items.title: Muster
items.text:
Muster is a self-hosted alert grouping and on-call service that sits after Alertmanager. It groups Alerts into Alert Groups, the problems people act on; keeps one editable message per Alert Group in Mattermost, in Slack, in Telegram, in any other messenger through a Bridge, or behind an outgoing webhook; and lets people acknowledge, resolve and snooze Alert Groups.

flowchart LR
  am["Alertmanager"] -- "Snapshots" --> integration
  subgraph muster["Muster"]
    integration["Integration"] --> routes["Routes"] --> groups["Alert Groups"]
  end
  subgraph destinations["Destinations"]
    mm["Mattermost"]
    sl["Slack"]
    tg["Telegram"]
    br["Bridge"]
    wh["Outgoing webhook"]
  end
  groups --> mm
  groups --> sl
  groups --> tg
  groups --> br
  groups --> wh

The Alertmanager of each cluster sends its notifications to an Integration of Muster. Routes pick Alerts by their labels, group them into Alert Groups and decide the Destinations they are delivered to, and Muster keeps the message of each Alert Group there up to date until the Alert Group is resolved.

items.title: Sections
items.text:
• Quick start: run Muster with Docker Compose, sign in, connect Alertmanager and send a test alert, in about five minutes.
  • First alert in a messenger: connect Telegram, route the Alert Groups of one service to a channel and acknowledge one from Telegram, step by step with screenshots.
  • Install: run Muster in production with Helm and an external PostgreSQL, and read the requirements and tested versions and how to verify a release.
  • Integrations: connect the Alertmanager of a cluster, connect Grafana Alerting directly or through an Alertmanager, and watch the path from Alertmanager with a Heartbeat.
  • Messengers: see what each Destination type can do, connect Mattermost, Slack and Telegram, reach any other messenger through a Bridge (and write one), link your messenger accounts, and set a proxy for a client.
  • Outgoing webhooks: send the lifecycle events of Alert Groups in the events mode, or keep a message in any chat in the template mode; recipes for a phone call, a status page, a second chat and an issue tracker.
  • Configure: change what messages and templates say, add links with Lookup tables and Link rules, set the Organization, and automate with API tokens.
  • Sign-in: Roles and ways to sign in; OpenID Connect with Keycloak, TOTP, and closed networks.
  • Concepts: what an Alert Group is, how Routes and Group keys group Alerts, the rules of Snapshots, Loud and Quiet messages, the statuses and commands, and Broken Destinations.
  • Operations: back up and restore, upgrade, rotate the master keys, run more than one replica, monitor Muster, set an outgoing heartbeat, use the command line, and read the Request log.
  • Runbooks: what each alert about Muster means and how to fix it.
  • Reference: metrics, log events, Internal alerts, environment variables, chart values, the API and the Bridge protocol.

items.title: AI agents
items.text: AI agents and coding assistants start at llms.txt: the map of this documentation for agents, with a Markdown version of every page and the full text in one file.

items.title: First alert in a messenger
items.text:
This tutorial takes one alert from Alertmanager to a Telegram channel and back: you connect Alertmanager, connect a Telegram bot, send Alert Groups of one service to a channel, and acknowledge the Alert Group from Telegram. It starts where Quick start ends: Muster runs and you are signed in as the Admin. It takes about fifteen minutes.

Telegram needs no address of Muster that Telegram can reach: Muster asks Telegram for updates itself. Before you start, in Telegram:

  • create a bot with @BotFather and copy its token, as Create the bot describes;
  • create a channel for the alerts, enable comments on it, and make the bot an admin of the channel and of its discussion group, as Enable comments on the channel and Make the bot an admin describe.

The screenshots show the channel @muster_alerts and the bot @muster_dev_b_bot; yours have your names.

items.title: 1. Create the Integration
items.text:
An Integration is the way one Alertmanager sends to Muster. Open Integrations, select Create integration, name it after your Alertmanager, such as Production Alertmanager, and select Create.

On the Integration's page, under Tokens, select Create token, name it, such as alertmanager, and select Create. The dialog shows the Token and the Alertmanager configuration once; copy both before you select Done. Add the configuration to your Alertmanager and reload it. In the screenshot both are hidden.

Connect Alertmanager explains every line of the configuration.

items.title: 2. Connect Telegram
items.text:
A Connection holds the credentials Muster uses to talk to a messenger, here a Telegram bot. Open Connections, select Create connection and choose Telegram. Enter a Name, such as Telegram, select Set a value next to Bot token and paste the bot's token. Keep the Bot API base URL https://api.telegram.org and the Update mode Long polling.

Select Check connection. The check runs in three steps against the values in the form and saves nothing; it names the bot when they pass. Then select Save.

Connect Telegram explains each field and each step of the check.

items.title: 3. Add a Destination
items.text:
A Destination is the channel Muster posts to. Open Destinations, select Create destination and choose Telegram. Choose the Connection of step 2, enter the Channel as @username, or its chat id for a private channel, give it a Name, such as alerts, and select Save. Saving runs the Destination check: the bot is an admin of the channel and of its discussion group. The saved Destination shows the discussion group it found.

Under Test and preview, on the tab Test, select Send test message. A message marked 🧪 appears in the channel, and the result shows the request Muster sent, with the bot token hidden. Links in the screenshots start with http://localhost:8080, the address of a development installation; yours start with your MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL.

Connect Telegram lists what the Destination check needs and what it says when it fails.

items.title: 4. Send Alert Groups to the Destination
items.text:
A Route picks Alerts by their labels and decides where their Alert Groups go. Alerts that no other Route takes go to the Default route, which has no Destination yet. Open Routes, select Create route and choose the profile On-call. Name the Route checkout and select Add matcher: the label service, =, the value checkout. In Group key, remove severity and cluster and add service, so that each alert name of each service is one Alert Group. Under Destinations, choose alerts in Add a Destination, then select Create.

Routes and Group keys explains Matchers, Group keys and the order of the Routes.

items.title: 5. Link your Telegram account
items.text:
A button in Telegram acts as a Muster User only through an Account link. Open your profile from the user menu and, under Messenger accounts, select Link Telegram. With more than one Telegram Connection, choose the one of step 2 and select Get link. Select Open Telegram, or scan the QR code with your phone, and press Start in the chat with the bot. The link works once and expires after a few minutes; in the screenshot the code and the time are hidden.

The dialog closes once the bot has linked your account, and your profile shows it.

Link your messenger accounts explains the other messengers.

items.title: 6. Send a test alert
items.text:
Send an alert of the service checkout, as Alertmanager would send it, with the request of Quick start and the token of step 1 in TOKEN:

TOKEN=mstr_int_...
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:8080/api/v1/ingest \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @- <<EOF
{
  "version": "4",
  "groupKey": "{}:{alertname=\"HighErrorRate\"}",
  "status": "firing",
  "receiver": "muster-prod-eu",
  "groupLabels": {"alertname": "HighErrorRate"},
  "commonLabels": {"alertname": "HighErrorRate", "service": "checkout", "severity": "critical"},
  "commonAnnotations": {"summary": "Error rate of checkout is above 5 %"},
  "externalURL": "http://localhost:9093",
  "alerts": [
    {
      "status": "firing",
      "labels": {"alertname": "HighErrorRate", "service": "checkout", "severity": "critical"},
      "annotations": {"summary": "Error rate of checkout is above 5 %"},
      "startsAt": "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)",
      "endsAt": "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z"
    }
  ]
}
EOF

Muster answers 202. Open Alert Groups: the Alert Group HighErrorRate is there, Firing, on the Route checkout. Its page shows the Alert, its labels, its delivery to alerts and its Timeline.

At the same moment the bot posts its Root message in the channel: the status, the title, the labels and the buttons. The Destination's Preview, based on the Alert Group, shows that message as Telegram draws it.

Alert Groups explains how Alerts become Alert Groups.

items.title: 7. Acknowledge it in Telegram
items.text:
In the channel, press Ack under the Root message. Telegram shows "Done: Acknowledge", the message changes to Acknowledged, and the Alert Group's page names you as its Owner. Its Timeline records that you acknowledged it through Telegram.

Statuses and commands lists what each button does.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
Mattermost, Slack and Bridges differ only in steps 2, 3 and 5:

  • Mattermost: create the Connection with the server's address and a bot token, add a Destination for a channel the bot is a member of, and link the account with a code the bot sends. Mattermost calls Muster for button presses, so it must reach MUSTER_INGEST_URL.
  • Slack: create the app and the Connection, invite the bot and create Destinations, and link the account. In Socket Mode, Slack needs no address of Muster.
  • Any other messenger through a Bridge, with a Destination for each channel.

Then set the time zone of the Organization, change what messages say, and watch the path from Alertmanager with a Heartbeat.

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
Run Muster with Docker Compose on one machine, sign in, connect Alertmanager and send a test alert. You need Docker with the Compose plugin, curl and openssl, and it takes about five minutes. The compose example runs one replica of Muster beside its own PostgreSQL; for a production installation, install with Helm.

flowchart LR
  am["Alertmanager or curl"] -- "Snapshots, port 8080" --> muster["Muster"]
  browser["Browser"] -- "web UI, port 8080" --> muster
  muster --> pg["PostgreSQL"]

items.title: Start Muster
items.text:
Download the compose example into a new directory:

mkdir muster && cd muster
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muster-io/muster/v0.1.4/deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml # x-release-please-version

Write its settings into .env next to it, with a generated master key and generated passwords:

cat >.env <<EOF
MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS=$(openssl rand -base64 32)
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8080
MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@example.org
MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
EOF
chmod 600 .env
  • MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS is the master key. It encrypts the secrets Muster keeps in the database, such as the tokens of messenger bots, and Muster refuses to start on a database without the key that wrote it. Keep a copy of the key, apart from the database backups: see Backup and restore.
  • MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL is the address people open, and links in messages point to it.
  • MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL and MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD create the first Admin at the first start. Use your own email if you like; it is also the login. Once an Admin exists, Muster ignores both.

Start Muster:

docker compose up -d --wait

Muster creates its schema at the first start. One port, 8080, serves the web UI, the API and ingestion.

items.title: Sign in
items.text:
Open http://localhost:8080 and sign in with the login admin@example.org and the password from .env:

grep MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD .env

Muster runs on a machine without HTTPS, such as a VM? Browsers keep the session only over HTTPS or on localhost, and the shortest way in is an SSH tunnel. On your own machine run ssh -L 8080:localhost:8080 <vm>, keep it open and browse to http://localhost:8080, with MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8080 as above. See Sign-in needs HTTPS or localhost.

Everything in the web UI and the API works only after sign-in: people sign in with a password or through OpenID Connect, and automation with tokens. Each User has a Role — Admin, Responder or Viewer — that decides what they see and change. Add the people of your team as Users under Access; each of them links their own messenger accounts in their profile, as Link your messenger accounts describes.

items.title: Create an Integration
items.text:
An Integration is the way one Alertmanager cluster sends to Muster.

  1. Open Integrations and select Create integration.
  2. Name it after your Alertmanager cluster, such as prod-eu, and select Create.
  3. On the Integration's page, under Tokens, select Create token, then Create.
  4. The dialog shows the Token and the Alertmanager configuration once. Copy both before you select Done: only a hash of the token is kept.

The Alertmanager configuration is a receiver that sends to Muster with the token, and a child route for it to place first under the top-level route:

receivers:
  - name: muster-prod-eu
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://localhost:8080/api/v1/ingest
        send_resolved: true
        max_alerts: 0
        http_config:
          authorization:
            type: Bearer
            credentials: mstr_int_…
route:
  routes:
    - receiver: muster-prod-eu
      continue: true
      repeat_interval: 10m
    # ... your existing child routes

Its URL comes from MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL, because the compose example serves ingestion on the same address. Keep MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8080 for your browser on this machine. When your Alertmanager runs on another machine, replace localhost in the receiver's url with an address of this machine that Alertmanager reaches. Browsers keep Muster's session only over HTTPS or on localhost: to open Muster from other machines, put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of port 8080, set MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL in .env to its https:// address and run docker compose up -d --wait again. Connect Alertmanager explains every line of the configuration, the catch-all child route to keep last, and the start delay.

items.title: Send a test alert
items.text:
You do not need Alertmanager for a first try: send what it would send. Put the token you copied into TOKEN, then post a Snapshot with one firing alert:

TOKEN=mstr_int_...
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:8080/api/v1/ingest \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @- <<EOF
{
  "version": "4",
  "groupKey": "{}:{alertname=\"QuickStartTest\"}",
  "status": "firing",
  "receiver": "muster-prod-eu",
  "groupLabels": {"alertname": "QuickStartTest"},
  "commonLabels": {"alertname": "QuickStartTest", "severity": "warning"},
  "commonAnnotations": {"summary": "A test alert from Quick start"},
  "externalURL": "http://localhost:9093",
  "alerts": [
    {
      "status": "firing",
      "labels": {"alertname": "QuickStartTest", "severity": "warning"},
      "annotations": {"summary": "A test alert from Quick start"},
      "startsAt": "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)",
      "endsAt": "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z"
    }
  ]
}
EOF

Muster answers 202. Open Alert Groups: the Alert Group QuickStartTest is there, firing, and its page shows the alert, its labels and its Timeline. It reached no messenger, because the alert went to the Default route, the Route that takes every Alert no other Route takes, and the Default route has no Destination yet.

To resolve it, send the same request with both "status": "firing" changed to "status": "resolved".

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Send your first alert to a messenger. First alert in a messenger connects Telegram, sends the Alert Groups of one service to a channel, and acknowledges one from Telegram, step by step.
  • Set the time zone. The Organization's time zone is UTC until you change it, so times in messages are UTC. Set it under Organization → General: see Organization settings.
  • Connect a messenger. Connect Mattermost, Slack or Telegram, add a Destination for a channel, and add the Destination to the Default route or to a Route of its own; see Routes and Group keys. Mattermost sends button presses to MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL here, so the Mattermost server must reach that address: unless it reaches Muster at http://localhost:8080, put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of port 8080 and set MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL to its https:// address first. Slack in Socket Mode needs no address of Muster that Slack can reach.
  • Use any other messenger through a Bridge. A Bridge is a small service that connects Muster to a messenger it does not support natively. Write a bridge with the library for Go, muster-bridge-go, or for Python, muster-bridge-python, or try the example bridge from examples/chat of the Go library: a small chat with a web page, to see Muster's messages without a real messenger. It runs next to this Quick start as one more service of the compose project.
  • Change what messages say, and add links to your dashboards and runbooks, as Messages and templates describes. API tokens and automation is for scripts and Terraform.
  • Connect your Alertmanager as Connect Alertmanager describes, and watch the path from it with a Heartbeat.
  • Learn how Muster groups alerts in Concepts.
  • Run it in production: install with Helm, and read Operations for backups, upgrades and monitoring.

docker compose down stops Muster and keeps its data; docker compose down -v deletes the database too.

items.title: Alert Groups
items.text:
An Alert Group is a set of Alerts that Muster treats as one problem. It is the thing people act on: it has a number like #412, a status, and at most one Owner, and each Destination that receives it shows it as a single message that Muster keeps up to date. Acknowledge it, snooze it or resolve it, and everyone looking at it sees the result.

This page explains what an Alert Group is and how it relates to the other things Muster handles. The pages that follow go deeper:

  • Routes and Group keys: how an Alert finds its Alert Group.
  • Snapshot semantics: how Alertmanager's notifications become Alerts, and when an Alert counts as gone.
  • Statuses and commands: the four statuses, the commands, ack timeouts and Reminders.
  • Loud and Quiet: which changes ring a phone, and whom they Mention.
  • Broken Destinations: what happens when a messenger stops answering.

items.title: The things Muster handles
items.text:
Four words sound alike and are not the same. Muster keeps them apart:

Term What it is Snapshot One notification from Alertmanager. It lists the current Alerts of one Alertmanager group. It is input, not an Alert. Alertmanager group The alerts Alertmanager notifies about together under one groupKey. It is Alertmanager's idea of "together", decided by the group_by of its route. Alert One firing problem reported by a source, identified by its full set of labels, such as one pod, one node or one domain. Alert Group The problem Muster shows people. It contains Alerts, and which ones go together is decided by a Route and its Group key, not by Alertmanager.

Muster does not copy Alertmanager's grouping. Alertmanager's groups exist to batch notifications. An Alert Group exists so that a person can say "I have this one". The two often look alike, but you can change either without the other.

items.title: What an Alert Group has
items.text:
Number, #N Assigned per Organization, without gaps, when the Alert Group is created. It is what people say aloud: "I took Status firing, acknowledged, snoozed or resolved. See Statuses and commands. Owner The user who acknowledged it. Only a user can be an Owner; a Service account cannot. Title The alertname that its Alerts share. When Alerts with different alertname values join it, the Group key values instead, such as cluster=prod, namespace=payments. It is set when the Alert Group is created and changes at most once, at that switch. Summary The summary annotation of the first of its Alerts that has one. It is set once. Route The Route that took its Alerts. It decides the Destinations and the timers. Severity level The highest Severity level of its firing Alerts: critical, warning or info. Urgent Set when its Route is marked urgent, or when its Severity level is critical and the Organization treats critical as Urgent (organization.critical_is_urgent, on by default). Reopen count How many times Muster reopened it. Alerts One entry per fingerprint, firing first, resolved ones struck through with their reason. Timeline The ordered record of everything that happened to it.

The Alert Group page shows all of this, the Alerts with their labels and annotations, the labels they share, and the previous Alert Groups with the same Route and Group key values. The page and the list work at phone width.

items.title: In the web UI
items.text:
1. Open Alert Groups. The list shows the Alert Groups of the chosen Time range, the last 7 days by default, newest first: the status, the number, the title, the severity, the Route and the Integrations first. The tabs above it — Open, Firing, Acknowledged, Snoozed, Resolved and All — choose the statuses and count each one; Search finds an Alert Group by its number, such as #412, or by text.

The table scrolls sideways inside its box to the columns further right: the Owner, the end of a Snooze, when each Alert Group started, how long it has lasted and its last change.

![The list scrolled to its right end: the Owner admin, the end of the Snooze, the start, the duration and the last change of each Alert Group](../assets/screenshots/concepts/alert-groups/02-list-columns.png){ .screenshot }

  1. Narrow the list with the filters beside it: the Routes, the Integrations, the Severity, Urgent, the Owner, label Matchers and more. They combine, and they live in the address, so a filtered list can be shared; Clear filters removes them. On a phone they open from Filters.

  2. Select the number or the title of an Alert Group to open its page: the status, the Owner, the command buttons, the Alerts, the labels, the deliveries to its Destinations and the previous Alert Groups with the same Route and Group key values.

  3. Further down, the Timeline lists what happened to it, with the actor and the Transport of each change, and the box to add a Note.

The commands act on the Alert Group from its page.

items.title: Live updates
items.text:
The list and the Alert Group page change as soon as something happens, without a reload. A mark in the header of every page says whether these live updates reach your browser, so that on a phone at night you know whether the list in front of you is current:

Mark Meaning Green filled dot, "Live" Live updates are on. Grey ring, "Connecting…" The page has loaded and is connecting. The text shows once this has taken 5 seconds. Amber half-filled dot, pulsing, "Reconnecting…" The connection has been lost for 5 seconds, and the browser keeps trying again. Red ring with a slash, "Offline" The connection has been lost for 30 seconds, or the page has not connected within 30 seconds of loading.

On a screen narrower than 640 pixels, such as a phone, only the dot shows, whatever the state, so that the navigation keeps its room; each state has its own shape as well as its colour, so you can tell them apart without the colour. A drop shorter than 5 seconds, such as a Muster replica restarting, leaves the mark as it was. Press the mark to read its state and what it means: in every state but "Live" it says that what you see may be out of date, while reconnecting or offline it names the time the connection was lost, and when offline it offers to reload the page. As soon as the connection is back, the list and the page are read again, so they show everything that happened meanwhile. The mark sends nothing to Muster.

items.title: How Alerts join an Alert Group
items.text:
When an Alert starts firing, Muster picks its Route and reads the values of the Route's Group key from the Alert's labels. Then, in this order:

  1. If an open Alert Group of that Route has the same Group key values, the Alert joins it.
  2. Otherwise, if the system resolved an Alert Group of that Route with the same values within the Reopen window, that Alert Group reopens.
  3. Otherwise a new Alert Group starts, with the next number.

An Alert that is already in an open Alert Group is not routed again: it stays there until the Alert Group is resolved, even if you change the Route's Matchers or Group key meanwhile.

What a new Alert does to an Alert Group depends on its status, because the status says whether anybody is paying attention:

The Alert Group is A new Alert joining it is firing a Loud event, added to the Thread in batches acknowledged a Quiet event; the acknowledgement stays, always snoozed a Quiet update of the Root message only; what accumulated is listed when the Snooze ends

items.title: Replacements
items.text: An exporter restarts and reports the same problem with a new pod label. That is a different Alert, since its labels differ, but it is the same problem. When a new Alert differs from a firing Alert of the same Alert Group only in Instance labels, Muster records a Replacement: a Quiet event in the Timeline that names the label that differs. The old Alert resolving is Quiet too. The Alert Group page suggests the real fix, which is to aggregate the label away in the rule, for example with without(pod, instance).

items.title: Instance labels
items.text: Instance labels are the labels that change when the process reporting an Alert restarts. The Organization lists them in organization.instance_labels; by default pod, instance, container and endpoint. See Instance labels in informational alerts for when to keep them out of your rules.

items.title: Reopening
items.text:
An Alert Group is resolved by the system when its last Alert resolves, whether Alertmanager said so, or the Alert went Gone or Stale, or its Integration was deleted. A person can resolve it too.

The two ways to resolve differ in what happens when the problem returns:

Resolved by When an Alert with the same Route and Group key values fires again The system Within the Reopen window (route.reopen_window, 15 minutes by default) the same Alert Group reopens: same number, Reopen count plus one, and it returns to the status it had before, with the same Owner if it was acknowledged. After the window, a new Alert Group starts. A person The Reopen window does not apply. If the Alerts that were still firing are still reported when the Grace period (route.grace_period, 15 minutes by default) ends, they are grouped again as if they had just fired. Within the Grace period, a new firing starts a new Alert Group at once.

A reopen is keyed by the Route and the Group key values, not by one Alert: any Alert with the same values brings the Alert Group back, whether it is one of its own Alerts or a new one. How loud a reopen is depends on where it returns: Loud into firing, Loud into acknowledged but Mentioning only the Owner, Quiet into snoozed.

A person who resolved the wrong Alert Group presses Unresolve in the web UI or the API. Unresolve is not offered in messengers, and it works only on an Alert Group that a person resolved, not on one that reopens by itself.

The reason is always visible. A resolution by the system carries the reason, such as "Alertmanager no longer reports this alert", and so does every other automatic change; the page, the Timeline and the message show it.

items.title: Where an Alert Group shows up
items.text:
A Route lists the Destinations that receive its Alert Groups. For each Alert Group and each of its Destinations, Muster keeps one Root message and brings it to the latest state each time something changes. Replies, such as new Alerts joining or a Reminder, go to the message's Thread. See Loud and Quiet for which changes are new messages and which are edits.

An Alert Group whose Route has no Destination, as with the Default route in the Quick start, exists only in Muster. Its page, the list, the statistics and the Timeline still work.

items.title: The Timeline
items.text:
The Timeline of an Alert Group shows, in order: Alerts added, resolved, replaced and continued; status changes with the actor and the Transport; Reopens; Notes; Takeovers; ack timeout notices, Reminders and their answers; use of the Fallback template; delivery events such as a Publication, a possible duplicate or a delivery that was Not delivered; moves to the Default route; and the periods when Muster itself was down. Each entry that records something Muster might tell people also shows whether it was Loud and whom it Mentioned.

You can filter the Timeline by kind and read it oldest first or newest first. Notes belong to it: Responders and Admins can add one, up to 4,000 characters (alert_group.note_max_length).

items.title: Changing a Route does not change an Alert Group
items.text:
Edits of a Route's settings apply at once, also to its open Alert Groups, whose messages are updated. They never change an Alert Group's status. A new Group key or new Matchers apply only to Alerts that start firing afterwards.

A Route that still has open Alert Groups cannot be deleted. Muster refuses and offers to move them to the Default route. A moved Alert Group keeps its Group key values, takes no new Alerts, and never reopens; it stays open until its Alerts resolve or a person resolves it.

items.title: Statistics
items.text:
Statistics counts the Alert Groups that started in a period and how fast people took and closed them: for each Route or each Integration, the number of Alert Groups and the median and the 95th percentile of the time to acknowledge and of the time to resolve. Days are split in your time zone.

  1. Open Statistics. Choose the Period — Last 7 days, Last 30 days, Last 90 days or Custom — and show it By route or By integration; add Routes or Integrations to narrow it.

  2. Select a Route or an Integration to see its Alert Groups per day of start, with the median times of each day.

items.title: How long Alert Groups are kept
items.text:
retention.alert_details

kept for: 90 days

Alerts in Alert Groups, Timeline entries, delivery events.

retention.alert_group_summaries

kept for: 2 years

The summary row of an Alert Group: number, title, summary, times, Route, status, and its Notes.

After the details are removed, search still finds the Alert Group by its title and number, and its page shows the summary with the notice that the Alerts and the Timeline were removed. The list shows Alert Groups whose lifetime overlaps the chosen time range, 7 days by default (alert_group.list_range), so an Alert Group that has been firing for weeks is always in the default view. Searching by number ignores the range.

items.title: Broken Destinations
items.text:
A Destination is Broken when Muster has decided that it cannot deliver there until something changes: the messenger refused the bot for good, or the messenger kept failing until Muster ran out of patience. A Broken Destination is not an error to dismiss. It means that the people it serves are not seeing their alerts, so Muster raises an alert about it.

This page explains when a Destination becomes Broken, what Muster does meanwhile, and how it recovers. For the steps when MusterDestinationBroken fires, use the runbook.

items.title: When a Destination becomes Broken
items.text:
Every failed attempt is sorted into a class, and the class decides what happens:

Retry after

examples: the messenger answers 429 and says how long to wait

Muster waits exactly that long and then sends the latest state. It is not counted as an attempt.

Transient

examples: a 5xx, a timeout, a network error

Muster retries with exponential backoff and jitter, from 2 seconds up to 5 minutes. After 10 attempts within 30 minutes (delivery.transient_budget) the Destination becomes Broken as unavailable.

Fatal

examples: the messenger refuses the bot or the request for good

The Destination becomes Broken at once.

Unknown

examples: an answer Muster does not recognize

Not retried. That one delivery ends as Not delivered, and the Destination stays healthy.

What is Fatal depends on the messenger:

  • Mattermost: 401 or 403, such as an invalid token or a bot removed from the channel, and 404 for the channel, which is not found or archived.
  • Slack: a token that Slack refuses (invalid_auth, token_revoked, token_expired and the like), a missing scope, and a channel the bot cannot use: channel_not_found, not_in_channel for a bot removed from the channel, and is_archived. A 429 is not Fatal: Muster holds the whole Connection for the seconds Slack asks.
  • Telegram: 401, and "bot was kicked" or missing rights, such as a bot that lost its admin rights in the channel.
  • Bridge: the bridge answers forbidden, for example because the bot was removed from the channel; the bridge's own text becomes the reason. A bridge that does not answer at all becomes Broken through the Transient budget.
  • Outgoing webhook: 401, 403, 404 and 410, and a request that the Organization's outbound address policy blocks, since every later request would be blocked too.

Several things look like trouble and do not make a Destination Broken:

  • A deleted Root message. Muster posts the Alert Group again once, Quietly, with the note "The previous message was deleted at HH:MM"; if that one is deleted too, the pair is marked "deleted in the messenger" and left alone. In Slack this holds while the bot is still in the channel and the channel is not archived; see Edits and deleted Root messages.
  • A Telegram Thread that lost the automatic copy of its Root message. The delivery state shows "Thread not attached".
  • A delivery that ends as Not delivered, such as a template that failed or a request the receiver rejected with 400.
  • A Bridge Connection whose bridge cannot be reached. The Connection does not become Broken itself; its Destinations do, through their own deliveries, and its Connection check shows the cause.
  • Failed polls of a bridge or of Telegram. The poller backs off.

items.title: What you see
items.text:
• The Destination and its Routes show a banner: "Broken since HH:MM: {reason}. Muster tries again every 5 minutes." The reason is the error the messenger answered, or "unavailable after repeated failures" and the last error.
  • The Internal alert MusterDestinationBroken is raised, with the severity critical and the labels destination and destination_name. Muster routes it by your Routes like any other Alert, so a Route for Internal alerts should lead to a Destination of another kind than the one that failed: if all your Telegram Destinations are Broken because Telegram is unreachable, an alert that goes to Telegram says nothing. See Routes and Group keys.
  • The chart rule MusterDestinationBroken is the backup for when Muster cannot deliver its own alert. Send it through an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster. See Internal alerts and the metrics.
  • The Alert Groups whose delivery waits show a delivery problem. The Alert Group list has the filter Delivery problem, and the page of each shows the state "Waiting: {Destination} is Broken".
  • The System status page lists the Broken Destinations and since when.

items.title: What Muster does meanwhile
items.text:
Everything except the delivery to that Destination goes on: ingestion, routing, Alert Groups, commands from the web UI and the API, timers, and every other Destination.

  • Deliveries wait instead of failing. Nothing is dropped, and Muster does not spend retries on a Destination it knows is down.
  • Muster probes the Destination every 5 minutes (delivery.broken_probe_interval). If a delivery is waiting, the probe is an attempt at the oldest one. If nothing is waiting, the probe is the Destination check, which asks the messenger whether the bot can still reach and post to the channel, without posting. An outgoing webhook has no Destination check, so its next delivery is the probe.
  • A new Alert Group is created and shown in Muster as usual, but its first Publication waits. Its ack timeout does not start until it is published, so a Route whose only Destinations are Broken sends no notices.

items.title: Recovery
items.text:
The Broken state ends when any of these succeeds:

  • the automatic probe;
  • Check on the Destination page, which runs the Destination check at once;
  • Send test message on the Destination page, when every step succeeds.

Fix the cause first. Typical fixes are a replaced bot token, adding the bot back to the channel or giving it its admin rights again, enabling comments on a Telegram channel, correcting the address or the proxy of the Connection or the Outbound addresses policy, or waiting out a messenger outage. When the fix is made, press Check; if you do nothing, the next probe notices by itself, with no Alert Group activity needed. The Internal alert then resolves.

items.title: What is sent after recovery
items.text:
Muster sends only the current state. It does not replay what it missed.

What happened during the outage After recovery An Alert Group started and is still firing It is published as a Loud new message. An Alert Group started and is no longer firing, but still open It is published Quietly. An Alert Group was already published, then changed Its Root message is edited once to the current state, with no Thread reply. An Alert Group started and resolved during the outage It is not published; it stays in the Timeline and in the web UI. Thread replies came due They are not sent.

Urgent Alert Groups are published first, within the Destination's rate limits.

An outgoing webhook in events mode is the exception: it is a stream of events, so every event that came due during the outage is sent after recovery, in order per Alert Group, with none dropped and no age limit. An outgoing webhook in template mode sends only the current state, like a messenger.

If an Alert Group resolved while its first Publication was still waiting for a retry, but the Destination was not yet Broken, it is still posted, Quietly, with the note "Delivered late: started HH:MM, resolved HH:MM while this Destination was unavailable".

items.title: Republishing past an edit window
items.text:
Muster edits a Root message for as long as its Alert Group is open, which can take days. Whether a messenger lets it depends on the messenger. This is not about a Broken Destination, but the messages that Muster can no longer edit look similar from the outside, so here is the whole picture.

Telegram None for the bot's own messages. A bot may edit them at any age, so Muster never republishes because of age. Slack None known for a bot's own messages. Whether a window that a workspace sets applies to a bot's messages hours or days old has not been verified; an edit Slack refuses ends that delivery as Not delivered. Mattermost The server setting ServiceSettings.PostEditTimeLimit, which is unlimited (-1) by default. Keep the default. If an administrator sets a limit, Muster's edits of older Root messages may be refused, and what Mattermost then answers has not been verified. See Keep posts editable. Bridge The bridge declares it in its info, as limits.edit_max_age_seconds, or declares none. Outgoing webhook Muster does not know the chat's rules. In template mode an update request that the chat refuses ends as Not delivered or Broken by the usual classes.

For a Bridge with an edit window, Muster stops editing a Root message 60 seconds before the window closes (bridge.edit_window_margin). After that:

  • A change that keeps the status of the Alert Group, such as new Alerts or Alerts that resolve, reaches only the Thread. The old Root message keeps the state of its last edit.
  • A change of status, such as Acknowledge, Resolve, Snooze or a Reopen, makes Muster publish a new Root message Quietly, in the same channel, and reply under the old one: "This message is no longer updated. The current one: {link}". Later Thread replies go under the new Root message.
  • The old message keeps working: a press on its buttons, or a Text command in its Thread, still acts on the Alert Group.
  • The Alert Group page shows "Past the edit window: updated on the next change of status" until then.

A bridge may also refuse an edit before the declared time, with the reason edit_window_closed. Muster treats that as the end of the window, not as a deletion. See Edit windows for the details.

items.title: After you delete a Destination
items.text: A deleted Destination receives one last edit of each open Root message, "No longer updated here; current state in Muster: {link}", and nothing after that. For a Bridge Root message past its edit window, the last edit is a Thread reply with the same text. An outgoing webhook in events mode sends no final event, and its queued events end as Not delivered.

items.title: Loud and Quiet
items.text:
Every change to an Alert Group is either Loud or Quiet. A Loud change should make people's devices ring. A Quiet change should only update what they see when they look. Muster fixes the loudness of every change; you decide only whom a Loud change Mentions.

The rule behind it is simple, and it is the same in Mattermost, Slack and Telegram: an edit never notifies anybody. Editing a message, even to add a Mention, does not ring a phone. So a Loud change is always a new message, a new Root message or a reply in the Thread, and a Quiet change is an edit of the Root message or a new message without a Mention.

items.title: Which changes are Loud
items.text:
A new Alert Group starts Loud, as a new Root message · mentions: the Destination's new_alert_group setting New Alerts join a firing Alert Group Loud, as a Thread reply; batched · mentions: new_alerts New Alerts join an acknowledged or snoozed Alert Group Quiet · mentions: nobody A Reopen into firing Loud · mentions: reopen A Reopen into acknowledged Loud · mentions: the Owner only A Reopen into snoozed Quiet · mentions: nobody A Snooze ends while Alerts still fire Loud, listing what accumulated · mentions: snooze_ended A rise to Urgent that ends a Snooze or removes an acknowledgement Loud, with the reason · mentions: the Owner it removed, and rise_to_urgent A rise in Severity level that changes nothing else Quiet · mentions: nobody A Takeover Loud · mentions: the previous Owner An ack timeout notice Loud · mentions: ack_timeout A Reminder Loud · mentions: the Owner Auto-unacknowledge Loud, with the reason · mentions: the Owner it removed The Owner is disabled or deleted Loud · mentions: nobody Several notices missed during downtime Loud, as one reply · mentions: as the notices it stands for Acknowledge, Unacknowledge, Snooze, Unsnooze, Resolve, Unresolve Quiet · mentions: nobody An Alert resolves, is replaced or continues, or its annotations change Quiet · mentions: nobody The system resolves the Alert Group Quiet, with a Thread reply that gives the reason · mentions: nobody A Note Quiet, and not sent to messengers · mentions: nobody

The pattern: Muster rings when something needs a human who may not be looking, such as a new problem, one that returned, one that nobody took, or one that someone took and went quiet. It does not ring for what a person just did, because that person is looking. The Takeover is the only result of a person's command that is Loud, because the previous Owner has just lost the Alert Group.

Delivery adds a few cases of its own:

Delivery event Loud or Quiet A Destination added to a Route receives its open Alert Groups Quiet A Destination recovers from Broken: an Alert Group still firing is published Loud The same recovery, for an Alert Group that is not firing, or an edit of a message already there Quiet A message published late, after the Alert Group already resolved Quiet, with a note A Root message posted again because it was deleted Quiet, with a note A Storm summary, when it first appears Loud A Storm summary's updates, and the Alert Groups posted after the Storm Quiet

You cannot change the loudness of an event. You can change whom it Mentions.

items.title: What Loud means in each Destination
items.text:
Mattermost

A Loud change is a new post with its Mentions: at the top of the attachment of a Root message or a Storm summary, in the text of a reply in the Thread.

A Quiet change is an edit, or a new post without a Mention.

Slack

A Loud change is a new message, a Root message or a reply in the Thread, with its Mentions.

A Quiet change is an edit, or a new message without a Mention.

Telegram

A Loud change is a new message, in the channel for a Root message and in the discussion group for a Thread reply.

A Quiet change is an edit, or a new message sent with disable_notification.

Bridge

A Loud change is a new message that the bridge posts with notify on, with its Mentions.

A Quiet change is an edit, or a new message that the bridge posts without a notification where it declares quiet_messages.

Outgoing webhook

A Loud change is an event with notify true (events mode), or .Notify true in a template (template mode).

A Quiet change is notify false.

A few details:

  • Mattermost. A reply in a Thread notifies the Thread's followers by their own settings, and a Mention makes the person a follower. So Quiet means "without a Mention", not "nobody is notified". A Loud Root message has its Mentions as the first line of its attachment, where a person's Mention, @channel, @here and @all notify; a push or desktop notification shows the summary line of the Alert Group, and an email shows no content. A Thread reply has its Mentions in its text. See Who gets notified.
  • Slack. Slack cannot send a message without a notification: whom a new message notifies depends on each member's settings for the channel and the Thread. So Quiet means "without a Mention", not "nobody is notified". An edit carries no Mention, so it drops the Mentions of the message it edits. See Who gets notified.
  • Telegram. disable_notification silences the sound but does not remove the push. Only members of the channel's discussion group get Thread replies, and the automatic copy of every Root message rings them, even for a Quiet one. Tell the people on call to join the group and mute the channel itself. See Known limitation: Quiet Root messages ring the group.
  • Bridge. Whether the bridge can post without a notification depends on the bridge. A bridge that does not declare quiet_messages posts a Quiet message as an ordinary one, without Mentions.
  • Outgoing webhook. Muster rings nothing itself. In events mode every event is sent, Quiet ones too, with notify telling what a person-facing system should do with it. Your receiver decides, for example, to call a phone only when notify is true. See events mode and Recipes.

items.title: Mentions
items.text: A Mention is a deliberate @-reference that Muster adds to a message so that a person is notified. Muster adds a Mention only where this page says it does. Alert data never mention anyone: an @ in a label or an annotation is neutralized with a zero-width space, so @channel in a label notifies nobody.

items.title: Whom a Loud change Mentions
items.text:
Each Destination has a Mention setting for each of six kinds of Loud change:

  • new_alert_group, new_alerts, reopen, ack_timeout, snooze_ended and rise_to_urgent.

For each, the Destination chooses nobody (the default for all six), everyone in the chat, chosen Muster users, or messenger groups. What a Destination type offers:

Destination Nobody Everyone in the chat Chosen users Messenger groups Mattermost yes @channel, @all or @here yes Mattermost group names Slack yes @channel or @here yes no Telegram yes no yes no Bridge yes no yes no Outgoing webhook yes yes, as data yes, as data yes, as data

Some Mentions are not a setting. A Reminder and an auto-unacknowledge always Mention the Owner, a Takeover Mentions the previous Owner, and a Reopen into acknowledged Mentions only the Owner.

items.title: Account links
items.text:
A Mention of a user needs an Account link: the tie between a Muster user and their account in the messenger. The people who are Mentioned, and the Owner above all, link their accounts from their profile; see Link your messenger accounts. Muster renders a Mention in the messenger's own form:

  • Mattermost: @username;
  • Slack: a Mention of the person's Slack account;
  • Telegram: a link to the person, whose text is the display name;
  • Bridge: a marker that a bridge with native_mentions renders as the messenger's mention and any other bridge as the person's name.

A user without an Account link is named by their display name as plain text, which notifies nobody. So choosing a user for a Mention setting, or being an Owner, rings a phone only once that person has linked their account. The footer of a Root message names a person by their messenger username without @, which does not notify them either.

For an outgoing webhook, Muster does not know the receiver's markup, so the Mention is data: the event's mentions list, and .Mentions in a template, with the target's type, id, name and login. Your receiver or your template turns it into whatever the receiving system understands.

items.title: Storm summaries
items.text:
When many Alert Groups start at once, one Route can flood a Destination. A Storm is a Route creating more new Alert Groups in one minute than its Storm threshold (route.storm_threshold, 20 by default). Then each of the Route's Destinations gets one Storm summary instead of a message per Alert Group:

  • The summary is Loud only when it first appears, and Mentions as a new Alert Group does (new_alert_group).
  • Urgent Alert Groups are still posted on their own, first.
  • Its updates and its final state are Quiet. When the rate has stayed below the threshold for 5 minutes (delivery.storm_calm_period), the summary shows its final state, and the Alert Groups that are still open are posted gradually and Quietly. Those that already resolved are not posted.
  • Messengers and the template mode of outgoing webhooks follow Storms. The events mode does not: it receives every event.

items.title: Why the rule is fixed
items.text: A rule of thumb for on-call: the phones should ring for problems that need a human, and nothing else. Because an edit is always silent, a person can acknowledge, snooze and resolve all day, and the message changes under their eyes without a sound; and because the loudness of every change is fixed, a team never has to wonder whether a change will ring. The Mention settings are the one place to tune who rings.

items.title: Routes and Group keys
items.text:
A Route decides what happens to an Alert after Muster has read it: which Alert Group it joins, who is told, and how the Alert Group is handled afterwards. A Group key decides which Alerts share an Alert Group. Together they are the two settings that shape what your team sees.

Do not confuse a Route with an Alertmanager route. An Alertmanager route is a rule inside Alertmanager that picks a receiver and a repeat interval. A Route of Muster is evaluated after the Alert has arrived, on the labels of the Alert.

items.title: How an Alert is routed
items.text:
1. The Alert arrives in a Snapshot of an Integration.
  2. The Integration's Static labels are added to it. If the Alert already has a label of that name, its own value wins, and Muster warns about the label.
  3. Muster walks the Routes in list order. The first Route whose Matchers all match takes the Alert.
  4. The Route's Group key says which Alert Group the Alert goes to. See Alert Groups.

Only an Alert that starts firing is routed. An Alert that already lives in an open Alert Group stays in it.

items.title: Routes
items.text:
A Route has:

  • a name, unique in the Organization, and a description;
  • Matchers, which pick the Alerts;
  • a position in the list;
  • an urgent mark;
  • a Group key;
  • the Destinations that receive its Alert Groups;
  • policy fields for how its Alert Groups are handled: the Reopen window and the Grace period, whether a rise to Urgent removes an acknowledgement, the Snooze durations, the Thread batching window and the Storm threshold, the templates and the language, and the ack timeout, the Reminders and auto-unacknowledge.

items.title: Matchers
items.text:
A Matcher is a condition on one label, written as in Alertmanager: =, !=, =~ and !~, where the last two take an RE2 regular expression. The Matchers of a Route are all required: they combine with AND. The Route editor builds them from fields; the API takes the same structure; an invalid expression is refused with a pointer to the field.

team="payments" and severity="critical" Takes Alerts of the payments team that are critical. namespace=~"prod-.*" Takes Alerts in any namespace that starts with prod-. alertname!="Watchdog" Takes everything except the Watchdog.

A missing label counts as an empty value. So team!="payments" also matches an Alert that has no team label.

In the Route editor, under Matchers:

  1. Select Add matcher. A row appears with the label, the operator and the value.
  2. Enter the label, such as team, choose the operator, = by default, and enter the value, such as payments. The × at the end of a row removes it.

items.title: Order, and the Default route
items.text:
Routes are evaluated in list order, and the first Route that matches takes the Alert. Put the narrow Routes first and the broad ones after them. Drag the Routes on the Routes page to reorder them.

The Default route is always last. It has no Matchers, cannot be deleted or moved, and takes every Alert that no other Route took. A small installation may keep only the Default route. A Route with no Destinations is fine too: its Alert Groups exist in Muster and in no messenger.

Edits to Routes use optimistic locking: if somebody changed the Routes while you were editing, your save is refused and you reload.

items.title: Route profiles
items.text:
When you create a Route, you choose a Route profile. A profile only fills in the settings; it is not stored, and you can change every field afterwards. There are two:

Ack timeout (route.ack_timeout) On-call: on; first notice after 15 minutes · Informational: off Reminders (route.reminders) On-call: on; first after 4 hours · Informational: off Snooze durations (route.snooze_durations) On-call: 1 h, 4 h, 24 h · Informational: 1 d, 3 d, 7 d Group key (route.group_key) On-call: alertname, severity, cluster · Informational: the same Reopen window and Grace period On-call: 15 minutes each · Informational: the same

Choose Informational for alerts nobody needs to act on at once, such as a certificate that expires in a month: no notices, no Reminders, and long Snooze durations. Choose On-call for the rest. See Statuses and commands for what the timers do.

items.title: Urgent
items.text:
An Alert Group is Urgent when its Route is marked urgent, or when its Severity level is critical and the Organization has organization.critical_is_urgent on (the default). An Urgent Alert Group is posted first when many arrive at once, and a rise to Urgent can end a Snooze or remove an acknowledgement.

By default the severity label maps to a Severity level: critical is critical, warning is warning, info and none are info, any other value counts as warning and is shown as received, and an Alert without the label counts as info. The Organization can change the label and the mapping.

items.title: Group keys
items.text:
The Group key of a Route is a list of label names. Alerts of the Route that have the same values for all of those labels go to the same Alert Group. A label that an Alert lacks counts as an empty value, so Alerts that all lack cluster group together.

The default Group key is alertname, severity and cluster. Take these four Alerts, all taken by one Route:

Alert alertname severity cluster namespace pod 1 KubePodCrashLooping warning prod payments api-1 2 KubePodCrashLooping warning prod payments api-2 3 KubePodCrashLooping warning prod search web-1 4 KubePodCrashLooping warning staging payments api-1 Group key Alert Groups Which Alerts alertname, severity, cluster (default) 2 1, 2 and 3 in one; 4 in another alertname, cluster, namespace 3 1 and 2; 3; 4 alertname, cluster, namespace, pod 4 one Alert Group per pod alertname 1 all four

There is no best key. A coarse key gives few Alert Groups that stay open longer, and a person takes the whole problem with one Acknowledge. A fine key gives more Alert Groups and a clearer ownership of each. Pick the labels that tell "who should look at this" apart. A good start is the labels your teams split on: the alert name, the cluster and the namespace or the service.

In the Route editor, the Group key shows its labels in order:

  1. To take a label out, select the × next to it.
  2. To add one, type its name in the field under the labels and select Add label.

items.title: Preview before you save
items.text:
The Group key editor previews what a key would do. It reads the Stored Snapshots of the chosen period (24 hours by default, at most the retention of Stored Snapshots; routing.group_key_preview_period) and shows how many Alert Groups the current and the proposed key would produce, with the 5 largest as examples (routing.group_key_preview_examples). It covers the Alerts that the Route would take at its place in the current order, each Alert once, and it works for a Route you are still creating. Use it before every change of a key.

  1. Change the Matchers or the Group key in the Route editor.
  2. Under Group key preview, choose the Period, 24 hours by default, and select Preview.
  3. Compare Current, the saved key, with Proposed, the key in the editor: each table lists the largest Alert Groups with the values of the key's labels and the number of Alerts. A new Route has only the proposed side. When you change the Matchers, the key or the period after a preview, the preview says so; select Preview again.

The screenshot shows the four Alerts of the table above: with namespace in place of severity, the Alerts of prod split by namespace.

items.title: Do not put Instance labels in the key
items.text: Instance labels change when the process that reports an Alert restarts, such as pod and instance. If one is in the Group key, every restart of a pod starts an Alert Group of its own and the old one stays open. Keep pod and instance out of the key unless one Alert Group per pod is what you want. When it is, restarts cause no trouble, since the Alert Group for a pod fires and resolves with that pod. Otherwise leave the labels out of the key, so that the restarted pod's Alert is recognised as a Replacement inside the same Alert Group. See Alert Groups and Instance labels in informational alerts.

items.title: Static labels
items.text: Static labels belong to an Integration, not to the Route. Muster adds them to every Alert of the Integration before it routes it, so the Matchers and the Group key can use them like labels the rules set. Their usual job is to name what the Alertmanager cluster knows and the rules do not, such as cluster=prod-eu. That is why the default Group key can include cluster: set it as a Static label on each Integration, and Alert Groups of different clusters stay apart even when the alerting rules never mention the cluster. See Static labels.

items.title: Create a Route
items.text:
1. Open Routes and select Create route. Choose a Route profile, On-call or Informational; Choose another profile takes you back.

  2. Enter a Name and, if you like, a Description. Add the Matchers, turn on Urgent if every Alert Group of the Route is Urgent, and check the Group key with its preview.

  3. Under Destinations, choose each Destination in Add a Destination. The list shows each one with its type and health; a Route without Destinations sends no messages.

  4. Check the policy below, filled in by the profile: Lifecycle (the Reopen window and the Grace period), Delivery (the Thread batching window and the Storm threshold), Snooze durations, Ack timeout and Reminders — see Statuses and commands — and Message, which Messages and templates explains.

  5. Select Create. The Routes list opens with the new Route just above the Default route, with its Matchers, its Group key and its open Alert Groups; drag it, or use its arrows, to change the order. Above the list, Muster may suggest Routes for its own alerts.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Only the Default route. Every Alert goes to one Route, grouped by alertname, severity and cluster. Add one Destination to the Default route and everything reaches one place. This is the setup of the Quick start plus a messenger.

Pages for payments. Create the Route payments-critical with the Matchers team="payments" and severity="critical", the On-call profile, the urgent mark on, and a Destination that is the payments team's channel. Put it above the Default route. Critical alerts of the payments team reach their channel and are Urgent. Their other alerts fall through to the Default route.

Certificates. Create the Route certificates with the Matcher alertname=~"Cert.*", the Informational profile and a Destination for the platform channel. These Alert Groups send no ack timeout notices and no Reminders, and they offer Snooze for a day, three days or a week.

Muster's own alerts. The Internal alerts, such as MusterDestinationBroken, are Alerts of the built-in "Muster" Integration and are routed by Routes like any other. Route them to a Destination of another kind than the one that failed. The Routes page offers a Route for alertname=~"Muster.*" once you have a Destination, and a Route for MusterHeartbeatLost when an Integration has a Heartbeat. See the Internal alerts.

items.title: What changes when you edit a Route
items.text:
• Settings, such as the timers, the templates and the Snooze durations, apply at once, also to open Alert Groups, whose messages are brought up to date.
  • A new Group key or new Matchers apply to Alerts that start firing afterwards. A fingerprint already in an open Alert Group stays there until that Alert Group is resolved.
  • No edit changes the status of any Alert Group.
  • Adding a Destination to a Route gives it the Route's open Alert Groups, Quietly. Removing one gives each open Root message one last edit that says it is no longer updated and links to Muster.
  • Deleting a Route that has open Alert Groups is refused. You can move them to the Default route first.

items.title: Snapshot semantics
items.text:
Alertmanager does not tell Muster "this alert started" and "this alert stopped" as separate events. It sends a Snapshot: the full state of one Alertmanager group at the moment of the notification, listing every alert it holds. Grafana's built-in Alertmanager sends Snapshots too, through a webhook contact point. Muster works out what changed by comparing Snapshots. This page explains the rules, and why an alert can be Gone or Stale without anybody sending a "resolved".

You only need this page to understand why Muster resolved something, or why it did not. The settings that matter are on Connect Alertmanager, in particular its Repeat intervals, and on Connect Grafana.

items.title: From a Snapshot to a message
items.text:
Receiving is store-first. Muster checks the Integration token and the size, stores the Snapshot exactly as received, and answers 202. A worker then processes it, on any replica, and everything that follows is a chain of small steps:

flowchart TD
  am["Alertmanager or Grafana"] -- "Snapshot" --> ingest["Ingest"]
  ingest --> stored[("Stored Snapshot")]
  stored --> processing["Processing"]
  processing -- "Alert changes" --> routing["Routing"]
  routing -- "Route" --> groups["Alert Group"]
  groups -- "lifecycle event" --> desired["Desired state"]
  desired --> worker["Delivery worker"]
  worker --> root["Root message"]
  1. Ingest stores the Snapshot as a Stored Snapshot and wakes a worker. It is kept for retention.stored_snapshots (14 days) for debugging, previews and replay.
  2. Processing splits the Snapshot into Alerts by fingerprint, adds the Integration's Static labels, and applies the rules below. It emits Alert changes: a new firing, a resolution with its reason, a Continuation, a change of annotations. It processes the Snapshots of an Alertmanager group in the order they arrived.
  3. Routing gives each newly firing Alert its Route and Severity level.
  4. The Alert Group takes the Alert: it joins an open one, reopens a resolved one, or starts a new one. Every change records a lifecycle event in the Timeline.
  5. The lifecycle event changes the Desired state of the Alert Group's message in each of its Destinations: what the Root message should look like right now.
  6. The delivery worker brings the actual message to the Desired state with one call, and the Root message in the messenger shows it. See Loud and Quiet for when that is an edit and when a new message.

Processing writes one log line per Snapshot, never one per Alert.

items.title: One Alertmanager group, one stream of Snapshots
items.text:
An Alertmanager group is the set of alerts that Alertmanager notifies about together under one groupKey. The Snapshots of one group form a stream, and Muster compares each with the ones before it. Alertmanager sends a Snapshot again each time the group changes and each time the route's repeat_interval elapses, and Muster learns from the gaps.

Two things about Snapshots matter in practice:

  • Copies from an HA pair are harmless. Two Alertmanagers in a pair send their own copy, 0 to 15 seconds apart, sometimes one of them incomplete. Muster processes an Alert once for the same fingerprint, status and startsAt, so a duplicate changes nothing. Snapshots of one group that arrive within the Integration's duplicate window (integration.duplicate_window, 45 seconds) count as one, and an Alert listed in either of them counts as listed.
  • A Snapshot's status is the group's, an Alert's status is its own. A Snapshot with status: firing can list alerts that are resolved, and each alert's own status decides for it.

items.title: Resolved
items.text:
The normal way an Alert ends is that Alertmanager lists it as resolved. Muster resolves it at once, with the reason that Alertmanager resolved it, in the latest Alert Group where that fingerprint is still firing.

  • A resolved for an Alert that is already resolved, or for an earlier firing of it, changes nothing. Prometheus re-sends a resolved alert for about 15 minutes, so the same resolved arrives several times.
  • A resolved with an older startsAt than the Alert's current one resolves the current firing when its endsAt is later than the current startsAt: the two firings overlap. The replicas of a Grafana HA pair evaluate the rules each on its own, so their copies of one alert can carry different startsAt, and the resolve of either replica ends the Alert. Without an endsAt, or with one not later than the current startsAt, it is a resolve of an earlier firing. Alertmanager merges overlapping firings of one alert, so with one rule evaluator a resolve it sends of an earlier firing ends before the next one starts. With an HA pair of rule evaluators, such as two Prometheus replicas, it can send one that ends later, and Muster resolves the Alert, as it would with the startsAt that Alertmanager merged.
  • A resolved for a fingerprint that fires nowhere is dropped, and counted.
  • A Snapshot whose status is resolved, sent when all the alerts of its group resolved, resolves every Alert of that group that still fires, also the ones it does not list. After a restart of both Alertmanagers of a pair, such a Snapshot can list only some of them and the others are never sent. A truncated Snapshot from Grafana is the exception; see Truncation.

items.title: Gone
items.text:
Sometimes Alertmanager stops listing an alert without saying that it resolved. The rule evaluator may have stopped, an alert may have been inhibited, or the route may have changed. Muster notices that the Alert is Gone:

An Alert is Gone in an Alertmanager group when it has been missing from at least two consecutive Snapshots of that group, over at least processing.gone_min_absence (5 minutes), counted from the first Snapshot that missed it to the latest one.

A Snapshot that lists it ends the count. Both conditions are needed, for good reasons. A restarted Alertmanager starts with an empty memory, and its first Snapshots can leave out a firing alert twice, a minute apart, because Prometheus re-sends firing alerts only every 2 minutes. The minimum absence covers that. A restarted instance of an HA pair is covered by the duplicate window, because the other instance sends the full Snapshot 15 seconds later.

Snapshots of one group Result Alert A missing at T and T+60 s, listed at T+120 s A stays firing; the count restarts Alert A missing at T, T+60 s and T+6 min A is Gone at T+6 min Alert A missing at T only A stays firing; one Snapshot never counts

An Alert that appears in several Alertmanager groups is resolved by absence only when it is Gone (or Stale) in every one of them.

items.title: Stale
items.text:
If the whole group sends nothing at all, there is no Snapshot to miss the Alert from. This happens when the group is silenced, inhibited or muted as a whole in Alertmanager. Muster calls an Alert Stale when it has heard nothing about it for too long:

An Alert goes Stale when its Alertmanager group has sent no Snapshot for stale_after, which is processing.stale_after_factor (3) times the repeat interval that Muster has learned for the group's Alertmanager route.

Muster learns the interval from the gaps between Snapshots whose notification_reason is repeat interval elapsed or, from senders without that field such as Grafana, between identical Snapshots, and uses the median of the last 9 gaps (processing.repeat_samples). Until it has learned an interval, stale_after is processing.stale_after_unlearned, 25 hours. Alertmanager sends a repeat on the first group_interval tick after repeat_interval has elapsed, so the gaps are about repeat_interval + group_interval. With a 10-minute repeat_interval and Alertmanager's default group_interval of 5 minutes, Muster learns an interval of about 15 minutes, and a silenced group's Alerts go Stale after about 45 minutes. With a daily interval it takes more than three days, which is why the Integration page warns about an interval longer than processing.long_repeat_warning (1 hour). See Repeat intervals.

Gone and Stale both resolve the Alert with the reason "Alertmanager no longer reports this alert — it resolved without notice, was silenced or inhibited in Alertmanager, or the Alertmanager routing changed". If a silenced alert's mute ends within about 14 minutes, Alertmanager still reports it as resolved, so it resolves normally; after that it only goes Stale.

items.title: The Heartbeat
items.text:
Stale resolution has a risk: if the path from Alertmanager to Muster breaks, Muster hears nothing, and every Alert would go Stale, although they may still fire. The Heartbeat removes the risk. It is a regular signal that proves the path works.

  • Stale applies only while the Integration's Heartbeat is live. An Integration without a Heartbeat, or still waiting for the first signal, never resolves an Alert as Stale. Gone still works.
  • While the Heartbeat is lost (no signal within integration.heartbeat_timeout, 5 minutes), the time does not count towards stale_after. From the last signal before the loss until the signal returns, nothing goes Stale. Muster's own downtime does not count either, beyond the timeout.
  • The Integration shows "No contact with Alertmanager since HH:MM", and Muster raises the Internal alert MusterHeartbeatLost.

So with a live Heartbeat and a learned 5-minute interval, an Alert whose group last arrived at T goes Stale at T+15 minutes. If the last Heartbeat signal also came at T, the Heartbeat was lost at T+5 minutes, and the signal returned at T+10 minutes, the Alert goes Stale at T+25 minutes: the 10 minutes from the last signal until its return did not count.

items.title: Truncation
items.text:
An Alertmanager webhook configuration with max_alerts above 0, like Grafana's webhook contact point with Max alerts above 0, keeps only the first alerts of a group in each notification, and counts the rest in truncatedAlerts. A truncated Snapshot lists only part of the group, so it can never be evidence that an Alert is missing.

  • Muster does not count a truncated Snapshot as absence. While Snapshots of the group keep arriving truncated, the unlisted Alerts stay alive, which can keep an Alert open that has resolved in reality.
  • Muster raises the Internal alert MusterSnapshotTruncated for the Integration while any group is truncated, and resolves it when none is left. The Integration page shows a warning too.
  • Grafana computes the status of a Snapshot from the alerts it lists, not from the whole group, so a truncated Snapshot from Grafana can say resolved while alerts it left out still fire. Muster recognises a Snapshot from Grafana by its top-level orgId, which Alertmanager never sends. A truncated one with status: resolved resolves only the Alerts it lists as resolved, never its whole group.
  • The fix is max_alerts: 0 on the Alertmanager receiver, or Max alerts 0, the default, on Grafana's webhook contact point. See Send every alert of the group, Connect Grafana and the runbook.

items.title: Continuation
items.text: A Prometheus restart whose first evaluation falls exactly on the alerts' endsAt can make Alertmanager send them again with a new startsAt and no resolved in between. A longer stop gives a resolved and a new firing. That first case is a Continuation: the Alert stays the same, its start time is updated, and nothing is Loud and nothing reopens. Once an Alert has resolved by any route, the next firing of the same fingerprint is a new firing.

items.title: Why an Alert resolved
items.text:
Every Alert resolved by Muster carries one of four reasons, which the Integration's Alerts view shows and the metric muster_alerts_resolved_total counts:

resolved Alertmanager sent resolved, for the Alert or for its whole group. gone Missing from at least two consecutive Snapshots for the minimum absence. stale Its group sent nothing for three learned repeat intervals, with a live Heartbeat. integration_deleted Its Integration was deleted.

When the last Alert of an Alert Group resolves, the Alert Group is resolved by the system with the reason of the last one. See Alert Groups for what happens if the problem returns. If processing ever misbehaves, muster ingest replay reprocesses Stored Snapshots, and because processing is idempotent it changes nothing that was already right.

items.title: Statuses and commands
items.text: An Alert Group is always in one of four statuses, and only a few things move it from one to another. Some are Commands that a person gives, from the web UI, the API, a button in a messenger, or a Text command in a Thread. The others are transitions that Muster makes on its own, always with a reason you can read.

items.title: The four statuses
items.text:
Status Meaning Firing The Alert Group has a live problem and nobody has taken it. Acknowledged A person has taken it and is handling it. That person is its Owner. Snoozed It is set aside until a chosen time, or with no end. Muster stays quiet about it meanwhile. Resolved It is closed, by a person or by Muster because its Alerts are gone.

New Alerts that join an open Alert Group change its status only through a rise to Urgent, and edits of a Route never change a status. Only the transitions below do.

stateDiagram-v2
    state "Resolved by the system" as ResolvedBySystem
    state "Resolved by a user" as ResolvedByUser

    [*] --> Firing : created
    Firing --> Acknowledged : Acknowledge
    Snoozed --> Acknowledged : Acknowledge
    Acknowledged --> Acknowledged : Takeover
    Acknowledged --> Firing : Unacknowledge
    Acknowledged --> Firing : auto-unacknowledge (system)
    Acknowledged --> Firing : rise to Urgent (system)
    Firing --> Snoozed : Snooze
    Acknowledged --> Snoozed : Snooze
    Snoozed --> Snoozed : Snooze with a new end
    Snoozed --> Firing : Unsnooze
    Snoozed --> Firing : Snooze ends (system)
    Snoozed --> Firing : rise to Urgent (system)
    Firing --> ResolvedByUser : Resolve
    Acknowledged --> ResolvedByUser : Resolve
    Snoozed --> ResolvedByUser : Resolve
    Firing --> ResolvedBySystem : all Alerts resolved (system)
    Acknowledged --> ResolvedBySystem : all Alerts resolved (system)
    Snoozed --> ResolvedBySystem : all Alerts resolved (system)
    ResolvedBySystem --> Firing : Reopen (system)
    ResolvedBySystem --> Acknowledged : Reopen (system)
    ResolvedBySystem --> Snoozed : Reopen (system)
    ResolvedByUser --> Firing : Unresolve
    ResolvedBySystem --> [*] : Reopen window ends
    ResolvedByUser --> [*] : Grace period ends

Resolved appears twice because the two ways back differ. After the system resolved an Alert Group, it reopens by itself if the problem returns within the Reopen window. After a person resolved it, nothing reopens it; the person can Unresolve it, or Muster starts a new Alert Group if the Alerts still fire after the Grace period. See Reopening.

The ack timeout runs only while an Alert Group is Firing, and an Alert Group is Unclaimed after its last notice. See Ack timeouts, Reminders and auto-unacknowledge.

items.title: Transitions Muster makes on its own
items.text:
Each carries its reason, which you see on the Alert Group page, in its Timeline and, in a messenger, in the Root message or a Thread reply.

Open → Resolved

reason you see: the reason of the last Alert

The last Alert resolved: Alertmanager sent resolved, or the Alert went Gone or Stale, or its Integration was deleted. This also ends a Snooze.

Resolved by the system → previous status

reason you see: the Reopen, with the Reopen count

An Alert with the same Route and Group key values fires within the Reopen window.

Snoozed → Firing

reason you see: the Snooze ended

The Snooze ends while Alerts still fire. It has no Owner, and the message lists what accumulated.

Snoozed or Acknowledged → Firing

reason you see: the rise to Urgent

A rise in Severity level makes the Alert Group Urgent. It ends a Snooze, unless the Snooze was set while the Alert Group was already Urgent, and removes an acknowledgement when the Route has route.urgent_rise_removes_ack on (the default).

Acknowledged → Firing

reason you see: "No answer to the last two Reminders"

The Route's auto-unacknowledge removes the acknowledgement of an Owner who stopped answering.

Acknowledged → Firing

reason you see: "The owner was disabled" or "The owner was deleted"

The Owner was disabled or deleted.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Command Allowed from Effect Acknowledge Firing, Snoozed The caller becomes the Owner. It ends a Snooze. By the current Owner it changes nothing. By another user it is a Takeover. Unacknowledge Acknowledged The Alert Group is Firing again, without an Owner, and the ack timeout starts over. Any user who may acknowledge can do it, not only the Owner.
