Resolve Firing, Acknowledged, Snoozed The Alert Group is Resolved by the person. A Note can come with it. Unresolve Resolved by a person The Alert Group is Firing again without an Owner. Web UI and API only. Snooze Firing, Acknowledged, Snoozed The Alert Group is Snoozed until a time in the future, until a Snooze preset, or with no end. A Snooze with a new end changes the end. Unsnooze Snoozed The Alert Group is Firing again without an Owner, and the ack timeout starts over. Add Note any A Note appears in the Timeline with its author. Web UI and API only. Still on it Acknowledged, while a Reminder waits The Owner answers the Reminder. See below.

Details:

  • Takeover. Acknowledging an Alert Group that somebody else owns moves it to you, without asking. The previous Owner is Mentioned in a Loud Thread reply, and your Reminders start from zero. The web UI says "Take over from {Owner}" on the button.
  • Snooze. The web UI and the API accept any future time, a Snooze preset, or no end. The API makes you say which: a request names exactly one of until, no_end and preset. A Snooze with no end asks you to confirm "This Alert Group stays snoozed until someone unsnoozes it". Messengers offer the Route's Snooze durations as separate buttons or a menu (route.snooze_durations: 1 hour, 4 hours and 24 hours on an On-call Route, 1 day, 3 days and 7 days on an Informational Route), and after them the two Snooze presets; see In messengers.
  • Unresolve is refused when the system resolved the Alert Group ("it reopens by itself when an alert returns"), when its Route was deleted, when a newer open Alert Group with the same key exists, and when all its Alerts have already resolved.
  • Notes are up to 4,000 characters (alert_group.note_max_length).
  • Bulk commands. In the list, select up to 100 Alert Groups (alert_group.bulk_max) and run Acknowledge, Resolve, Snooze or Unsnooze on all of them. Each goes through the rules on its own and the result lists the outcome per Alert Group. One refusal never stops the others. A bulk Acknowledge skips an Alert Group that another user owns ("skipped: owned by {Owner}"), so it never takes over by accident.
  • Refusals carry a stable code and a message, such as "already resolved", "not acknowledged" or "not permitted". The API answers 409 for a precondition and 403 for a permission.
  • Commands on one Alert Group are serialized. Two people acknowledging at the same moment leave the later one as Owner and one Takeover in the Timeline.

Every command is a Quiet event except the Takeover. See Loud and Quiet.

items.title: Snooze presets
items.text:
A Snooze preset ends a Snooze at the start of the working day instead of after a duration. Muster turns it into an end when the command runs:

Until tomorrow 09:00 API value: tomorrow · ends at: the next start of the working day Until Monday 09:00 API value: week_start · ends at: the next start of the working day on the first day of the week

"Next" is strictly after now. With the working day starting at 09:00:

  • At 02:00, "Until tomorrow 09:00" ends at 09:00 the same day. The night belongs to the day before it, so "tomorrow" is the morning about to come, seven hours away.
  • At 08:59 it ends one minute later: the preset means "until the working day starts".
  • At 09:00 sharp, and at any later time of the day, it ends at 09:00 the next day.
  • There is no working-week calendar, so on Friday evening "Until tomorrow 09:00" ends on Saturday at 09:00. For a weekend, use week_start, which ends on Monday at 09:00.
  • The start is the time on the clock on the day of the end. A start that the clocks skip moves forward by the change: 02:30 on the night the clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00 is 03:30. A start that the clocks show twice, when they go back, is the first of the two.

The end is stored as a time. A later change of the settings or of a time zone never moves a Snooze already set, and the Snooze ends like any other: if Alerts still fire, the Alert Group is Firing again without an Owner, with a Loud message.

Time zone. The preset counts in the time zone that the request names in time_zone. Without one, it counts in the profile time zone of the user who snoozes, also through a Personal access token, and otherwise in the Organization's time zone (organization.time_zone). A Service account has no profile, so it always gets the Organization's. A press on a button in a messenger and a Text command carry no time zone, so they count in the profile time zone of the linked user who pressed or wrote, and otherwise in the Organization's.

Settings. Two Organization settings define the presets, as the fields workday_start and week_start of the organization in the API:

organization.workday_start

default: 09:00

The start of the working day, HH:MM on the 24-hour clock.

organization.week_start

default: monday

The first day of the week, monday to sunday.

API. A Snooze takes preset, tomorrow or week_start, as a third choice beside until and no_end, with an optional time_zone:

{"preset": "tomorrow", "time_zone": "Europe/Berlin"}

A time_zone without preset is refused with 422 unsupported, and a time zone Muster does not know with 422 invalid_format. A bulk Snooze with a preset computes the end once, so every Alert Group gets the same end. GET /api/v1/snooze-presets, with an optional time_zone, answers the end that each preset would set now and the time zone it used; it needs the Permission to snooze and changes nothing. The Audit log entry of a preset Snooze names the preset and the time zone beside the end. See the API reference.

items.title: In the web UI
items.text: The Snooze dialog of an Alert Group offers both presets after the Route's Snooze durations and before "Until" and "No end", also on a Route without durations; the bulk Snooze of the list, which has no durations, offers them first. Under each preset the dialog shows the end it would set now, such as "Ends Oct 20, 2026, 09:00": Muster computes it when the dialog opens, on its own clock and in your time zone (the one of your profile, else your browser's), and the dialog sends that time zone with the preset. Admins set the start of the working day and the first day of the week on Organization → General. In the profile, a hint under the time zone says that presets pressed in messengers end in that time zone, and in the Organization's while the profile follows the browser.

items.title: In messengers
items.text:
On a Route with Snooze durations, the Root message of a firing or an acknowledged Alert Group offers both presets as two more Snooze buttons after the durations: "Until tomorrow 09:00" and "Until Monday 09:00", or «До завтра 09:00» and «До понедельника 09:00» on a Route in Russian. The time is organization.workday_start and the day organization.week_start, so with the week starting on Sunday the second button reads "Until Sunday 09:00". A snoozed Alert Group offers no Snooze button, and a Route without Snooze durations offers no preset either, because an empty route.snooze_durations means no Snooze from messengers. Telegram shows the presets on a row of their own under the durations, and a bridge with a limit on buttons drops them first; see Bridge. Slack offers the durations and then the presets as the options of one Snooze… menu, since its web client folds the buttons beyond five in a row.

The labels are part of the message. After a change of organization.workday_start or organization.week_start, each Root message shows the new labels at its next update, and a press on a button shown before the change already ends at the new start of the working day: the preset is computed when the command runs. On a bridge without buttons, the presets are Text commands.

items.title: Who may
items.text: A Responder or an Admin may acknowledge, resolve, snooze and add Notes. A Viewer may read and may not act: the command is refused. A Service account may run the commands its Role allows, except Acknowledge and Still on it, because an Owner is always a User. A Personal access token acts as its User, with at most that User's Permissions. Every command is recorded in the Audit log with its actor and the Transport.

items.title: Commands in the web UI
items.text:
The page of an Alert Group offers the commands its status allows, and the list offers them for several Alert Groups at once (Bulk commands).

  1. Open the Alert Group from Alert Groups. Its command buttons are at the top: Acknowledge, Resolve and Snooze for a firing one.

  2. To add a Note, type it under Add a note, further down the page, and select Add note. It appears in the Timeline with you as its author.

  3. Snooze opens its dialog: the Route's Snooze durations, the Snooze presets, Until a date and time of your choosing, or No end, which asks you to confirm with I understand. Select Snooze.

  4. Resolve opens a dialog with an optional Note, recorded with the resolve.

  5. After Acknowledge, the page names you as the Owner and offers Unacknowledge, Resolve and Snooze. Another user sees Take over from {Owner} instead of Acknowledge.

items.title: Where a command comes from
items.text:
The Transport is the way a command reaches Muster. It is recorded with the command, and Muster applies the same rules to all of them.

Web UI how: buttons on the Alert Group page and in the list, with dialogs for Snooze and Resolve · notes: everything above, including bulk commands, Notes and Unresolve API how: POST to /api/v1/alert-groups/{id}/acknowledge and its siblings, with a session or a token · notes: the same; see the API reference Mattermost how: a button on the message · notes: Acknowledge, Unacknowledge, Resolve, Snooze, Unsnooze, Still on it Slack how: a button on the message, and the Snooze… menu with the durations and then the presets · notes: the same Telegram how: an inline button on the message · notes: the same Bridge how: a button on the message, if the bridge declares buttons; or a Text command in the Thread, if it declares thread_messages · notes: the same system how: Muster itself · notes: the automatic transitions above, shown in the Timeline

Messengers never offer Unresolve or Notes, and never a Snooze with no end. A person who presses a button in a messenger must have linked their messenger account to their Muster user; see Link your messenger accounts. A press from an unlinked account changes nothing, and the person is told privately how to link it.

items.title: What each button does
items.text:
The buttons of a Root message depend on the status of its Alert Group:

Status Buttons Firing Ack, Resolve, Snooze Acknowledged Unack, Resolve, Snooze Snoozed Ack, Unsnooze, Resolve Resolved none; a link "Open in Muster"
  • Ack takes the Alert Group: you become its Owner, the Reminders start, and the message shows who has it. If somebody else has it, Ack takes it over from them.
  • Unack gives it back. The Alert Group becomes Firing again with no Owner, and the ack timeout starts over.
  • Resolve closes the Alert Group by hand. If Alerts still fire, the message shows "⚠ N alerts still firing in Alertmanager", and after the Grace period the Alerts that still fire start a new Alert Group.
  • Snooze sets it aside. It offers the Route's Snooze durations, such as 1 hour, 4 hours and 24 hours, one choice for each, then the two Snooze presets "Until tomorrow 09:00" and "Until Monday 09:00", which end at the next start of the working day, or at its start on the first day of the week, in your profile time zone, or else the Organization's. When the time is up and Alerts still fire, the Alert Group comes back Firing and a Loud message says so.
  • Unsnooze ends the Snooze early. The Alert Group becomes Firing again.
  • On a Reminder, Still on it tells Muster you are still handling the Alert Group, and Unack gives it up.
  • A Storm summary and an ack timeout notice carry only links to Muster. A test message carries the buttons of its status, but pressing them changes nothing: you get "This is a test message; nothing was changed".

A press edits the Root message to show the result. A press that Muster refuses, such as a Resolve by a Viewer, is answered privately to the person who pressed, and nothing changes.

items.title: Text commands
items.text:
Some messengers have no buttons, or a bridge does not offer them. A Text command is a Command written as a reply in a Thread. Only a Bridge Destination takes them, and only when the bridge declares thread_messages. A Root message that is not resolved then ends with a line such as "Reply in the Thread: ack · resolve · snooze 1h".

A reply is a Text command when its whole text, trimmed, in any case and with an optional leading /, is one of:

Text command Same in Russian Command ack взял Acknowledge unack отпускаю Unacknowledge resolve решено Resolve snooze <duration> отложить <duration> Snooze unsnooze вернуть Unsnooze still on it ещё работаю (also еще работаю) Still on it

The <duration> is one of the Route's Snooze durations, written in minutes, hours or days: 30m, 4h or 1d, and 30м, 4ч or 1д in Russian. It can also name a Snooze preset: tomorrow (завтра) for the next start of the working day, or the first day of the week (organization.week_start), such as monday (понедельник), for the start of the working day on that day. So snooze tomorrow, /Snooze Tomorrow and отложить понедельник (with the week starting on Monday) all work. A day is written as it stands alone: понедельник, вторник, среда, четверг, пятница, суббота, воскресенье. Every word works whatever the Route's language is. The writer needs an Account link, and the same permissions as for a button.

Muster answers a Text command in the Thread, for example "Done: Acknowledged #42", or with the reason it refused. A duration that is not one of the Route's, or a day other than the first day of the week, is answered with what the Route offers: "Snooze for one of: 1h, 4h, 24h, tomorrow, monday". The sentence and the durations are in the writer's profile language, and the two preset words in the Route's language. A Route without Snooze durations takes no preset either, and answers "This Alert Group's Route has no Snooze durations; nothing was changed." Any other text is ignored and never answered, so people can talk in the Thread. The Thread of an older Root message works too: a Text command there acts on the Alert Group like any other, also when the message is past its edit window. A Text command older than an hour (bridge.event_max_age) is dropped. If the bridge forwards only the messages that mention its bot, the line says "mentioning the bot", and the command must mention it. See Write a bridge for how a bridge reports a Thread message.

items.title: Ack timeouts, Reminders and auto-unacknowledge
items.text: Three timers make sure nobody forgets: one for an Alert Group nobody has taken, one for an Alert Group somebody took and then went quiet, and an optional one that takes the Alert Group back. They are Route settings; the On-call profile turns the first two on and the Informational profile turns everything off.

items.title: Ack timeout
items.text:
The ack timeout runs while an Alert Group is Firing. It starts at the Alert Group's first Publication in a Destination, and starts over each time it becomes Firing again. Acknowledge, Snooze and Resolve stop it.

When nobody acknowledges, Muster sends up to three notices, at doubling intervals from the Route's first interval (route.ack_timeout, 15 minutes on an On-call Route). With 15 minutes they come at 15, 45 and 105 minutes after the start. Each is a Loud Thread reply that Mentions whom the Destination's ack_timeout setting says. After the last notice the Alert Group is Unclaimed: its message shows "⚠ Nobody has taken this", and the Alert Group list has an Unclaimed filter, column and badge. Unclaimed ends when the Alert Group stops being Firing.

An Alert Group that has not been published, as when its Route has no Destination or only Broken ones, has no ack timeout until its first Publication.

items.title: Reminders
items.text:
When somebody acknowledges, Muster reminds the Owner while the Alert Group stays open (route.reminders, on an On-call Route). The first Reminder comes 4 hours after the acknowledgement, and each next interval doubles up to 24 hours: at 4, 12, 28 and 52 hours, then every 24 hours. Each is a Loud Thread reply that Mentions the Owner, with the buttons Still on it and Unack.

  • Still on it is recorded in the Timeline and does not change the interval. The Owner can also answer from the Alert Group page or the API.
  • A Takeover starts the Reminders over for the new Owner. A Reopen into acknowledged continues them. A snoozed Alert Group gets none. There are no quiet hours.
  • An Owner who is disabled or deleted loses the acknowledgement: the Alert Group becomes Firing without an Owner, and the ack timeout starts over.
  • After Muster was down, the overdue notices of one Alert Group collapse into one Loud Thread reply that says how many were missed.
  • Buttons on Reminders are signed like the others, but are not updated after a key rotation. Once the old key is removed, a press is answered "This button has expired; use the buttons on the Alert Group's message".

items.title: Auto-unacknowledge
items.text:
If an Owner goes home and says nothing, the Alert Group would stay acknowledged forever. Auto-unacknowledge (route.auto_unacknowledge, off by default) takes it back. The Owner answers a Reminder by pressing Still on it, by running any command on the Alert Group or by adding a Note before the next Reminder is due. When the Owner has answered neither of the last two Reminders (timers.auto_unacknowledge_after), the next Reminder is not sent. Instead Muster unacknowledges the Alert Group with the reason "No answer to the last two Reminders". It becomes Firing without an Owner, a Loud Thread reply gives the reason and Mentions the Owner, and the ack timeout starts over.

For example, Carol acknowledges at 10:00 and goes home. She answers neither the Reminder at 14:00 nor the one at 22:00. At 14:00 the next day, instead of a third Reminder, Muster unacknowledges the Alert Group and Mentions Carol, and the ack timeout notices begin again.

The Alert Group page shows the next scheduled notice or Reminder.

items.title: API tokens and automation
items.text: Everything the web UI does, a script can do through the API, as a person or as a non-person identity. This page shows how to get a token, how to call the API, and what to expect from it. The API reference lists every operation, its Permission and its answers; the binary serves the same specification at /api/v1/openapi.yaml.

items.title: Two kinds of token
items.text:
A Personal access token acts as a User. It has the Permissions you choose, never more than you hold, and it loses what your Role loses. Use it for your own scripts. Its prefix is mstr_pat_.

A Service account is an identity that is not a person, such as Terraform or a pipeline. It has a name, a Role and any number of tokens, whose prefix is mstr_sat_. It cannot sign in to the web UI and has no Account links.

A Service account cannot become an Owner

The Owner of an Alert Group is always a User. Acknowledge from a Service account is refused with 409 and the code owner_must_be_user. It may Resolve, Snooze and add Notes, and the Timeline shows the Service account as the actor. A Personal access token acts as its User, so acknowledging with one makes that User the Owner.

An Integration token (mstr_int_) is a third kind and is not for the API: it sends alerts and Heartbeats only, and the API does not accept it. See Connect Alertmanager.

The prefix mstr_ and the kind in it let secret scanners find a token that leaked into a repository. If one does, revoke it.

items.title: Create a Personal access token
items.text:
Tokens are created in the web UI. A token cannot create or revoke another token, so there is no API call to start from nothing.

  1. Open Profile, Personal access tokens, and select Create token.
  2. Give it a Name that says where it is used, such as laptop-scripts.
  3. Under Permissions tick what the script needs. You see only the Permissions you hold. A script that reads Alert Groups needs alert-groups:read; one that also acknowledges needs alert-groups:acknowledge.

  4. Choose Expires on: 30 days, 90 days, 365 days or a date of your own. A token may have No expiry (token.expiry is none by default), but the page warns about a token that never expires: choose a date.

  5. Select Create. The dialog shows the token once. Copy it with Copy before you select Done: only a hash is kept.

The list shows when each token was created, when and from which address it was last used, and when it expires. Revoke stops a script that uses it at once. The Audit log records a request made with a token as "alex via token laptop-scripts".

items.title: Create a Service account
items.text:
1. Open Access → Service accounts and select Create service account.

  2. Give it a Name and a Role: Admin, Responder or Viewer. You can give only a Role whose Permissions you hold. Select Create.

  3. On its page, under Tokens, select Create token, give it a name and an expiry, select Create, and copy the value once.

  4. The page of the Service account shows its Role, its status and its tokens, with Disable and Delete.

Its tokens act with the Role of the account, and changing the Role changes every token at once. To change a token without a gap, create the second token, switch the pipeline to it and revoke the first. Disable stops all its tokens until you Enable it; Delete revokes them for good.

items.title: Call the API
items.text:
Send the token as a bearer token. The API is under /api/v1 of the address people open, MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL:

MUSTER=https://muster.example.org
TOKEN=mstr_pat_...
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$MUSTER/api/v1/alert-groups?status=firing&limit=20"

The answer is JSON: items and next_cursor. A request with no token, or a wrong one, gets 401; one with a token that lacks the Permission gets 403. Every operation in the reference names the Permission it needs.

Snooze the Alert Group AGK7M3QX9P2RTA until a time (the token needs alert-groups:snooze):

curl -sS -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"until": "2026-10-20T08:00:00Z"}' "$MUSTER/api/v1/alert-groups/AGK7M3QX9P2RTA/snooze"

A call on the interactive path, such as a check of a Connection, answers 503 with Retry-After when Muster's limit toward the messenger leaves no room within 5 seconds (delivery.interactive_budget); retry after the pause.

A few operations need the web session and refuse a token with 403 (session_required): changing your own password, TOTP, Account links and tokens.

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
Identifiers URLs carry the public_id of a resource, such as AGK7M3QX9P2RTA, never the #N of an Alert Group. Pagination limit is 50 by default and at most 500 (api.page_size). A page carries next_cursor; send it back as cursor for the next page. There are no offsets. Changing configuration

Routes, Destinations, the Organization and other configuration carry an ETag, in a header and in the body. Read it, then update with PUT and If-Match set to it. A stale value gets 412, a missing header 428. This stops two writers from overwriting each other.

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$MUSTER/api/v1/organization" | grep -i '^etag'

Then send the changed Organization with -X PUT -H 'If-Match: <that value>'. An omitted optional field keeps its stored value, and an explicit null clears one that can be cleared.

Errors RFC 9457 problems (application/problem+json) with a stable type and code, and errors[] with a JSON pointer to each invalid field. Times and units RFC 3339 in UTC; durations in whole seconds in *_seconds; retention in *_days. Secrets Write-only. A read shows whether a secret is set and when it changed, never its value.

items.title: Rate limit
items.text: The API is limited per token: 20 requests per second with bursts of 100 (api.rate_limit), counted on each Muster replica. A request over the limit gets 429 with Retry-After in seconds; wait that long and retry. Another token is not affected. Web sessions and ingestion are not limited.

items.title: Tokens of OIDC users
items.text:
A Personal access token of a User who signs in through OpenID Connect follows the identity provider. If the provider refuses the person at a background re-check, the token gets 401 with the code oidc_recheck_required and the text "Sign in through OIDC to make your tokens work again", and works again after the person's next OIDC sign-in, without a new token. When the provider granted no offline token, the tokens also stop once the last OIDC sign-in is older than the Organization's grace period (auth.oidc_token_grace, 7 days; Organization → Security, see Organization settings). Your profile shows the date until which your tokens work. Service account tokens are not affected, which is why automation belongs on a Service account.

A web session has its own lifetimes: see Sign-in.

items.title: Messages and templates
items.text: Muster shows every Alert Group as one Root message in each Destination, and edits it as the Alert Group changes. Without any setup the message is complete: the status, the number and title, the environment and start time, the labels, the summary, the Alerts, the links and the buttons. This page is for the Admin who wants to change what it says: the template of a Route, whom a message mentions, and the links it carries.

items.title: What you can change, and what you cannot
items.text:
A Route has three templates, under Routes → a Route → Message. Each is Built-in or Custom.

Root message The body of the message: the environment, the start time, the labels, the summary and the Alerts. The status colour, the heading, the links, the notices, the footer and the buttons always come from Muster, so no template can lose the buttons or the link to the Alert Group. Alert line The line of each Alert in the list of Alerts. It is also called the Line template. Ack timeout notice The reply Muster sends when nobody acknowledges an Alert Group in time.

Language of the same section sets the language of the built-in texts of the Route, English or Russian (route.language, English by default). Times in messages are absolute and use the Organization's time zone, never relative: see Organization settings.

Choosing Custom fills the editor with the source of the built-in template in the Route's language, so you start from what people see today and edit it. Choosing Built-in again keeps your text until you leave the page.

Each editor has a Preview under it. Choose the Sample it renders against: a Built-in example, the Recent snapshots of this route, or the Stored Snapshots of one Integration; and the Markup of the preview, Mattermost, Slack or Telegram. When you save, Muster parses every template and runs it against the most recent Stored Snapshots of the Route (up to 20, template.dry_run_sample, or the built-in example when there are none). A template that does not parse, or that calls a function Muster does not have, is not saved: the editor marks the error at its line and column.

The Outgoing webhook Destinations have templates of their own, written the same way: see template mode.

items.title: Edit a Route's message
items.text:
1. Open Routes and the Route, and scroll to Message. Choose the Language of its built-in texts. Each template shows Built-in or Custom, with its Preview under it.

  2. Choose Custom for the template you change, such as Alert line, and edit the source in the editor; it starts from the built-in template. The Preview renders it as you type, against the Sample you choose, in the markup of Mattermost, Telegram or Slack. A Route without recent Stored Snapshots renders against the built-in example. The template language lists what a template reads.

  3. Select Save. A template with an error is not saved, and the editor marks the error at its line and column.

items.title: The template language
items.text:
Templates are Go templates, the language of Alertmanager's own templates, and run in a sandbox:

  • The functions are those of Alertmanager's templates under their own names (toUpper, toLower, title, join, match, reReplaceAll, safeHtml, stringSlice, date, tz, humanizeDuration, toJson and more), so an Alertmanager template usually carries over. On top of them come the string, list, map, conversion and regular expression (RE2) functions of the sprout library, now and since from Muster's clock, and two Muster functions: lookup (see Links) and mention.
  • There is no function that reads the environment, files or the network; env does not exist. Muster has no list of functions in the web UI: sprout's documentation and Alertmanager's template reference are the function reference, and the editor names an unknown function when you save.
  • Loops are capped, a template may run for 2 seconds, and the output is cut at about 50,000 characters (template.output_cap).
  • A label or annotation that is not there is empty text, as in Alertmanager: {{ .Labels.cluster }} prints nothing and passes "" to a function, so toJson gives "", not null. Tell a missing value apart with if or or, as in {{ or .CommonLabels.team "none" }}.

What the Root message template reads:

.AlertGroup Number, Title, Summary, Status, Route, SeverityLevel, Urgent, StartedAt, URL, ReopenCount, Owner. .Alerts, .Status, .GroupLabels, .CommonLabels, .CommonAnnotations, .ExternalURL As in Alertmanager's templates. .Alerts.Firing and .Alerts.Resolved select by status.

The line template reads one Alert directly, as .Labels, .Annotations, .Status, .StartsAt, .EndsAt, .GeneratorURL and .Fingerprint, and .AlertGroup as above.

Alert data is safe by construction. Label and annotation values arrive already escaped for the Destination's markup, cut at 4 KB each (message.value_cap), and an @ in them is neutralised with a zero-width space, so @channel in a label notifies nobody. Links in messages are http or https only.

Two small examples

A line template that shows the pod and its summary:

{{ .Labels.pod }}: {{ .Annotations.summary }}

A Root message template that shows the summary and the pods that fire:

{{ .AlertGroup.Summary }}
{{ range .Alerts.Firing }}- {{ .Labels.pod }}
{{ end }}

Check both in the preview with a sample that has Alerts before you save.

If a template that was saved fails later, on data it did not expect, Muster does not drop the message. It renders the Fallback template instead, which shows every label under Muster's heading, footer and buttons. The Route shows Template error with the time and the error, the Timeline records that the fallback was used, and the Internal alert MusterTemplateError fires until the template renders again; see its runbook. Organization → System status lists the template errors.

A long message is shortened to the limit of the messenger by cutting the list of Alerts first, then the label sections. It always keeps the title, status, footer, buttons and the link. The list shows up to 10 lines of Alerts (message.alerts_listed); above that it shows the distinct values of each label that differs, and "Full list in Muster".

items.title: Whom a message mentions
items.text:
Each Destination has a Mentions section for six kinds of Loud event: nobody by default, or everyone in the chat, chosen Muster users, or messenger groups, as far as the messenger offers them (destination.mentions). The Loud and Quiet page lists what each Destination type takes and why a user needs an Account link to be mentioned.

In a template, {{ mention "all" }}, {{ mention "channel" }}, {{ mention "here" }}, {{ mention "owner" }} and {{ mention "group" "oncall" }} write a trusted Mention that Muster renders for the messenger. A literal @all written in a template is escaped and mentions nobody.

items.title: Links
items.text: Links to other tools come from data, not from code in a message: Link rules read Lookup tables. They appear as one line in the message and as the Links block on the Alert Group page.

items.title: Add a Lookup table
items.text:
A Lookup table is a table of values: a key and one value per named column. Limits: 50 columns and 10,000 rows, names and column names up to 200 characters, a description up to 2,000, a key or value up to 4,096 (lookup_table.size_max).

  1. Open Organization → Lookup tables and select Create table.

  2. Enter the Name that Link rules read the table by, and a Description if you like. Under Rows, name the first column, add more with Add column, and add each row with Add row: its Key and a value per column.

  3. Select Create. The list of Lookup tables shows the table with its number of rows.

items.title: Add a Link rule
items.text:
A Link rule turns an Alert Group, or each value of a label, into a link. Its fields:

Name Shown as the text of the link. Matchers Conditions on the Alert Group's common labels. A label that only some Alerts carry counts as missing. Without Matchers the rule applies to every Alert Group. Scope Alert Group gives one link. Each value of label gives one link per distinct value of a label among the Alerts. URL template A Go template. It reads .Labels (the common labels for the scope Alert Group, the labels of the first Alert with the value otherwise), .Value (the label's value) and the data of the Root message template. lookup "table" key "column" reads one cell and gives an empty text when the table, the key or the column does not exist. A template that writes nothing, or something that is not an http or https URL, gives no link.
  1. Open Organization → Link rules and select Create rule.

  2. Fill in the fields above. The Preview under the URL template shows the link that the rule makes for the Sample you choose, a built-in example or a recent Alert Group.

  3. Select Create. The list of Link rules shows the rule beside the built-in Explore.

All the Link rules of one message together read at most 100 rows with lookup in one render (template.lookups_per_render); the 101st is a template error, and a Link rule that fails is left out of the message and counted.

Example: a dashboard per cluster.

  1. Create the Lookup table dashboards with the column url and one row for each cluster: the key prod-eu, the value https://grafana.example.org/d/abc123/prod-eu.
  2. Create the Link rule Dashboard, scope Alert Group, with the URL template {{ lookup "dashboards" .Labels.cluster "url" }}. An Alert Group without a common cluster looks up an empty key and gets no link: a missing label is empty text.
  3. The preview of the rule shows the link for a sample. Alert Groups with cluster="prod-eu" now carry Dashboard.

A rule with the scope Each value of label and the label pod can build one log link per pod: https://logs.example.org/search?pod={{ .Value | urlquery }}.

Muster adds links without a rule as well: the annotations runbook_url and dashboard_url, shown as Runbook and Dashboard, and the generatorURL of the first firing Alert, shown as Source.

The built-in Link rule Explore opens the query of the Alert in Grafana's Explore. It reads the Lookup table grafana with the columns address (the address of your Grafana) and datasource_uid, and the key is the value of the environment label, else of the cluster label. It cannot be deleted, renamed or given another scope; its Matchers and URL template can be changed. A Lookup table that a Link rule reads cannot be deleted or renamed.

The API has lookup-tables and link-rules for the same: see the API reference. A list of Lookup tables comes at most 50 to a page (lookup_table.page_max), since each carries its rows.

items.title: Thread replies
items.text: Lifecycle events that are Thread replies, such as a Takeover or a Reopen, are sent at once. Only new Alerts are batched, by the Route's Thread batching window (Routes → a Route → Delivery, route.thread_batching_window, 60 seconds by default): the first new Alert is sent at once and opens the window, and the new Alerts that arrive within it are sent as one reply when it closes. After a quiet period longer than the window, the next one is again immediate. A reply lists the first 10 new Alerts and then "…and K more" (delivery.thread_alerts_listed).

items.title: Organization settings
items.text:
The Organization is the owner of all Users, Routes and data in Muster; there is one. Its settings change behaviour for everyone, so only Admins open them: choose Organization in the main navigation, then a page of its sub-navigation. Every change is recorded in the Audit log (Organization → Audit log) with a before and after, and two Admins editing the same page do not overwrite each other: the second save is refused with "Someone else changed these settings. Reload to see them.", and you reload and apply your change again.

The defaults below are what a new installation has.

items.title: General
items.text:
Organization → General

Name (organization.name, Muster) The name of the Organization. Time zone of messages (organization.time_zone, UTC) The time zone of every time in a message in a messenger. It is UTC until you change it, so a new installation shows times such as "started 07:12" in UTC. Times in messages are absolute, never "5 minutes ago". Each User sees the web UI in their own time zone, which they set in their profile. Start of the working day (organization.workday_start, 09:00) and First day of the week (organization.week_start, monday) The Snooze presets "Until tomorrow 09:00" and "Until Monday 09:00" end at this time of day and on this day, in the time zone of the person who snoozes. A change applies to Snoozes set afterwards; a Snooze already set does not move. See statuses and commands.
  1. Open Organization; General opens first.

  2. Change the Name, the Time zone of messages — type in Search time zones to narrow the list —, the Start of the working day or the First day of the week, and select Save. "Saved." confirms it.

items.title: Severity levels
items.text:
Organization → Severity levels

Alerts say how bad they are in a label. Muster turns its values into three Severity levels: critical, warning and info.

Severity label (organization.severity_label, severity) The label that carries the severity. Mapping (organization.severity_mapping) Values of that label and their level. By default critical is critical, warning is warning, and info and none are info. A label that is missing counts as info; any other value counts as warning and is shown as received. Emoji and colours (organization.severity_styles) The emoji and the colour of each level: critical 🟥 #d32f2f, warning 🟧 #f57c00, info 🟦 #1976d2. Values seen (organization.severity_values_window, the last 14 days) The values of the severity label that arrived, with their counts. A value with no mapping is marked "No mapping — counts as warning" and has a Map action. If your alerts use P1 and page, map them to critical here.
  1. Open Organization → Severity levels.

  2. Under Mapping, select Add value, enter the value, such as P1, and choose its level; or select Map next to a value under Values seen. Select Save.

items.title: Alert handling
items.text:
Organization → Alert handling

Critical is Urgent (organization.critical_is_urgent, on) An Alert Group whose Severity level is critical is Urgent. See Loud and Quiet. Instance labels (organization.instance_labels, pod, instance, container, endpoint) A new Alert that differs from a firing one only in these labels is a Replacement: it stays in the same Alert Group, and the Timeline names the label that changed.

Changes to Severity levels and Instance labels apply to Alerts evaluated from then on. Open Alert Groups keep their status.

  1. Open Organization → Alert handling.

  2. Turn Critical is Urgent on or off, and change the Instance labels: Add label adds one, the × next to a label removes it. Select Save.

items.title: Security
items.text:
Organization → Security

TOTP required (organization.totp_required, Nobody) Nobody, Local users (Users who sign in with a password) or Everyone (OIDC users too). A person the policy covers who has no TOTP sets it up right after their next sign-in. See TOTP. Token grace for OIDC users without an offline token (auth.oidc_token_grace, 7 days) Applies to Users who sign in through OpenID Connect when the identity provider granted no offline token. Their Personal access tokens work while their last OIDC sign-in is no older than this; after that they get 401 with the code oidc_recheck_required until the person signs in through OIDC again. Service account tokens are not affected. See API tokens and automation.
  1. Open Organization → Security.

  2. Choose who must have TOTP under TOTP required, and change the Token grace for OIDC users without an offline token (days). Select Save.

items.title: Outbound addresses
items.text:
Organization → Outbound addresses

The Outbound address policy (organization.outbound_policy) says which network addresses Muster may call: Destinations, Connections, the identity provider, proxies and the outgoing heartbeat. The check runs after the name is resolved, so a name that points at a blocked address is blocked.

  • Standard (the default) allows private addresses and blocks loopback.
  • Strict allows only public addresses and the entries you allow.

Allowed and Denied (organization.outbound_allowed, organization.outbound_denied, both empty) take a network such as 10.0.0.0/8, an address, a host name or a domain such as *.example.org. A denied entry always wins. Some addresses are always blocked and no allowed entry opens them: link-local, cloud metadata, unspecified and multicast addresses. A chat server on the loopback address, for one, needs 127.0.0.0/8 in Allowed under Standard.

  1. Open Organization → Outbound addresses.

  2. Choose the Outbound address policy. Add entries with Add allowed entry and Add denied entry, and remove one with the × next to it. Select Save.

The screenshot is of a development installation, whose test chat servers listen on the loopback address.

items.title: Retention
items.text:
Organization → Retention

Stored Snapshots (days) (retention.stored_snapshots, 14) Snapshots kept as received, for debugging, previews and replay. Alert details (days) (retention.alert_details, 90) Alerts inside Alert Groups, Timeline entries and delivery events. Never Notes. Alert Group summaries (days) (retention.alert_group_summaries, 730) The summary row of an Alert Group, with its Notes. Audit log (days) (retention.audit_log, 365) Who changed or did what.

Each period is 1 to 36,500 days. The summaries must be kept at least as long as the details, because details go first; a save that breaks this is refused (retention_order).

  1. Open Organization → Retention.

  2. Enter the number of days of each period and select Save.

items.title: Audit log
items.text:
Organization → Audit log (Admins only) records who changed or did what, newest first, for the last 7 days by default: the time, the actor with the token or the Transport it acted through, the action, the resource and the changes with their values before and after. Secrets show only that they changed. Entries are kept for retention.audit_log days, as Retention sets.

  1. Open Organization → Audit log.

  2. Narrow it with the filters: From and To, the Actor, the Action, such as organization.updated, and the Resource type, such as organization; select Apply, and Clear filters to see everything again. The filters are kept in the address, so a link to a filtered list can be shared.

  3. Read the changes of an entry in its Changes: each field with its value before and after.

items.title: Elsewhere
items.text: Other Organization pages have their own guides: Keyring in Key rotation, Outgoing heartbeat (outgoing_heartbeat.url, unset) in Outgoing heartbeat, Lookup tables and Link rules in Messages and templates, and System status in Monitoring.

items.title: The API
items.text: GET /api/v1/organization reads the Organization and its ETag; PUT /api/v1/organization replaces the fields above with If-Match set to that ETag, as API tokens and automation shows. The fields are name, time_zone, workday_start, week_start, severity_label, severity_mapping, severity_styles, critical_is_urgent, instance_labels, outgoing_heartbeat (required, with proxy, whose enabled is required; url is write-only and kept when omitted), retention (stored_snapshots_days, alert_details_days, alert_group_summaries_days, audit_log_days), totp_required (nobody, local_users or everyone) and oidc_token_grace_seconds. The outbound policy is GET and PUT /api/v1/organization/outbound-policy, and the values seen are GET /api/v1/organization/severity-values. Reading the Organization needs any sign-in; reading the outbound policy and the values seen needs organization:read, and changing anything needs organization:write; only the Admin Role holds both. workday_start and week_start are optional on an update.

items.title: The database
items.text: Muster keeps everything in PostgreSQL 14 or newer, and nothing else stateful: no Redis and no queue. At start Muster refuses an older PostgreSQL and stops with an error that names the cause. It needs one extension, pg_trgm, which ships with PostgreSQL and which the database owner can create (a trusted extension since PostgreSQL 13); the first migration creates it. Neither the Helm chart nor the compose example backs up the database: see Backup and restore, and keep the master key apart from the backups.

items.title: As a URL or as fields
items.text:
Give the database to Muster in one of two forms. The settings are in the environment reference.

A URL MUSTER_DATABASE_URL, such as postgres://muster:<password>@db.example.org:5432/muster?sslmode=require Fields MUSTER_DATABASE_HOST, MUSTER_DATABASE_PORT (default 5432), MUSTER_DATABASE_NAME, MUSTER_DATABASE_USER, MUSTER_DATABASE_PASSWORD or MUSTER_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE, MUSTER_DATABASE_SSLMODE (default prefer)

When both forms are set, the URL wins and Muster logs a warning that names both. Muster ignores every PG* variable, such as PGHOST, PGSSLMODE, PGSSLROOTCERT, PGOPTIONS and PGPASSFILE, and the password file ~/.pgpass. Give any other libpq setting as a parameter of the URL instead, such as sslrootcert, options or target_session_attrs. Percent-encode the values as libpq requires, = as %3D and a space as %20, for example options=-c%20search_path%3Dmuster. A URL that libpq rejects stops Muster at start with an error that names the parameter; the URL in the error includes the sslmode that Muster appends when the URL names none. Only libpq's default certificate files still apply when the URL names none: ~/.postgresql/root.crt, and ~/.postgresql/postgresql.crt with postgresql.key; these are files, not variables, and the Muster image has none. Any secret can come from a *_FILE variable.

Prefer the fields when the host, user and name are plain values and only the password is a secret: the Helm chart does exactly that, with database.host, database.port, database.name, database.user and database.sslmode as values and the password from a key of the Secret as MUSTER_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE. Use the URL when you need a setting that has no field, such as pool_max_conns or sslrootcert; in the chart, database.urlKey names the key of the Secret that holds the whole URL, and the field values are then ignored.

A replica's main pool holds max(10, CPUs) connections unless the URL sets pool_max_conns. The pool_* parameters size the main pool only: a session connection derived from the URL drops them, and one given by MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_URL ignores them. On top of that, each replica keeps about three session connections (see PgBouncer). Size max_connections of PostgreSQL for all replicas together.

Create the database and its user before the first start. The user owns the database, because Muster creates its tables, indexes and partitions itself:

CREATE ROLE muster LOGIN PASSWORD '<password>';
CREATE DATABASE muster OWNER muster;

Muster applies its migrations at the first start: the compose example sets MUSTER_MIGRATE_ON_START, and the chart runs muster migrate in an init container.

items.title: CloudNativePG
items.text:
CloudNativePG runs PostgreSQL clusters on Kubernetes. A Cluster for Muster creates the database and its owner:

apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: muster-db
  namespace: muster
spec:
  instances: 3
  storage:
    size: 10Gi
  bootstrap:
    initdb:
      database: muster
      owner: muster

CloudNativePG serves the primary at the Service muster-db-rw (and the replicas read-only at muster-db-ro) and enables TLS on its own. It generates the password and keeps it in the Secret muster-db-app, with the keys username, password, host, port, dbname and uri among others. The chart reads the database from that Secret when you name it in database.existingSecret; the Secret muster of Install with Helm then holds only the master keys and the password of the first Admin:

existingSecret: muster
database:
  existingSecret: muster-db-app
  urlKey: uri

The uri key holds a URL such as postgresql://muster:<password>@muster-db-rw.muster:5432/muster. It names no sslmode, so Muster connects with its default, prefer, which uses the TLS of CloudNativePG but does not insist on it. To require TLS, give the connection as fields and take only the password from the Secret, which also keeps the password out of the pod's environment:

existingSecret: muster
database:
  existingSecret: muster-db-app
  host: muster-db-rw.muster.svc
  name: muster
  user: muster
  sslmode: require
  passwordKey: password

When you give the Cluster a Secret of your own under bootstrap.initdb.secret, CloudNativePG generates no muster-db-app, and your Secret holds no uri: use the fields form above, with your Secret in database.existingSecret and passwordKey: password.

Add an spec.backup section to the Cluster (see the CloudNativePG documentation) and test a restore, together with the master key, before you rely on it.

items.title: Managed PostgreSQL
items.text:
A managed PostgreSQL service works when it offers version 14 or newer and a role that owns an empty database. Check:

  • Version. PostgreSQL 14 or newer. Muster is tested on 14 and 17.
  • Extensions. Only pg_trgm; allow it where the service keeps an allow-list of extensions. Muster does not use pg_partman; it creates its partitions itself.
  • Session features. Muster needs session advisory locks and LISTEN/NOTIFY. Plain endpoints of managed services provide them. A pooler endpoint that your provider adds in transaction mode does not: see PgBouncer.
  • Failover. Name the endpoint that follows the primary, not an instance.
  • TLS. Most services require it. Set sslmode as below.
  • Connections. Check the connection limit of the plan against the pool sizes above.

Run muster doctor against the database after you set it up. It checks the version, the session features, the pooler mode and whether each connection is encrypted.

items.title: PgBouncer
items.text:
Muster uses two kinds of database connections:

  • The main connection carries every query. It may go through PgBouncer in transaction mode.
  • The session connection carries what needs a real session: the advisory lock of the Leader, the LISTEN connection that wakes the workers and feeds live updates to the web UI, partition maintenance and the migrations. A transaction pooler would lose their session state between statements.

Without a separate setting, the session connection is the main connection. At start, Muster takes an advisory lock over it and completes a LISTEN/NOTIFY round trip. Behind a transaction pooler this fails within five seconds, and Muster stops with an error that names MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_URL.

So when the main connection goes through PgBouncer in transaction mode, give Muster a session connection that reaches PostgreSQL directly or through a pooler in session mode:

MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_URL A whole URL for the session connection. MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_HOST MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_PORT Only the host and the port; the user, password, database, sslmode and the other parameters are those of the main connection, without its pool_* parameters.

In the chart, these are database.sessionHost and database.sessionPort. With CloudNativePG, the main connection can use a Pooler object in transaction mode, whose Service takes the Pooler's name, here muster-db-pooler-rw, and the session connection the -rw Service of the Cluster:

database:
  host: muster-db-pooler-rw.muster.svc
  sessionHost: muster-db-rw.muster.svc
  sessionPort: 5432

PgBouncer 1.21 or newer

Muster's driver uses prepared statements on the main connection. In transaction mode, PgBouncer supports them from version 1.21, and only when max_prepared_statements is above 0. An older PgBouncer, or a value of 0, makes queries fail with errors about missing prepared statements. Set max_prepared_statements to a few hundred, such as 200. A pooler in session mode, or no pooler, needs no such setting.

PgBouncer is optional. Most installations connect straight to PostgreSQL, and then no session setting is needed.

items.title: TLS
items.text:
MUSTER_DATABASE_SSLMODE (or sslmode in the URL) takes the values of PostgreSQL's client library:

disable encrypts: never · checks the server: nothing allow encrypts: only when the server insists · checks the server: nothing prefer (default) encrypts: when the server offers TLS, else falls back to plain text · checks the server: nothing require encrypts: always · checks the server: nothing: protects against listening in, not against an impostor verify-ca encrypts: always · checks the server: the certificate chain against a trusted CA verify-full encrypts: always · checks the server: the chain, and that the certificate names the host you connect to

prefer makes a fresh installation work, but it also connects without encryption to a server that has none. Muster tells you: muster doctor reports each connection as encrypted or not, and a start with an unencrypted connection logs a warning. For anything but a single machine, set require at least, and verify-full where you can: the certificate then proves that the server is yours.

verify-ca and verify-full check against the file named by sslrootcert in MUSTER_DATABASE_URL, which must exist in the container; without it, against ~/.postgresql/root.crt when that file exists, and otherwise against the root certificates of the system. The fields form has no such setting. With MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_HOST and MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_PORT, the session connection takes the sslmode of the main connection; a MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_URL carries its own, prefer when it names none.

items.title: Install with Helm
items.text:
The Helm chart runs Muster on Kubernetes 1.30 or newer. It deploys Muster and its Services, and optionally an Ingress or Gateway API routes, a PodDisruptionBudget, a ServiceMonitor, a NetworkPolicy, alert rules and a dashboard. It does not include PostgreSQL: Muster takes an external database. For a first try on one machine, use the Quick start with Docker Compose instead.

flowchart LR
  browser["Browser"] -- "muster.example.org" --> app["app Service, 8080"]
  am["Alertmanager"] -- "ingest.example.org" --> ingest["ingest Service, 8081"]
  app --> pod["Muster pods"]
  ingest --> pod
  pod --> pg["PostgreSQL"]
  prom["Prometheus"] -- "/metrics" --> internal["internal Service, 8082"]
  internal --> pod

items.title: Get the chart
items.text:
Each release publishes the chart as an OCI artifact in the registry of the image:

helm install muster oci://ghcr.io/muster-io/charts/muster --version <version> \
  --namespace muster --create-namespace -f values.yaml

<version> is a Muster release without the v, such as 0.1.0 for the release v0.1.0. The chart's appVersion is the release's tag, and image.tag defaults to it, so each chart runs the image of its own release.

The release signs the chart with cosign, keyless, as it signs the image; Verify a release shows how to check the signature before you install. Artifact Hub lists the released versions of the chart, each with its changes and the image it runs, pinned by digest: Muster on Artifact Hub.

items.title: Create the Secret
items.text:
The chart never generates the master keys. Create a Secret yourself and name it in existingSecret; rendering fails without it. The Secret holds, under the key names that the values masterKeysKey, database.passwordKey and bootstrapAdmin.passwordKey name:

secret-keys

the default of masterKeysKey

Holds the master key of the Keyring, as openssl rand -base64 32 prints it.

database-password

the default of database.passwordKey

Holds the password of the database user, unless database.existingSecret names another Secret for it.

bootstrap-password

no default; set bootstrapAdmin.passwordKey

Holds the password of the first Admin.

kubectl create namespace muster
kubectl -n muster create secret generic muster \
  --from-literal=secret-keys="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  --from-literal=database-password='<the database password>' \
  --from-literal=bootstrap-password="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"

The pods mount the Secret as files and read the values through MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS_FILE, MUSTER_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE and MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE, so no secret appears in the pod's environment, except the whole database URL when you name its key in database.urlKey.

When another operator keeps the database credentials in a Secret of its own, name that Secret in database.existingSecret instead of copying the password: database.passwordKey and database.urlKey then name keys of that Secret, and the master keys and the password of the first Admin stay in existingSecret. For the Secret muster-db-app that CloudNativePG generates:

existingSecret: muster
database:
  existingSecret: muster-db-app
  urlKey: uri

The database shows the form with sslmode.

Keep a copy of the master key

Muster refuses to start on a database without the key that wrote it, and a restored database is useless without it. Keep a copy apart from the database backups: see Backup and restore.

A tool that manages Secrets, such as External Secrets or Sealed Secrets, works the same way: it only has to produce a Secret of that name with those keys.

items.title: Ship the Secret's source in the release
items.text:
With GitOps tools such as Argo CD or Flux, the object that produces the Secret can be part of the same release: extraObjects takes a list of extra manifests, and the chart renders each as a document of its own. An item is a map or a string that holds a YAML manifest; both go through tpl, so a manifest can name .Values and .Release and keeps the key names in one place. An ExternalSecret of External Secrets Operator that fills the Secret from a secret store:

existingSecret: muster

bootstrapAdmin:
  email: admin@example.org
  passwordKey: bootstrap-password

extraObjects:
  - apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
    kind: ExternalSecret
    metadata:
      name: '{{ .Values.existingSecret }}'
    spec:
      refreshInterval: 1h
      secretStoreRef: { kind: ClusterSecretStore, name: vault }
      target: { name: '{{ .Values.existingSecret }}' }
      data:
        - secretKey: '{{ .Values.masterKeysKey }}'
          remoteRef: { key: muster/keys, property: secret-keys }
        - secretKey: '{{ .Values.bootstrapAdmin.passwordKey }}'
          remoteRef: { key: muster/keys, property: bootstrap-password }
        - secretKey: '{{ .Values.database.passwordKey }}'
          remoteRef: { key: muster/database, property: password }

Quote a value that is only a template, as above, so that the item stays valid YAML. bootstrapAdmin.passwordKey has no default, so set it before naming it. With database.existingSecret, the database password comes from that Secret instead, and its line is left out.

tpl renders every {{ of an item, so one meant for another tool, such as the template of an ExternalSecret, is escaped as {{ `{{ .password | urlquery }}` }}; unescaped, it renders empty. Write the strings inside {{ }} with backticks, not double quotes: the chart writes a map item back as YAML before tpl runs, which breaks a line longer than 80 characters at a space, and a backtick string may span that break, which YAML then joins again, while a double-quoted string fails with unterminated quoted string. A string item is used as it is written.

With database.urlKey, a key named {{ .Values.database.urlKey }} takes the place of the passwordKey line, for example a database URL that External Secrets Operator builds from the password, which urlquery encodes for the URL. Add it to the values above, with existingSecret and bootstrapAdmin, in place of their extraObjects:

database:
  urlKey: database-url

extraObjects:
  - apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
    kind: ExternalSecret
    metadata:
      name: '{{ .Values.existingSecret }}'
    spec:
      refreshInterval: 1h
      secretStoreRef: { kind: ClusterSecretStore, name: vault }
      target:
        name: '{{ .Values.existingSecret }}'
        template:
          mergePolicy: Merge
          data:
            '{{ .Values.database.urlKey }}': 'postgresql://muster:{{ `{{ .password | urlquery }}` }}@muster-db-rw.muster.svc:5432/muster?sslmode=require'
      data:
        - secretKey: '{{ .Values.masterKeysKey }}'
          remoteRef: { key: muster/keys, property: secret-keys }
        - secretKey: '{{ .Values.bootstrapAdmin.passwordKey }}'
          remoteRef: { key: muster/keys, property: bootstrap-password }
        - secretKey: password
          remoteRef: { key: muster/database, property: password }

On the first install the pods wait in Init:0/1, with FailedMount events, until External Secrets Operator has created the Secret; this is normal, and they start once it exists. A SealedSecret works the same way; a string item suits it, since the encrypted data is pasted as it is:

extraObjects:
  - |
    apiVersion: bitnami.com/v1alpha1
    kind: SealedSecret
    metadata:
      name: {{ .Values.existingSecret }}
    spec:
      encryptedData:
        secret-keys: <the output of kubeseal>
        database-password: <the output of kubeseal>
        bootstrap-password: <the output of kubeseal>

items.title: Values
items.text:
A short values.yaml for an installation with an Ingress and an external database:

existingSecret: muster

database:
  host: muster-db-rw.muster.svc
  name: muster
  user: muster
  sslmode: require

publicURL: https://muster.example.org
ingestURL: https://ingest.example.org

bootstrapAdmin:
  email: admin@example.org
  passwordKey: bootstrap-password

replicas: 2
podDisruptionBudget:
  enabled: true

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  app:
    hosts:
      - host: muster.example.org
    tls:
      - secretName: muster-tls
        hosts: [muster.example.org]
  ingest:
    hosts:
      - host: ingest.example.org
    tls:
      - secretName: muster-ingest-tls
        hosts: [ingest.example.org]

publicURL is required: the chart renders without it, but Muster stops at start. The notes that helm install prints warn about a missing publicURL or a missing database. bootstrapAdmin creates the first Admin once; after the first Admin exists, Muster ignores it. Everything else about the installation — Connections, Integrations, Routes, people — is configuration in the database and changes in the web UI and the API, never in the chart.

The full list of values, with types and defaults, is the chart values reference. The chart rejects a value it does not know. Environment variables that have no value of their own go into extraEnv; the environment reference lists them.

The chart sets MUSTER_MIGRATE_ON_START off and runs muster migrate in an init container instead, under a database lock, so that the pods of a rollout do not migrate at once. The pods run as a non-root user with a read-only root file system. The readiness probe checks only the database, and a startup probe gives a slow start up to five minutes.

items.title: The two public addresses
items.text:
Muster has two addresses that other systems use, and the chart takes both as values:

publicURL

environment variable: MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL

Used for people: the web UI, links in messages, the OIDC redirect.

ingestURL

environment variable: MUSTER_INGEST_URL

Used for machines: Alertmanager, Heartbeats, Mattermost button callbacks, the Telegram webhook, and the button presses of Slack Connections in the HTTP event mode.

ingestURL defaults to publicURL. Muster never derives either from an Ingress or a route: set them to the addresses that people and machines really use, or the links it builds will be wrong.

Muster serves ingestion on its own listener (8081) apart from the web UI and the API (8080), and the chart gives each a Service. A separate address for ingestion lets you expose the two differently: the web UI only inside the company network, and ingestion to Alertmanagers in other networks, or the other way round, with different TLS settings, rate limits and firewall rules on each. It also keeps a burst of Snapshots away from the web UI's address. When you have no such need, give both the same host name and send the paths /api/v1/ingest, /api/v1/heartbeat and /api/v1/callbacks/ (with everything below them) to the ingest Service and everything else to the app Service, as Connect Alertmanager describes.

The third listener, 8082, serves /health/live, /health/ready and /metrics. It has a Service and no Ingress or route; do not expose it outside the cluster.

items.title: Ingress
items.text: ingress.enabled creates two Ingress objects, one for the app Service and one for the ingest Service. List the hosts of each under ingress.app.hosts and ingress.ingest.hosts, with their tls blocks, and set ingress.className and ingress.annotations for your controller. A host takes an optional path (/ by default) and pathType (Prefix). Annotations apply to both Ingress objects. Set the body size limit of your controller to at least 16 MB for the ingest host, because Muster accepts Snapshots up to that size.

items.title: Gateway API
items.text:
httpRoute.enabled creates two HTTPRoute objects (gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1) instead of Ingress objects, one for each Service. Name the Gateway in httpRoute.parentRefs and the host names in httpRoute.app.hostnames and httpRoute.ingest.hostnames:

httpRoute:
  enabled: true
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
      namespace: gateway
  app:
    hostnames: [muster.example.org]
  ingest:
    hostnames: [ingest.example.org]

The chart does not create the Gateway and its certificates. The Gateway API resources must be installed in the cluster and the Gateway must accept routes from the namespace of Muster. Use ingress or httpRoute, not both.

items.title: Replicas and the PodDisruptionBudget
items.text:
replicas is 1 by default. All replicas are active: each serves the web UI and ingestion and works on the queues, and a Leader among them does the few jobs that must run only once. With more than one replica:

  • Set podDisruptionBudget.enabled to true. The budget allows one unavailable pod (maxUnavailable), so a node drain never takes all replicas down at once.
  • Spread the pods over nodes with topologySpreadConstraints or affinity.
  • If the main database connection goes through PgBouncer in transaction mode, set database.sessionHost (and sessionPort) to a session-capable endpoint. See the database.
  • Keep the clocks of all nodes in sync with NTP; Muster compares them with the database's clock and logs a warning on a skew, and the chart rule MusterClockSkew raises an alert.

Rolling updates run between adjacent minor versions only, and the init container of each new pod applies the database migrations before the pod starts. Take a backup first.

items.title: Watch Muster
items.text: serviceMonitor.enabled makes the Prometheus Operator scrape /metrics of the internal Service. alerting.prometheusRule.enabled or alerting.vmRule.enabled renders the alert rules, and dashboard.configMap.enabled or dashboard.grafanaDashboard.enabled the Grafana dashboard. The rules and the dashboard are reference material; the Runbooks explain each alert, and the metrics reference lists what Muster exports.

items.title: Requirements and tested versions
items.text:
What Muster needs, which versions it was checked against, how its own versions are numbered, and how to verify that a release you download is the one the project built. "Tested" means different things for different rows, so each row says which.

  • CI means an automated job that runs on the project's pull requests or nightly, and fails the build.
  • Development stand means a person ran the behaviour against a real server of that version and recorded what it did, but no job repeats it. These facts are the ground the messenger and Alertmanager features rest on; the fake servers that CI uses imitate them.

items.title: Requirements
items.text: PostgreSQL 14 or newer, directly or or through a pooler whose session connection is session-capable. Nothing else stateful: no Redis, no queue. See The database. Where Muster runs Binaries and container images for Linux; binaries also for macOS; both on amd64 and arm64. The container image is linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. The Quick start needs Docker with the Compose plugin. Kubernetes 1.30 or newer, for the Helm chart. A browser For the web UI, one that keeps a Secure cookie: over HTTPS, or on localhost. See Sign-in needs HTTPS or localhost.

items.title: Tested versions
items.text: PostgreSQL 14 and 17 in CI: make test-integration runs the integration tests on both, in containers, on every pull request. The compose example and the development database run PostgreSQL 17. Kubernetes and Helm Kubernetes 1.33.0 in CI: make helm-check lints the chart, renders it with the values files of the repository and validates the result strictly against the schemas of 1.33.0. Helm v4.3.0 does the rendering, and also packages the chart for a release. Nothing is run in a cluster by CI, and other versions from 1.30 are not checked. Alertmanager v0.34.1 on a development stand, with Prometheus v3.15.0 and vmalert v1.153.0: how it repeats, groups, restarts and truncates is measured there. Other versions of Alertmanager send the same webhook; if one behaves differently, the Snapshot semantics page and the Heartbeat are how you notice. Grafana OSS 13.2.4 on a development stand, as one instance on SQLite and as a pair of replicas on PostgreSQL 17, through the webhook contact point of its built-in Alertmanager. See Connect Grafana. Mattermost 11.2.2, a test server on the development stand, through REST API v4 with a bot account. CI runs the same behaviour against a fake Mattermost server. See Mattermost. Slack Slack's cloud Web API and Socket Mode, on a development stand: a free workspace with a test app and a test channel. CI runs against a fake. See Slack. Telegram The cloud Bot API 10.3, on a development stand, with a test bot and a test channel. CI runs against a fake. See Telegram. The web UI Its component tests and its end-to-end tests run in Chromium in CI. Other browsers are not tested.

items.title: Version numbers
items.text:
Muster's versions are 0.N.x, and 1.0 is a long way off.

  • 0.N is layer N of the roadmap. L1, Alert Groups in messengers, is released as 0.1.x; L2 will be 0.2.x, L3 0.3.x, and so on. Layer N+1 starts with the release 0.(N+1).0, which the maintainers set with release-please's release-as.
  • 0.N.x releases bring fixes and small changes, and nothing that breaks an installation: settings, the API under /api/v1 and the database keep working without a change on your side.
  • Breaking changes come only with the next layer's minor version, and its release notes say what to change before you upgrade. See Upgrades for how to upgrade.

items.title: Upgrade notes
items.text: 0.1.1 Migration 0020 is expand only: it adds the column oidc_settings.groups_claim_seen_at, and replicas of 0.1.0 that are already running keep working on it during a rolling update. 0.1.0 refuses to start on schema 20, so going back to 0.1.0 needs the database backup taken before the upgrade, as Upgrades describes.

items.title: Image tags
items.text:
The images are ghcr.io/muster-io/muster and the tags are:

  • vX.Y.Z: a release. Use it, so that an upgrade is a decision you make.
  • latest: the newest release that is not a prerelease. A prerelease tag, such as v1.4.0-rc.1, never moves it.
  • edge: the newest commit on master, a development image.
  • sha-<7 hex digits>: the development image of one commit.

items.title: Verify a release
items.text:
A release is built by the workflow release.yml of the repository, on a tag vX.Y.Z. It signs the container image and the Helm chart with cosign, keyless, with the identity of that workflow run, so a valid signature proves that the image or the chart was built by that workflow on that tag. The development images, edge and sha-…, are not signed and carry no SBOM attestation: the workflow that builds them skips signing. Install cosign v3 or newer (the release signs with v3.1.3, in the new signature format), then verify the image:

VERSION=vX.Y.Z
cosign verify ghcr.io/muster-io/muster:$VERSION \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/muster-io/muster/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/$VERSION" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

It prints the verified signature and exits 0. To accept any release tag, replace --certificate-identity with --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/muster-io/muster/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v'. The signature covers the multi-architecture index and the image of each platform. To pin what you run, deploy the digest you verified, ghcr.io/muster-io/muster@sha256:…, rather than the tag.

The Helm chart is signed the same way, by the same workflow run. Its tag is the version without the v:

VERSION=vX.Y.Z
cosign verify ghcr.io/muster-io/charts/muster:${VERSION#v} \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/muster-io/muster/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/$VERSION" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

To install exactly the chart you verified, verify it by its digest and install by the same digest. helm pull prints the digest as Digest: sha256:…:

helm pull oci://ghcr.io/muster-io/charts/muster --version ${VERSION#v}
cosign verify ghcr.io/muster-io/charts/muster@sha256:… \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/muster-io/muster/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/$VERSION" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
helm install muster oci://ghcr.io/muster-io/charts/muster@sha256:… \
  --namespace muster --create-namespace -f values.yaml

The SBOM of the image is an attestation that BuildKit attaches when the image is pushed, not a cosign attestation. Read it with Docker:

docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/muster-io/muster:$VERSION --format '{{ json .SBOM }}'

It prints the software bill of materials, one per platform.

The archives are attached to the GitHub release: muster_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz for Linux and macOS on amd64 and arm64, checksums.txt with their SHA-256 sums, and one SPDX JSON software bill of materials per archive. Download the archive and checksums.txt into one directory and check it:

sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt

On macOS use shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing. checksums.txt is not signed: it finds a broken or swapped download from the same release, not a swapped release. For that, verify the image.

items.title: Connect Alertmanager
items.text:
Muster receives alerts from Alertmanager through an Alertmanager receiver with a webhook. Each delivery is a Snapshot of one Alertmanager group: every alert of the Alertmanager group that still fires, and its resolves. Muster stores each request exactly as received, answers 202 once it is written, and processes it afterwards.

In the examples, MUSTER_INGEST_URL is https://ingest.muster.example.org.

items.title: One Integration per Alertmanager cluster
items.text:
Create one Integration for each Alertmanager cluster that sends to Muster. An HA pair — two or more Alertmanager instances that gossip with each other — is one cluster and gets one Integration: both instances send the same notifications, and Muster folds their copies together within the Integration's duplicate window. Two independent Alertmanagers, such as one per region, get one Integration each, so that each has its own repeats, its own Static labels and its own health.

Static labels are added to every alert of the Integration before routing, for example cluster=prod-eu, so that Routes and messages can tell the clusters apart.

Alertmanager pushes its Snapshots to Muster by webhook: the Integration's connection mode is webhook-only (integration.connection_mode), the only mode in this version.

items.title: Create a token and paste the snippet
items.text:
1. In Muster, open Integrations and select Create integration. Enter a Name after the Alertmanager cluster, such as prod-eu, and add its Static labels with Add label, such as cluster=prod-eu. Keep the Duplicate window of 45 seconds. Select Create.

  2. On the Integration page, select Create token, give the token a Name if you like, such as alertmanager, and select Create. Muster shows the token and a ready Alertmanager snippet, the Alertmanager configuration, once; copy it with Copy before you select Done. Only a hash of the token is kept, so a lost token cannot be shown again: create a new one.

  3. Paste the snippet into the Alertmanager configuration, as the rest of this section explains, and reload Alertmanager.

The snippet has two parts. The Alertmanager receiver goes into receivers:

receivers:
  - name: muster-prod-eu
    webhook_configs:
      - url: https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/ingest
        send_resolved: true
        max_alerts: 0
        http_config:
          authorization:
            type: Bearer
            credentials: mstr_int_…
  • send_resolved: true sends resolves, which close alerts in Muster at once.
  • max_alerts: 0 sends every alert of the Alertmanager group. Muster treats each Snapshot as the whole Alertmanager group; a Truncated Snapshot makes it warn.
  • The token travels as Authorization: Bearer. A sender that cannot set a header may append the token to the URL instead, as /api/v1/ingest/<token>; Muster's logs name only the route, never such a path.

The route goes first under the top-level route, before your other child routes:

route:
  routes:
    - receiver: muster-prod-eu
      continue: true
      repeat_interval: 10m
    # ... your existing child routes
    # The last child route: a catch-all without matchers for the receiver of the top-level route.
    # - receiver: <your default receiver>
  • With no matchers, the route takes every alert, and continue: true passes each alert on to the child routes after it, so Muster runs beside your current Alertmanager receivers while you try it.
  • Keep a catch-all child route last. Alertmanager sends an alert to the receiver of the top-level route only when no child route matches it. The Muster route matches every alert, so without a catch-all, an alert that none of your other child routes matches goes to Muster alone and your default receiver stops getting it. Add a last child route without matchers for your default receiver, or make sure an existing later child route already catches everything.

For example, a configuration that sends critical alerts to oncall and everything else to the top-level default:

route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - receiver: oncall
