      matchers: ['severity="critical"']

becomes:

route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - receiver: muster-prod-eu
      continue: true
      repeat_interval: 10m
    - receiver: oncall
      matchers: ['severity="critical"']
    - receiver: default

A critical alert goes to muster-prod-eu and oncall, any other alert to muster-prod-eu and default. Without the last line, a warning would reach only Muster. amtool config routes test --config.file=alertmanager.yml severity=warning prints the receivers an alert reaches; it should list Muster and your default receiver.

  • Keep repeat_interval between 5 and 15 minutes (10 minutes in the snippet, snippet.repeat_interval). See Repeat intervals for why.

Reload Alertmanager (POST /-/reload or SIGHUP). The Integration page then shows the time of the last Snapshot and the Stored Snapshots as received. In the screenshots, the addresses start with http://localhost:8081, the ingest address of a development installation; yours start with your MUSTER_INGEST_URL.

Further down, Stored Snapshots lists each Snapshot as received, newest first, with its group key and its state; select one to see its body.

items.title: Repeat intervals
items.text:
Keep the repeat_interval of the route that sends to Muster between 5 and 15 minutes. It is a setting of the route, not of the receiver, so a route that sends only some alerts to Muster can have its own.

Muster learns from the repeats. An Alertmanager group sends a Snapshot again each time repeat_interval elapses, and Muster measures the gaps between those Snapshots. Two rules depend on them:

  • An Alert is Gone when at least two consecutive Snapshots of its Alertmanager group, and at least processing.gone_min_absence (5 minutes), do not list it any more. This is how Muster notices an alert that Alertmanager dropped without a resolved notification.
  • An Alert goes Stale when its Alertmanager group sends no Snapshot at all for processing.stale_after_factor (3) times the learned repeat interval, for example when the group is silenced in Alertmanager. It applies only while the Integration's Heartbeat is live. Until Muster has learned the interval, it waits processing.stale_after_unlearned (25 hours).

Alertmanager sends a repeat on the first group_interval tick after repeat_interval has elapsed, so the gaps are about repeat_interval + group_interval. With 10 minutes and Alertmanager's default group_interval of 5 minutes, Muster learns an interval of about 15 minutes, and an Alert of a silenced group goes Stale after about 45 minutes. With a daily interval it takes more than three days, and the Integration page warns about an interval longer than processing.long_repeat_warning (1 hour) and shows the route to put in Alertmanager. A short interval does not make Muster noisy: Muster sends one message per Alert Group and edits it, so a repeat changes nothing that people see. It only makes Muster faster to notice that an alert is gone.

The routes Muster has learned, with their intervals and the time each needs to resolve by absence, are on the Integration page.

items.title: Send every alert of the group
items.text: Set max_alerts: 0 on the webhook configuration, as the snippet does. Alertmanager's default is no limit, but a max_alerts above 0 makes it keep only the first alerts of a group in each notification and count the rest in truncatedAlerts. A truncated Snapshot lists only part of the Alertmanager group, so Muster cannot tell an alert that is missing from one that was cut off. It never takes a truncated Snapshot as proof of absence: it keeps the unlisted Alerts firing as long as Snapshots of that group keep arriving, which can keep a resolved Alert open. It raises the Internal alert MusterSnapshotTruncated for the Integration and counts the Snapshot in muster_ingest_truncated_snapshots_total. If you see that alert, set max_alerts: 0 on the receiver and reload Alertmanager; the runbook has the steps.

items.title: Static labels
items.text:
Static labels belong to the Integration, not to Alertmanager. Add them in the Integration's settings, such as cluster=prod-eu; Muster adds them to every Alert of the Integration before it routes the Alert, so a Route and a Group key can use them as if the rules had set them.

  1. Open the Integration and select Edit, or set them in the form of a new Integration.

  2. Under Static labels, select Add label and enter the label's name and value, one label per row; Remove label takes a row away. Select Save.

  3. Use them for what the Alertmanager cluster knows and the rules do not: the cluster, the region, the environment. The default Group key of a Route includes cluster, so Alert Groups of different clusters stay apart.

  4. An Alert that already has the label keeps its own value. Muster then warns about the label on the Alert and in its Alert Group's Timeline, and the Alerts view of the Integration shows the warning. A Static label never overwrites a label that a rule set.

items.title: Instance labels in informational alerts
items.text:
Instance labels are the labels that change when the process that reports an Alert restarts, such as pod and instance. The Organization lists them in organization.instance_labels (by default pod, instance, container and endpoint).

Keep them out of informational alerts, the ones nobody needs to act on at once, such as those of a Route with the Informational profile. A restarted pod reports the same problem under a new pod label, which is a different Alert. Muster recognises that case: it records a Replacement, a Quiet event in the Timeline that names the label that differs, and the Alert Group page suggests fixing the rule. But every restart still adds an Alert and a Timeline entry to an Alert Group that was meant to be calm, and if the label is also in the Route's Group key, each pod gets an Alert Group of its own.

Aggregate the label away in the rule instead, for example sum without(pod, instance) (...) in the expression. Keep the label where it helps a person find the culprit, in an annotation rather than a label. For alerts about one particular pod that people must act on, Instance labels are fine: there each pod is a separate problem.

items.title: Start delay
items.text:
When Alertmanager starts, it does not know the alerts that were firing before. It learns them again as the rule evaluators (Prometheus, vmalert) send them, and until then its Alertmanager groups list only part of their alerts. A Snapshot sent in that time is partial, and Muster would take the missing alerts as Gone.

Set --dispatch.start-delay so that Alertmanager waits before it sends. It must be at least twice the longer of the rule evaluation interval and the rule evaluator's resend delay, plus a margin. Prometheus re-sends a firing alert only every second evaluation at its defaults, so with a 1-minute evaluation interval use about 2.5 minutes or more:

alertmanager --dispatch.start-delay=2m30s ...

With 90 seconds, the first Snapshot after a start was still partial in tests.

items.title: HA pairs need a persistent volume
items.text: Give every instance of an HA pair a persistent volume for its data directory (--storage.path). Without one, a restarted instance loses its silences and its notification log: it can notify silenced alerts and send partial Snapshots until the other instance catches it up.

items.title: Token rotation
items.text:
An Integration may hold several tokens. To rotate one without losing a webhook:

  1. Create a second token and paste its snippet (or only the new credentials) into the Alertmanager configuration.
  2. Reload Alertmanager and check that the token list shows a recent use of the new token.
  3. Revoke the old token. It is refused from the next request.

A request with a revoked token is refused with 401 and counted under the Integration in muster_ingest_requests_total{outcome="unauthorized"}, so the chart rule MusterIngestRejected shows an Alertmanager that still uses an old token.

items.title: Behind a reverse proxy
items.text:
Muster serves ingestion on its own listener, MUSTER_LISTEN_INGEST (:8081 by default), apart from the UI and API on MUSTER_LISTEN_APP. Set MUSTER_INGEST_URL to the address Alertmanager uses; it defaults to MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL, and the snippets are built from it.

With separate listeners, route /api/v1/ingest and /api/v1/heartbeat (with everything below them) to the ingest port. A reverse proxy that serves both on one host name, for example, sends these two paths to :8081 and everything else to :8080. Keep the proxy's body size limit at 16 MB or more: Muster accepts bodies up to ingest.body_limit (16 MB) and answers 413 above it. Do not let the proxy log request paths with the token, or prefer the Authorization header, which proxies do not log by default.

With one listener for both (MUSTER_LISTEN_INGEST equal to MUSTER_LISTEN_APP), the same port serves ingestion and the API.

items.title: What Muster answers
items.text:
Answer When Alertmanager 202 The body was stored, whatever it holds done 401 No token, an unknown or revoked token, a token of a deleted Integration, or an API token does not retry 413 The body is larger than 16 MB does not retry 500 The body could not be written retries

Muster never answers 400: a body that is not JSON, or not an Alertmanager payload, is stored and fails later in processing, where the Stored Snapshot shows the error.

items.title: Connect Grafana
items.text:
Grafana Alerting reaches Muster in one of two ways: directly, from Grafana's built-in Alertmanager through a webhook contact point, or through an external Alertmanager that Grafana forwards its alerts to. Both carry Grafana-managed alert rules.

flowchart LR
  rules["Grafana alert rules"] --> builtin["Grafana's built-in Alertmanager"]
  builtin -- "Snapshots, webhook contact point" --> direct["Muster Integration for Grafana"]
  rules -. "alerts" .-> am["External Alertmanager"]
  prom["Prometheus rules"] -- "alerts" --> am
  am -- "Snapshots" --> shared["Muster Integration for the Alertmanager"]
  • Directly needs nothing between Grafana and Muster. Grafana's built-in Alertmanager sends Alertmanager's webhook format with a few fields of its own, and Muster reads each notification as a Snapshot, as from any Alertmanager.
  • Through an external Alertmanager suits you when you already run an Alertmanager for Prometheus rules and want one Integration in Muster for both.

In the examples, MUSTER_INGEST_URL is https://ingest.muster.example.org. Muster was tested with Grafana OSS 13.2.4, as a single instance and as an HA pair.

items.title: Connect Grafana directly
items.text: The steps, in this order: create an Integration and its token in Muster, create a webhook contact point in Grafana, and send the alerts to it with a notification policy.

items.title: One Integration per Grafana cluster and organization
items.text:
Create one Integration for each Grafana cluster, and for each Grafana organization in it, that sends to Muster.

  • An HA pair — two or more Grafana replicas that share a database and gossip with each other — is one cluster and gets one Integration. See HA pairs.
  • Each Grafana organization gets an Integration of its own. The groupKey of a Snapshot names the notification policy and the group, not the organization, so two organizations with the same notification policies send the same groupKeys, and one Integration would take their Snapshots for one Alertmanager group.
  • Give the Integration Static labels for what the rules do not say, such as cluster=prod-eu.

items.title: Create the Integration and a token
items.text:
1. In Muster, open Integrations and select Create integration. Enter a Name, such as grafana-prod, and add the Static labels with Add label, such as cluster=prod-eu. Select Create.

  2. On the Integration page, select Create token, give the token a Name if you like, such as grafana, and select Create. Muster shows the token once, with a snippet for Alertmanager; Grafana needs only the Token (mstr_int_…), the credentials of that snippet. Copy it with Copy before you select Done.

  3. Create the contact point and the notification policy in Grafana, as the next two sections say. Once Grafana sends its first Snapshot, the Integration page shows it under Snapshots: the time of the last one and how many were received. In the screenshot, the address starts with http://localhost:8081, the ingest address of a development installation; yours starts with your MUSTER_INGEST_URL.

items.title: Create a webhook contact point
items.text:
In Grafana, open Alerting → Contact points → Add contact point and choose the integration Webhook:

  1. URL: the Integration's ingest URL, MUSTER_INGEST_URL followed by /api/v1/ingest: https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/ingest.
  2. HTTP Method: POST.
  3. Authorization header: the scheme Bearer, and the Integration token as its credentials.
  4. Max alerts: 0, the default, which sends every alert of the group. Muster treats each Snapshot as the whole Alertmanager group; see Limits.
  5. Disable resolved message: off, the default. Resolves close Alerts in Muster at once.
  6. No custom payload: Muster reads the payload that Grafana sends by default, and a custom one replaces it.

Check these names against the version of Grafana that you run, because the places of the settings in the interface change between versions. The same contact point in a provisioning file, together with the notification policy of the next step:

apiVersion: 1

contactPoints:
  - orgId: 1
    name: muster
    receivers:
      - uid: muster
        type: webhook
        disableResolveMessage: false
        settings:
          url: https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/ingest
          httpMethod: POST
          authorization_scheme: Bearer
          authorization_credentials: ${MUSTER_TOKEN}

policies:
  - orgId: 1
    receiver: muster
    group_by: [grafana_folder, alertname]
    repeat_interval: 10m

Grafana replaces ${MUSTER_TOKEN} with the variable of its environment when it reads the file, so the token stays out of the file. The file leaves out Max alerts (maxAlerts), so it is 0. Grafana does not let you edit resources provisioned from files in its interface, this contact point and the notification policy tree included: change the file, then restart Grafana or reload the provisioned files through its Admin API.

items.title: Send the alerts with a notification policy
items.text:
In Alerting → Notification policies, send the alerts to the contact point:

  • Keep Grafana's default grouping, group_by: [grafana_folder, alertname], and let Muster make Alert Groups with its Routes and Group keys. See Do not merge rules into one group.
  • Set repeat_interval between 5 and 15 minutes (10 minutes in the example). See Repeat intervals.
  • The example makes Muster the contact point of the default policy, which takes every alert. A provisioned policies entry is the whole notification policy tree of the organization and replaces the one set in the user interface. If Grafana also notifies other contact points, add Muster instead as the first nested policy, without matchers, with continue: true and its own repeat_interval, and keep a last nested policy for your default contact point, as for the Alertmanager route.
  • Grafana's built-in Alertmanager sends the notifications, so keep it receiving Grafana-managed alerts, the default in Alerting → Settings.

On its first start, Grafana applies provisioned policies within about a minute. Grafana sends the first Snapshot when an alert fires; the Integration page then shows the time of the last Snapshot and the Stored Snapshots as received, as in Create the Integration and a token.

items.title: Repeat intervals
items.text:
Repeats are how Muster learns when an alert is Gone or Stale, as with Alertmanager; see Repeat intervals. Grafana sends no notification_reason, so Muster recognises a repeat as a Snapshot identical to the one before it and learns the interval from those.

Grafana sends a repeat on the first group_interval tick after repeat_interval has elapsed. With 10 minutes and Grafana's default group_interval of 5 minutes, Muster learns an interval of about 15 minutes; with Grafana's default repeat_interval of 4 hours, an Alert of a silent group would go Stale only after more than 12 hours. Control the noise in Muster, not with a long interval: Muster sends one message per Alert Group and edits it, so a repeat changes nothing that people see.

items.title: Do not merge rules into one group
items.text:
Keep each Grafana notification group to the alerts of one rule, as the default grouping by grafana_folder and alertname does, and do not group many rules together, for example by a label that they share.

After a restart, Grafana knows the alerts of a rule again only once it has evaluated the rule. A group of rules with different evaluation intervals then sends Snapshots without the slower rules' alerts until their first evaluation: in a test, the alert of a rule evaluated every 8 minutes was missing from its group's Snapshots for about 7 minutes. Muster can take such an alert for Gone, and its return for a new firing, which is Loud. Grafana has no setting like Alertmanager's start delay. The alerts of one rule all return with its first evaluation, and Muster's Routes put them into Alert Groups as they would any other alerts.

items.title: Simplified routing
items.text: A contact point chosen in the rule itself (simplified routing) puts the label __grafana_route_settings_hash__, a hash of the rule's notification settings, into the route path of the groupKey. Editing those settings starts a new groupKey, and the old one falls silent, as when the matchers of an Alertmanager route change: an Alert that the new groupKey lists stays firing, and one that only the old groupKey listed resolves only by going Stale, which needs a live Heartbeat. Notification policies avoid this.

items.title: What Grafana sends
items.text:
• Every end of an alert is an explicit resolve: a value back under the threshold, a series that is missing for two evaluations, a paused rule and a deleted rule. Muster resolves the Alert at once, with the reason resolved. Grafana gives the resolve the annotation grafana_state_reason (MissingSeries, Paused or RuleDeleted); Muster takes annotations from firing alerts only, so that reason shows in the Stored Snapshot, not on the Alert.
  • NoData and Error are alerts of their own. A rule whose query returns no data, with the no-data state No Data, resolves its alert and fires an alert DatasourceNoData in a group of its own, with the label rulename (the rule's title), datasource_uid and ref_id beside the rule's labels. When data returns, the rule's alert fires again as a new firing and DatasourceNoData resolves. The error state Error gives an alert DatasourceError with the label rulename the same way, as Grafana documents it; it has not been tested with Muster. A Route can match both by alertname.
  • Links. The Source link of an Alert Group opens the rule's page in Grafana, the alert's generatorURL: <root_url>/alerting/grafana/<rule uid>/view?orgId=1. Set Grafana's root_url to the address people open. The built-in Link rule Explore builds its link from the Prometheus query of a generatorURL, which Grafana's does not have, so it makes no link for Grafana's alerts.

items.title: HA pairs
items.text:
An HA pair needs nothing more than its one Integration and one contact point. Normally one replica sends; when both do, Muster folds their copies together within the Integration's duplicate window.

The replicas evaluate the rules each on its own, so their copies of one alert can carry different startsAt. Muster takes the resolve of either replica: a resolve whose firing overlaps the current one resolves it (see Resolved). Such copies can also make Muster record a Quiet Continuation for an Alert once. Grafana's ha_single_node_evaluation, which makes one replica evaluate the rules for both, has not been tested with Muster.

items.title: Heartbeat
items.text:
The Heartbeat page's setup is for Alertmanager. The same idea in Grafana — an always-firing rule with a notification policy of its own, a repeat_interval of about one minute, and a second webhook contact point at the Integration's Heartbeat URL, https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/heartbeat, with resolved messages disabled — has not been verified with Grafana.

Without a Heartbeat, Muster never resolves an Alert as Stale: an Alert whose Grafana group stops sending altogether stays firing in Muster. Gone still works. A cron job that requests the Heartbeat URL keeps the Heartbeat live too, but it proves only the network: when Grafana itself stops, its groups fall silent and their Alerts go Stale.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• Truncation. With Max alerts above 0, a Snapshot lists only part of its group. Muster keeps the unlisted Alerts alive and raises the Internal alert MusterSnapshotTruncated (runbook). Grafana computes the status of a Snapshot from the alerts it lists, so a truncated Snapshot can say resolved while alerts it left out still fire; Muster recognises a Snapshot from Grafana by its top-level orgId, and a truncated status: resolved from Grafana resolves only the Alerts it lists as resolved. When a whole group resolves, its last Snapshot too lists only the first alerts, and Grafana sends nothing more for the group until one of its alerts fires again: the Alerts it left out stay firing in Muster until they go Stale, which needs a live Heartbeat. Set Max alerts to 0; for the Alerts already left firing, see the runbook.
  • The Integration page speaks of Alertmanager, the part that Grafana's built-in one plays. Its Alertmanager routes are Grafana's notification policies; its warning about a long repeat interval shows an Alertmanager route, where for Grafana you set the repeat_interval of the policy; its truncation warning names max_alerts, which is Max alerts in Grafana.
  • What Muster answers, Token rotation and Behind a reverse proxy apply to Grafana as they are.
  • Not tested with Muster: Grafana's retries of a webhook after an error or a timeout; Grafana's silences and mute timings; several Grafana organizations on one Integration; a custom payload; HMAC signing (Muster checks the Integration token only); ha_single_node_evaluation; DatasourceError; the Heartbeat through Grafana.

items.title: Connect Grafana through an external Alertmanager
items.text:
Grafana-managed alert rules can also reach Muster the same way as Prometheus rules do: Grafana forwards its alerts to an external Alertmanager, and that Alertmanager has the Muster receiver from Connect Alertmanager. One Alertmanager can serve Grafana and Prometheus together, with one Integration in Muster for the whole Alertmanager cluster.

Prefer this way when you already run an Alertmanager for Prometheus rules and want one Integration for both: the Heartbeat route of the Heartbeat page then watches the path of Grafana's alerts too.

items.title: Send Grafana's alerts to the Alertmanager
items.text:
In Grafana, two settings are needed, and both must be on.

  1. Add the Alertmanager as a data source: Connections → Data sources → Alertmanager. Set the Alertmanager Implementation (Prometheus, for a plain Alertmanager) and the HTTP URL, and turn on Receive Grafana Alerts.
  2. In Alerting → Settings (called Administration in some versions), enable that Alertmanager so that it shows that it receives Grafana-managed alerts.

From then on Grafana forwards all its Grafana-managed alerts to the Alertmanager. The same data source in a provisioning file, which covers step 1 only; step 2 is still done in Alerting → Settings:

apiVersion: 1

datasources:
  - name: Alertmanager
    type: alertmanager
    url: http://alertmanager.monitoring.svc:9093
    access: proxy
    jsonData:
      implementation: prometheus
      handleGrafanaManagedAlerts: true

The option in the user interface is Receive Grafana Alerts; its jsonData name is handleGrafanaManagedAlerts. The names above are those of the Grafana documentation of the Alertmanager data source; check the version of Grafana that you run, because the places of the settings in the interface change between versions.

Then follow Connect Alertmanager: create an Integration for the Alertmanager, paste the receiver and the route into its configuration, and keep the catch-all child route last.

items.title: Labels
items.text:
Grafana adds two labels of its own to every Grafana-managed alert: alertname, the name of the alert rule, and grafana_folder, the title of the folder that holds the rule. Labels that you set on the rule, such as severity or team, come with them. Route and Group key on these labels in Muster as on any others:

  • Set severity on your rules: it is part of the default Group key, and Routes can match it.
  • alertname is also part of the default Group key, so rules of different names make different Alert Groups.
  • Grafana rules have no cluster label of their own: add it to the Integration as a Static label. Through an Alertmanager shared with Prometheus, you can instead give Grafana's alerts an Integration of their own.
  • A rule on a query that returns one series per pod or instance makes one alert per series, with those labels. Keep Instance labels out of informational alerts; a Grafana rule can reduce the series to one with an aggregation.
  • Directly from Grafana, an Alert's fingerprint is the one in the body, which also covers the rule's hidden uid, so two rules with the same labels make two Alerts.

Muster shows the labels of each alert on the page of its Alert Group. If a label you expected is missing, open the Stored Snapshot on the Integration page, which shows the request as Grafana or the Alertmanager sent it.

items.title: Heartbeat
items.text:
A Heartbeat proves, for one Integration, that the path from your cluster to Muster works: Prometheus evaluates rules, Alertmanager sends notifications, and the network carries them to Muster. Alertmanager sends Muster a signal about once a minute; when the signals stop, Muster calls people. It is part of the recommended setup of every Integration.

In the examples, MUSTER_INGEST_URL is https://ingest.muster.example.org.

items.title: Why it matters
items.text:
Without a Heartbeat, a silent Alertmanager looks exactly like a healthy cluster with nothing to report. With one:

  • Muster notices when Alertmanager goes quiet. After the Heartbeat timeout without a signal, the Integration is Heartbeat lost and Muster raises the Internal alert MusterHeartbeatLost (severity critical). Its labels are integration (the Integration's id), integration_name and the Integration's Static labels, so a Route can send it to the team of that cluster.
  • Muster can resolve alerts as Stale. An Alertmanager group that is silenced, inhibited or muted as a whole sends nothing at all, not even its resolves, so Muster resolves its alerts once it has not seen them for three learned repeat intervals. It does that only while it knows that it would have heard from Alertmanager: while the Heartbeat is live. An Integration without a Heartbeat never resolves alerts as Stale.

items.title: Turn it on
items.text:
On the Integration page, turn the Heartbeat on. The timeout is 5 minutes by default (integration.heartbeat_timeout); keep it a few times the interval at which Alertmanager signals. The Heartbeat then waits for the first signal: nothing is raised and nothing goes Stale until it arrives, however long that takes. The first signal makes it live.

  1. Open Integrations and the Integration. Next to its name, the Heartbeat badge says Not configured, and a banner warns that Muster will not notice when Alertmanager goes quiet. The list of Integrations shows the same badge in its column Heartbeat.

  2. Select Edit. Under Heartbeat, turn on Watch for Heartbeat signals, keep or change the Timeout in minutes, and note the Heartbeat URL. Select Save. A new Integration can have the Heartbeat on from the start: the same switch is in its form.

  3. The badge says Waiting until the first signal arrives.

  4. Select Create token and Create. With the Heartbeat on, the dialog also shows the Heartbeat configuration: add it to Prometheus and Alertmanager as The snippet explains, and reload them.

  5. The first signal makes the badge Live, and the banner goes.

While the Heartbeat is off, Muster answers a signal with 204 and records nothing, so turning it on later always starts from waiting. Turning it off resolves an open MusterHeartbeatLost.

items.title: The Heartbeat URL
items.text:
Each Integration has its Heartbeat URL on the ingest listener:

https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/heartbeat

It accepts GET and POST with one of the Integration's tokens as Authorization: Bearer <token>, or appended to the path as /api/v1/heartbeat/<token>, and answers 204. The body is ignored. A missing, wrong or revoked token, or an API token, is refused with 401. Muster's logs name only the route, never a path with a token.

items.title: The snippet
items.text:
With the Heartbeat on, Create token also shows a Heartbeat snippet, once, with the token in it. It has three parts.

An alert that always fires, as a Prometheus rule:

groups:
  - name: muster-heartbeat
    rules:
      - alert: MusterHeartbeat
        expr: vector(1)

kube-prometheus-stack already has such an alert, Watchdog. With it, skip the rule and match alertname="Watchdog" in the route instead.

A child route for it, first under the top-level route:

route:
  routes:
    - receiver: muster-heartbeat-prod-eu
      matchers: ['alertname="MusterHeartbeat"']
      continue: true
      group_wait: 0s
      group_interval: 1m
      repeat_interval: 1m

repeat_interval: 1m (snippet.heartbeat_repeat_interval) makes Alertmanager send the always-firing alert about once a minute, and continue: true passes it on to your other routes, such as a dead man's switch.

A receiver that sends it to the Heartbeat URL, without resolves:

receivers:
  - name: muster-heartbeat-prod-eu
    webhook_configs:
      - url: https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/heartbeat
        send_resolved: false
        http_config:
          authorization:
            type: Bearer
            credentials: mstr_int_…

Reload Alertmanager. Within a minute or two the Integration's Heartbeat becomes live.

items.title: A cron job also works, but proves less
items.text:
Any client that requests the Heartbeat URL regularly keeps the Heartbeat live, for example a cron job:

curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/heartbeat

It proves only that the network from that host to Muster works. The Alertmanager route proves much more: that Prometheus evaluates rules, that Alertmanager routes and sends notifications, and that they reach Muster, which is exactly the path your alerts take. Prefer it.

items.title: When the Heartbeat is lost
items.text:
No signal within the timeout makes the Integration Heartbeat lost:

  • Muster raises MusterHeartbeatLost as a firing Alert of the built-in "Muster" Integration, and the Integration shows since when Muster has had no contact: the time of the last signal.
  • Stale resolution pauses. The time without a live Heartbeat, from the last signal before the loss until the signal returns, does not count towards an alert's time to go Stale, so a broken path never resolves alerts that may still fire.
  • The chart's rule MusterHeartbeatLost on muster_heartbeat_lost is the backup when Muster itself cannot deliver.

On the Integration page, the badge says Lost and the banner names the time of the last signal; the list of Integrations and Organization → System status show the loss too.

The next signal makes the Heartbeat live again and resolves MusterHeartbeatLost. Deleting the Integration resolves it too.

After Muster itself was down, the timeout counts from the moment the Leader started leading again, so that Muster's own outage does not make every Integration Heartbeat lost. A downtime longer than the timeout does not count towards staleness either; a shorter one does, which is at most the timeout against at least three repeat intervals.

items.title: Messengers
items.text:
Muster delivers Alert Groups to Destinations. A Destination is a place where Alert Groups arrive: a channel of a messenger, or an outgoing webhook. There are five types:

  • Mattermost, through a bot account on your Mattermost server;
  • Slack, through the bot of a Slack app, to a channel the bot is a member of;
  • Telegram, through a bot, to a channel with comments;
  • Bridge, for any other messenger: a small service that you or someone else writes speaks the Bridge protocol with Muster and talks to the messenger;
  • Outgoing webhook, which sends the lifecycle events of Alert Groups, or requests you build from templates, to any HTTP endpoint.

A Connection holds the credentials Muster uses to reach one messenger: a bot on a Mattermost server, the bot of a Slack app, a Telegram bot, or a Bridge. Many Destinations can share a Connection. An outgoing webhook has no Connection; the Destination carries its own address, Secrets and proxy.

To start, create the Connection, check it, create a Destination for a channel, and add the Destination to a Route. A Route decides which Alert Groups reach which Destinations; see Routes and Group keys.

items.title: What each Destination type can do
items.text:
Every entry is true for this release. An entry that depends on the bridge says "if the bridge declares it": a Bridge offers only what its info announces, and Muster adapts to the rest. Write a bridge lists the features.

Needs a Connection
  • Mattermost — yes
  • Slack — yes
  • Telegram — yes
  • Bridge — yes
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — no
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — no
One message per Alert Group, kept up to date
  • Mattermost — yes
  • Slack — yes
  • Telegram — yes
  • Bridge — yes
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — no: one request per event
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — yes, through your requests
Edits of the Root message
  • Mattermost — yes
  • Slack — yes, no window known
  • Telegram — yes
  • Bridge — yes, until the bridge's edit window
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — no
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — yes, through the update request
Buttons
  • Mattermost — yes
  • Slack — yes, with the Snooze menu
  • Telegram — yes
  • Bridge — if the bridge declares buttons
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — no
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — no
Without buttons
  • Mattermost — the web UI and the API
  • Slack — the web UI and the API
  • Telegram — the web UI and the API
  • Bridge — Text commands in the Thread if the bridge declares thread_messages; otherwise the web UI and the API
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — the web UI and the API
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — the web UI and the API
Thread
  • Mattermost — replies under the Root message
  • Slack — replies under the Root message
  • Telegram — the comments of the Root message, in the channel's discussion group
  • Bridge — replies under the Root message
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — no: each event is separate
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — optional reply_in_thread, with an optional open_thread
Loud
  • Mattermost — a new post with Mentions
  • Slack — a new message with Mentions
  • Telegram — a new message
  • Bridge — a new message that the bridge posts with notify
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — notify is true
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — .Notify is true
Quiet
  • Mattermost — an edit, or a post without a Mention
  • Slack — an edit, or a message without a Mention
  • Telegram — an edit, or a message sent with disable_notification
  • Bridge — an edit, or a message without a notification if the bridge declares quiet_messages
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — notify is false
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — .Notify is false
Mentions
  • Mattermost — nobody, @channel @all @here, users, Mattermost groups
  • Slack — nobody, @channel @here, users
  • Telegram — nobody, users
  • Bridge — nobody, users
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — nobody, everyone, users, groups, as data
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — the same, as data
Account links
  • Mattermost — yes: a code the bot sends by direct message
  • Slack — yes: a code the bot sends by direct message
  • Telegram — yes: a link that opens the bot
  • Bridge — yes: a token sent to the bot, and a code if the bridge can find people and send direct messages
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — not needed: no one presses anything
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — not needed
Rate limits
  • Mattermost — Connection 5 requests/s; Destination the same by default
  • Slack — Connection 50 requests/min; Destination 30 requests/min, sends and edits together
  • Telegram — Connection 15 messages/s; Destination 10 requests/min, sends and edits together
  • Bridge — Connection 10 requests/s, Destination 30 requests/min, or half of what the bridge's info declares
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — Destination 5 requests/s
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — Destination 5 requests/s
Edit window
  • Mattermost — none by default; the server setting PostEditTimeLimit is unlimited, so keep it
  • Slack — none known for a bot's messages
  • Telegram — none for the bot's own messages
  • Bridge — the bridge declares it, or none; Muster publishes a new Root message past it
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — not applicable
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — the chat's own; Muster does not know it
Storms
  • Mattermost — one Storm summary per Route
  • Slack — one Storm summary per Route
  • Telegram — one Storm summary per Route
  • Bridge — one Storm summary per Route
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — every event is sent, no summary
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — one Storm summary
Proxy
  • Mattermost — on the Connection
  • Slack — on the Connection
  • Telegram — on the Connection
  • Bridge — on the Connection
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — on the Destination
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — on the Destination
Destination check
  • Mattermost — yes
  • Slack — yes, conversations.info
  • Telegram — yes
  • Bridge — yes, checkChannel, which posts nothing
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — no
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — no
Test message and preview
  • Mattermost — yes
  • Slack — yes, the test message cannot press its own button
  • Telegram — yes
  • Bridge — yes
  • Outgoing webhook, events mode — yes, sends the event test
  • Outgoing webhook, template mode — yes, sends the create request

Notes on the entries:

  • Rate limits. These are the defaults of the limiters, and you can change them. Mattermost's own rate limit is off by default; when an administrator turns it on, it allows 10 requests per second per client address, so keep the limiters of all Connections to one server below that together. Slack limits each method per app and workspace, and about one message per second per channel; its Connection limiter is 50 requests a minute and its Destination limiter
  • A Telegram chat takes about 20 messages and edits per minute, which is why its Destination limiter is half of that. A bridge says its own limits in its info, and its rate_limited answers always win. A 429 from a messenger holds the Destinations that share it, for as long as it asks.
  • Slack and Quiet. Slack cannot send a message without a notification, so Quiet means "without a Mention"; an edit carries no Mention. See Connect Slack.
  • Account links. Pressing a button as a Muster user, and being Mentioned, need an Account link. See Link your messenger accounts.
  • Loud and Quiet. Edits never notify anybody, so every Loud change is a new message. See Loud and Quiet.
  • Edit windows. See Broken Destinations.
  • Destination check. It asks the messenger whether the bot can still post, without posting. Muster runs it when you save a Destination, from Check, and as the probe of a Broken Destination when nothing waits. An outgoing webhook has no Destination check, so a Broken one is probed by its next delivery.

items.title: Pages
items.text:
• Connect Mattermost: the bot account, the setting that lets the server call Muster for button presses, and who gets notified.
  • Connect Slack: the app and its manifests for Socket Mode and for HTTP, the tokens, the bot in the channels, and who gets notified.
  • Connect Telegram: the bot, a channel with comments, long polling or a webhook; Telegram in restricted networks for networks where it is blocked.
  • Connect a messenger through a bridge, and Write a bridge for a messenger Muster does not support.
  • Outgoing webhooks: the events mode, the template mode and some recipes.
  • Proxies: the proxy of each client, and what the outbound address policy checks.
  • Link your messenger accounts: how people tie their messenger accounts to their Muster user.
  • Request log: the recent requests Muster sent to a messenger, a bridge or an outgoing webhook, with secrets masked, for troubleshooting.

items.title: Link your messenger accounts
items.text:
An Account link ties your Telegram account, your account on a Mattermost server, your account in a Slack workspace, or your account on a messenger that Muster reaches through a Bridge, to your Muster User. With it, a button you press under an Alert Group in a messenger runs as you — the Timeline names you and shows the messenger you pressed in — and Mentions in the messenger name you, as does the footer of a Root message you acknowledged, snoozed or resolved, which mentions you there in the messenger's own form.

A Telegram account belongs to one User across every Telegram Connection. A Mattermost account belongs to one User per Mattermost Connection, since each Connection is its own server, and so does a Slack account, per Slack Connection, and an account reached through a Bridge, per Bridge Connection. You have at most one Telegram account and one account per Mattermost, Slack or Bridge Connection; linking another one replaces the earlier link, and linking the same account again keeps its link and updates its username and name.

items.title: Why links start in your profile
items.text: Every link starts in your signed-in Muster session, and the secret travels from there to your messenger account — never the other way. Nobody can link your account by typing your name into a chat, and nobody can link their account to your User: only the account that receives the secret Muster gave you in your own session gets linked. That is why linking needs no extra password or TOTP code, and why an API token, an Admin's included, cannot start, confirm or remove a link of its own User.

items.title: Link Telegram
items.text:
1. In your profile, open Messenger accounts and select Link Telegram — or Relink Telegram once you have a Telegram link, which the new link replaces.

  2. Choose the Telegram Connection, when there are several, and select Get link. Muster shows a link https://t.me/<bot>?start=<token> as Open Telegram and as a QR code to scan with your phone. Open it on the device where you use Telegram, within 10 minutes (account_link.telegram_token_ttl); the link works once.

  3. Telegram opens a chat with the bot. Press Start.

  4. The bot answers "Linked to Muster user {your name} ({your login})", and your profile shows the link at once.

If the bot answers "This link is invalid or expired. Start again from your Muster profile.", the link was used already, expired, belongs to another Telegram bot of Muster, or was never issued: start again from your profile. If it answers "This account is linked to another user. Its owner or an admin can unlink it.", that Telegram account is linked to someone else; nothing changed.

items.title: Link Mattermost
items.text:
1. In your profile, open Messenger accounts and select Link Mattermost. Choose the Connection, enter Your Mattermost username — with or without the @ — and select Send code.

  2. The Connection's bot sends you a direct message: "You requested a link to Muster. Do not share this code." with an 8-character code. If you did not ask for it, ignore it.

  3. Type the code into your profile within 10 minutes (account_link.mattermost_code); capital and small letters are the same. Select Link. The bot confirms "Linked to Muster user {your name}".

A code allows 5 attempts; after five wrong codes it stops working, even with the right code, and you request a new one. A new request replaces your earlier one. You can request 5 codes an hour, and one Mattermost account gets at most 3 codes an hour, whoever asks (account_link.mattermost_code_requests); beyond that, wait until the oldest request is an hour old. A username the server does not know, a bot account and a deactivated account cannot be linked. An account that is linked to another User is refused.

The bot must be allowed to open direct messages with you; see Direct messages.

items.title: Link Slack
items.text:
1. In your profile, open Messenger accounts and select Link Slack. Choose the Connection, enter Your Slack email or name and select Send code. An email finds your account for sure; a name is compared with the name and the display name of each account, regardless of case.

  2. The Connection's bot sends you a direct message: "You requested a link to Muster. Do not share this code." with an 8-character code. It shows in the Messages tab of the bot's app, which is read-only, so you can read the code and cannot write to the bot. If you did not ask for it, ignore it.

  3. Type the code into your profile within 10 minutes (account_link.slack_code); capital and small letters are the same, and select Link. The bot confirms "Linked to Muster user {your name}".

If Muster answers "No Slack account with this email or name was found.", check what you typed. If it answers "Several Slack accounts have this name. Enter the email instead.", do. A bot, a deleted account and Slackbot cannot be linked, and an account that is linked to another User is refused.

A code allows 5 attempts; after five wrong codes it stops working, even with the right code, and you request a new one. A new request replaces your earlier one. You can request 5 codes an hour, and one Slack account gets at most 3 codes an hour, whoever asks (account_link.slack_code_requests); beyond that, wait until the oldest request is an hour old.

The bot can send the code only while the Messages tab of its app is on. Slack documents that with it off it refuses the direct message, and then Muster answers that the Messages tab of the Slack app is turned off; the problem is messages_tab_disabled. Ask the admin of the Slack app to turn the tab on under App Home, then request a new code. The refused request still counts toward the limits above, so if you tried several times before the tab was on, you may have to wait up to an hour. See Connect Slack.

items.title: Link through a Bridge
items.text:
A Bridge Connection reaches a messenger through a bridge, which tells Muster in its info what it can do for Account links. Every bridge takes a token that you send to its bot. A bridge that can look people up and start a direct chat with them also offers a code that its bot sends you, as Mattermost does. Your profile offers what the Connection's bridge declares.

Once linked, a Mention of you in a message of that Connection names you by the name the bridge reported for your account, which a bridge with native mentions turns into its messenger's mention. The footer of a Root message you acknowledged, snoozed or resolved mentions you the same way when Muster posts it to a bridge with native mentions; an edit carries no Mentions, so there, and through any other bridge, the footer names you by that name. Without a link, a Mention is your Muster name as plain text, which notifies nobody.

items.title: By a token sent to the bot
items.text:
1. In your profile, open Messenger accounts and select Link through {Connection} of the Bridge Connection.

  2. On the tab Token, Muster shows a token of 43 characters, with Copy, and, when the bridge declares a link that opens a chat with its bot, that link as well. Within 10 minutes (account_link.bridge_token_ttl), send the token to the bot of that Connection in a direct message, or open the link, which hands the token to the bot. The token works once, and only with the bot of the Connection you chose.

  3. The bot answers "Linked to Muster user {your name} ({your login})", and your profile shows the link with the name and the handle the bridge reported for your account.

If the bot answers "This link is invalid or expired. Start again from your Muster profile.", the token was used already, expired, was started for another Connection — another bridge, or another bot of the same bridge — or was never issued: start again from your profile. If it answers "This account is linked to another user. Its owner or an admin can unlink it.", that account is linked to someone else; nothing changed.

items.title: By a code by direct message
items.text:
The code is offered only when the bridge declares how it finds people — its lookup kind, one of email address, login, username or user id — and that its bot can start a direct chat. Your profile names the field after that kind: Email, Login, Username or User id.

  1. In your profile, select Link through {Connection} of the Bridge Connection and the tab Code. Enter your email address, login, username or user id in the messenger, as the field asks, and select Send code.
  2. The bot sends you a direct message: "You requested a link to Muster. Do not share this code." with an 8-character code. If you did not ask for it, ignore it.

  3. Type the code into your profile within 10 minutes (account_link.bridge_code); capital and small letters are the same. Select Link: the link is made at once, and the bot sends no confirmation.

If the bridge finds no one, Muster answers "No account with this email was found." — or login, username or user id. If the bot may not write to you, Muster answers "The bot cannot send you a direct message. Send it the token instead." The limits are those of Mattermost: 5 attempts per code, a new request replaces your earlier one, 5 code requests an hour for you and at most 3 codes an hour for one account, whoever asks (account_link.bridge_code_requests). An account that is linked to another User is refused.

items.title: Several Connections of one messenger
items.text:
An Organization may have several Connections of one messenger, such as two Mattermost bots on one server, two Slack apps or a second Telegram bot. What a link covers differs by messenger:

  • Mattermost links are per Connection. Each Mattermost Connection is its own Identity space, even when two Connections use bots on the same server: two bots on one server need two links, made one after the other from Link Mattermost with each Connection. Your profile lists one row per Connection.
  • Slack links are per Connection. Each Slack Connection is its own Identity space, even when two Connections serve the same workspace with two apps: two Connections need two links, made one after the other from Link Slack with each Connection. Your profile lists one row per Connection.
  • Bridge links are per Connection. Each Bridge Connection is its own Identity space, also when two Connections reach the same bridge with two bots: two Connections need two links, made one after the other, and a token started for one of them links nothing when you send it to the other's bot. Your profile lists one row per Connection.
  • A Telegram link is valid for all Telegram bots. Telegram has one Identity space, so the link you make through any Telegram Connection lets you press buttons sent by every Telegram bot of Muster. Your profile shows it as "Telegram · @ · for all Telegram bots", with "linked via " below.

    One chat reached through two Connections is two Destinations, and each posts its own message for every Alert Group. This is allowed, but the Route editor warns when two or more of a Route's Destinations deliver to the same chat — one Telegram chat, or one Mattermost server and channel — since their messages appear twice. The Destinations list, the Route editor and the Alert Group page name each Destination's Connection and channel, so you can tell them apart.

items.title: Unlink
items.text:
Nothing can be unlinked from a chat. Removing a link, like making one, is recorded in the Audit log with who did it and from where.

  1. In your profile, open Messenger accounts. It lists each link with the messenger, the Connection, the account, when it was last used and when it was linked.

  2. Select Unlink on the row, and Unlink again in the dialog. Presses from that account no longer act as you.

items.title: What Admins can do
items.text: Admins see the links of every User on the user page, under Account links, and can remove any of them — their own from the web session only, as above. They cannot create a link for someone else. Deleting a User removes their links and voids the links they had started.

items.title: What a press answers
items.text:
Who pressed What happens The private answer An account without a link Nothing changes "Your Telegram account is not linked to Muster. Link it in your profile: {link}" — or the same for Mattermost or Slack, and "Your account is not linked to Muster. Link it in your profile: {link}" through a Bridge; the link goes to your profile and carries no secret A linked Viewer Nothing changes "You are not permitted to do this" A linked User who is disabled Nothing changes "Your Muster account is disabled" A linked Responder or Admin The Command runs as that User "Done: {command}", or why it was refused

The Audit log records account_link.link, account_link.unlink and account_link.link_rejected with the User, the messenger, the account's id and username, and the Connection; a rejection says why: token_unknown, token_used, token_expired, wrong_connection, wrong_code or conflict.

items.title: Connect a messenger through a bridge
items.text:
A bridge connects Muster to a messenger that Muster does not support natively. It is a separate service that speaks the Bridge protocol with Muster on one side and talks to your messenger on the other: Muster sends it every message as an envelope — the status, the title, a link, the text and the buttons — and the bridge renders the envelope in its messenger. A Bridge Connection is one bot of your messenger behind one bridge: one token is one bot. Muster posts one Root message per Alert Group to a channel of that messenger, edits it as the Alert Group changes, and replies in its Thread for what happens later, as it does for Mattermost, Slack and Telegram.

To write a bridge, read Write a bridge; the protocol itself is the Bridge protocol reference.

In the examples, MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL is https://muster.example.org, MUSTER_INGEST_URL is https://ingest.muster.example.org and the bridge listens on https://bridge.example.org. The steps use the web UI; the examples do the same with the API, with a Personal access token of an Admin in MUSTER_TOKEN.
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Create the Connection
items.text:
From your bridge, you need:

  • its base URL, an http or https address with an optional path prefix, such as https://bridge.example.org/muster. Muster sends every request to <base URL>/v1/…, and only there, with User-Agent: Muster/<version>;
  • the token it gave your bot. Muster sends it as Authorization: Bearer on every request, stores it encrypted and never shows it again.

Choose how the bridge reports events — the presses of buttons and the messages people write in a Thread — with the event delivery mode:

  • poll (connection.bridge.event_delivery, the default) when the bridge cannot reach Muster. The Leader asks the bridge for new events, so the bridge needs no address of Muster.
  • push when the bridge can reach MUSTER_INGEST_URL. The bridge posts each event to the Connection's callback address, https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/bridge/CN…, which the Connection shows in callback_url, signed with a push secret that you configure on both sides. The push secret has the Standard Webhooks form, whsec_ followed by base64, and is write-only like the token.

A Connection also has a proxy, for a bridge that Muster reaches only through one, and a limiter: 10 requests per second by default, shared by all its Destinations. When the bridge answers that it is rate-limited, Muster waits as long as it asks, whatever the limiter allows.

  1. Open Connections, select Create connection and choose Bridge.

  2. Enter a Name, the Base URL and, after Set a value, the Token. Choose the event delivery mode, Polling or Push; with push, also the push secret.

  3. Select Check connection, below the form. It runs the steps of What the check shows against the values in the form and saves nothing.

  4. Select Save, then Check connection on the saved Connection: Muster keeps what the bridge offers, which the page shows.

With the API:

curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/connections \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"bridge","name":"Team chat","base_url":"https://bridge.example.org/muster",
       "bot_token":"the-token-of-the-bot","event_delivery":"poll","proxy":{"enabled":false},
       "limiter":{"limit":10,"per_seconds":1}}'

For push, set "event_delivery":"push" and add "push_secret":"whsec_…".
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: What the check shows
items.text:
Check the Connection after you create it, and after every change of the bridge:

curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/connections/CNK7M3QX9P2RTA/checks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN"

The check calls the bridge's getInfo and shows two steps, each with its latency and whether it went through the proxy:

  1. info: the bridge's name and version, the messenger's name, the protocol version — Muster speaks 1 — what the bridge offers, such as buttons and Thread messages, its limits, such as the longest text of a message, how it finds people for Account links, and its event delivery modes. Muster keeps this copy on the Connection and reads it again before a call that depends on it once it is older than 10 minutes, so a change in the bridge reaches Muster without a restart.
  2. event_delivery: whether the bridge offers the Connection's event delivery mode.

A failed step names its cause with a code:

token_invalid The bridge refused the token. protocol_version_unknown The bridge speaks a protocol version that this Muster does not speak. protocol_mismatch The answer does not match the protocol, or is larger than 64 KiB. event_delivery_not_offered The bridge does not offer the Connection's event delivery mode. proxy_refused The Connection's proxy refused its credentials (407). timeout, connect_failed, dns_failed, tls_failed Muster got no answer from the bridge. blocked The outbound address policy does not allow the bridge's address. request_failed The bridge answered with another error; the message names its class and the bridge's text.
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Check before saving
items.text:
The check above reads a saved Connection. Check connection in the form of a new Connection, or on the page of a saved one while the form holds changes, checks the values in the form before anything is saved, with POST /api/v1/connections/checks. It saves nothing: the info it reads is returned, not stored, and the Audit log gets no entry.

  • With the token typed, the steps info and event_delivery run against the base URL in the form, through the proxy in the form, with that token.
  • Without one, a saved Connection (connection_id) uses its stored token only when the base URL — a trailing / aside — and the proxy are the saved ones: the stored token is sent only to the saved address, through the saved proxy. After a change of the base URL or of the proxy, the check makes only a dry probe, GET <base>/v1/info without the token, which a bridge answers with 401 and a problem (application/problem+json). An address that answers otherwise fails with not_bridge, a 404 with wrong_path_prefix, another status with a problem with unexpected_status; after a dry probe that passes, info and event_delivery ask you to type the token again to check the new address or proxy, or to save first. A new Connection without a token gets the dry probe alone too.
curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/connections/checks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"bridge","base_url":"https://bridge.example.org/muster","event_delivery":"poll",
       "bot_token":"the-token-of-the-bot"}'
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Add a Destination
items.text:
A Bridge Destination is one channel of the messenger, named by its channel id — the channel as your messenger names it, which the bridge's documentation explains how to find. Its Mention settings take nobody or chosen users; everyone in the chat and messenger groups are not available through a bridge. Its limiter allows 30 requests per minute by default, sends and edits together.

  1. Open Destinations, select Create destination and choose Bridge.

  2. Choose the Connection, enter the Channel id and a Name.

  3. Select Save, which runs the Destination check below. The saved Destination shows the channel's name as the bridge reports it.

  4. Under Test and preview, on the tab Test, select Send test message: the bridge posts a message marked 🧪, and the result shows the envelope Muster sent. Links in the screenshot start with http://localhost:8080, the address of a development installation; yours start with your MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL. See Test messages and previews.

With the API:

curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/destinations \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"bridge","name":"alerts","connection_id":"CNK7M3QX9P2RTA","channel_id":"C024BE91L",
       "mentions":{"new_alert_group":{"everyone":"none","user_ids":[],"groups":[]},
                   "new_alerts":{"everyone":"none","user_ids":[],"groups":[]},
                   "reopen":{"everyone":"none","user_ids":[],"groups":[]},
                   "ack_timeout":{"everyone":"none","user_ids":[],"groups":[]},
                   "snooze_ended":{"everyone":"none","user_ids":[],"groups":[]},
                   "rise_to_urgent":{"everyone":"none","user_ids":[],"groups":[]}},
       "limiter":{"limit":30,"per_seconds":60}}'

Saving the Destination runs its Destination check, the one item channel: the bridge's checkChannel, which posts nothing. It passes when the bot can post, edit and reply in the channel, and the Destination then shows the channel's name as the bridge reports it. It fails with the bridge's own text when the bridge refuses the channel — it does not exist, or the bot is not in it — with proxy_refused when the Connection's proxy refuses its credentials, and with the class of the bridge's answer otherwise; a Destination that fails the check is not saved. POST /api/v1/destinations/DS…/checks runs the same check at any time.
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: What Muster posts
items.text:
• The envelope. Every Root message carries its status with a colour and an emoji, the title #N and the Alert Group's title, the link "Open in Muster" to the Alert Group page, and its text in CommonMark: the labels, the summary, one line per Alert, the links, the notices and the footer. A Thread reply carries its text in CommonMark. Alert data are escaped, so a label value cannot format the message, link anywhere or mention anyone. A Loud message asks the bridge to notify; a Quiet one does not.
  • The length. The text fits the longest text the bridge declares, read from the Connection's copy of its info: a long Root message drops its Alert lines first, then the label sections, but always keeps its title, its status, its footer, its buttons and its link to Muster. The bridge may still shorten what it renders, and says so.
  • Buttons. When the bridge offers buttons, a Root message carries the buttons of its status — Ack, Resolve, one per Snooze duration and the two Snooze presets "Until tomorrow 09:00" and "Until Monday 09:00", for example — with a style hint for each, the presets neutral like the durations, at most as many as the bridge allows. Beyond that limit the Snooze buttons go first, whatever their labels: the "Until Monday" preset (the first day of the week), then the "Until tomorrow" preset, then the durations from the longest. A firing Root message on an On-call Route has seven buttons, so a bridge that allows five gets Ack, Resolve and the three durations, and one that allows six also "Until tomorrow 09:00". Without buttons, a bridge that forwards the messages of a Thread gets a last line in each Root message that is not resolved, such as "Reply in the Thread: ack · resolve · snooze 1h", and takes the presets as Text commands such as snooze tomorrow.
  • Edits and Thread replies. An edit sends the whole envelope of the new state, Quiet and without Mentions. A Thread reply goes under the Root message with the Thread reference the bridge returned last.
  • The footer. "Acknowledged by", "Snoozed by" and "Resolved by" name a person with an Account link for the Connection by a Mention marker in a new Root message to a bridge with native mentions, Loud or Quiet; in an edit, which carries no Mentions, and through any other bridge, by the name the bridge reported for their account.
  • Posts are not repeated. Every new message carries an idempotency key, the same for every retry of it. When an answer is lost — a timeout, or a connection cut after the request — Muster retries with the same key, the bridge answers with the message it posted already, and Muster edits it to the current state. When the bridge did not know the key, the retry may have posted a second message: the Timeline records a possible duplicate.
  • The token never shows in a log line, an error, the Timeline or a metric; a test shows it as [redacted].
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Edit windows
items.text:
Some messengers let a bot edit a message only for a while after posting it. A bridge for such a messenger declares how long in its info, as limits.edit_max_age_seconds, and Muster stops editing its Root messages in time. A bridge that declares no limit (null) has none: Muster edits each Root message for as long as its Alert Group changes.

  • When Muster stops editing. Muster makes no edit of a Root message once it is as old as the bridge's limit less 60 seconds, counted from its Publication on Muster's clock, so that a last edit does not race the messenger's: with a limit of 600 seconds, the last edit is made within 9 minutes. Muster reads the limit from the Connection's copy of the info, as for every call. When the messenger refuses an edit earlier than declared, the bridge answers gone with the reason edit_window_closed: this is not a deletion, and Muster treats the Root message as past its window at once. A Root message that Muster posts again after it was deleted has a window of its own.
  • Alerts reach only the Thread. Past the window, a change that keeps the status of the Alert Group — new Alerts, Alerts that resolve, the counters — no longer changes the Root message, which keeps the state of its last edit; the Thread replies that such a change makes are sent as usual.
  • A change of status posts a new Root message. When the status changes past the window — Acknowledge, Resolve, Snooze, a Reopen — Muster posts a new Root message with the current state, Quietly, to the same channel, and replies under the old one: "This message is no longer updated. The current one: {link}", with a link to the new message when the bridge returned one and to the Alert Group page otherwise. Later Thread replies go under the new Root message, which has a window of its own. This reply is sent once: when the bridge refuses it, the failure is recorded with the delivery event and the reply is not sent again.
  • A new Root message is not left behind. When the answer to the post of a new Root message is lost, Muster posts it again with the same key, even if the status has changed back meanwhile, so that a message the bridge may have taken is never left with a stale status and live buttons: a bridge that took the first post answers with that message instead of posting a second one. When the Destination left the Route meanwhile, the post carries the final text; when the bridge answers with the earlier post, which shows an older state, Muster then gives that message the final edit.
  • The old message keeps working. A press on the buttons of an older Root message, or a Text command in its Thread, acts on the Alert Group as on the current one.
  • The final edit is a Thread reply. When the Destination leaves the Route or is deleted, each open Root message gets a final edit, "No longer updated here; current state in Muster: {link}"; past the window, Muster sends the same text as a Thread reply instead.
  • Storm summaries are never posted again. Past its window, a Storm summary keeps the state of its last edit.
  • What the delivery shows. GET /api/v1/alert-groups/AG…/deliveries shows past_edit_window as true for a Destination whose Root message is past its window, while the delivery stays delivered, or pending while a new Root message is due. Each new Root message posted past the window is the delivery event republished_past_edit_window in the Alert Group's Timeline, with the error of the reply under the old message when it failed, and the log line bridge_republished_past_edit_window, with the ids of the old and the new message.
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Test messages and previews
items.text:
A test message checks how a Destination looks without touching any Alert Group:

curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/destinations/DSK7M3QX9P2RTA/tests \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"source":{"kind":"example"}}'

It posts one message of the kind test, Quiet, marked "🧪 Test message" before its text, with the buttons of its status, whose presses change nothing. It goes through the same limiters as delivery, and the result shows the step message with the request — the token masked — the bridge's answer and its error class. Use {"source":{"kind":"alert_group","alert_group_id":"AG…"}} to render a recent Alert Group of one of the Destination's Routes instead of the example. POST …/previews with the same body returns, without posting anything, the envelope the test would post, as JSON in the item message.
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Broken Destinations
items.text:
A Bridge Destination becomes Broken when the bridge refuses it — it answers forbidden, for example because the bot was removed from the channel — with the bridge's text as the reason, or when the bridge keeps failing or does not answer for the whole Transient budget: 10 attempts within 30 minutes. A bridge that asks Muster to wait does not make a Destination Broken unless it asks for more than 15 minutes (bridge.retry_after_max); an answer the bridge calls invalid ends that one delivery as Not delivered and leaves the Destination healthy. When the bridge answers that a Root message is gone, Muster publishes the Alert Group again, once; an edit refused as gone with the reason edit_window_closed is not a deletion, but the end of the message's edit window.

While a Destination is Broken, Muster tries again every 5 minutes: with the oldest waiting delivery, or, when nothing waits, with the Destination check, which posts nothing. The first success ends the Broken state, and so does a successful check or test message. See MusterDestinationBroken. A Bridge Connection whose bridge cannot be reached does not become Broken itself: its Destinations do, and its Connection check shows the cause.
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Account links
items.text: A press or a Mention through a bridge names a person through their Account link for that Connection; see Link your messenger accounts.
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Check from the command line
items.text: muster doctor prints one line per Bridge Connection, with the result of getInfo, and one line per Bridge Destination, with the result of checkChannel, without posting anything.
path: Connect a messenger through a bridge

items.title: Connect Mattermost
items.text:
Muster posts to Mattermost through the REST API with a bot account: one post per Alert Group, the Root message, which Muster edits as the Alert Group changes, and replies in its Thread for what happens later. People act on the Alert Group with the buttons of the post. Muster uses no incoming webhook and no plugin.

In the examples, MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL is https://muster.example.org, MUSTER_INGEST_URL is https://ingest.muster.example.org and the Mattermost server is https://chat.example.org.

items.title: Create the bot account
items.text:
1. In the System Console, under Integrations → Bot Accounts, turn on Enable Bot Account Creation.
  2. In Integrations → Bot Accounts, add a bot, for example muster. Give it the role Member: Muster needs no system admin role and no post:all or post:channels permission, because it posts only to channels the bot is a member of. With the role Member, the answers to button presses show in the Thread of the Root message; see Where answers to presses show.
  3. Copy the bot's access token. Mattermost shows it once.
  4. Add the bot to the team, and to every channel a Destination posts to. A public channel is enough; a private channel works the same once the bot is a member.

The bot token works even when Enable Personal Access Tokens is off, its default.

items.title: Create the Connection
items.text:
1. In Muster, open Connections, select Create connection and choose Mattermost.

  2. Enter a Name and the Server URL, the address people open Mattermost at, such as https://chat.example.org. Select Set a value next to Bot token and paste the bot's access token.

  3. Select Check connection, below the form. The check reads the bot's own user with the token and shows the bot's name. When the bot may not make ephemeral posts, it passes with a warning: see Where answers to presses show.

  4. Select Save. The saved Connection shows its callback address, which Mattermost calls when someone presses a button: MUSTER_INGEST_URL followed by /api/v1/callbacks/mattermost/CN…. In the screenshot it is http://localhost:8081, the ingest address of a development installation; yours starts with your MUSTER_INGEST_URL. Let button presses reach Muster says what the server needs to call it.

items.title: Check before saving
items.text:
Check connection checks the values in the form, before anything is saved: in the form of a new Connection, as above, and on the page of a saved one while the form holds changes. It saves nothing: no bot name is recorded and the Audit log gets no entry.

  • With the bot token typed in the form, the check reads the bot's own user at the server URL in the form, through the proxy in the form, and shows the bot's name.
  • Without a token typed, the page of a saved Connection uses its stored token only when the server URL and the proxy are the saved ones: the stored token is sent only to the saved address, through the saved proxy. After a change of the server URL or of the proxy, the check makes only a dry probe: GET <server>/api/v4/system/ping without a token, which a Mattermost server answers to anyone with 200 and "status":"OK". It tells a wrong address, a wrong path prefix (404) and a server that is not Mattermost apart, and the step Token asks you to type the bot token again to check the new address or proxy, or to save first. A new Connection without a token gets the dry probe alone too.

The check is POST /api/v1/connections/checks, which needs connections:write; with a Personal access token of an Admin in MUSTER_TOKEN:

curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/connections/checks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"mattermost","server_url":"https://chat.example.org","bot_token":"the-bot-token"}'

Add "connection_id":"CN…" to check the changes of a saved Connection, whose stored token the rule above may use.

items.title: Add a Destination
items.text:
A Mattermost Destination is one channel of one team that the bot is a member of.

  1. Open Destinations, select Create destination and choose Mattermost.

  2. Choose the Connection, the Team and the Channel. The list shows the channels the bot is a member of: add the bot to a channel to send there. The Name takes the channel's name; change it if you like.

  3. Select Save. Saving runs the Destination check: the bot is a member of the channel, which belongs to the team and is not archived. A Destination that fails the check is not saved, and the check names what failed.

  4. Under Test and preview, on the tab Test, select Send test message. Muster posts a message marked 🧪; the result shows the request it sent and Mattermost's answer. Links in the screenshot start with http://localhost:8080, the address of a development installation; yours start with your MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL.

    Muster then presses the message's first button through the bot. The step Button press says whether the press reached Muster at the callback address; when it did not, read Let button presses reach Muster.

Check on the Destination page runs the Destination check at any time.

items.title: Direct messages
items.text: Account links send a person a direct message from the bot: the bot opens the direct channel with the person's user id and posts there. Make sure your server lets the bot open direct messages with the people who link their accounts — for example, if Enable users to open Direct Message channels with is restricted to members of a team, add the bot to the teams of those people.

items.title: Let button presses reach Muster
items.text:
A press on a button makes the Mattermost server call Muster at the Connection's callback address, which the Connection page shows:

https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/mattermost/CN…

When that address resolves to a private or otherwise reserved address — the usual case inside one network — the Mattermost server refuses to call it unless the host is listed in ServiceSettings.AllowedUntrustedInternalConnections (Environment → Developer → Allow untrusted internal connections to in the System Console). Add the host of MUSTER_INGEST_URL, for example:

"ServiceSettings": {
  "AllowedUntrustedInternalConnections": "ingest.muster.example.org"
}

Without it, a person who presses a button sees only a generic Action integration error; only the Mattermost server log says why ("address forbidden … in a reserved range and not in AllowedUntrustedInternalConnections"). The test message of a Destination presses its own button through the bot and tells you whether the press reached Muster.

Whatever the person who pressed must read — that the press was refused, that their Mattermost account is not linked to Muster yet, or that the button could not be verified — arrives as a message only they can see. A press from an account without an Account link changes nothing. A request that does not come from a button of a Muster post in one of the Connection's channels gets no answer at all.

items.title: Where answers to presses show
items.text:
