Muster first sends the answer as an ephemeral message, which shows in the channel, marked "(Only visible to you)". Mattermost allows that only with the create_post_ephemeral permission, which by default only the system admin role has. Without it, Mattermost refuses the ephemeral message, and Muster returns the same text in its answer to the press: Mattermost then shows it from System in the Thread of the Root message. With collapsed reply threads, Mattermost's default, it is not shown in the channel view; the person opens the Thread to read it. Either way the answer is never lost.

Check connection tells you which applies: when the bot's roles do not grant create_post_ephemeral, the check passes with a warning that answers will show in the Thread of the Root message, and muster doctor prints the Connection as a WARN line. The warning names the bot whose token the Connection holds, as @username, and the roles Muster read for it, for example system_user, so you can see which account the token belongs to. To show answers in the channel, give the bot that permission, for example the system admin role. Otherwise keep the role Member and let people read the answers in the Thread.

Promote the bot account itself, not the person who owns it, and check that it is the bot the warning names: a bot of another Connection, or an older token of another bot, keeps its own roles. As a system admin, open Integrations → Bot Accounts from the product menu, select Edit on the bot, set Role to System Admin and select Update; or run mmctl roles system-admin <bot-username>. Then run Check connection again: the warning is gone once the bot's roles grant the permission.

items.title: Rate limit
items.text: Mattermost's rate limit is off by default. When an admin turns it on (RateLimitSettings.Enable, which takes a server restart), it allows 10 requests per second, with a burst of 100, per client address. All Connections of one Muster installation to the same Mattermost server usually come from one address and share that bucket, so keep their limiters together below it. The default limiter of a Connection is 5 requests per second. A 429 from Mattermost holds every request of the Connection, to any of its Destinations, for the seconds of its Retry-After.

items.title: Keep posts editable
items.text: Muster edits a Root message for as long as its Alert Group is open, which can be days. Keep ServiceSettings.PostEditTimeLimit at -1, its default, so that posts can be edited at any age.

items.title: Who gets notified
items.text:
• Edits notify nobody, even an edit that adds a Mention. That is why every Loud event is a new post: a new Root message, or a reply in the Thread.
  • Thread replies notify the Thread's followers by their own notification settings, and a Mention makes the person mentioned a follower of the Thread. "Quiet" therefore means "without a Mention", not "nobody notified".
  • A Loud Root message carries its Mentions — @channel, @here, @all, a Mattermost group, or a person's @username through their Account link — as one line at the top of the attachment, directly under its title. There a person's @username, @channel, @here and @all notify as they do anywhere in a post; whether a group's Mention notifies from an attachment has not been checked. The post's own text is empty: everything is in the attachment, so the post shows its title once. What a notification shows follows from that: an email notification shows no content; a push notification, when the server's PushNotificationContents is full, and a desktop notification show the attachment's summary line — the status, #N and the title — which Muster sets as its fallback and the channel does not show; a push notification under generic shows a fixed text such as "… notified the channel." An edit removes the line of Mentions. A reply in the Thread carries its Mentions in its own text. A {{ mention "channel" }} in a Route's template shows in the attachment as text and, on a Loud post, adds its Mention to the line of Mentions.
  • Alert data never mention anyone: an @ in a label or annotation is shown as text and notifies nobody.
  • The footer of a Root message — "Acknowledged by", "Snoozed by", "Resolved by" — writes a person with an Account link for the Connection as @username, so that Mattermost shows their name with their profile; a person without one is their Muster name as text. An edit notifies nobody, but a new post with the footer, after a republish, may notify that person.

items.title: Check from the command line
items.text: muster doctor prints one line per Mattermost Connection and per Mattermost Destination with the same checks, without sending anything.

items.title: Proxies
items.text: Muster has no proxy for the whole installation. Each client that talks to the outside has a proxy setting of its own, so that traffic that must go through a proxy does, and traffic that must not, such as the identity provider's, goes straight. HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY are never read, in any process of Muster.

items.title: Where you set a proxy
items.text:
Client Where a Mattermost, Slack, Telegram or Bridge Connection the Connection's proxy section an outgoing webhook Destination the Destination's proxy section the identity provider (OpenID Connect) the OIDC settings the Organization's outgoing heartbeat its settings

The setting is off by default. Every one of these has the same form:

  • Use a proxy, a switch. Switching it off keeps the other fields, so that you can switch it on again.
  • Type: http, https or socks5.
  • Address, as host:port with a port from 1 to 65535.
  • Username and password, when the proxy needs them. The username must not contain a colon or a line break and is at most 255 bytes long.

The three types differ in how Muster talks to the proxy:

Type Muster speaks to the proxy Notes HTTP plain HTTP for an HTTPS target, Muster asks the proxy for a tunnel with CONNECT HTTPS HTTP over TLS the connection to the proxy is encrypted SOCKS5 the SOCKS5 protocol the proxy resolves the name of the target

items.title: The password
items.text: The proxy password is a secret like the others: it is encrypted with the master key, write-only in the API and the web UI (they show whether it is set, never the value), and replaced with [redacted] in every log line and error. A stored password is used only with the proxy type and address it was saved with. When you change either, type the password again.

items.title: Checks take the same path
items.text: The connection check of a Connection, and the test of a Destination, go through the saved proxy just as real traffic does. If the check works, delivery works by the same route. A check run from the form before saving uses the proxy in the form instead. A token that is already stored goes only to the saved address of its Connection, through its saved proxy: with a changed but unsaved address or proxy and no token typed, the check makes only a probe without the token.

items.title: What the outbound address policy checks
items.text:
Every outbound connection of Muster is checked by the Organization's outbound address policy, standard or strict, with its lists of allowed and denied networks, host names and domains. The Admins edit the policy under Organization → Outbound addresses. Through a proxy, two things are checked:

  1. The proxy's own address. It is checked like any other target, after name resolution. A proxy setting cannot reach a link-local or cloud metadata address, such as 169.254.169.254, and a proxy on a loopback address works only when an allowed network contains it.
  2. The target. The proxy resolves the target's name, so Muster resolves it too, and every address it gets must pass the policy; for a target given as an IP address, that address is checked. A request to a name that resolves to a blocked address is refused before it is sent, without retry, and the error names the rule.

In a closed network, only the proxy may be able to resolve outside names. When Muster cannot resolve the target's name itself, it checks the name instead: a name that matches a denied entry is blocked, and in strict mode only a name that matches an allowed entry passes. A request that passes is sent without an address check, and Muster logs that.

Muster cannot see where the proxy finally connects to. The Admin who sets the proxy chooses to trust it.

items.title: Telegram
items.text: Telegram is often reached through a proxy where it is blocked. Telegram in restricted networks shows the proxy on the Connection, and the alternatives: a reverse proxy under your own domain and a self-hosted Bot API server.

items.title: Slack
items.text: A Slack Connection has no address field, since Slack's address is fixed, so a proxy sees only Slack's hosts. It must allow CONNECT to slack.com; in Socket Mode also to the hosts under slack.com that the socket uses; and to hooks.slack.com, where Muster sends the answer to a press when it cannot send it in the channel. When only the proxy can resolve outside names and the policy is strict, add slack.com and *.slack.com to Allowed: the domain entry covers the socket's hosts and hooks.slack.com, but not slack.com itself. See Connect Slack.

items.title: Connect Slack
items.text:
Muster posts to Slack through the Web API with the bot of a Slack app that you create from a manifest and install in your workspace: one message per Alert Group, the Root message, which Muster edits as the Alert Group changes, and replies in its Thread for what happens later. People act on the Alert Group with the buttons of the message and its Snooze… menu. Muster uses no incoming webhook, no Events API subscription and no user token.

In the examples, MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL is https://muster.example.org and MUSTER_INGEST_URL is https://ingest.muster.example.org.

items.title: Socket Mode or HTTP
items.text:
A button press reaches Muster in one of two event modes, set on the Connection (connection.slack.event_mode). Choose before you create the app, because the app's manifest differs.

Socket Mode The Leader holds a WebSocket connection to Slack, so Slack needs no address of Muster: Muster only calls out. It is the way when Muster has no address that Slack can reach. It needs the app-level token. Only the Leader holds the socket, so a press made while the Leader changes is lost: the person sees Slack's error, and Muster does not count on Slack to send it again. A handover takes well under a minute; see High availability. HTTP

Slack posts every press to the Connection's callback address, which the Connection page shows:

https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/slack/CN…

Slack must reach this address over HTTPS. Any replica receives the press, so no press is lost while the Leader changes. It needs the app's Slack signing secret: Muster verifies the signature of every press with it, and refuses a request whose timestamp is further than slack.request_tolerance (5 minutes) from its own clock, so keep the clocks of Muster's nodes right. A request with a wrong or missing signature, a stale timestamp, an unknown Connection or a Connection in Socket Mode is answered 401 with the same body, which reveals nothing about which Connections exist; a body over 1 MiB, or one without a payload, is answered 400.

If Slack is the only client outside your network that reaches the ingest listener, expose only /api/v1/callbacks/ on the address Slack reaches, for example with a reverse proxy that forwards that path alone to the ingest port. MUSTER_INGEST_URL is also the address of Alertmanagers and Heartbeats: when they come from outside too, publish their paths as well, or give Slack's callbacks a route of their own. See The two public addresses.

A Slack app sends its presses to the sockets alone while its Socket Mode is on, and over HTTP alone while it is off, so the app and the Connection must agree: a Connection receives presses only in its own mode.

items.title: One Slack app per Connection
items.text:
Slack hands each press to any one of the app's open socket connections, and Muster binds a press to a Destination of the Connection that receives it. Two Connections on one Slack app, in one Muster or in two, would therefore share its presses at random, and a press that reaches the wrong Connection is refused as "This button could not be verified". Over HTTP an app has one Request URL, so it serves one Connection. Create a Slack app for each Connection, a test copy of Muster included.

Muster notices it. When Slack tells the Leader that the app has more socket connections than the Leader holds, another program is connected to the same app, usually a second Connection or Muster, or a script: the Check connection of a Connection in Socket Mode passes with the warning another_client_connected, the Connection page shows the same warning, muster doctor prints a WARN line, and the Leader logs slack_socket_shared. Presses go on working, but some of them are lost to the other program. Muster takes the count at each hello: when a socket reconnects, at the planned refresh hours after the previous one, and when the Connection is saved with a change, which restarts its socket at once. So the warning can stay for hours after its cause is gone; to clear it, save the Connection with its app-level token entered again. How long Slack counts the connection of a Leader that crashed has not been verified.

items.title: Create the app from a manifest
items.text:
1. Open Your Apps in Slack, select Create New App → From a manifest, choose the workspace and paste one of the manifests below, in YAML.
  2. Check the summary Slack shows and create the app.

items.title: The manifest for Socket Mode
items.text:
display_information:
  name: Muster
  description: Muster alert groups
features:
  app_home:
    home_tab_enabled: false
    messages_tab_enabled: true
    messages_tab_read_only_enabled: true
  bot_user:
    display_name: Muster
oauth_config:
  scopes:
    bot:
      - chat:write
      - channels:read
      - groups:read
      - im:write
      - users:read
      - users:read.email
settings:
  interactivity:
    is_enabled: true
  org_deploy_enabled: false
  socket_mode_enabled: true
  token_rotation_enabled: false

items.title: The manifest for HTTP
items.text:
It differs from the first in the Interactivity Request URL, the callback address of the Connection, and in Socket Mode, which is off:

display_information:
  name: Muster
  description: Muster alert groups
features:
  app_home:
    home_tab_enabled: false
    messages_tab_enabled: true
    messages_tab_read_only_enabled: true
  bot_user:
    display_name: Muster
oauth_config:
  scopes:
    bot:
      - chat:write
      - channels:read
      - groups:read
      - im:write
      - users:read
      - users:read.email
settings:
  interactivity:
    is_enabled: true
    request_url: https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/slack/CNAGK7M3QX9P2R
  org_deploy_enabled: false
  socket_mode_enabled: false
  token_rotation_enabled: false

The Connection page shows its callback address only once the Connection is saved, and saving it needs the bot token of the installed app. Create the app with the address above, create the Connection, then copy its callback address into Interactivity & Shortcuts → Request URL of the app.

items.title: What the manifest sets
items.text:
The app and its bot are named Muster. The bot posts under the name in the app's settings: Muster does not ask for chat:write.customize, so a name that a message carries would be ignored. To use another name, change both names in the manifest.

The Messages tab is on and read-only Account links send a person a code by direct message from the bot, and the direct messages of an app show in its Messages tab. Read-only means that the person reads the code and cannot write to the bot. Keep the tab on: Slack documents that with it off it refuses the bot's direct message, and the request for a code then fails with the problem messages_tab_disabled (409), which has not been seen yet on a real workspace. A refused request still counts toward the limits of Account links, 5 requests an hour for a person and 3 for one Slack account (account_link.slack_code_requests), so after you turn the tab on again, a person who tried several times may have to wait up to an hour. Turn it on under App Home → Show Tabs → Messages Tab. See Link Slack. The Home tab is off Muster publishes no Home tab. Interactivity is on Buttons and menus send nothing to Muster without it. Over HTTP it holds the Request URL. Socket Mode is on, or off for HTTP See Socket Mode or HTTP. Token rotation is off With rotation, the bot token expires and Slack issues a new one. Muster stores the token you enter and has no way to renew it, so a rotating token ends as token_expired and every Destination of the Connection becomes Broken. The app is not deployed to an organization One Connection serves one app in one workspace. There is no event subscription Muster does not use the Events API: it hears only the presses of buttons and menus.

items.title: The scopes
items.text:
Muster needs these six bot scopes and no other. Check connection reads the scopes Slack grants the token and fails with missing_scope, naming the missing ones.

chat:write Posts, edits and deletes the bot's own messages, and answers the people who press its buttons. channels:read Reads a public channel to check a Destination, and lists the public channels the bot is a member of. groups:read The same for private channels. im:write Lets the bot open a direct chat with a person. The Connection check fails without it. The code of an Account link is sent with chat.postMessage to the person's user id, which needs chat:write; whether Slack also needs im:write for that has not been verified, so Muster keeps the scope. users:read Finds a person by name for an Account link, and reads the app of the bot so that the check can tell whether both tokens belong to one app. users:read.email Finds a person by email for an Account link.

Muster never joins a channel on its own, so it asks for no channels:join: you invite the bot.

items.title: Install the app and create the tokens
items.text:
1. In the app's settings, open Install App and install it in the workspace. Slack then shows the Bot User OAuth Token under OAuth & Permissions; it starts with xoxb-. Copy it. Anyone with the token controls the bot.
  2. In Socket Mode, open Basic Information → App-Level Tokens and generate a token with the scope connections:write. It starts with xapp-. Copy it. Anyone with this token can open sockets of the app and take its presses.
  3. Over HTTP, open Basic Information → App Credentials and copy the Signing Secret. Anyone with it can send Muster presses that pass the signature check.

Muster stores all three secrets encrypted, never shows them again and writes them to no log line.

items.title: Create the Connection
items.text:
1. In Muster, open Connections, select Create connection and choose Slack.

  2. Enter a Name, choose the Event mode, and enter the Bot token and, in Socket Mode, the App-level token, or over HTTP the Slack signing secret, each after Set a value. A Slack Connection has no address field, since Slack's address is fixed.

  3. Select Check connection. The check runs in steps and shows the latency of each and whether it went through the proxy:

    1. Token: auth.test with the bot token, which names the bot and the workspace and fails if the token is not a bot's;
    2. Scopes: every scope of the manifest is granted;
    3. App-level token, in Socket Mode: the token belongs to the same app as the bot token, and Slack opens a connection for it. The check opens no WebSocket.

  4. Select Save. On the saved Connection, Check connection records the bot, the workspace and the app, which the page then names.

Over HTTP no request can show that Slack reaches the callback address or that the Slack signing secret is right, because a bot cannot press its own button. The first press does: see The test message.

Check connection also works in the form before anything is saved. It checks the values in the form and saves nothing, and no bot name is recorded. A stored token goes to Slack only through the saved proxy: after a change of the proxy, type the tokens again to check, or save first.

items.title: Invite the bot and create Destinations
items.text:
A bot posts only to channels it is a member of. In Slack, invite the bot to each channel a Destination posts to, public or private:

/invite @Muster

In Muster, create a Destination of type Slack with the Connection and the channel:

  1. Open Destinations, select Create destination and choose Slack.

  2. Choose the Connection and the Channel. The form lists the public and private channels the bot is a member of; for a channel that is not listed, type its id as Slack shows it in the channel's details, C… or G…. A direct chat or a person cannot be a Destination. Give the Destination a Name.

  3. Select Save, which runs the Destination check below. The saved Destination shows the channel's name.

  4. Under Test and preview, on the tab Test, select Send test message: a message marked 🧪 appears in the channel. In the screenshot the request line, which names a development server, is hidden, and links start with http://localhost:8080, the address of a development installation; yours start with your MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL. See The test message.

Saving runs the Destination check, which asks Slack about the channel with conversations.info and refuses a Destination that fails:

  • channel_not_found: no such channel, or a private channel the bot is not in;
  • channel_archived: the channel is archived;
  • bot_not_in_channel: "Invite the bot to the channel: /invite @{bot}", where {bot} is the bot's name as Slack reports it for the bot token, such as muster.

The bot's name appears in that hint only after Check connection has run on the saved Connection; before that it says only "Invite the bot to the channel."

Check on the Destination page runs the same check at any time. When Slack refuses the bot later, for example because someone removed it from the channel, the Destination becomes Broken; Muster runs the check every few minutes while nothing waits for the Destination, and ends the Broken state once it passes again, for example after someone invites the bot back. See Broken Destinations.

items.title: Link accounts
items.text: A button acts as a Muster User, and a Mention reaches a person, only through an Account link. The person enters their Slack email or name in their profile, and the bot sends a code by direct message, in the Messages tab of the app. The code has 8 characters, is valid for 10 minutes and allows 5 attempts (account_link.slack_code). See Link Slack.

items.title: Where answers to presses show
items.text:
A successful press is not answered: the Root message changes. Whatever the person who pressed must read — that the press was refused, that their Slack account is not linked to Muster yet, or that the button could not be verified — shows in the channel as a message only they can see, marked "Only visible to you". Unlike Mattermost, Slack needs no permission beyond chat:write for it. For a press on a Thread reply, such as a Reminder, the answer shows in the Thread. The one success that is answered is "Still on it", which changes no message.

Slack does not guarantee such a message: the person must be active and in the channel. When Slack refuses it, Muster sends the same text to the press's response_url, on hooks.slack.com; an answer that fails both ways is logged and not tried again. Answers are in the language of the User the account is linked to, and in English for an account without a link.

A replica handles at most 2 presses at a time (slack.parallel_presses); the others wait, already confirmed to Slack. A press whose deadline ends while it waits for a slot, 30 seconds after it was handed over (slack.press_deadline), is answered, in English, that it failed. At most 64 presses wait for a slot in a process (slack.max_waiting_presses): one more, and a press still waiting or running at the end of the shutdown's grace period, fails without an answer and is logged. None of these bounds is configurable.

items.title: Who gets notified
items.text:
Slack cannot send a message without a notification: whom a new message notifies depends on each member's settings for the channel and the Thread. So, as in Mattermost, Quiet means "without a Mention", not "nobody is notified".

  • Edits are Quiet. An edit of the Root message carries no Mention, so a Loud change is always a new message: a new Root message, or a reply in the Thread. The edit drops the Mentions that the Root message had; Slack may then remove them from the person's list of mentions.
  • Mentions are @channel and @here, as the Destination's Mention settings ask, and the people chosen in them, through their Account links. A person without a link is named by their display name as text, which notifies nobody. A Slack Destination takes neither @all nor groups. The footer of a Root message — "Acknowledged by", "Snoozed by", "Resolved by" — writes a person with an Account link for the Connection as their Mention, which Slack shows as their name, in an edit as in a new message; a person without one is their display name as text.
  • Thread replies stay in the Thread: Muster never also broadcasts them to the channel.
  • Alert data and template text never mention anyone. An &, < or > in a label or an annotation is escaped, and so is @. A literal <!here> or <@U…> written in a template is shown as text and notifies nobody. Only the Destination's Mention settings, {{ mention "here" }} and its siblings, and linked people notify.

See Loud and Quiet.

items.title: Rate limits
items.text:
Muster limits itself, and Slack limits it too.

connection.slack.limiter 50 requests a minute for every call of the Connection to the Web API together, the minimum Slack documents for the methods that edit and delete. destination.slack.limiter 30 requests a minute for the sends and edits of a Destination together, half of Slack's "one message per second per channel".

Slack limits each method per app and workspace. When it answers 429, Muster holds every request of the Connection, for any of its Destinations, for the seconds of Retry-After; this is not counted as a failed attempt, and does not make a Destination Broken. A 429 without Retry-After counts as a transient failure. You can change both limiters.

items.title: Edits and deleted Root messages
items.text:
Muster edits a Root message for as long as its Alert Group is open, which can be days. Slack lets a bot edit its own messages, and no edit window is known for them. Whether a window that your workspace sets applies to the messages of a bot, hours or days old, has not been verified; an edit that Slack refuses that way ends that delivery as Not delivered and does not make the Destination Broken.

When someone deletes a Root message, Muster finds out at its next edit, when Slack answers message_not_found. It checks that the bot is still in the channel and the channel is not archived, and then posts the Alert Group again once, Quietly, with a note. If the bot is gone or the channel archived, the Destination becomes Broken instead. A Root message that already had replies stays in the channel as "This message was deleted." with its replies, and Muster's later replies still go under it until the next edit finds it gone.

A Root message deleted before it had any reply takes no reply: Slack posts a reply to it into the channel, as an ordinary message, and answers as if it had worked. Muster notices, deletes that message at once and posts the Alert Group again. The reply may stay in the channel for a moment. If Slack refuses the deletion, Muster does not try again: the stray reply stays until someone deletes it, and the delivery records why.

items.title: The test message
items.text:
Send test message on the Destination page posts one message marked "🧪 Test message", with the buttons of its status, and Preview shows the message as Muster would send it. No Alert Group changes.

A bot cannot press its own button in Slack, so the test message cannot prove that presses reach Muster, as Mattermost's does. Press a button of the test message yourself: Muster answers you "This is a test message; nothing was changed", even from an account without a link. That answer proves that presses reach Muster and, over HTTP, that the Slack signing secret is right.

items.title: The proxy
items.text:
A Slack Connection has a proxy section like the others; see Proxies. The proxy must allow CONNECT to slack.com; in Socket Mode also to the hosts under slack.com that the socket uses; and to hooks.slack.com, where the fallback answers to presses go. Where only the proxy can resolve outside names and the Organization's outbound address policy is strict, add slack.com and *.slack.com to Allowed: the domain entry covers hooks.slack.com and the socket's hosts, but not slack.com itself. See Proxies.

Muster accepts a Socket Mode address only on slack.com or a host below it, and an answer address only on hooks.slack.com. If the socket cannot open, the Leader backs off (slack.socket_backoff, from 1 second up to 5 minutes), logs slack_socket_failed, and does not make any Destination Broken. It waits slack.hello_timeout, 10 seconds, for Slack's greeting on a new socket.

items.title: Request log
items.text: The Request log of a Slack Connection records its calls to the Web API named as Slack names them, such as chat.postMessage and apps.connections.open. Over HTTP it records each press that reaches the callback address as interactive, with Muster's answer, refused ones included. In Socket Mode it records each envelope that carries an envelope id under the type of the envelope, with the socket's host as its address and Muster's confirmation as its answer; the app subscribes to no events, so only interactive envelopes arrive. Slack's greetings, disconnects and keep-alive frames are not recorded. The answers Muster sends to a press's response_url are recorded as response_url, with the address masked: look there when an answer never shows. Tokens, the Slack signing secret and the signature are masked, and so are the address of the socket, the response_url of a press, the signed ids of buttons and the code of an Account link. See Request log.

items.title: Check from the command line
items.text: muster doctor prints one line per Slack Connection and per Slack Destination with the same checks, without sending anything, and a WARN line for a Connection whose app another program shares.

items.title: Telegram in restricted networks
items.text:
Muster talks to Telegram only by calling out to the Bot API, https://api.telegram.org by default. Where the network of your installation cannot reach it — Telegram is blocked, or the cluster has no direct way out — there are three ways to reach it. Use them in this order:

  1. A proxy on the Connection, when a proxy can reach Telegram.
  2. A reverse proxy under your own domain, when you run a host that can reach Telegram.
  3. A self-hosted Bot API server, only when neither of the first two works. It has sharp edges that the first two avoid.

All three keep the bot in Telegram's cloud or move it to one server you control; none needs a change to the Destinations.

items.title: 1. A proxy on the Connection
items.text:
Each Connection may send its requests through its own proxy, while the rest of Muster — other Connections, the identity provider, outgoing webhooks — keeps its own path. On the Connection page, under Proxy, turn on Use a proxy and set:

  • Type: HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS5;
  • Address: host:port of the proxy;
  • Username and Password, if the proxy asks for them. The password is stored encrypted and never shown again.

Leave the Bot API base URL at https://api.telegram.org: the HTTPS connection to Telegram runs through the proxy end to end, so the proxy never sees the bot token in the request path. Press Check connection: every step shows its latency and whether it went "through the proxy" or "direct", and a proxy that refuses Muster's credentials is named as such. Pressed before you save a new proxy, the check sends the stored token nowhere and makes only the dry probe through it, unless you type the bot token again (see Check before saving).

The proxy's own address is checked by the Organization's outbound address policy (Outbound addresses, /admin/organization/outbound) like any other target: the standard policy allows private addresses and blocks loopback; the strict policy blocks a proxy on a private address unless an allowed network covers it. HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY are never read; the proxy is set only on the Connection.

items.title: 2. A reverse proxy under your own domain
items.text:
When a host that you run can reach api.telegram.org — for example a small virtual machine in another network — put a reverse proxy on it, under a name of your installation's own domain such as tg.muster.example.org, in front of api.telegram.org. Muster then calls your domain, and only that host talks to Telegram.

The reverse proxy must:

  • connect to api.telegram.org over HTTPS with the upstream SNI and the Host header set to api.telegram.org;
  • allow the upstream to answer for longer than the long-polling timeout. In the long polling update mode, Muster asks Telegram to hold each getUpdates request open for up to 25 seconds and waits up to 35 seconds for the answer; give the proxy timeouts of 60 seconds;
  • limit the request body size. Muster sends no files, only messages of at most 4,096 characters and their buttons, so 1 MB is plenty;
  • turn the access log off, or write it without the request URI: every request path carries the bot token, as in /bot123456789:AA…/sendMessage;
  • answer only Muster: put everything under a secret path prefix, a long random string that is never logged, and refuse every other path, or allow only Muster's egress addresses with an address allowlist, or both.

Then set the Connection's Bot API base URL to the reverse proxy, with the prefix: https://tg.muster.example.org/8f1c2e…. Muster sends its requests to <base>/bot<token>/<method>. A new base URL needs the bot token again, so that the stored token never reaches an address you did not mean; type it again and press Check connection before you save: the check runs its three steps against the new address with the typed token; without the token it makes only the dry probe there (see Check before saving). Its first step is a dry probe, GET <base>/bot0:x/getMe without your token, which api.telegram.org answers with 401 and JSON: it tells a wrong host, a wrong path prefix or a server that is not a Bot API apart before your token goes anywhere. Use an https base URL; with http, Muster warns that the token travels in clear text.

items.title: nginx
items.text:
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name tg.muster.example.org;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/tls/tg.muster.example.org.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/tls/tg.muster.example.org.key;

    # Every request path carries the bot token.
    access_log off;
    client_max_body_size 1m;

    # The secret path prefix; replace it with your own long random string.
    location /8f1c2e…/ {
        # An address allowlist instead of, or besides, the prefix:
        # allow 203.0.113.0/28;
        # deny all;

        proxy_pass https://api.telegram.org/;
        proxy_ssl_server_name on;
        proxy_ssl_name api.telegram.org;
        proxy_ssl_verify on;
        proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt;
        proxy_set_header Host api.telegram.org;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;

        # Above the long-polling timeout of getUpdates.
        proxy_connect_timeout 10s;
        proxy_send_timeout 60s;
        proxy_read_timeout 60s;
    }

    location / {
        return 404;
    }
}

proxy_pass with a trailing / strips the prefix, so Telegram receives /bot<token>/<method>. nginx's error log names the request of a failed upstream call too; keep it where only administrators can read it.

items.title: Caddy
items.text:
tg.muster.example.org {
    # Caddy writes no access log unless the site has a log directive: leave it out.
    request_body {
        max_size 1MB
    }

    # The secret path prefix; replace it with your own long random string.
    handle_path /8f1c2e…/* {
        # An address allowlist instead of, or besides, the prefix:
        # @outside not remote_ip 203.0.113.0/28
        # respond @outside 404

        reverse_proxy https://api.telegram.org {
            header_up Host api.telegram.org
            transport http {
                tls_server_name api.telegram.org
                # Above the long-polling timeout of getUpdates.
                dial_timeout 10s
                response_header_timeout 60s
            }
        }
    }

    handle {
        respond 404
    }
}

handle_path strips the prefix before the request goes upstream. Caddy gets and renews the certificate of tg.muster.example.org itself. Caddy's error log entries carry the request URI, with the token, when an upstream call fails; keep that log where only administrators can read it.

items.title: 3. A self-hosted Bot API server
items.text:
Telegram publishes the source of its Bot API server (tdlib/telegram-bot-api), and a bot can be moved to a server you run. That server connects to Telegram's data centres itself, over Telegram's own protocol, not through api.telegram.org; it needs a direct route to them (its --proxy option applies only to the webhook requests it sends, not to its connection to Telegram). Use it only when neither a proxy nor a reverse proxy works: it changes where the bot lives, and every warning below applies.

  • It needs an api_id and an api_hash. The server starts only with --api-id and --api-hash, which you register at my.telegram.org with a personal Telegram account. Use a dedicated account for it, not a person's own: the server's access depends on that account.
  • A bot lives on one server at a time. While it is on your server, Telegram's cloud does not serve it, and the other way round. Every installation and every script that uses the token must use the same server.
  • logOut drops unread updates, and the way back to the cloud is closed for 10 minutes. Moving a bot off the cloud starts with logOut on api.telegram.org. Updates that Muster has not fetched by then — button presses and messages of the discussion group — are lost, and after logOut the bot cannot log in to the cloud again for 10 minutes.
  • Any request with the bot's token to api.telegram.org moves the bot back to the cloud, silently. Even a getMe from a script or a health check on another host is enough. Muster keeps sending to your server, which no longer receives the bot's updates: button presses and messages of the discussion group go missing without an error. Never call api.telegram.org with this token from anywhere while the bot is on your server.
  • The server has no authentication of its own. Anyone who reaches it can use it with any bot token. Never expose it to the internet or to networks other than Muster's; put it on a private address that only the replicas reach.
  • Tokens are visible on its statistics port. --http-stat-port serves statistics that include the bots' tokens. Leave it off, or bind it to loopback with --http-stat-ip-address 127.0.0.1 so that it stays local.
  • Do not use --local. In local mode the server accepts local paths and file:// URIs in requests and answers with absolute paths of its own disk, so anyone who reaches it can make it serve the server's files. Muster sends and receives no files and needs none of it.
  • There are no releases. The project publishes no releases or tags, and container images built from it carry no version you can rely on. Build your own image, or pin a third-party image by digest (image@sha256:…), never by a tag such as latest.
  • Route MusterDestinationBroken of Telegram Destinations elsewhere. When the server stops, every Telegram Destination of that bot becomes Broken at once. Route the Internal alert MusterDestinationBroken of Telegram Destinations to a Destination that is not in Telegram — Mattermost or an outgoing webhook — and its chart rule around Muster.

The server's address is an ordinary target of the outbound address policy: the standard policy allows a private address and blocks loopback.

items.title: Move a bot between servers
items.text:
Muster has no wizard for this; the move is a manual procedure. Plan for a short gap in which presses and messages of the discussion group are lost.

What Muster does with deleteWebhook: it calls deleteWebhook only when a Connection leaves the webhook update mode — saved from Webhook to Long polling — and calls it at the base URL saved before, the server the bot is leaving. When that call fails, the save fails ("deleteWebhook failed: …") and nothing changes. Changing only the base URL while the Connection stays in the webhook mode calls setWebhook at the new base URL and never deleteWebhook at the old one. Deleting a Connection in the webhook mode also calls deleteWebhook, best effort, at its saved base URL: the outcome is logged (telegram_webhook_deleted or telegram_webhook_delete_failed) and never fails the deletion. Muster never calls logOut or close.

From Telegram's cloud to your server:

  1. Start the Bot API server as above and check from a replica that it answers: curl -s http://bot-api.internal.example.org:8081/bot0:x/getMe returns 401 and JSON. The server listens on plain HTTP (port 8081 by default); with an http base URL Muster warns that the token travels in clear text, which is acceptable only on a private network or through a tunnel.
  2. If the Connection uses the webhook update mode, switch it to Long polling and save while the old server still answers, so that Muster's own deleteWebhook reaches it. If the save fails, fix the path to the old server first.
  3. Stop every other process that uses the bot's token.

  4. Optionally call deleteWebhook yourself on the old server, then logOut:

    curl -s "https://api.telegram.org/bot$TOKEN/deleteWebhook"
curl -s "https://api.telegram.org/bot$TOKEN/logOut"

    The deleteWebhook before logOut is a best-effort step: if it fails, go on with logOut; it does not stop the move. 5. On the Connection, set the Bot API base URL to your server, enter the bot token again, and save. 6. Press Check connection: the dry probe, then getMe and getWebhookInfo with your token against the saved base URL. Run muster doctor too; it checks the saved Connections the same way. 7. Switch back to the webhook update mode if you used it: Muster calls setWebhook on your server.

From one server you run to another, use the same steps on the old server, as Telegram documents in Moving a bot from one local server to another, in one of two ways:

  • call logOut on the old server instead of on api.telegram.org; updates not yet fetched are lost;
  • or call deleteWebhook and then close on the old server, and move the bot's subdirectory — named by the bot's user id, the number before the colon in its token — from the old server's working directory to the new server's; no updates are lost. close answers 429 during the first 10 minutes after the bot started on that server.

Back to Telegram's cloud: the same steps in the other direction — switch to long polling while your server still answers, logOut on your server, then set the base URL back to https://api.telegram.org with the token. The cloud takes the bot back only when 10 minutes have passed since its logOut from the cloud.

See also Telegram's logOut, close and Using a Local Bot API Server.

items.title: Connect Telegram
items.text:
Muster posts to a Telegram channel through the Bot API with a bot: one channel post per Alert Group, the Root message, which Muster edits as the Alert Group changes. Everything that happens later goes to the channel's discussion group, the group that Telegram creates when comments are enabled on the channel. People act on the Alert Group with the buttons under the post.

In the examples, MUSTER_INGEST_URL is https://ingest.muster.example.org and the bot is @muster_alerts_bot.

items.title: Create the bot
items.text:
1. In Telegram, open @BotFather and send /newbot. Give the bot a name and a username, for example @muster_alerts_bot.
  2. Copy the bot token that BotFather sends, such as 123456789:AA…. Anyone with the token controls the bot; Muster stores it encrypted and never shows it again.
  3. Leave the bot's privacy mode on, the default. Muster needs no other setting in BotFather.

items.title: Create the Connection
items.text:
1. In Muster, open Connections, select Create connection and choose Telegram.

  2. Enter a Name, select Set a value next to Bot token and paste the bot token. Keep the Bot API base URL https://api.telegram.org unless Telegram is blocked in your network; for a proxy or another address, see Telegram in restricted networks. Keep the Update mode Long polling unless Telegram can reach Muster: see Long polling or webhook.

  3. Select Check connection, below the form. The check runs in steps and shows the latency of each and whether it went through the proxy:

    1. a dry probe, GET <base>/bot0:x/getMe without your token, which only a Bot API answers with 401 and JSON — it tells a wrong address, a wrong path prefix, a proxy that refuses or a web server that is not a Bot API apart before your token goes anywhere;
    2. getMe with your token, which names the bot;
    3. getWebhookInfo, which says whether a webhook is set and how many updates wait.

  4. Select Save. On the saved Connection, Check connection records the bot, which the page then names.

items.title: Check before saving
items.text:
Check connection checks the values in the form, before anything is saved: in the form of a new Connection, as above, and on the page of a saved one while the form holds changes. It saves nothing: no bot name is recorded and the Audit log gets no entry.

  • With the bot token typed in the form, the check runs its three steps against the base URL in the form, through the proxy in the form, with that token.
  • Without a token typed, the page of a saved Connection uses its stored token only when the base URL — a trailing / aside — and the proxy are the saved ones: the stored token is sent only to the saved address, through the saved proxy, since a proxy you have not saved would see it in the path of an http base URL. After a change of the base URL or of the proxy, the check makes only the dry probe there, GET <base>/bot0:x/getMe without your token, and getMe and getWebhookInfo ask you to type the bot token again to check the new address or proxy, or to save first. A new Connection without a token gets the dry probe alone too.

The check is POST /api/v1/connections/checks, which needs connections:write; with a Personal access token of an Admin in MUSTER_TOKEN:

curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/connections/checks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"telegram","bot_api_base_url":"https://api.telegram.org","update_mode":"long_polling",
       "bot_token":"123456789:AA…"}'

Add "connection_id":"CN…" to check the changes of a saved Connection, whose stored token the rule above may use.

items.title: Enable comments on the channel
items.text:
A Telegram Destination is a channel with comments. Comments on a channel post live in the channel's discussion group, and Muster writes everything about an Alert Group after its Root message there.

  1. Create the channel, or open an existing one.
  2. In the channel's settings, open Discussion and add a group, or let Telegram create one. This enables comments, and Telegram links the group to the channel.

You never enter the group in Muster: the Destination check finds it through the channel.

items.title: Make the bot an admin of the channel and of the group
items.text:
1. In the channel's settings, under Administrators, add the bot. Telegram adds a bot to a channel only as an admin: added as a subscriber, it stays outside the channel. Allow it to post messages and to edit messages of others; Muster needs both, because it edits its own posts as the Alert Group changes.
  2. In the discussion group's settings, under Administrators, add the bot as well. An admin may always post in the group. The bot must be an admin, not a plain member: Telegram does not send a bot that is a plain member the copies of the channel's posts in the group, which the Threads of the Root messages hang under.

items.title: Add a Destination
items.text:
A Telegram Destination is the channel only: Muster finds its discussion group.

  1. Open Destinations, select Create destination and choose Telegram.

  2. Choose the Connection and enter the Channel: its chat id, such as -1001234567890, or @username for a public channel. Give the Destination a Name.

  3. Select Save. Saving runs the Destination check:

    • getChat on the channel: it exists and is a channel, and it names its discussion group;
    • getChatMember for the bot in the channel: an admin allowed to post and to edit messages;
    • getChatMember for the bot in the discussion group: an admin there.

    A Destination that fails the check is not saved, and the check says what to fix:

    • "Comments are not enabled for this channel. Enable comments in the channel settings in Telegram; this creates its discussion group."
    • "The bot is not an admin of the discussion group {group}. Make the bot an admin there, allowed to post messages."
    • "The bot is not an admin of the channel.", "The bot may not post messages in the channel." or "The bot may not edit messages in the channel."

    The saved Destination shows the channel and the discussion group it found.

  4. Under Test and preview, on the tab Test, select Send test message. A message marked 🧪 appears in the channel; the result shows the request Muster sent, with the bot token as bot[redacted], and Telegram's answer. Links in the screenshot start with http://localhost:8080, the address of a development installation; yours start with your MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL.

Muster keeps sending to that channel and that group: when comments are moved to another group later, or the @username to another channel, the check fails with "The channel or its discussion group changed since the Destination was saved. Save the Destination again." until you save it. Check on the Destination page runs the same check at any time, and muster doctor prints one line per Telegram Destination with its result. When Telegram refuses the bot later — for example, someone removed its admin rights — the Destination becomes Broken; Muster runs the same check every few minutes while nothing waits for the Destination, and ends the Broken state once the check passes again.

items.title: Long polling or webhook
items.text:
Muster receives the bot's updates — button presses and the messages of the discussion group — in one of two update modes, set on the Connection:

  • Long polling, the default. The Leader asks Telegram for updates with getUpdates. Muster needs no public address: it only calls out to Telegram. Only one process may poll a bot: when a second one starts — another Muster installation with the same token, or a test script — Telegram ends one of the polls with 409 Conflict, and the two then take turns. Muster backs off and logs telegram_poll_conflict; the Destination does not become Broken. Give each installation its own bot.
  • Webhook. Telegram posts each update to Muster at https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/telegram/CN…, under MUSTER_INGEST_URL, with a secret token header that Muster checks. Saving the Connection in this mode calls setWebhook; leaving the mode, or deleting the Connection, calls deleteWebhook. Use the webhook mode when Telegram can reach MUSTER_INGEST_URL over HTTPS.

Where Telegram is blocked, a Connection can reach the Bot API through a proxy or through another Bot API address; see Telegram in restricted networks.

items.title: Join the discussion group and mute the channel
items.text:
For the people on call:

  • Join the discussion group, and mute the channel itself. Telegram copies every channel post into the discussion group, so each new Alert Group reaches the members of the group once, through its copy, with the Thread of its replies under it.
  • Only members of the discussion group are notified about the replies in a Thread — even a reply that mentions them. Someone who only subscribed to the channel sees the Root messages, but not what happens to them later.

items.title: Known limitation: Quiet Root messages ring the group
items.text: A Quiet Root message is sent with disable_notification, which in Telegram silences the notification but does not remove it. Members of the discussion group still get a notification with sound for every new Alert Group, because Telegram notifies them about the copy of the post in the group, and that copy cannot be sent without sound.

items.title: What Muster sends
items.text:
• The Root message is a regular message in Telegram's HTML: the status and #N with the title, linked to the Alert Group page, the labels in an expandable quote, the summary, one line per Alert — never a table, which phones cannot show — the link to Muster and the footer. The footer — "Acknowledged by", "Snoozed by", "Resolved by" — names a person with a Telegram Account link by a link to their account with their Muster name, as a Mention does, and anyone else by their name as text. Alert data are escaped, so a label value cannot format the message or mention anyone. A message is at most 4,096 characters: a long one drops its Alert lines first, then the label sections, but always keeps its title, status, footer, buttons and link to Muster.
  • Every edit of the Root message carries all its buttons again, because Telegram removes the buttons of a message edited without them. The bot may edit its own messages at any age.
  • Muster never replies inside the channel: a reply there would be a new post that notifies every subscriber.
  • The bot token never appears in a log line, an error, the Timeline or a metric: logs show the scheme and host of the Bot API address only, and the token in a request path is written as bot[redacted].

items.title: Write a bridge
items.text: A bridge connects Muster to a messenger that Muster does not support natively. This page is for the people who write one. It starts with the bridge libraries, which do the protocol's part of a bridge, and then describes the Bridge protocol step by step for a bridge written without a library. If you run a bridge that somebody else wrote, read Connect a messenger through a bridge instead.

items.title: What a bridge is, and when to write one
items.text:
Muster has native support for Mattermost, Slack and Telegram. For any other messenger, Muster talks to a bridge: a small HTTP service that you write and run. Muster calls the bridge to post, edit and reply to messages. The bridge calls the messenger. When people press a button or write in a Thread, the bridge reports it back to Muster as an event.

Write a bridge when your team uses a messenger with a bot API that Muster does not support. A bridge does not need to live in Muster's repository, and it may stay closed: the protocol is MIT licensed (see Licence).

flowchart TB
  subgraph muster["Muster"]
    calls["Delivery worker and interactive path"]
    poller["Poller"]
    callback["Push callback on the ingest listener"]
    handler["Commands and Account links"]
    health["Destination health"]
  end
  subgraph bridge["Your bridge"]
    api["Bridge protocol: the /v1/ operations"]
    queue["Event queue"]
  end
  messenger["Your messenger"]

  calls -- "getInfo, postMessage, editMessage, replyInThread, checkChannel, answerEvent, findUsers, sendDirectMessage" --> api
  api -- "calls the messenger's own API" --> messenger
  messenger -- "presses, Thread messages, direct messages, deletions" --> queue
  poller -- "poll mode: pollEvents" --> queue
  queue -. "push mode: bridgeEvent, signed" .-> callback
  poller --> handler
  callback --> handler
  api -. "answers and error classes" .-> health
  health -- "Broken, every 5 minutes: the oldest waiting delivery, or checkChannel when nothing waits" --> api

Muster is always the caller of the /v1/ operations, and the bridge is always the caller of the messenger. Events travel the other way, in one of two modes that the Admin chooses on the Bridge Connection: Muster polls the bridge with pollEvents, or the bridge pushes each event, signed, to Muster's callback address. The bridge answers every call with a result or an error class, and Muster turns those into the health of the Destination: a Destination whose bridge keeps failing, or refuses the channel, becomes Broken until a check succeeds (see Run your bridge).

Terms follow Muster's glossary: a Root message is the one editable message that shows an Alert Group in a channel of the messenger, its Thread holds the replies under it, and a Mention is a deliberate @-reference. A Bridge Connection in Muster is one bot of your messenger behind one bridge: one token is one bot.

items.title: Start with a library
items.text: Most bridge authors should not write the protocol again. A bridge library does the protocol's part of a bridge, and you write only the calls to your messenger.

items.title: What a library does, and what is left to you
items.text:
A library:

  • serves every operation of the protocol under /v1/;
  • checks the token of each bot in constant time, and keeps the events and idempotency keys of each bot apart;
  • validates every request against api/bridge.yaml and every answer before it is sent, and enforces the bridge's limits;
  • keeps each Idempotency-Key with its result and answers a repeated key with that result and replayed: true;
  • builds the answer to getInfo from the features and limits you give it;
  • answers failures as problems with an error class, and never logs a token or a push secret;
  • queues events for pollEvents, and pushes them with Standard Webhooks signatures and retries;
  • turns a direct message that carries an Account link token into an account_link event.

You write:

  • the calls to your messenger: post, edit, reply in a Thread, check a channel and show an answer to a person, and, where the messenger offers them, finding a person, sending a direct message and deleting a message;
  • the mapping of the messenger's failures to the five error classes (see Error classes);
  • the reports of what people do: a press, a message in a Thread, a deleted message and a direct message;
  • the rendering of the envelope in the messenger's markup (see Rendering the envelope).

The Go library, muster-bridge-go, is released from its own repository, under the MIT licence and without a CLA. The same holds for every bridge library of the project.

items.title: The Go library
items.text:
The Go module is github.com/muster-io/muster-bridge-go, and its package is bridge.

go get github.com/muster-io/muster-bridge-go

Each release of a library is a tag vX.Y.Z, and go get without a version takes the newest release. Versions stay 0.x until Muster 1.0, and every library release speaks the protocol versions Muster supports at that time, today protocol version 1; a breaking protocol change is a new protocol version, not a new major version of a library.

1. Implement bridge.Messenger. It has five methods, each given the name of the bot whose token Muster sent: PostMessage, EditMessage, ReplyInThread, CheckChannel and AnswerEvent. The sketch below is for Parley, a fictional messenger; its client parleyClient stands for whatever library your messenger has.

// parleyMessenger is the bridge's calls to the fictional messenger Parley.
type parleyMessenger struct{ api *parleyClient }

// mention is how Parley writes a mention of a person.
func mention(p bridge.Mention) string { return "<@" + p.ExternalId + ">" }

func (m *parleyMessenger) PostMessage(ctx context.Context, bot string, in bridge.MessageInput) (
    bridge.MessagePosted, error) {
    body := bridge.ReplaceMentions(in.Body, in.Mentions, mention)
    id, err := m.api.Send(ctx, in.ChannelId, render(in.Title, body))
    if err != nil {
        return bridge.MessagePosted{}, classify(err)
    }
    return bridge.MessagePosted{MessageId: id}, nil
}

func (m *parleyMessenger) EditMessage(ctx context.Context, bot, messageID string, in bridge.MessageContent) (
    bridge.MessageEdited, error) {
    if err := m.api.Edit(ctx, messageID, render(in.Title, in.Body)); err != nil {
        return bridge.MessageEdited{}, classify(err)
    }
    return bridge.MessageEdited{}, nil
}

func (m *parleyMessenger) ReplyInThread(ctx context.Context, bot, messageID string, in bridge.ThreadReplyInput) (
    bridge.ThreadReplyPosted, error) {
    var thread string
    if in.ThreadRef != nil {
        thread = *in.ThreadRef
    }
    body := bridge.ReplaceMentions(in.Body, in.Mentions, mention)
    id, thread, err := m.api.Reply(ctx, messageID, thread, body)
    if err != nil {
        return bridge.ThreadReplyPosted{}, classify(err)
    }
    return bridge.ThreadReplyPosted{MessageId: id, ThreadRef: thread}, nil
}

func (m *parleyMessenger) CheckChannel(ctx context.Context, bot, channelID string) (string, error) {
    name, err := m.api.ChannelName(ctx, channelID)
    if err != nil {
        return "", classify(err)
    }
    return name, nil
}

// AnswerEvent answers an Account link in its direct chat, a Thread message in its Thread, and a press privately.
func (m *parleyMessenger) AnswerEvent(ctx context.Context, bot string, ev bridge.ReportedEvent, text string) (
    bridge.AnswerShownShownAs, error) {
    switch ev.Type {
    case bridge.EventTypeAccountLink:
        if err := m.api.SendDirect(ctx, ev.Chat, text); err != nil {
            return "", classify(err)
        }
        return bridge.AnswerShownShownAsDirect, nil
    case bridge.EventTypeThreadMessage:
        if _, _, err := m.api.Reply(ctx, ev.MessageID, ev.ThreadRef, text); err != nil {
            return "", classify(err)
        }
        return bridge.AnswerShownShownAsThread, nil
    default:
        if err := m.api.Whisper(ctx, ev.Chat, text); err != nil {
            return "", classify(err)
        }
        return bridge.AnswerShownShownAsEphemeral, nil
    }
}

For the features you declare, also implement UserFinder (when UserLookup is not none), DirectMessenger (when the bridge offers direct messages) and Deleter (when it offers deletion). bridge.New refuses a configuration whose features lack their interface, or whose info would not match the protocol, and names the reason.

2. Answer failures with error classes. A method returns bridge.TransientError, bridge.RateLimitedError, bridge.GoneError (with bridge.ReasonEditWindowClosed for an edit that the messenger refuses only for the message's age), bridge.ForbiddenError or bridge.InvalidError. Any other error, and a panic, is answered as transient.

// classify tells Muster what a failure of Parley means. Only the bridge knows.
func classify(err error) error {
    var pe *parleyError
    if !errors.As(err, &pe) {
        return bridge.TransientError("Parley did not answer.")
    }
    switch pe.Code {
    case "slow_down":
        return bridge.RateLimitedError(time.Duration(pe.RetryIn)*time.Second, bridge.ProblemScopeChannel,
            "Parley asks to slow down.")
    case "message_not_found", "thread_removed":
        return bridge.GoneError("The message no longer exists.")
    case "edit_too_old":
        return bridge.GoneError("The message can no longer be edited.", bridge.ReasonEditWindowClosed)
    case "channel_not_found", "not_a_member", "bot_banned", "no_permission":
        return bridge.ForbiddenError("The bot is not a member of this channel.")
    case "user_blocked_bot":
        return bridge.ForbiddenError("This person cannot receive a message from the bot.")
    case "text_too_long", "bad_request":
        return bridge.InvalidError("Parley refused the request.")
    default:
        return bridge.TransientError("Parley is not available.")
    }
}

3. Create the bridge with bridge.New. Give it the bot's token in Config.Bots, the features in Config.Capabilities and the limits in Config.Limits, and mount b.Handler() behind an HTTP server. The code below is the body of a function that returns an error.

token, err := os.ReadFile("/run/secrets/muster-token")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
messenger := &parleyMessenger{api: &parleyClient{}}

b, err := bridge.New(bridge.Config{
    Name:          "parley-bridge",
    Version:       "0.1.0",
    MessengerName: "Parley",
    Bots:          []bridge.Bot{{Name: "main", Token: strings.TrimSpace(string(token))}},
    Limits:        bridge.Limits{MaxBodyLength: 4000},
    Capabilities: bridge.Capabilities{
        Buttons: &bridge.Capabilities_Buttons{MaxPerMessage: 5, MaxPerRow: 5, DataMaxBytes: 64,
            Styles: []bridge.ButtonStyle{bridge.ButtonStylePrimary, bridge.ButtonStyleSuccess,
                bridge.ButtonStyleNeutral, bridge.ButtonStyleDanger}},
        ThreadMessages: new(bridge.CapabilitiesThreadMessagesAll),
        PrivateAnswers: &[]bridge.CapabilitiesPrivateAnswers{bridge.CapabilitiesPrivateAnswersEphemeral},
    },
    UserLookup: bridge.InfoUserLookupNone,
}, messenger)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer b.Close(context.Background())

srv := &http.Server{
    Addr:              "127.0.0.1:8095",
    Handler:           b.Handler(),
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
    // No WriteTimeout: pollEvents holds a request open for up to 60 seconds.
}
return srv.ListenAndServe()

MaxBodyLength is the longest body that your bridge always accepts, after its own rendering; the protocol's smallest value is 500, and the library takes at most 100000. Capabilities lists the optional features: a nil member is a feature the bridge does not offer, and Muster never calls an operation that the bridge did not declare. To serve the handler under a path prefix, mount it with http.StripPrefix.

No WriteTimeout

pollEvents holds a request open for up to 60 seconds. Serve the handler with no WriteTimeout, or one above 75 seconds. A shorter one cuts a poll off without an answer, and its events reach Muster late. ReadHeaderTimeout and IdleTimeout are safe to set.

4. Report what happens in the messenger. When a person presses a button, writes in a Thread, deletes a message of the bot or writes to the bot, call b.Press, b.ThreadMessage, b.MessageDeleted or b.DirectMessage. Each returns at once, so confirm a press to your messenger within its deadline whatever Muster does. Give the messenger's own id of the update as UpdateID: an update that the messenger delivers twice is then queued once.

// onPress is called when a person presses a button in Parley. chat is what AnswerEvent needs to whisper to
// the person; the library keeps it with the event and never sends it to Muster.
func onPress(ctx context.Context, b *bridge.Bridge, updateID, messageID, data, chat string, who bridge.Person) error {
    // ... confirm the press to Parley first, then report it. Press returns at once.
    return b.Press(ctx, "main", bridge.Press{
        UpdateID: updateID, MessageID: messageID, User: who, Data: data, Chat: chat,
    })
}

Chat comes back as ReportedEvent.Chat when Muster answers the event; b.ThreadMessage and b.DirectMessage take one too.

A direct message whose whole text is an Account link token becomes an account_link event; any other direct message is ignored.

5. Turn Mention markers into mentions. bridge.ReplaceMentions(body, mentions, render) replaces each marker [@Name](muster-mention:ref) by what render returns for its entry in mentions, as the sketch above does. For a bridge without NativeMentions, pass a nil render and the markers become plain names.

6. Push, if you want it. Give a bot a bridge.PushTarget with the callback address that its Bridge Connection shows and the push secret you entered on it, in Config.Bots or later with b.SetPush. b.Close stops the pushers.

7. Use a Store that survives restarts. bridge.NewMemoryStore, the default, keeps the idempotency keys and the queued events in memory. A restart forgets them: a retried request that Muster sends after the restart then posts a second message, and events that Muster has not collected are lost. Implement bridge.Store over your database and set Config.Store. Long polls and pushers are woken in the process that queued an event, so with several processes over one store, run each bot in one process only.

8. Check it. Run muster bridge check against your bridge (see Test your bridge).

The library's repository has a complete bridge in one file, examples/minimal: its messenger lives in memory and writes every message the bot posts to the log. From a clone of the repository, with Go 1.26 or newer, run it with a token, the one a Bridge Connection in Muster would hold:

git clone --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/muster-io/muster-bridge-go && cd muster-bridge-go
printf example-token > /tmp/bt
go run ./examples/minimal -token-file /tmp/bt

It listens on 127.0.0.1:18095, knows the channels alerts and ops and the people alice and bob, and offers every feature of the protocol. In another terminal:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' 127.0.0.1:18095/v1/info          # 401: no token
curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer example-token' 127.0.0.1:18095/v1/info \
  | jq -c '{protocol_version, user_lookup}'                                 # {"protocol_version":"1","user_lookup":"login"}

Then run muster bridge check against it, here from Muster's image, which reaches the host's loopback with --network host on Linux only:

docker run --rm --network host -v /tmp/bt:/token:ro ghcr.io/muster-io/muster:latest bridge check \
  http://127.0.0.1:18095 --token-file /token --channel alerts --forbidden-channel nobot --handle alice \
  --no-interactive

PASS info
PASS channel_check
PASS post
PASS replayed_key
PASS buttons
PASS edit
PASS thread_reply
PASS thread_ref
PASS forbidden_channel
PASS user_lookup
PASS direct_message
PASS delete
PASS poll
SKIP press: --no-interactive
SKIP push: --no-interactive
PASS answer

The package documentation on pkg.go.dev describes what the library does for every operation.

items.title: The Python library
items.text:
The Python library is muster-bridge on PyPI, and its import package is muster_bridge. It needs Python 3.11 or newer and depends only on Starlette, httpx and pydantic 2. Like the Go library, it is released from its own repository, muster-bridge-python, under the MIT licence and without a CLA.

python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install muster-bridge

Its versions stay 0.x until Muster 1.0 and speak the protocol versions Muster supports, as the Go library's do.

The library serves the protocol as an ASGI application, BridgeApp, and calls your code with async methods on the event loop that serves the bridge. Call your messenger with an asynchronous client, or move a blocking call off the loop with asyncio.to_thread.

1. Implement Messenger. It is a protocol of five coroutines, each given the name of the bot whose token Muster sent: post_message, edit_message, reply_in_thread, check_channel and answer_event. Define them with async def. The sketch below is for Parley, the same fictional messenger; its asynchronous client ParleyClient stands for whatever library your messenger has.

from muster_bridge import (
    AnswerShownShownAs,
    Mention,
    MessageContent,
    MessageEdited,
    MessageInput,
    MessagePosted,
    ReportedEvent,
    ThreadReplyInput,
    ThreadReplyPosted,
    replace_mentions,
)


def mention(m: Mention) -> str:
    """Write a mention of a person as Parley does."""
    return f"<@{m.external_id}>"


class ParleyMessenger:
    """The bridge's calls to the fictional messenger Parley."""

    def __init__(self, api: ParleyClient) -> None:
        self.api = api

    async def post_message(self, bot: str, message: MessageInput) -> MessagePosted:
        body = replace_mentions(message.body, message.mentions, mention)
        try:
            message_id = await self.api.send(message.channel_id, render(message.title, body))
        except ParleyError as error:
            raise classify(error) from error
        return MessagePosted(message_id=message_id)

    async def edit_message(self, bot: str, message_id: str, content: MessageContent) -> MessageEdited:
        try:
            await self.api.edit(message_id, render(content.title, content.body))
        except ParleyError as error:
            raise classify(error) from error
        return MessageEdited()

    async def reply_in_thread(self, bot: str, message_id: str, reply: ThreadReplyInput) -> ThreadReplyPosted:
        body = replace_mentions(reply.body, reply.mentions, mention)
        try:
            reply_id, thread = await self.api.reply(message_id, reply.thread_ref, body)
        except ParleyError as error:
            raise classify(error) from error
        return ThreadReplyPosted(message_id=reply_id, thread_ref=thread)

    async def check_channel(self, bot: str, channel_id: str) -> str:
        try:
            return await self.api.channel_name(channel_id)
        except ParleyError as error:
            raise classify(error) from error

    async def answer_event(self, bot: str, event: ReportedEvent, text: str) -> AnswerShownShownAs:
        """Answer an Account link in its direct chat, a Thread message in its Thread, and a press privately."""
        try:
            if event.type == "account_link":
                await self.api.send_direct(event.chat, text)
                return AnswerShownShownAs.direct
            if event.type == "thread_message":
                await self.api.reply(event.message_id, event.thread_ref, text)
                return AnswerShownShownAs.thread
            await self.api.whisper(event.chat, text)
            return AnswerShownShownAs.ephemeral
        except ParleyError as error:
            raise classify(error) from error

For the features you declare, also implement UserFinder (find_user, when user_lookup is not none), DirectMessenger (send_direct_message, when the bridge offers direct messages) and Deleter (delete_message, when it offers deletion). BridgeApp raises ConfigError for a configuration whose features lack their methods, or whose info would not match the protocol, and names every reason.

2. Answer failures with error classes. A method raises Transient, RateLimited (with the wait retry_after in seconds, and scope "channel" or "bot"), Gone (with edit_window_closed=True for an edit that the messenger refuses only for the message's age), Forbidden or Invalid. Each takes a detail that Muster shows the Admin, so keep secrets out of it. Any other exception is answered as transient, with a generic detail that carries none of its text.

from muster_bridge import BridgeError, Forbidden, Gone, Invalid, RateLimited, Transient


def classify(error: ParleyError) -> BridgeError:
    """Tell Muster what a failure of Parley means. Only the bridge knows."""
    match error.code:
        case "slow_down":
            return RateLimited("Parley asks to slow down.", retry_after=error.retry_in, scope="channel")
        case "message_not_found" | "thread_removed":
            return Gone("The message no longer exists.")
        case "edit_too_old":
            return Gone("The message can no longer be edited.", edit_window_closed=True)
        case "channel_not_found" | "not_a_member" | "bot_banned" | "no_permission":
            return Forbidden("The bot is not a member of this channel.")
        case "user_blocked_bot":
            return Forbidden("This person cannot receive a message from the bot.")
        case "text_too_long" | "bad_request":
            return Invalid("Parley refused the request.")
        case _:
            return Transient("Parley is not available.")

3. Create the bridge with BridgeApp. Give its Config the bot's token in bots, the features in capabilities and the limits in limits, and serve the BridgeApp with uvicorn or another ASGI server.

from pathlib import Path

import uvicorn

from muster_bridge import (
    Bot,
    BridgeApp,
    ButtonStyle,
    Capabilities,
    CapabilitiesButtons,
    CapabilitiesPrivateAnswer,
    CapabilitiesThreadMessages,
    Config,
    Limits,
)

token = Path("/run/secrets/muster-token").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()

config = Config(
    name="parley-bridge",
    version="0.1.0",
    messenger_name="Parley",
    bots=[Bot(name="main", token=token)],
    limits=Limits(max_body_length=4000, edit_max_age_seconds=None),
    capabilities=Capabilities(
        buttons=CapabilitiesButtons(
            max_per_message=5,
            max_per_row=5,
            data_max_bytes=64,
            styles=[ButtonStyle.primary, ButtonStyle.success, ButtonStyle.neutral, ButtonStyle.danger],
        ),
        thread_messages=CapabilitiesThreadMessages.all,
        private_answers=[CapabilitiesPrivateAnswer.ephemeral],
    ),
    user_lookup="none",
)
bridge = BridgeApp(config, ParleyMessenger(ParleyClient()))

uvicorn.run(bridge, host="127.0.0.1", port=8095)

max_body_length is the longest body that your bridge always accepts, after its own rendering; the protocol's smallest value is 500, and the library takes at most 100000. Limits also needs edit_max_age_seconds, how long the bot can edit a message after posting it, or None when edits never expire. A member of Capabilities left None is a feature the bridge does not offer, and Muster never calls an operation that the bridge did not declare.

To serve the bridge under a path of a Starlette or FastAPI application, mount it there and pass its lifespan to the application. The base URL of the Bridge Connection then ends with that path.

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI(lifespan=bridge.lifespan)
app.mount("/bridge", bridge)

Starlette runs the lifespan of the top-level application only, and the bridge's lifespan starts and stops its pushers. An application with a lifespan of its own enters the bridge's in it, with async with bridge.lifespan(app):. A BridgeApp has one lifespan, and its end stops the pushers for good: a program or a test that starts the application again makes a new BridgeApp.

A read timeout above 75 seconds

pollEvents holds a request open for up to 60 seconds. uvicorn sets no timeout that cuts such a request short, but a proxy in front of the bridge needs a read timeout above 75 seconds. A shorter one cuts a poll off without an answer, and its events reach Muster late.

4. Report what happens in the messenger. When a person presses a button, writes in a Thread, deletes a message of the bot or writes to the bot, await bridge.press(...), bridge.thread_message(...), bridge.message_deleted(...) or bridge.direct_message(...), all four coroutines, in the event loop that serves the bridge. Each queues the event and returns at once, so confirm a press to your messenger within its deadline whatever Muster does. Give the messenger's own id of the update as update_id: an update that the messenger delivers twice is then queued once.

from muster_bridge import BridgeApp, Person


async def on_press(bridge: BridgeApp, update_id: str, message_id: str, data: str, chat: str, who: Person) -> None:
    """Report a press in Parley.

    chat is what answer_event needs to whisper to the person; the library keeps it with the event and never sends it
    to Muster.
    """
    # ... confirm the press to Parley first, then report it. press returns at once.
