    await bridge.press("main", message_id=message_id, user=who, data=data, update_id=update_id, chat=chat)

chat comes back as ReportedEvent.chat when Muster answers the event; thread_message and direct_message take one too. Person and the other models validate when they are built, so cut a display name to 200 characters before you build the Person of a report. A report raises UnknownBotError for a bot that the Config lacks, NotOfferedError for a feature that the bridge does not offer, and InvalidEventError for an event that would not match the protocol. From another thread, hand the coroutine to the event loop with asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe.

A direct message whose whole text is an Account link token becomes an account_link event; any other direct message is ignored.

5. Turn Mention markers into mentions. replace_mentions(body, mentions, render) replaces each marker [@Name](muster-mention:ref) by what render returns for its entry in mentions, as the sketch above does. For a bridge without native_mentions, pass None as render and the markers become plain names.

6. Push, if you want it. Give a bot a PushTarget with the callback address that its Bridge Connection shows and the push secret you entered on it, in Bot(push=...) or later with bridge.set_push(bot, target), from the thread of the event loop that serves the bridge. The end of the bridge's lifespan, or await bridge.aclose(), stops the pushers; the events stay queued for polling.

7. Use a Store that survives restarts. MemoryStore, the default, keeps the idempotency keys and the queued events in memory. A restart forgets them: a retried request that Muster sends after the restart then posts a second message, and events that Muster has not collected are lost. Implement the protocol Store over your database and pass it as Config(store=...). Long polls and pushes are woken in the process that queued an event, so with several processes over one store, run each bot in one process only.

8. Check it. Run muster bridge check against your bridge (see Test your bridge).

The library's repository has a complete bridge in one file, examples/memory_bridge.py: its messenger lives in memory and writes every message the bot posts to the log. With the library installed as above, clone the repository, install uvicorn beside the library and run the example with a token, the one a Bridge Connection in Muster would hold:

git clone --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/muster-io/muster-bridge-python && cd muster-bridge-python
pip install uvicorn
printf example-token > /tmp/bt
python examples/memory_bridge.py --token-file /tmp/bt

Like the Go library's example, it listens on 127.0.0.1:18095, knows the channels alerts and ops and the people alice and bob, and offers every feature of the protocol, or only those that BRIDGE_FEATURES lists. The curl calls and the muster bridge check command of the Go library give the same answers against it. Outside the protocol, the example serves POST /demo/press, which presses the first button of a message as a person, so that a script can play the person of an interactive check. It has no authentication of its own: keep it on loopback.

The library's README and the docstrings of the package describe what the library does for every operation.

items.title: The example bridge
items.text:
The example bridge is built on the Go library and lives in its repository, in examples/chat. It is a small chat that runs in memory, with a web page: channels, Threads, buttons, direct chats between a person and the bot, and users found by login. It offers every feature of the protocol, one by one switchable, and both event delivery modes. Use it to try Muster without a real messenger, and as a reference for your own bridge.

Its image is ghcr.io/muster-io/muster-example-bridge, tagged vX.Y.Z with each release of the Go library; edge follows the master branch of the library's repository.

docker run --rm -p 8095:8095 -e BRIDGE_TOKEN=example-token ghcr.io/muster-io/muster-example-bridge:v0.1.0

The page is then at http://127.0.0.1:8095/, and the protocol under /v1/ on the same port. BRIDGE_FEATURES limits the features the example offers, comma-separated: with BRIDGE_FEATURES=thread_messages, for one, it shows no buttons, and people answer with Text commands in Threads.

The page has no authentication

The protocol under /v1/ needs the token, but the example's page and its JSON API under /chat/api/ have no authentication of their own: whoever reaches them reads every message and acts as any person. Keep the example on your machine's loopback, or put it behind an authenticating proxy.

Next to muster dev:

  1. Start muster dev from a Muster checkout (make dev) and sign in.
  2. Start the example on the host's loopback at 127.0.0.1:18095. From a checkout of the library, go run ./examples/chat -token-file <file> listens there by default. With the image on Linux, use --network host, mount the token file, and give -listen 127.0.0.1:18095 -token-file /token, because the image listens on :8095 otherwise. The image runs as the user 65532, so the mounted file must be readable by that user, for example with mode 0644. muster dev lets Muster call loopback addresses; elsewhere the Organization's outbound address policy blocks them, and you allow the example's address there.
  3. Create a Bridge Connection with the base URL http://127.0.0.1:18095, the token you gave the example and the event delivery Polling. Check connection shows "Messenger: Example chat" and the features the example offers.
  4. Create a Destination on that Connection for the channel alerts. Send test message makes the message "🧪 Test message" appear in #alerts on the page.
  5. Alert Groups that a Route sends to the Destination appear in #alerts, one Root message each. A press acts for the Muster User whose account is linked to the person who pressed, so link an account first: copy the token from your profile, pick the person under "You are", open their direct chat with the bot under "Direct", and send the token.

Next to the Quick start: run the example as one more service of the compose project, so that Muster reaches it by name and nothing on the host's loopback is involved.

  1. In the directory of the Quick start, where docker-compose.yml and .env are, add a token to .env and write a file compose.override.yaml next to them, which Docker Compose merges into the project by itself. docker compose up -d --wait then starts the example, and leaves Muster running if it already runs:

    echo "EXAMPLE_BRIDGE_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 16)" >> .env
cat >compose.override.yaml <<'EOF'
services:
  example-bridge:
    image: ghcr.io/muster-io/muster-example-bridge:v0.1.0
    environment:
      BRIDGE_TOKEN: ${EXAMPLE_BRIDGE_TOKEN}
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8095:8095"
    restart: unless-stopped
EOF
docker compose up -d --wait

    The example's page is published on the loopback of the host only, at http://127.0.0.1:8095/, because it has no authentication (see the warning above). On a VM, reach it with an SSH tunnel, ssh -L 8095:localhost:8095 <vm>. The whole port is published, so /v1/ is reachable on the host's loopback too, and it needs the token. Muster reaches the example inside the compose network. 2. Create a Bridge Connection with the base URL http://example-bridge:8095, the token from .env (grep EXAMPLE_BRIDGE_TOKEN .env) and the event delivery Polling. The Organization's outbound address policy is Standard, which allows the private address that the name resolves to; only loopback is blocked. 3. Then do the check of step 3 above, which shows "Messenger: Example chat", and steps 4 and 5: a Destination for the channel alerts, and an account link to press buttons. Do not create the loopback Connection of step 3.

To remove the example and keep Muster and its data, run docker compose rm -sf example-bridge and delete compose.override.yaml. Do not run docker compose down -v for this: it deletes Muster's database too.

For Push, choose a push secret (see Push), enter it in the Connection, and restart the example with BRIDGE_PUSH_URL set to the callback address that the Connection shows, and the secret in BRIDGE_PUSH_SECRET or in the file of -push-secret-file. With the compose service, set BRIDGE_PUSH_URL in the override's environment to the callback address with the service name of Muster, http://muster:8080/api/v1/callbacks/bridge/<id>, not localhost: the example reaches Muster inside the compose network.

items.title: The protocol without a library
items.text:
This part describes the protocol in the order a bridge author implements it. The full definition is the Bridge protocol reference, rendered from api/bridge.yaml; the page Bridge protocol in the Reference gives its version and the specification itself. Every request and answer below follows that specification. The values in the examples are examples only.

Conventions.

  • Every path is under /v1/. GET /v1/info returns protocol_version "1". A bridge ignores request fields it does not know, and Muster ignores fields of info it does not know. A change that breaks existing bridges gets a new major path.
  • Muster sends the Connection's token on every request as Authorization: Bearer <token>. The bridge answers 401 to a missing or wrong token. Muster sends the token only to the base URL saved on the Connection, and follows no redirects.
  • The Bridge Connection's base URL may have a path prefix. Muster sends every request to <base URL>/v1/….
  • message_id and channel_id are opaque strings of up to 512 characters. Muster percent-encodes each as one path segment, and the bridge decodes it.
  • Request bodies are JSON, with Content-Type: application/json. Errors are application/problem+json.
  • One token is one bot. A bridge that serves several Connections tells them apart by the token.

What every bridge implements: getInfo, postMessage, editMessage, replyInThread, checkChannel, answerEvent, and events by pollEvents, by the bridgeEvent push, or by both. A bridge sends at least account_link events, because every bridge takes Account link tokens. Everything else is optional and declared in the capabilities of info.

items.title: getInfo
items.text:
Muster calls it on every Connection check, and again before a call that depends on it when its copy is older than 10 minutes. A bridge whose features change is therefore picked up without a restart of Muster.

GET /v1/info HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "protocol_version": "1",
  "bridge": { "name": "parley-bridge", "version": "0.1.0" },
  "messenger": { "name": "Parley" },
  "capabilities": {
    "buttons": { "max_per_message": 5, "max_per_row": 5, "data_max_bytes": 64,
                 "styles": ["primary", "success", "neutral", "danger"] },
    "thread_messages": "all",
    "direct_messages": { "bot_can_start": true },
    "private_answers": ["ephemeral"],
    "native_mentions": true,
    "quiet_messages": true,
    "status_color": true
  },
  "limits": { "max_body_length": 4000, "edit_max_age_seconds": null },
  "user_lookup": "login",
  "event_delivery": ["poll", "push"],
  "link_url_template": "https://chat.example.org/bots/muster?start={token}"
}
  • messenger.name is shown on the Connection and the Destinations.
  • limits.max_body_length is the longest body you always accept, in code points, at least 500. limits.edit_max_age_seconds is how long after posting the bot can still edit a message, at least 300, or null when edits never expire.
  • user_lookup is what a person enters to be found for an Account link by code: email, login, username, user_id or none.
  • event_delivery lists the modes you offer, poll, push or both. Each Connection chooses one.
  • link_url_template is an http or https link that opens a chat with the bot and hands it the Account link token, with {token} where the token goes. Use null or leave it out when your messenger has no such link.

The answer must match the protocol and be smaller than 64 KiB, or the Connection check fails.

items.title: checkChannel
items.text:
The Destination check. It must not post anything. Answer 200 only when the bot can post, edit its own messages and reply in Threads in the channel. Muster runs it when a Destination is saved, when a person presses Check, and every few minutes while the Destination is Broken.

POST /v1/channels/ch-alerts/check HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{ "channel_id": "ch-alerts", "name": "alerts" }

name is the channel's name as people see it. When the channel does not exist, or the bot cannot use it, answer forbidden with a detail that a person can act on:

{
  "title": "Forbidden",
  "status": 403,
  "detail": "The bot is not a member of this channel.",
  "class": "forbidden"
}

items.title: postMessage
items.text:
Posts a Root message, a Storm summary or a test message. The request carries an Idempotency-Key, and the answer names the message for later edits and Thread replies.

POST /v1/messages HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: <key>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "channel_id": "ch-alerts",
  "kind": "root",
  "status": "firing",
  "color": "#d32f2f",
  "emoji": "🔴",
  "title": "#42 HighErrorRate",
  "link": {
    "url": "https://muster.example.org/alert-groups/AGK7M3QX9P2RTA",
    "label": "Open in Muster"
  },
  "body": "[@Alice Smith](muster-mention:m1)\n\nprod · started 14:03\n\n> **namespace** payments\n\n- `api-7f9c` error rate 12 %\n- `api-5d2a` error rate 9 %\n\n[Runbook](https://wiki.example.org/runbooks/high-error-rate)",
  "buttons": [
    { "label": "Ack", "style": "primary", "data": "a1.k2.QmFzZTY0U2lnbmF0dXJlRXhhbXBsZQ" },
    { "label": "Resolve", "style": "success", "data": "a2.k2.U2Vjb25kU2lnbmF0dXJlRXhhbXBsZQ" }
  ],
  "mentions": [
    { "ref": "m1", "external_id": "u-alice", "display_name": "Alice Smith" }
  ],
  "notify": true
}

{
  "message_id": "m-77",
  "thread_ref": null,
  "url": "https://chat.example.org/c/alerts/m-77",
  "truncated": false,
  "replayed": false
}
  • kind is root, storm_summary or test. status is firing, acknowledged, snoozed, resolved or storm.
  • message_id is opaque to Muster: encode in it whatever you need to edit the message and reply under it.
  • thread_ref may be returned when the messenger's Thread id is known at once; otherwise the first replyInThread returns it (see thread_ref).
  • url is a link that opens the message in your messenger, if it has one. Muster shows it on the Alert Group page and links to it from the Thread of an older Root message.
  • truncated is true when you shortened the body to fit your messenger (see Rendering the envelope).

items.title: editMessage
items.text:
Replaces the whole message with the envelope of its new state. An edit is always Quiet and never carries Mentions, so its body has no channel_id, kind, mentions or notify. An empty buttons removes the buttons. Editing to the state that the message already shows is a success.

PATCH /v1/messages/m-77 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "status": "acknowledged",
  "color": "#f57c00",
  "emoji": "🟠",
  "title": "#42 HighErrorRate",
  "link": {
    "url": "https://muster.example.org/alert-groups/AGK7M3QX9P2RTA",
    "label": "Open in Muster"
  },
  "body": "prod · started 14:03\n\n> **namespace** payments\n\n- `api-7f9c` error rate 12 %\n- `api-5d2a` error rate 9 %",
  "buttons": [
    { "label": "Unack", "style": "neutral", "data": "a3.k2.VGhpcmRTaWduYXR1cmVFeGFtcGxl" },
    { "label": "Resolve", "style": "success", "data": "a2.k2.U2Vjb25kU2lnbmF0dXJlRXhhbXBsZQ" }
  ]
}

{ "truncated": false }

A message that no longer exists is gone. An edit that the messenger refuses because the message is older than it allows is gone with the reason edit_window_closed (see Edit windows).

items.title: replyInThread
items.text:
Posts a reply in the Thread of a message, usually a Root message. Muster sends the last thread_ref it received for that message, or null when it has none, and the bridge creates the Thread if its messenger needs that.

POST /v1/messages/m-77/thread-replies HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: <key>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "thread_ref": null,
  "body": "New alert: `api-1c3e` error rate 14 %",
  "buttons": [],
  "mentions": [],
  "notify": false
}

{
  "message_id": "m-78",
  "thread_ref": "t-77",
  "truncated": false,
  "replayed": false
}

message_id of the answer is the reply; a press on its buttons names it. A Thread that no longer exists, or a message that was deleted, is gone. A reply may carry buttons, such as "Still on it" on a Reminder, when the bridge declares buttons.

items.title: Events and answerEvent
items.text:
The rest of the required protocol is the way a person's actions reach Muster, and the way Muster answers them:

  • pollEvents, GET /v1/events, returns the events after a cursor, and the bridgeEvent push posts each event, signed, to Muster's callback address. A bridge offers either or both; the Admin chooses one per Connection. See Events.
  • answerEvent, POST /v1/answers, shows Muster's answer to the person behind an event. See Presses within 3 seconds, and answers later.

items.title: Optional: deleteMessage, findUsers and sendDirectMessage
items.text:
• DELETE /v1/messages/{message_id} is offered when capabilities.delete is declared. Muster L1 never deletes messages; the operation is reserved so that a later version of Muster can remove its test messages without a new protocol version. A message that no longer exists is a success, 204.
  • GET /v1/users?handle=alice is offered when user_lookup is not none. Muster calls it when a person asks to link an account by a code. The answer lists the one account with that handle, or none; a handle you cannot search for is invalid.
  • POST /v1/direct-messages is offered when capabilities.direct_messages is declared with bot_can_start. Muster uses it to send the code of an Account link. An account that cannot receive a message from the bot is forbidden.
GET /v1/users?handle=alice HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{ "items": [ { "external_id": "u-alice", "display_name": "Alice Smith", "handle": "alice" } ] }

POST /v1/direct-messages HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: <key>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "user_external_id": "u-alice",
  "body": "You requested a link to Muster. Do not share this code.\n\n**K7M3Q9XT**"
}

{ "message_id": "dm-12", "replayed": false }

items.title: Required and optional features
items.text:
The capabilities of info declare the optional features. A missing member means the feature is not offered, and Muster adapts:

buttons Without it: Muster sends no buttons. When the bridge has thread_messages, a Root message that is not resolved ends with the commands line, such as "Reply in the Thread: ack · resolve · snooze 1h", and people write Text commands in the Thread. Without either, the link to Muster is the only way to act. thread_messages Without it: Muster receives no Text commands. all reports every message of a person in a Thread of a message of the bot, mentions_only only those that mention the bot (the commands line then says "mentioning the bot"). direct_messages with bot_can_start, and a user_lookup other than none Without it: Account links work by token only: the person sends the token to the bot. With both, a person can also link by a code that the bot sends. private_answers Without it: Muster's answer to a press appears in the Thread of the message instead of privately. ephemeral is a message only the person sees, popup a short plain-text pop-up. native_mentions Without it: a Mention marker is rendered as the person's name in plain text, which notifies nobody. quiet_messages Without it: a Quiet message (notify: false) is posted as an ordinary message, without Mentions. status_color Without it: the bridge shows the emoji of the status instead of the color. deletion_events Without it: Muster learns that a Root message was deleted from gone on its next edit or Thread reply, instead of at once. delete Without it: Muster L1 never deletes messages, so nothing changes. link_url_template Without it: the profile shows the Account link token without a link that opens the bot. edit_max_age_seconds Without it: a value of null means Muster edits a Root message for as long as its Alert Group changes.

A bridge sends press events only with buttons, thread_message events only with thread_messages, and message_deleted events only with deletion_events. Muster handles every event type whatever its copy of info says, so an event sent just after a feature was switched on is not lost.

items.title: Rendering the envelope
items.text:
Muster sends a JSON envelope: the status, color and emoji, the title, the link, the body and the buttons. The bridge renders it in its messenger's markup. Muster never writes a messenger's markup for a bridge.

The body is CommonMark 0.31 with one extension, strikethrough (~~text~~) as GitHub Flavored Markdown writes it.

  • Muster uses paragraphs, hard line breaks, emphasis, strong emphasis, strikethrough, code spans, links, bullet lists and block quotes.
  • Muster never uses headings, tables, images or raw HTML.

Use a CommonMark parser rather than patterns, and map each construct to the closest thing your messenger has. The title is plain text. Show it as the heading of the message, linked to link. Alert data in the body is already escaped for CommonMark, and it cannot mention anyone or form a link.

Links are http and https links, plus Mention markers.

Mention markers are links of the form [@Display Name](muster-mention:<ref>), where ref names an entry of mentions. A bridge with native_mentions renders the marker as its messenger's mention of the entry's external_id, which notifies that person. Any other bridge renders the link text alone, as plain text. The Mentions of a Loud message form the first line of its body. The external_id is the account's id in the messenger as the bridge reported it when the account was linked.

Colours and emoji. color is #rrggbb in lower case, for messengers that colour messages. emoji is the status as an emoji, for messengers that do not: 🔴 firing, 🟠 acknowledged, ⚪ snoozed, 🟢 resolved, ⛈ storm.

Loud and Quiet. notify: true is a Loud message: it should notify people as the messenger's new messages do, and it carries the mentions of the envelope. notify: false is Quiet: with quiet_messages declared, send it without a notification. Edits are always Quiet. Do not make an edit ring anyone.

Buttons. Each button has a label (up to 64 characters), a style hint (primary, danger, neutral or success), and data. The data is opaque and signed by Muster; return it unchanged with the press. Map a style that your messenger lacks to the closest one, or show a plain button. Muster sends at most max_per_message buttons, and drops Snooze buttons first: the preset of the first day of the week ("Until Monday 09:00"), then the preset of the next morning ("Until tomorrow 09:00"), then the durations from the longest. A firing Root message on an On-call Route has seven buttons, Ack, Resolve, three durations and the two presets, so a bridge that declares max_per_message: 5 gets Ack, Resolve and the three durations.

Length and safe truncation. Muster keeps the body within limits.max_body_length code points of the CommonMark it sends. Choose that limit so that a body of that length fits your messenger after your rendering. When the rendered message is still too long, you make the final cut where your markup needs it, and answer truncated: true. Cut by whole code points, never inside an entity, a tag or a surrogate pair, and close any markup you opened. A request whose body exceeds max_body_length is invalid.

items.title: Idempotency-Key
items.text:
Every request that creates something carries an Idempotency-Key header: postMessage, replyInThread, sendDirectMessage and answerEvent. The key is one to 255 printable ASCII characters without spaces. Muster reuses a key when it retries a request, also after a crash or a timeout.

The bridge must:

  • store each key per token: the same key sent with another Connection's token is another request;
  • keep each key with its successful (2xx) result for at least 24 hours, because Muster may retry long after the first attempt, and a bridge that forgot the key would post a second message;
  • answer a repeated key with that first result and replayed: true, whatever the body of the repeated request, without creating anything again;
  • store nothing for a failed request, so that its retry is a new attempt;
  • answer a repeated key whose first request is still running with transient;
  • pass the key on to the messenger when the messenger has an idempotency mechanism of its own.

Muster treats a postMessage whose answer says replayed as the same message, and follows it with an editMessage of its current state, because the retry may carry a newer state than the request whose answer was lost. If the bridge did not know the key, the retry posts a second message, and Muster records a possible duplicate in the Alert Group's Timeline.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant M as Muster
  participant B as Bridge
  participant X as Messenger

  M->>B: POST /v1/messages with Idempotency-Key K1
  B->>X: post the message
  X-->>B: posted
  Note over B: stores K1 with its result for 24 hours, per token
  B--xM: the answer is lost, Muster times out
  M->>B: POST /v1/messages with the same Idempotency-Key K1
  B-->>M: 201 with message_id and replayed true, nothing is posted again
  M->>B: PATCH /v1/messages/message_id with the current state
  B->>X: edit the message
  B-->>M: 200 truncated false
  M->>B: POST /v1/messages/message_id/thread-replies with Idempotency-Key K2 and thread_ref null
  B->>X: reply in the Thread
  B-->>M: 201 with thread_ref
  M->>B: POST the next reply with Idempotency-Key K3 and that thread_ref
  B-->>M: 201 with the same thread_ref

items.title: thread_ref
items.text:
The messenger decides how a Thread is named, and some messengers need a Thread to be created before the first reply. The thread_ref carries that between calls, so that the bridge needs no store of its own that maps messages to Threads:

  • postMessage may return a thread_ref when the Thread's id is known at once, and may leave it out or return null.
  • replyInThread carries the last thread_ref Muster received for that message, from postMessage or from an earlier reply, or null when it has none. When it is null, create the Thread if your messenger needs that.
  • replyInThread always returns a thread_ref. Muster stores it and sends it with the next reply of the same Thread.

A thread_ref is opaque to Muster, up to 512 characters, and it may equal the message id. In a thread_message event, the thread_ref is the same value, or null.

items.title: Presses within 3 seconds, and answers later
items.text:
The bridge confirms a press to its messenger itself, within the messenger's deadline and at most 3 seconds after the press, before Muster has seen it. Messengers expect that quick answer; Muster would be too late. Only then does the bridge report the press to Muster as an event.

When Muster has something to say to the person, it answers with a separate answerEvent call, made before it acknowledges the event: before it answers a push with 204, or polls with the next cursor. Muster makes the call within a few seconds of receiving the event, or not at all. A press that works is not answered; the edited Root message shows its result. A refusal, a failure, a press from an account without an Account link and a press on a test message are answered.

POST /v1/answers HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: <key>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "event_id": "ev-1001", "text": "Done: Acknowledged #42" }

{ "shown_as": "ephemeral", "replayed": false }

The bridge shows text to the person who caused the event event_id, as plain text of at most 500 characters, and answers where:

A press Privately (ephemeral or popup) when the messenger allows it, with private_answers, and the press is recent enough; otherwise in the Thread of the message (thread). A thread_message In that Thread (thread), never as a pop-up. An account_link In the direct chat it came from (direct).

An event that the bridge no longer knows, or can no longer answer anywhere, is gone.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor P as Person
  participant X as Messenger
  participant B as Bridge
  participant M as Muster

  P->>X: presses a button
  X->>B: callback with the button's data
  B->>X: confirms the press at once, within 3 seconds
  B->>B: queues a press event
  alt Poll mode
    M->>B: GET /v1/events with the cursor
    B-->>M: the events and next_cursor
  else Push mode
    B->>M: POST the signed event to the callback address
  end
  M->>M: verifies the button's data and runs the Command
  opt Muster has something to say
    M->>B: POST /v1/answers with event_id and text
    B->>X: shows the text to the person
    X-->>P: privately (ephemeral or pop-up), or in the Thread
    B-->>M: 200 with shown_as
  end
  alt Poll mode
    M->>B: the next GET /v1/events with next_cursor
  else Push mode
    M-->>B: 204
  end
  Note over M: A press that works is not answered, the edited Root message shows the result

Muster ignores, without answering, a press or a Thread message about a message that it did not post through that Connection. It drops a press or a Text command whose occurred_at is more than an hour old.

items.title: Error classes
items.text:
Errors are RFC 9457 problems (application/problem+json) with a class member that the bridge chooses, because only the bridge knows what its messenger's codes mean. Muster acts on the class:

transient

A temporary failure: the messenger is down, a timeout.

Muster retries with exponential backoff; repeated failures make the Destination Broken.

rate_limited

The messenger or the bridge throttles; send Retry-After in seconds.

Muster waits exactly that long, for the channel, or for every channel of the bot when scope is bot; not counted as a failure; a wait longer than 15 minutes (bridge.retry_after_max), or none given, is treated as transient.

gone

The message no longer exists: deleted, or its Thread is gone.

Muster publishes the Alert Group again once; with reason edit_window_closed, treats the message as past its edit window.

forbidden

The channel is missing, the bot was removed from it or lacks a right, the bot was blocked.

Muster marks the Destination Broken until a check succeeds.

invalid

The request cannot succeed as sent: too long, malformed, an unknown id.

Muster ends that delivery as Not delivered, without retrying.

The problem members are title, status, an optional detail, the class, and for rate_limited a scope of channel (the default) or bot. The detail is shown to the Admin as the reason, as untrusted text, so write it for a person and never put a secret in it.

{ "title": "The messenger is not available.", "status": 503, "class": "transient" }

{ "title": "Too many requests", "status": 429, "class": "rate_limited", "scope": "channel" }

The 429 carries Retry-After: 7, for example.

{ "title": "The message no longer exists.", "status": 404, "class": "gone" }

{ "title": "The message is too long for this messenger.", "status": 400, "class": "invalid" }

Who decides gone. Only the bridge. Muster never treats a message as gone because of a status code, and a 404 without the class gone is invalid. A bridge that means gone says so in class. Use it for a message, a Thread or an event that no longer exists. Muster reacts by publishing the Alert Group again, once, so do not use it for anything else.

Why a missing channel is forbidden. A channel that does not exist, or that the bot cannot see, is forbidden, never gone. gone makes Muster post the message again, and that would fail again at once. forbidden marks the Destination Broken with your detail, which the Admin reads ("The bot is not a member of this channel."), and Muster probes it with checkChannel until the channel works again.

An answer without a class. Muster still classifies a problem without a class, or an answer that is not a problem, by its status, so a plain framework error does no harm:

401, 403 class: forbidden 408 class: transient 429, and 503 with Retry-After class: rate_limited Other 5xx, timeouts and network errors class: transient 404, 410, a redirect and everything else class: invalid

No status is ever read as gone. Muster also follows no redirects, and treats one as a configuration error.

An example mapping. Parley, a fictional messenger, answers its own error codes. The bridge for Parley maps them like this, as the classify function above does:

502, a timeout, unavailable class: transient · why: the messenger is down slow_down, with retry_in seconds class: rate_limited · why: send Retry-After; use scope bot if the limit holds for the whole account message_not_found, thread_removed class: gone · why: the message or its Thread is deleted edit_too_old class: gone with reason edit_window_closed · why: the message exists, but cannot be edited any more channel_not_found, not_a_member, bot_banned, no_permission class: forbidden · why: the channel is unusable until somebody fixes it text_too_long, bad_request class: invalid · why: this request cannot succeed user_blocked_bot on a direct message class: forbidden · why: the account cannot receive a message from the bot

items.title: Edit windows
items.text:
Some messengers let a bot edit a message only for a while. Declare how long in limits.edit_max_age_seconds. Muster then stops editing a Root message once it is as old as that, less 60 seconds, measured from its publication on Muster's clock, without sending a failing request. If the messenger refuses an edit earlier than declared, answer gone with reason edit_window_closed:

{
  "title": "The message can no longer be edited.",
  "status": 404,
  "class": "gone",
  "reason": "edit_window_closed"
}

This is not a deletion. Muster marks the Root message as past its window. When the status of the Alert Group changes after that, Muster posts a new Root message, Quietly, to the same channel, and replies under the old Thread: "This message is no longer updated. The current one: {link}", where the link is the new message's url when you returned one, and the Alert Group page otherwise. Later Thread replies go under the new Root message. Any other change leaves the old Root message as it is. The old message keeps working: a press on its buttons, and a Text command in its Thread, act on the Alert Group as on the current one, so the bridge must keep reporting them.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor P as Person
  participant M as Muster
  participant B as Bridge
  participant X as Messenger

  M->>B: PATCH /v1/messages/old_id after a change of status
  B->>X: edit the message
  X-->>B: refused, the message is too old
  B-->>M: 404 with class gone and reason edit_window_closed
  Note over M: marks the Root message as past its edit window
  M->>B: POST /v1/messages with the new state, Quiet, new Idempotency-Key
  B->>X: post the new Root message
  B-->>M: 201 with the new message_id and url
  M->>B: POST /v1/messages/old_id/thread-replies, a pointer to the new message
  B->>X: reply in the old Thread
  B-->>M: 201
  Note over M: later Thread replies go under the new Root message
  P->>X: presses a button of the old message
  X->>B: callback
  B->>M: press event with the old message_id
  M->>M: runs the Command on the Alert Group as for the current message

items.title: Events
items.text:
The bridge reports what people do in the messenger as events. Every event has a stable id, a type and occurred_at; Muster handles each id of a Connection once. An id is up to 200 printable ASCII characters without spaces, because it travels as the webhook-id header of a push. A bridge delivers every event at least once, so Muster deduplicates.

press

needs: buttons

A person pressed a button of a message of the bot, already confirmed to the messenger.

thread_message

needs: thread_messages

A person, never the bot itself, wrote in the Thread of a message of the bot.

account_link

needs: always

A person sent the bot an Account link token, or opened the link_url_template link.

message_deleted

needs: deletion_events

A message of the bot was deleted in the messenger.

{
  "id": "ev-1001",
  "type": "press",
  "occurred_at": "2026-10-18T14:05:12Z",
  "message_id": "m-77",
  "user": { "external_id": "u-alice", "display_name": "Alice Smith", "handle": "alice" },
  "data": "a1.k2.QmFzZTY0U2lnbmF0dXJlRXhhbXBsZQ"
}

{
  "id": "ev-1002",
  "type": "thread_message",
  "occurred_at": "2026-10-18T14:07:40Z",
  "message_id": "m-77",
  "thread_ref": "t-77",
  "user": { "external_id": "u-alice", "display_name": "Alice Smith", "handle": "alice" },
  "text": "ack"
}

message_id of a thread_message is the message whose Thread it is in, as in the path of replyInThread, usually the Root message, never the id of a reply. text is plain text of at most 4000 characters, with mentions of the bot removed.

{
  "id": "ev-1003",
  "type": "account_link",
  "occurred_at": "2026-10-18T14:09:03Z",
  "token": "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFG",
  "user": { "external_id": "u-alice", "display_name": "Alice Smith", "handle": "alice" }
}

{
  "id": "ev-1004",
  "type": "message_deleted",
  "occurred_at": "2026-10-18T14:11:30Z",
  "message_id": "m-77"
}

items.title: Polling
items.text:
Offer poll in event_delivery and implement pollEvents. Muster, on the Leader, calls it in a loop:

GET /v1/events?cursor=<next_cursor>&wait=25 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "events": [
    {
      "id": "ev-1001",
      "type": "press",
      "occurred_at": "2026-10-18T14:05:12Z",
      "message_id": "m-77",
      "user": { "external_id": "u-alice", "display_name": "Alice Smith", "handle": "alice" },
      "data": "a1.k2.QmFzZTY0U2lnbmF0dXJlRXhhbXBsZQ"
    }
  ],
  "next_cursor": "c-5"
}
  • Return the events after cursor, oldest first, at once when there are any. Without cursor, return all of them. When there are none, hold the request open until one arrives or until wait seconds have passed, and then return an empty list. wait is 0 to 60, 25 by default (bridge.poll_wait is the 25 that Muster sends). Muster waits for your answer up to wait plus 15 seconds.
  • next_cursor is opaque to Muster. Muster handles the batch and sends the next_cursor with its next call; only then may you forget the events before that cursor. Keep events that Muster has not passed for at least 24 hours.
  • A cursor that you do not know is invalid; Muster then polls again without one. Return only the events of the token's bot.
  • Only one Muster replica polls a Connection at a time, but after a handover two calls may overlap. That is why events are deduplicated by id.

items.title: Push
items.text:
Offer push in event_delivery. The Admin chooses it on the Connection and enters a push secret. The bridge posts each event, one per request, to the callback address that the Connection shows:

<MUSTER_INGEST_URL>/api/v1/callbacks/bridge/<connection id>

The request is signed as Standard Webhooks specifies:

webhook-id The event's id, kept across retries. webhook-timestamp The Unix time of this attempt, in seconds. webhook-signature v1, followed by the base64 of HMAC-SHA256 over <webhook-id>.<webhook-timestamp>.<body>.

The push secret is whsec_ followed by the base64 of at least 24 random bytes. The HMAC key is the decoded bytes: strip the prefix whsec_ and base64-decode the rest. The signed content is the three values joined with full stops, followed by the exact body that you send. webhook-signature may hold several signatures separated by spaces, which is how a secret is rotated. Muster refuses a webhook-timestamp more than 5 minutes away from its own clock, so keep your clock right, and sign each attempt with the time of that attempt.

Generate a secret and enter it on both sides:

printf 'whsec_%s\n' "$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)"

Muster answers:

Answer Means The bridge 204 Muster handled the event, now or before forgets the event 400 the event can never be handled drops it 401 the signature, the Connection or its mode is wrong keeps the event, retries after fixing its configuration anything else, a timeout a temporary failure retries with backoff for at least an hour, same webhook-id

Muster answers 401 for a bad signature, an unknown Connection and a Connection in poll mode alike, so the endpoint reveals nothing about which Connections exist.

In the protocol the bridge signs and Muster verifies. The snippets below show both sides: the signer is what your bridge needs, and the verifier is what Muster checks, which is useful in your tests. Both were run against Muster's own code.

package pushsig

import (
    "crypto/hmac"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/base64"
    "errors"
    "regexp"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

// timestampPattern is what Muster accepts as webhook-timestamp: Unix seconds, digits only.
var timestampPattern = regexp.MustCompile(`^[0-9]{1,12}$`)

// key decodes a push secret: whsec_ and the standard base64 of the key.
func key(secret string) ([]byte, error) {
    encoded, ok := strings.CutPrefix(secret, "whsec_")
    if !ok {
        return nil, errors.New("the push secret does not start with whsec_")
    }
    k, err := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(encoded)
    if err != nil || len(k) == 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("the push secret is not whsec_ and base64")
    }
    return k, nil
}

// signature is v1, a comma and the base64 HMAC-SHA256 of "<id>.<timestamp>.<body>".
func signature(k []byte, id, timestamp string, body []byte) string {
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, k)
    mac.Write([]byte(id + "." + timestamp + "."))
    mac.Write(body)
    return "v1," + base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil))
}

// Sign returns the value of webhook-timestamp and of webhook-signature for the event with this id, sent now.
// The bridge sets webhook-id to the id of the event, and retries the event with the same webhook-id, with a new
// timestamp and signature.
func Sign(secret, id string, now time.Time, body []byte) (timestamp, sig string, err error) {
    k, err := key(secret)
    if err != nil {
        return "", "", err
    }
    timestamp = strconv.FormatInt(now.Unix(), 10)
    return timestamp, signature(k, id, timestamp, body), nil
}

// Verify checks the three headers of a pushed event the way Muster does. The header may hold several
// signatures separated by spaces; one that matches is enough.
func Verify(secret, id, timestamp string, body []byte, header string, now time.Time) error {
    k, err := key(secret)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    want := []byte(signature(k, id, timestamp, body))
    matched := false
    for _, part := range strings.Fields(header) {
        if hmac.Equal([]byte(part), want) {
            matched = true
        }
    }
    if !matched {
        return errors.New("no signature matches")
    }
    if !timestampPattern.MatchString(timestamp) {
        return errors.New("the timestamp is not Unix seconds")
    }
    sent, err := strconv.ParseInt(timestamp, 10, 64)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if d := now.Sub(time.Unix(sent, 0)); d > 5*time.Minute || d < -5*time.Minute {
        return errors.New("the timestamp is more than 5 minutes from the clock")
    }
    return nil
}

For a bridge in Python:

import base64
import hashlib
import hmac
import re
import time


def _key(secret: str) -> bytes:
    """Decode a push secret: whsec_ and the standard base64 of the key."""
    if not secret.startswith("whsec_"):
        raise ValueError("the push secret does not start with whsec_")
    key = base64.b64decode(secret.removeprefix("whsec_"), validate=True)
    if not key:
        raise ValueError("the push secret is not whsec_ and base64")
    return key


def _signature(secret: str, msg_id: str, timestamp: str, body: bytes) -> str:
    mac = hmac.new(_key(secret), f"{msg_id}.{timestamp}.".encode() + body, hashlib.sha256)
    return "v1," + base64.b64encode(mac.digest()).decode()


def sign(secret: str, msg_id: str, body: bytes, now: float | None = None) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Return the values of webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature."""
    timestamp = str(int(now if now is not None else time.time()))
    return timestamp, _signature(secret, msg_id, timestamp, body)


def verify(secret: str, msg_id: str, timestamp: str, body: bytes, header: str,
           now: float | None = None) -> bool:
    """Check the three headers of a pushed event the way Muster does."""
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]{1,12}", timestamp):
        return False
    want = _signature(secret, msg_id, timestamp, body).encode()
    matched = False
    for part in header.split():
        if hmac.compare_digest(part.encode(), want):
            matched = True
    drift = (now if now is not None else time.time()) - int(timestamp)
    return matched and abs(drift) <= 300

Verification compares in constant time, so that the time it takes tells nothing about the signature. It accepts a header with several signatures when one of them matches, and refuses a timestamp more than 5 minutes from the clock. Sign and send the exact bytes of the body: a re-serialized body has another signature.

items.title: Account links
items.text:
An Account link ties a Muster User to their account in the messenger. A press, a Text command or a Mention names a person only through it, and it is started in the person's Muster profile, never from the messenger. Every bridge takes a token; a bridge that can look people up and write to them also offers a code. See Link your messenger accounts for what the person sees.

  • By token. The profile shows a token of 43 characters of base64url, valid for 10 minutes and for one use. The person sends it to the bot in a direct message, or opens your link_url_template link, which hands it to the bot. The bridge sends an account_link event. The token is the whole text of the direct message, trimmed and after an optional /start. Muster links the sender's account and answers with answerEvent, which you show in the direct chat the event came from: "Linked to Muster user …".
  • By code. It is offered only with direct_messages and bot_can_start, and a user_lookup other than none. The person enters their handle, of the kind user_lookup declares, in their Muster profile. Muster calls findUsers, then sendDirectMessage with the code and a warning, and the person types the code into the profile. The bot sends no confirmation.
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor P as Person
  participant W as Muster profile
  participant M as Muster
  participant B as Bridge
  participant X as Messenger

  alt By token
    P->>W: selects Link and chooses the Connection
    W-->>P: a token of 43 characters, and the link from link_url_template
    P->>X: sends the token to the bot in a direct message
    X->>B: the direct message
    B->>B: the text is a token, so it queues an account_link event
    B-->>M: the event, by poll or push
    M->>M: links the sender's account to the User
    M->>B: POST /v1/answers with event_id, Linked to Muster user
    B->>X: shows the answer in the direct chat
  else By code
    P->>W: enters the handle, such as a login
    W->>M: asks for a code
    M->>B: GET /v1/users with handle
    B-->>M: items with the account
    M->>B: POST /v1/direct-messages with the code and a warning
    B->>X: sends the direct message
    X-->>P: the code
    P->>W: types the code
    W->>M: confirms, and the link is made
  end

items.title: muster bridge check
items.text:
muster bridge check <url> runs the protocol against a bridge, without a Muster database, master key or configuration. It writes no file and stores nothing, and never changes the bridge's configuration. It does post, edit and reply in the channel of --channel, delete its own message there when the bridge offers deletion, and write to the person of --handle.

muster bridge check http://127.0.0.1:18095 --token-file ./token --channel alerts \
  --forbidden-channel nobot --handle alice --no-interactive
--token-file <file> The bridge's token, alone in the file (required). --channel <id> A channel the bot can post to (required). --forbidden-channel <id> A channel the bot cannot use, which must answer forbidden; without it the step forbidden_channel is skipped. --handle <handle> A person to look up and write to; without it user_lookup and direct_message are skipped. --push-listen <addr> Where the push listener listens, 127.0.0.1:0 by default. --push-url <url> Where the bridge reaches the push listener, the listener's own address by default. --push-secret-file <file> The push secret, whsec_ and base64, instead of a generated one. --no-interactive Skip press and push, which need a person.

Flags may come before or after the URL. The check prints one line per step as it ends: PASS <step>, FAIL <step>: <reason> or SKIP <step>: <why>. The steps run in this order: info, channel_check, post, replayed_key, buttons, edit, thread_reply, thread_ref, forbidden_channel, user_lookup, direct_message, delete, poll, press, push and answer. A failed info ends the run. replayed_key posts the same request again with its Idempotency-Key, which must return the same message_id with replayed.

PASS info
PASS channel_check
PASS post
PASS replayed_key
PASS buttons
PASS edit
PASS thread_reply
PASS thread_ref
PASS forbidden_channel
PASS user_lookup
PASS direct_message
PASS delete
PASS poll
SKIP press: --no-interactive
SKIP push: --no-interactive
PASS answer

It exits 0 when no step failed, 1 when one did, and 2 on a usage error. A step for an optional feature that the bridge does not declare is skipped.

Without --no-interactive, the check also needs a person. For a bridge that offers push, it opens a push listener and prints PUSH <url> <secret> (or PUSH <url> with --push-secret-file): point your bridge's push target there with that secret. Before it waits, up to five minutes, for a press, it prints WAIT press: …, message_id <id>; press a button of that message in your messenger, or play the person in a script.

The check runs from the muster binary, or from Muster's image:

docker run --rm --network host -v "$PWD/token:/token:ro" ghcr.io/muster-io/muster:latest bridge check \
  http://127.0.0.1:18095 --token-file /token --channel alerts --forbidden-channel nobot --handle alice \
  --no-interactive

(--network host gives the container your loopback on Linux only.)

items.title: The fake bridge of muster dev
items.text: muster dev starts a fake bridge on 127.0.0.1:18094 that offers every feature and both event delivery modes, and creates a Bridge Connection "Example Bridge" to it in poll mode, with the token muster-dev-bridge-token. The fake serves a second bot with the token muster-dev-bridge-token-b, which muster dev creates no Connection for, so you can run the check against it without touching the demo. Its channels are ch-alerts and ch-alerts-prod, and ch-nobot is one it refuses with forbidden. It records every request at /_fake/requests and takes scripted faults at /_fake/faults. It is for Muster's own tests and for trying Muster; it is not a messenger.

items.title: The example bridge
items.text: The example bridge passes every step of the check, and skips the optional ones when BRIDGE_FEATURES switches them off. Use it as a second opinion when your own bridge fails a step.

items.title: Check a bridge before saving it
items.text: The Admin can check a bridge before saving the Connection. Check connection in the form of a Bridge Connection runs the steps info and event_delivery against the base URL and token typed in the form, and stores nothing; see Check before saving.

items.title: See what Muster sent
items.text: The Request log tab of the Bridge Connection (Connections → a Connection → Request log) shows the recent requests that Muster sent to your bridge and the answers it got, and the events that reached Muster's callback address, with secrets masked. Open a record for the request with its headers and body, and the problem your bridge answered. See Request log.

items.title: Run your bridge
items.text:
• The token and the push secret. One token is one bot. Keep both in a secret store or a file with restricted access, not in the image or on a command line. To change the push secret without a refused push, sign with both the old and the new secret while it changes in Muster: webhook-signature may hold both signatures, separated by a space, and Muster accepts the header when one of them matches. The Go library's PushTarget holds one secret, so it signs with one: between the change in Muster and b.SetPush with the new secret, Muster answers its pushes 401. The library keeps those events and retries them, for at least an hour and at once after b.SetPush, so none is lost when the bridge gets the new secret within that hour.
  • Logs. Never log a token, a push secret, an Account link token, or an Authorization header. The Account link token is a credential until it is used. A detail that you answer is shown to the Admin, so keep secrets out of it too.
  • Who calls you. Muster sends User-Agent: Muster/<version> on every request, only to the base URL saved on the Connection, and follows no redirects. Serve the bridge over HTTPS when it is reachable from beyond a trusted network. A bridge that cannot reach Muster should use polling.
  • Timeouts. Answer quickly, and return an error class rather than hang: Muster waits only so long for an answer, and treats a timeout as transient. A pollEvents call may be held for up to 60 seconds, so do not put a shorter timeout in front of it.
  • Monitoring. Muster monitors your bridge through the health of its Destinations. A Destination that the bridge refuses with forbidden, or that keeps failing for the whole Transient budget (10 attempts within 30 minutes), becomes Broken, with your detail as the reason. A bridge that asks Muster to wait does not make a Destination Broken unless it asks for more than 15 minutes. While a Destination is Broken, Muster probes it every 5 minutes, with checkChannel when nothing waits, and the first success ends the state. The Internal alert MusterDestinationBroken tells the operators; its runbook is MusterDestinationBroken. A Bridge Connection whose bridge cannot be reached does not become Broken itself: its Destinations do.

items.title: Licence
items.text:
• The protocol, api/bridge.yaml, is MIT licensed. A bridge may stay closed: nothing in the protocol obliges you to publish your bridge, or to license it under Muster's licence.
  • The bridge libraries and the example bridge are MIT licensed. They are developed in their own repositories, which take contributions under the MIT licence and without a CLA.
  • Muster itself is AGPL-3.0-only. A contribution to api/bridge.yaml in Muster's repository is a contribution to Muster and falls under the CLA that Muster's repository asks for.

items.title: Backup and restore
items.text:
Muster keeps all its state in PostgreSQL, and encrypts its secrets with the master keys from the environment. Neither the Helm chart nor the compose example backs up anything, so you back up two things, separately:

The database

Holds Integrations, Routes, Alert Groups, people, the Audit log and every Secret, encrypted.

Without it, everything is gone.

The master keys (MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS)

Hold the keys that decrypt the Secrets and sign the buttons in messages.

Without them, Muster refuses to start on the database, and its encrypted Secrets cannot be read.

items.title: Why they are kept apart
items.text:
A database backup alone reveals no bot token, OIDC client secret or proxy password, because Muster encrypts them before they reach the database. A backup together with the master keys reveals all of them. Store the two in different places and give them different access: the dump in your backup storage, the keys where you keep your other secrets, such as a password manager or the secret store of your cluster.

Without the master key that wrote the database, Muster refuses to start on it, and nobody can read the Secrets in it. Muster cannot recover them, and it has no way to start that database again with a new key: keep the key safe.

After a key rotation, back up the new key list too. A backup taken before the rotation needs the old key to restore.

items.title: Back up the database
items.text:
Muster has no backup format of its own. Use the tools of PostgreSQL:

  • A dump. pg_dump writes a consistent copy while Muster runs:

    pg_dump --format=custom --file=muster-$(date +%F).dump "$MUSTER_DATABASE_URL"

    With the compose example, run it in the database container:

    docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U muster --format=custom muster > muster-$(date +%F).dump

  • Continuous backup. With CloudNativePG, add spec.backup to the Cluster; see the database. A managed PostgreSQL offers its own snapshots and point-in-time recovery. Either is better than a nightly dump when you cannot lose an hour of Alert Groups.

Take a backup before every upgrade, and test a restore before you rely on it.

items.title: Restore
items.text:
1. Stop every Muster replica. In Kubernetes, scale the Deployment to 0; with compose, stop the muster service.

  2. Restore the database into an empty database. For a dump:

    pg_restore --clean --if-exists --no-owner --dbname="$MUSTER_DATABASE_URL" muster-2026-10-19.dump

    A CloudNativePG or managed restore creates a new cluster from the backup; point database.host at it. When the chart reads the database from the Secret that CloudNativePG generates, point database.existingSecret at the new cluster's -app Secret too: it holds a new password and, in its uri, the new host. 3. Put the same master keys back into MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS. The key that was active when the backup was taken must be in the list. Keys are identified by their material, so any copy of the same key works. 4. Start Muster, in the version that wrote the backup or in a newer one that the upgrade rules allow. It applies the migrations that are missing (see Upgrades) and checks the key canary. A wrong or missing key stops the start with "master key does not match the database". 5. Run muster doctor with the same environment as the server, and read every line. See the CLI.

After the restore, Muster treats the time since the last "alive" mark as downtime. For a while, the web UI says that Muster is recovering and its data may be incomplete, and overdue timers fire once, collapsed. That is expected.

items.title: What to check
items.text:
• muster doctor exits 0. The key_canary line is OK, which proves that the keys match the database. The keyring line is OK when no older key is in use; it is WARN while a Secret or an open Root message still needs an older key, and it says when a key is no longer used and can be removed.
  • Organization → System status shows one Leader and every replica, and no Destination you did not expect as Broken.
  • Open an Alert Group and press a button in its messenger message. A press works only when the master keys are right.
  • Messengers and Alertmanagers reach the restored Muster at MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL and MUSTER_INGEST_URL. If you restored into an installation with other addresses, change them in the environment and check the Connections.

items.title: The command line
items.text:
The muster binary is the server and its command line. Without a command it runs the server. The commands are for emergencies, for setup and for diagnosis; everything else is in the web UI and the API. muster help lists them; its output, abridged:

Usage: muster [command]

Commands:
  migrate   Apply the database migrations under the migration lock
  doctor    Check the database, its connections, the master keys and the clock; only reads
  admin     Emergency access with --actor <name> <login>: admin reset-password sets a password read from standard
            input, admin reset-totp removes a lost second factor
  ingest    ingest replay --since <duration> [--integration <name>] --actor <name> reprocesses Stored Snapshots
  secrets   secrets rotate-key --activate <id> --actor <name> activates a master key that every live replica holds
  bridge    bridge check <url> --token-file <file> --channel <id> runs the Bridge protocol against a bridge, without a
            database; muster bridge help lists its flags
  dev       Development mode: fake servers and development defaults
  version   Print the version and commit
  help      Show this help

Every command exits 0 on success, 1 on a failure and 2 on a usage error, such as a missing flag.

items.title: Environment
items.text:
The commands that use the database read the same MUSTER_* variables as the server. Run them in the environment of the server, not in a bare shell:

kubectl -n muster exec deploy/muster -- muster doctor
docker compose exec muster muster doctor

The image has no shell, so run the binary directly. A command that reads a password from standard input needs kubectl exec -i or docker compose exec -T.

doctor, migrate, secrets rotate-key Need the database settings, MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL and the master keys (MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS or MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS_FILE). admin, ingest replay Need the database settings and MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL; they do not open the Keyring. bridge check, version Need nothing.

The environment reference lists the variables, and the database the ways to set the connection.

items.title: --actor
items.text: The commands that change data require --actor <name>: admin reset-password, admin reset-totp, ingest replay and secrets rotate-key. The name says who runs the command. Muster writes it, with the Transport cli, to the Audit log, so that a change made from a terminal has a person next to it like a change made in the web UI. Without --actor the command exits 2 before it connects, and nothing changes. migrate and doctor take no --actor.

items.title: muster doctor
items.text:
muster doctor

Checks and only reads. Each check prints one line, OK, WARN or FAIL, then its name and detail. The command exits 1 when a check fails. A warning does not fail it.

database Looks at: the main connection works. postgresql_version Looks at: PostgreSQL 14 or newer. session_connection Looks at: the session connection supports advisory locks and LISTEN, and the mode of each pooler. tls_main, tls_session Looks at: whether each connection is encrypted; WARN, not FAIL, when it is not. key_canary Looks at: the master keys can decrypt the canary, so they belong to this database. keyring Looks at: the active key is held, and which other keys are still needed, removable or not active yet. clock_skew Looks at: the replica's clock against the database clock, WARN above 2 seconds. connection <name>, destination <name> Looks at: the check of every Connection and every Destination that has one.

Run it after an install, after a restore, after an upgrade, and when you suspect the database, a pooler or the keys.

items.title: muster migrate
items.text:
muster migrate

Applies the migrations under a session advisory lock and logs the versions it applied. It refuses to run on a schema newer than the binary knows and names both versions. The Helm chart runs it in an init container. See Upgrades.

items.title: muster admin
items.text:
muster admin reset-password --actor <name> <login>
muster admin reset-totp --actor <name> <login>

Emergency access when no Admin can sign in. Flags come before the login.

  • reset-password reads the new password from standard input: without echo after a prompt on a terminal, otherwise the first line. It sets it on the User with that login and ends the User's sessions. On a User who signs in through OpenID Connect, it also removes the OIDC identity, so the User signs in with the password from then on.
  • reset-totp removes the TOTP and the recovery codes of the User, for a lost second factor, and ends their sessions. Under a TOTP policy that covers the User, they enrol again at the next sign-in. See TOTP.
printf '%s\n' "$NEW_PASSWORD" | kubectl -n muster exec -i deploy/muster -- \
  muster admin reset-password --actor alice admin@example.org

items.title: muster ingest replay
items.text:
muster ingest replay --since <duration> [--integration <name>] --actor <name>

Reprocesses Stored Snapshots, for example after a bug in processing was fixed.

  • --since is the period back from now, such as 1h or 90m. A period longer than the retention of Stored Snapshots is cut to it.
  • --integration limits the replay to the Integration with that name.

The command sets the Stored Snapshots of the period back to pending in one transaction and records ingest.replayed in the Audit log; the running replicas process them again in arrival order. Processing is idempotent per Alert, so Snapshots that were processed change nothing, while one that failed is processed with the current code. The command prints how many Stored Snapshots it replayed.

items.title: muster secrets rotate-key
items.text:
muster secrets rotate-key --activate <id> --actor <name>

Activates a master key, re-encrypts the Secrets and the key canary, and makes the Leader re-sign the buttons of open Root messages. It refuses while a live replica does not hold the key. --activate is the key id that Organization → Keyring shows. The two steps around it, and what to do afterwards, are in Key rotation.

items.title: muster bridge check
items.text:
muster bridge check <url> --token-file <file> --channel <id> [flags]

Runs the Bridge protocol against a bridge, step by step, and prints one line per step: PASS, FAIL with the reason, or SKIP. It needs no database, master key or configuration, writes nothing, and never changes the bridge's configuration. It exits 0 when no step failed, 1 when one did, and 2 on a usage error.

Flags: --token-file and --channel are required; --forbidden-channel, --handle, --push-listen, --push-url, --push-secret-file and --no-interactive are optional. Their meaning, the steps and a worked example are in Write a bridge.

items.title: muster version
items.text:
muster version

Prints the version and the commit, in the form muster <version> (commit <sha>). The metric muster_build_info carries the same two labels.

items.title: muster dev
items.text: muster dev runs Muster with fake messenger servers and a published development master key. It is for working on Muster; do not use it for an installation.

items.title: High availability
items.text: Run more than one replica of Muster when you want the web UI, ingestion and delivery to survive the loss of a node or a restart. The Helm chart defaults to one replica, and the compose example runs one. Two replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget are an option, not a requirement.

items.title: All replicas are active
items.text: Every replica serves the web UI, the API and ingestion, and runs the workers for ingestion, delivery and timers. The workers claim rows from PostgreSQL with a lease, so a timer such as an ack timeout, a Reminder or the end of a Snooze fires on whichever replica is free. A replica that stalls delays nothing beyond its lease.

items.title: The Leader
items.text:
A few tasks must run once, not once per replica. One replica, the Leader, runs only those. The list is closed:

Task What it does Telegram polling long polling of getUpdates for Connections in that update mode; Telegram answers 409 to a second poller Bridge polling polls the events of Bridge Connections in the poll event delivery mode, with one cursor per Connection Slack's Socket Mode holds one Socket Mode connection per Slack Connection in the socket event mode; presses made during a handover are lost, the http event mode avoids that Heartbeat and Stale checks find Integrations that are Heartbeat lost and Alerts that went Stale partitions and retention create partitions ahead of time, drop expired ones, and delete what the retention periods remove pruning removes ended sessions, expired requests and links, the records of gone replicas, and the Request log past its bounds database gauges the metrics computed from the database: open Alert Groups, the ingestion backlog, delivery queues, Broken Destinations, Storms the "alive" mark every 30 seconds, so that a restarted Muster knows how long it was down the outgoing heartbeat the call to your dead man's switch OIDC secret expiry check raises MusterOIDCSecretExpiring re-render after a key rotation re-signs the buttons of open Root messages (Key rotation)

Nothing else depends on the Leader. Every task is safe to run twice, because a handover can overlap for a moment.

items.title: How a replica becomes Leader
items.text:
The Leader holds a session advisory lock in PostgreSQL on a dedicated connection, the session connection. Every replica tries to take the lock every leader.ping_interval (5 seconds); one succeeds. The Leader proves that it still holds the lock by pinging over that session at the same interval. If no ping succeeds for leader.fencing_timeout (15 seconds), it stops all Leader tasks and closes the connection, and it may compete for the lock again later.

When a Leader crashes, its connection closes and PostgreSQL releases the lock at once. When its node disappears or the network splits, PostgreSQL would keep the session for hours by default. Muster sets idle_session_timeout on the lock session and TCP keepalives, so PostgreSQL ends a silent session and releases the lock within leader.server_bound (30 seconds). The fencing timeout is shorter than that, so the old Leader normally stops before another replica can take over. The values are built in; they are not settings.

sequenceDiagram
  participant A as "Replica A (Leader)"
  participant PG as "PostgreSQL"
  participant B as "Replica B"
  A->>PG: "ping over the lock session, every 5 s"
  B->>PG: "try the lock, every 5 s: taken"
  Note over A: "the node of A is lost"
  Note over A: "A stops its Leader tasks after 15 s without a ping"
  PG-->>PG: "ends the silent session within 30 s, the lock is free"
  B->>PG: "try the lock: acquired"
  Note over B: "B is the Leader: muster_leader is 1"
  B->>PG: "writes the alive mark, runs the Leader tasks"

A handover after the loss of a node takes well under a minute. During it, Telegram and Bridge polling, Slack's Socket Mode connections, the periodic checks and the outgoing heartbeat pause. Ingestion, delivery and timers do not. Telegram and the bridges keep what arrives meanwhile. A press made in Socket Mode before the new Leader connects is lost and its person sees Slack's error: Muster does not count on Slack to send it again.

items.title: When no replica leads
items.text:
The gauge muster_leader is 1 on the Leader and 0 on the others. When the "alive" mark is older than 2 minutes (leader.absence_notice), the web UI shows a notice that no replica is leading. The chart rule MusterNoLeader fires when no replica has led for 2 minutes; see its runbook.

While there is no Leader:

  • Bridge Connections in the poll mode and Telegram Connections in the long polling mode receive no button presses and no Text commands. When a Leader returns, a Bridge press or Text command older than bridge.event_max_age (1 hour) is dropped unanswered; a Telegram press is dropped unanswered when the Connection received no updates for longer than telegram.press_max_age (1 hour) before it. Connections in the push mode of a Bridge and the webhook mode of Telegram keep working.
  • Slack Connections in the socket event mode hold no Socket Mode connection: a press made meanwhile is lost, and the person sees Slack's error. Connections in the http event mode keep working.
  • No Integration becomes Heartbeat lost and no Alert goes Stale.
  • Partition maintenance, retention and pruning pause; the gauges that only the Leader exports go stale.
  • The outgoing heartbeat stops, so a dead man's switch alerts you.

Ingestion, delivery, timers, the web UI and the API keep working.

items.title: After downtime
items.text: When every replica was down, the next Leader reads the "alive" mark, records the period, and adds a Timeline entry to open Alert Groups. Timers that came due during the downtime fire once, collapsed. For a while the web UI says Muster is recovering.

items.title: The session connection
items.text: The Leader lock and the LISTEN connections need a real session. If the main database connection goes through PgBouncer in transaction mode, set MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_HOST and MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_PORT (in the chart, database.sessionHost and database.sessionPort), or MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_URL, to an endpoint that reaches PostgreSQL directly or through a pooler in session mode. At start, Muster checks that advisory locks and LISTEN work over it and stops with an error that names the setting otherwise. See PgBouncer.

items.title: Two replicas
items.text:
In the Helm values:

replicas: 2
podDisruptionBudget:
  enabled: true
  maxUnavailable: 1

The PodDisruptionBudget keeps a node drain from stopping both pods at once. Spread the pods over nodes with topologySpreadConstraints or affinity. See Install with Helm for the other values. PostgreSQL is the single stateful component, so its own availability, such as a CloudNativePG cluster with two instances, sets the limit of the installation.

Replicas of different minor versions run side by side only during a rolling upgrade.

items.title: Clocks
items.text:
Replicas share one database and take the time from their own system clocks. Run NTP, or the time service of your cloud provider, on every node and on the database server. A replica measures its clock against the database every minute and exports it as muster_clock_skew_seconds; it logs a warning above process.clock_skew_warning (2 seconds), and the chart rule MusterClockSkew fires after 5 minutes.

A skew moves the timestamps a replica writes and the timers and windows it evaluates, and it can make TOTP codes, OIDC ID tokens and the timestamps of outgoing webhook signatures fail. It can also make the lease of a row or of the Leader lock expire too early or too late, so that work runs twice or waits. See the MusterClockSkew runbook, and check the clock with muster doctor.

items.title: Key rotation
items.text:
Muster encrypts its Secrets and signs the buttons of its messages with the master keys in MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS. These keys form the Keyring; one of them is active and encrypts and signs, and all of them can still decrypt and verify. Which key is active is stored in the database, not in the environment. Muster never generates a master key and never writes the environment: you add a new key yourself, then tell Muster to use it.

Rotate when a key may have leaked, when a person who knew it leaves, or on a schedule you keep. The rotation takes two deliberate steps, so that a rolling restart never leaves a replica unable to read what another one wrote.

items.title: Step 1: add the new key everywhere
items.text:
1. Generate a key: openssl rand -base64 32.
  2. Add it to MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS, after the current key, separated by a comma. With the Helm chart the value comes from the key secret-keys of your Secret (masterKeysKey); MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS_FILE takes one key per line.
  3. Roll the change out to every replica. Muster applies a changed environment only on start, so restart the pods.

Both keys stay in the list. The key that is active does not change yet, and nothing is re-encrypted.

Each replica records the key ids it holds every 30 seconds, and counts as live while its record is younger than 2 minutes. Open Organization → Keyring. It lists every key by its id, which one is Active, and for each key Held by the replicas that have it and Missing on those that do not. The new key has the state Not active yet, because it has never been active. Muster never calls such a key removable.

items.title: Step 2: activate it
items.text:
Run the command with the same environment as the server (see the CLI), giving the id of the new key as the Keyring page shows it:

muster secrets rotate-key --activate <id> --actor alice

--actor names who runs the command and goes to the Audit log. Muster refuses to activate a key while a live replica does not hold it, names those replicas, and exits 1. Wait until the Keyring page shows no replica as Missing on, or until the replica that lacks the key stops being live, and run the command again.

When every live replica holds the key, one transaction:

  • makes the key active,
  • re-encrypts every stored Secret and the key canary with it, and
  • records keyring.key_activated in the Audit log.

The replicas switch to the key without a restart. Then the Leader recomputes the message of every open Alert Group whose buttons the old key signed, so that the delivery worker edits each Root message and signs its buttons with the new key. The edits go through the usual limits of the messengers, so a large backlog takes a while.

items.title: Remove the old key
items.text:
The old key is still needed while a Secret or an open Root message depends on it. The Keyring page shows each older key as Still needed until nothing does; then it says Key <id> is no longer used and can be removed from MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS. muster doctor prints the same on its keyring line, with the number of encrypted values and open Root messages that still need each key. Only a key that was active before is ever called removable.

Then remove the key from MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS and roll the change out. Removing the key before Muster says so breaks what still depends on it; the start of a replica that lacks the active key fails with "master key does not match the database".

Keep the old key in your records until the backups that need it are gone: a backup taken before the rotation restores only with the key that was active then.

items.title: What stops working when the old key goes
items.text:
• Buttons in Thread replies. Muster re-signs only the buttons of Root messages. A Reminder, for example, is a Thread reply, and keeps the signature it was sent with. Once the old key is gone, a press on such a button is answered privately: "This button has expired; use the buttons on the Alert Group's message". Nothing changes in the Alert Group, and the Root message works.
  • Web pages that were open before the rotation. The CSRF token that a web page sends with each change carries the id of the key that signed it, and verifies while Muster holds that key. A page that has been open since before the rotation has the old token. Once the old key is gone, the next change from that page is refused (403, csrf_invalid) and the page says "The page is out of date. Reload it and try again." Reload the page, and it works again with a token of the new key. Nobody has to sign in again.

Nothing else changes: Personal access tokens and Service account tokens are stored as hashes and are not affected, and the Signing secret of an outgoing webhook Destination does not change (Muster only re-encrypts it).

items.title: If something goes wrong
items.text: Replicas {names} do not hold key {id} yet. cause: a live replica has not restarted with the new key · what to do: finish the rollout, or wait until the record of a gone replica expires key {id} is not in the master keys of this process cause: you ran the command without the new key in MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS · what to do: give the command the same environment as the server A replica stops with "master key does not match the database" cause: it lacks the active key · what to do: add the key back to its environment Exit code 2 cause: --activate or --actor is missing · what to do: add the flag

items.title: Monitoring
