items.text: Muster exports Prometheus metrics, ships alert rules and a Grafana dashboard in its Helm chart, and raises Internal alerts about its own problems. Use all three: the metrics and the rules tell you from outside, and the Internal alerts reach you through Muster itself.

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
Muster serves /metrics on the internal listener, port 8082 by default (MUSTER_LISTEN_INTERNAL), next to /health/live and /health/ready. It never pushes metrics. Do not expose that listener outside the cluster.

With the Prometheus Operator, set serviceMonitor.enabled: true. The chart then creates a ServiceMonitor for the internal Service, with serviceMonitor.interval (default 30 seconds) and serviceMonitor.scrapeTimeout (default 10 seconds), and extra labels from serviceMonitor.labels for the selector of your Prometheus. Without the operator, scrape the internal Service yourself, or the pods on port 8082.

Every metric is in the metrics reference. Entities appear by their immutable id; their names are in the *_info metrics, which the dashboard joins. No metric carries an alert label, a user or an Alert Group number.

items.title: Alert rules
items.text:
The chart renders one group of rules, named muster, when you enable one of:

alerting.prometheusRule.enabled renders: a PrometheusRule · needs: the Prometheus Operator CRDs alerting.vmRule.enabled renders: a VMRule · needs: the VictoriaMetrics Operator CRDs

Both take extra labels (alerting.prometheusRule.labels, alerting.vmRule.labels) for the rule selector of your operator. Each rule has a description and a runbook_url that points to its runbook, built from alerting.runbookBaseURL and the version of Muster the chart deploys.

What you can tune:

  • alerting.jobSelector is the label matcher that selects Muster's series in every rule. By default it is job="muster", the job the ServiceMonitor gives. Change it when your scrape job has another name.
  • alerting.rules.<Name>.enabled switches one rule off, and .for sets how long its condition holds before it fires.
  • Some rules have thresholds: window (the range of the rate or increase), seconds (MusterDeliverySlow: p95 delivery latency; MusterClockSkew: the skew), size (MusterDeliveryQueueGrowing), backlog and delaySeconds (MusterIngestBacklog), unauthorized (MusterIngestRejected) and failures (MusterLoginFailures).

The defaults are in the chart values reference, and the expression of each rule is on its runbook page. The rules are covered by unit tests in CI.

The five rules with severity critical are MusterDown, MusterNoLeader, MusterDeliveryFailing, MusterDestinationBroken and MusterHeartbeatLost. The others are warning.

items.title: Send the critical rules around Muster
items.text:
Do not route the critical rules through Muster

A rule such as MusterDown or MusterDeliveryFailing fires when Muster cannot do its job. If Alertmanager sends it to Muster, the alert goes exactly where it cannot be delivered. Use an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster for them, to a receiver you trust to work when Muster does not.

The chart rules carry the labels alertname (starting with Muster) and severity: critical or warning, plus the labels Prometheus adds from the series. Match on both, and put the bypass route first, above the route that sends everything to Muster, with continue false (the default) so that the alert stops there. Here it is added to the configuration of Connect Alertmanager, whose receivers muster-prod-eu, oncall and default stay as they are:

route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - receiver: platform-direct          # not Muster
      matchers: ['alertname=~"Muster.+"', 'severity="critical"']
    - receiver: muster-prod-eu
      continue: true
      repeat_interval: 10m
    - receiver: oncall
      matchers: ['severity="critical"']
    - receiver: default

receivers:
  # ... muster-prod-eu, oncall and default
  - name: platform-direct
    webhook_configs:
      - url: https://chat.example.org/hooks/<id>          # a chat or a pager of your own
        send_resolved: true

The matchers use alertname=~"Muster.+" for the rules of this chart; severity="critical" limits the bypass to the ones that need it, so the warnings still reach Muster, and every other alert still reaches Muster and your own receivers. Point the receiver platform-direct at a path that does not depend on Muster.

The Internal alerts of Muster itself do not go through Alertmanager, so this route does not see them.

items.title: Dashboard
items.text:
The chart ships one dashboard, "Muster", with the fixed uid muster, a data source variable, and the variables namespace/job, integration, route and destination. It has four rows: Overview, Ingestion, Delivery and Platform. You enable it in either or both ways, each behind its own flag:

dashboard.configMap.enabled

renders: a ConfigMap with the dashboard JSON

For the Grafana sidecar; dashboard.configMap.labels defaults to grafana_dashboard: "1".

dashboard.grafanaDashboard.enabled

renders: a GrafanaDashboard of the Grafana Operator

References that ConfigMap, so it needs dashboard.configMap.enabled too; instanceSelector, folder and allowCrossNamespaceImport are values.

items.title: Internal alerts
items.text:
Muster raises its own problems as Internal alerts: MusterSnapshotTruncated, MusterHeartbeatLost, MusterDestinationBroken, MusterTemplateError and MusterOIDCSecretExpiring. They are Alerts of the built-in "Muster" Integration, which has no tokens and cannot be changed. They go through Routes like any Alert, and they reach nobody until a Route sends them to a Destination. The Internal alerts reference lists them with their labels.

Give them a Route:

  1. Open Routes. At the top of the list, Muster suggests Send Muster's own alerts to a Destination when no Route other than the Default route matches them.
  2. Choose a Destination, and press Create the route. The Route matches alertname=~"Muster.*".

Use a Destination that does not depend on what the alert reports: not the one that is Broken. A second messenger, or an outgoing webhook to a chat of your own, serves well. When a Route for MusterHeartbeatLost exists, the Internal alerts Route goes directly below it. Every Internal alert has a runbook, and MUSTER_RUNBOOK_BASE_URL (set by the chart from alerting.runbookBaseURL) is the base of its link.

Two Internal alerts have a chart rule with the same name, MusterHeartbeatLost and MusterDestinationBroken. The rule is the backup for when Muster cannot deliver; the Internal alert carries the labels of what it is about: the Integration, with its Static labels, for MusterHeartbeatLost, and the Destination for MusterDestinationBroken.

items.title: Watching that Muster is alive
items.text:
Metrics and rules need Prometheus. To notice that Muster, its cluster or its network is down altogether, configure the outgoing heartbeat: an external service alerts you when the calls stop.

The System status page shows the same from the inside: see System status.

items.title: System status
items.text:
Organization → System status (Admins only) shows the state of the installation from the inside. It only reads: it lists what is wrong, and you fix it on the pages it links to.

  1. Open Organization → System status. At the top, the version of Muster and the Replicas: every live replica, the Leader marked, with the key ids it holds and when its record was last refreshed. Below them, Recovery after downtime and the Delivery queues.

  2. Further down: Broken Destinations, Integrations needing attention — Heartbeat lost or Snapshots truncated —, Template errors, Storms, and the Outgoing heartbeat, with the result of its last call or a link to set one up. Each says None when there is nothing to show.

items.title: Outgoing heartbeat
items.text: The metrics and the Internal alerts tell you about a Muster that runs. They cannot tell you that Muster, its node, its cluster or its network is gone: a dead service raises nothing. For that, Muster calls a URL of your choice at a regular interval, and a service outside Muster alerts you when the calls stop. This is a dead man's switch, and the call is the outgoing heartbeat. It is the opposite direction of a Heartbeat, which watches the path to Muster.

items.title: Pick a service
items.text:
Any service that expects a regular HTTP request and alerts when it misses, and that sits outside the cluster Muster runs in, will do:

  • Uptime Kuma: a monitor of the type Push; it gives a URL and alerts when no call arrives within the interval.
  • Any dead man's switch service that accepts an HTTP GET and alerts when the calls stop.

Set its expected period a little above Muster's interval of 1 minute, such as 2 or 3 minutes, so that a single slow call does not alert. Send its alert somewhere that does not depend on Muster.

items.title: Set it up
items.text:
Open Organization → Outgoing heartbeat, as an Admin.

  1. Enter the Heartbeat URL of the service.
  2. If Muster must reach it through a proxy, fill the proxy form; it is the same form as everywhere, see Proxies.
  3. Save.

The URL is a Secret: such URLs carry a token. Muster encrypts it with the Keyring, never shows it again, and removes it from every log line and error. The page shows whether it is set, and the Organization settings have no way to read it back. To change it, enter the whole new URL.

Without a URL nothing is sent, and System status suggests setting one up: "Set up an outgoing heartbeat so that a stopped Muster is noticed."

items.title: What Muster sends
items.text:
Interval 1 minute (outgoing_heartbeat.interval) Method GET (outgoing_heartbeat.method) Timeout 10 seconds for one request (outgoing_heartbeat.timeout) Retry None: a failure is counted and logged, and the next tick is the retry.

Only the Leader sends it, so it stops when no replica leads, and it stops when Muster is down. Both are what you want a dead man's switch to see. See High availability. The call goes through the outbound address policy like every other outbound request, so a service on a private network needs an allowed entry under Organization → Outbound addresses when the policy is strict.

items.title: What the System status page shows
items.text:
Organization → System status has a section Outgoing heartbeat with the last result:

  • Last sent {time}: OK
  • Last sent {time}: {reason}, where the reason is, for example, that the host name does not resolve, that no answer came in time, that the TLS handshake failed or that the URL refused the request
  • Not sent yet, right after a start or a change

The settings page shows the same as Last result: OK, sent {time}, Last result: not sent yet and Last result: nothing is sent without a URL. Check it after you save: it proves that Muster reaches the service.

items.title: Request log
items.text: The Request log keeps the recent HTTP requests Muster sent to a messenger, a bridge or an outgoing webhook, and those that reached a Connection's addresses, each with its answer and with secrets masked. It shows what Muster sent and what came back when a Root message looks wrong, a check fails or a button press does nothing, without a packet capture. It is neither the Audit log, which says who changed what, nor the Delivery events, which say what happened to an Alert Group's delivery: the Request log keeps the requests themselves, for a short time.

items.title: What is recorded
items.text:
Each attempt of a request is a record of its own.

Requests Muster sends for a Connection or an outgoing webhook Destination: Root messages, their edits, Thread replies, final edits, Storm summaries and deletions; test messages, and the button press a Mattermost test makes through the bot (a Slack test makes none, because a bot cannot press its own button); answers to people, such as ephemeral messages and callback answers; the requests of Account links, such as finding a person and sending a direct message; channel lists, bridge info and webhook registration; event polling (Telegram getUpdates, Bridge pollEvents), and the request that opens a Slack Socket Mode connection; and the requests of checks and tests — the Connection check, the check before saving, also of a Connection that does not exist yet, the Destination check, the test message and the probe of a Broken Destination.

Requests that reach Muster on the ingest listener, each with the answer Muster gave, refused ones included — a bad signature, a wrong secret token, a Connection in the other event delivery mode:

press /api/v1/callbacks/mattermost/{connection_id} A button press in Mattermost. update /api/v1/callbacks/telegram/{connection_id} A Telegram update in the webhook mode. push /api/v1/callbacks/bridge/{connection_id} An event a bridge pushes. interactive /api/v1/callbacks/slack/{connection_id} A button press in Slack, in the HTTP event mode. In Socket Mode there is no request to Muster: each envelope that carries an envelope id is recorded as received under its own type, with the socket's host as its URL, the envelope as its request and Muster's confirmation as its answer, without a status; the app subscribes to no events, so only interactive envelopes arrive. Slack's hello, disconnect and keep-alive frames are not recorded.

A record holds:

  • the time, and the direction: Sent (→) or Received (←);
  • the operation as its protocol names it: the method of the Telegram Bot API (sendMessage, editMessageText, getUpdates), the operation of Mattermost's REST API in lower camel case (createPost, patchPost, getPing), the operation of the Bridge protocol (getInfo, postMessage, pollEvents), the method of Slack's Web API as Slack names it (chat.postMessage, chat.update, apps.connections.open), response_url for an answer sent to a press's response_url, event or the request of a template (create, update, open_thread, reply_in_thread) for an outgoing webhook, and press, update, push or interactive for requests that reached Muster;
  • the method, the URL, the request headers and body, and the answer's status, headers and body — none for a request that got no answer;
  • the latency in milliseconds, the path — direct or through the proxy — and the attempt;
  • for a request that failed, its error class, what failed — the codes of the checks, such as a DNS lookup that failed or no answer in time — and the error text;
  • for a request of a check or a test, its kind — Connection check, Check before saving, Destination check, Test message or Broken probe — and its check run, which the requests of one check or test share;
  • the Connection or the outgoing webhook Destination it belongs to, and the Destination and the Alert Group it concerns, when it concerns one.

items.title: What is not recorded
items.text:
• A long poll that ended without events: an empty getUpdates of Telegram or pollEvents of a bridge.
  • A request to a callback address whose path names no Connection, or a deleted one.
  • The requests of OIDC sign-in and of the outgoing heartbeat.
  • The requests of muster doctor and muster bridge check, which run outside the server.

items.title: Bounds
items.text:
The bounds are built in; nothing configures them.

request_log.max_records The newest 500 records of each Connection, of each outgoing webhook Destination, and of the checks before saving of new Connections in an Organization. request_log.max_age 7 days on the business clock. request_log.body_max 16 KB (16,384 bytes) of each request or answer body.
  • A record past either bound is neither listed nor shown, even before it is deleted. The Leader deletes such records every minute (the task request_log_pruning).
  • A longer body is cut at a character boundary and marked with its full size: the record shows "Cut at 16 KB of {size} KB". Bodies are stored as text; bytes that are not UTF-8 are replaced.
  • A URL is kept up to 16 KB and the names and values of a request's or an answer's headers up to 64 KB in all; what is cut ends with "…".
  • The body of a request that reached Muster, or of Muster's answer, that is larger than 256 KB, or that was not read to the end, is kept as its size only: the record shows "Not kept: {size} KB, too large or not read to the end".
  • Writing a record never fails or delays the request it records beyond the write itself, which may take at most 2 seconds. A record that cannot be written is dropped, logged as request_log_write_failed and counted in muster_request_log_write_failures_total; see Log events and Metrics.

items.title: Masking
items.text:
Nothing secret is stored. Muster masks a record before it writes it: the requests it sends where they are made, which knows each request's secrets, and the requests that reach it in one place shared by the three callback addresses. Every masked value reads [redacted].

  • Secrets a request carries, wherever they appear — the URL, the headers and both bodies: a bot token, also inside a Telegram URL, the proxy password, an outgoing webhook's Secrets and Signing secret, a bridge's push secret, a secret in a query.
  • Headers whose values are always masked, whatever they hold: Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token, X-Slack-Signature and webhook-signature, the signature header of outgoing webhooks and of pushed Bridge events.
  • The URL keeps no user information, and the path of a Connection's base URL, which may be a secret — such as the path of a bridge behind a reverse proxy — is shown as [redacted], as in errors.
  • Values that authenticate a person: the signed action ids of buttons, which authenticate a Mattermost or a Slack press, and the tokens and codes of Account links — /start <token> in a Telegram update, the token of an account_link event, the code in a direct message.
  • What Slack sends and answers with: the bot token and the app-level token, the Slack signing secret, the address that apps.connections.open answers with, whose single-use ticket opens a socket, the response_url of a press, and the legacy verification token that every Slack payload still carries.

Headers and bodies are untrusted text. The record view shows them as plain text and never renders HTML or Markdown.

items.title: Who may read it
items.text:
To list the records of a Connection, or of a check run needs: connections:read To list the records of a Destination needs: destinations:read To open a record of a Connection, or of a check before saving needs: connections:read To open a record of an outgoing webhook Destination needs: destinations:read

A messenger Destination's requests are its Connection's: its list shows the records of its Connection that concern it, and opening one of them needs connections:read. The built-in Roles — Admin, Responder and Viewer — hold both Permissions; a Personal access token may hold fewer.

items.title: Where to find it
items.text:
The Request log of a Connection, or of an outgoing webhook Destination, is a tab of its page:

  1. Open Connections → a Connection, of any type, or Destinations → an outgoing webhook, and select the tab Request log. A messenger Destination's page has no tab of its own. The list shows, newest first, the time in your time zone, the direction arrow, the operation with the kind of check below it, the status — or, without an answer, what failed — and the latency; Load more shows older records.

  2. Narrow the list by Direction, Status — the class 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx or No answer — and Operation, and select Apply. The filters are kept in the address, such as ?tab=request-log&direction=inbound&status_class=4xx, so a link to a filtered list can be shared.

  3. Select an operation to open its record: the request — method, URL, headers, body — and the answer — status, headers, body — side by side on a wide screen and one under the other on a narrow one; a JSON body is indented. Copy URL, Copy headers and Copy body copy each, the body as it is stored rather than indented. A record links to its Destination, its Alert Group and the other requests of its check.

The same records show in two more places:

  • The Alert Group page → Delivery → Requests on each Destination's row: what was sent to that Destination for this Alert Group and what came back.
  • Requests of this check under the result of the Connection check, of the check before saving and of the Destination's check and test: the requests that check or test made.

The API reads the same records: listRequestLog and getRequestRecord in the API reference, with the check run in the results of the Connection check, the check before saving, the Destination check and the Destination test.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
• Button presses in Mattermost do nothing. Filter the Connection's Request log by Received. No press at all means that the Mattermost server does not reach Muster: see Let button presses reach Muster. A press that Muster answered shows the answer the person got, such as the text that their account is not linked.
  • Button presses in Slack do nothing. In the HTTP event mode, filter the Connection's Request log by Received. No interactive at all means that Slack does not reach Muster: see Socket Mode or HTTP. An interactive answered 401 means a wrong Slack signing secret, a clock further than slack.request_tolerance from Slack's, or a Connection in Socket Mode. In Socket Mode, an interactive is recorded for each press, and the Connection page says whether another program shares the app.
  • A Root message looks wrong. On the Alert Group page, open Requests of that Destination: the createPost, sendMessage or postMessage shows the body Muster sent and what the messenger answered.
  • A bridge refuses a message. The Connection's Request log shows the postMessage, the problem the bridge answered with its detail, and the latency.
  • A check before saving fails. Requests of this check shows what the address answered, such as an HTML page of a reverse proxy instead of the bridge's info.
  • Pushed events are refused. A bridge that signs its pushes with an old secret shows each push answered 401.
  • An outgoing webhook fails. The Destination's Request log, filtered by 5xx, shows each attempt with the endpoint's status and body.

items.title: Upgrades
items.text: Muster follows semantic versioning (major.minor.patch). A release publishes the container image ghcr.io/muster-io/muster, binaries, and the Helm chart as an OCI artifact in the same registry. The changelog of each release is on the releases page of the repository, written from the commit messages.

items.title: The rules
items.text:
• Patch and minor versions. Update to the next version, or to any patch version of the same minor version.
  • Rolling updates only between adjacent minor versions. From 1.4.x to 1.5.x, replica by replica, is supported. From 1.4.x to 1.7.x is not: go through 1.5 and 1.6, or stop every replica before you start the new version.
  • Back up first. Take a database backup before every upgrade, because of the next rule.
  • No downgrades. Migrations only go forward in production. A binary refuses to start on a schema newer than it knows and names both versions. To go back, restore the backup you took before the upgrade, together with the master keys of that time, and run the old version on it. Everything written since is lost.
  • Read the release notes of every version you skip. Settings that change are named there.

items.title: Upgrade with Helm
items.text:
1. Take a backup.
  2. Change the version: helm upgrade muster oci://ghcr.io/muster-io/charts/muster --version <version> -n muster -f values.yaml. The chart's image.tag defaults to its appVersion, so the chart and the image move together. If you pin image.tag, change it too.
  3. Watch the rollout: kubectl -n muster rollout status deploy/muster.
  4. Run muster doctor (see the CLI) and open Organization → System status: it shows the version and commit that serve the page, and under Replicas which replica is the Leader.

The chart does not migrate in the server. Each new pod runs muster migrate in an init container before its server container starts, and MUSTER_MIGRATE_ON_START stays off. The pods of a rollout do not migrate at once, because migrations run under a database lock. Kubernetes starts a new pod before it stops an old one, so the web UI and ingestion stay up with one replica too; run two replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget if you also want to survive the loss of a node.

items.title: Upgrade with Docker Compose
items.text: The compose example sets MUSTER_MIGRATE_ON_START to true: the server migrates when it starts. Take a backup, change the image (set MUSTER_IMAGE, or download the compose file of the new release), and run docker compose up -d. With a single replica nothing else is needed.

items.title: Migrations
items.text:
Migrations are SQL files built into the binary. They run through muster migrate or, when MUSTER_MIGRATE_ON_START is true, at server start, in both cases under a session advisory lock and with the applied versions in the log.

Every migration follows expand and contract: a release only adds what the previous release can ignore, and removes what the previous release no longer uses in a later release. That is why a rolling update between adjacent minor versions works: while the new schema is in place, the replicas of the old version still run on it.

To migrate before you update the servers, run the command of the new version with the environment of the server:

muster migrate

It needs the database settings and MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS of the server (see the CLI). It exits non-zero on a schema newer than the binary knows.

items.title: During a rolling update
items.text: Replicas of two adjacent minor versions serve at the same time, and either may be the Leader. Do not leave an installation in this state: finish the rollout.

items.title: Runbooks
items.text:
One page for every alert Muster can raise: the rules of the Helm chart, evaluated by Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics from Muster's metrics, and the Internal alerts that Muster raises itself. Each page says what the alert means, its impact, how to diagnose it and how to fix it.

Alert Severity Source MusterDown critical chart rule MusterNoLeader critical chart rule MusterDeliveryFailing critical chart rule MusterDestinationBroken critical both MusterHeartbeatLost critical both MusterDeliverySlow warning chart rule MusterDeliveryQueueGrowing warning chart rule MusterIngestBacklog warning chart rule MusterIngestRejected warning chart rule MusterTemplateError warning both MusterClockSkew warning chart rule MusterLoginFailures warning chart rule MusterSnapshotTruncated warning Internal alert MusterOIDCSecretExpiring warning Internal alert

items.title: Two sources
items.text:
• Chart rules are evaluated by your monitoring from the metrics Muster serves at /metrics, and reach people through your Alertmanager like any other rule. Their thresholds, windows and job selector are values of the chart; the expressions on these pages are the defaults.
  • Internal alerts are raised by Muster itself, as Alerts of the built-in Integration "Muster" that every Organization has. Ordinary Routes pick them by their labels and deliver them like any other Alert Group; see Internal alerts.
  • An alert listed as both is an Internal alert with a chart rule of the same name for the same condition. The chart rule is the backup for when Muster cannot deliver the Internal alert itself.

Send the critical chart rules through an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster, to a pager or a chat that Muster does not manage: when Muster is down or cannot deliver, it cannot deliver an alert about that either.

items.title: Runbook links
items.text:
Every Internal alert carries a runbook_url annotation that opens its page here, for the version of Muster that raised it, and the chart rules link to the same pages:

<MUSTER_RUNBOOK_BASE_URL>/<version>/operations/runbooks/<alertname>/

MUSTER_RUNBOOK_BASE_URL is https://muster-io.github.io/muster by default, the published site; point it at your own copy of the site where people cannot reach the public one. <version> is the major.minor of a release, such as 1.2 for 1.2.3, or latest for any version that is not a release X.Y.Z: a development build, the sha-… and edge images and pre-releases. For example, MusterOIDCSecretExpiring of a development build links to https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/MusterOIDCSecretExpiring/.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
A replica's clock differs from the database clock by more than 2 seconds. The chart rule is:

max by (instance) (abs(muster_clock_skew_seconds{job="muster"})) > 2

It fires after 5 minutes, with severity warning and the label instance. It is a chart rule only. Each replica measures its clock against the database every minute and exports the difference as muster_clock_skew_seconds, positive when the replica is ahead.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
Every replica takes the time from its own system clock, and the replicas share one database, so a replica that is off disagrees with the others:

  • Timestamps it writes — of Alerts, Alert Groups and Timeline entries — are off by the skew, and the timers and windows it evaluates, such as Snooze ends, Ack timeouts and the Reopen window, run early or late.
  • TOTP codes may be refused at sign-in.
  • ID tokens of the identity provider may be refused as not yet valid or expired, so OIDC sign-in fails.
  • Signatures of outgoing webhooks carry a timestamp that receivers may reject.
  • Leases of claimed rows and of the Leader lock expire too early or too late, which can make work run twice or wait.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Find the replica: muster_clock_skew_seconds by instance.
  2. Read its log lines clock_skew (skew_seconds, warning_seconds): logged on every measurement above process.clock_skew_warning (2 s).
  3. Run muster doctor on the same host or node. The line clock_skew prints the measured skew, and warns with "… against the database clock, more than 2s" above the limit.
  4. Check time synchronisation on the node of the replica and on the database server: whether NTP (chrony, systemd-timesyncd or the cloud provider's time service) runs and is in sync.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Synchronise the clocks of the nodes and of the database server with NTP. The skew is measured again every minute, and the alert resolves 5 minutes after it falls under 2 seconds.
  • When only one node is off, move the replica to another node until its clock is fixed.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
A Destination has deliveries waiting and has not had a successful delivery for 10 minutes. The chart rule is:

max by (destination) (muster_delivery_queue{job="muster"}) > 0 unless on (destination) sum by (destination) (increase(muster_delivery_attempts_total{job="muster",outcome="delivered"}[10m])) > 0

It fires after 5 minutes, with severity critical and the label destination, the Destination's id; muster_destination_info{destination="…"} gives its name. It is a chart rule only. It fires before the Destination becomes Broken as well as after: Muster retries a Transient error with a growing pause (delivery.transient_backoff, from 2 s up to 5 min) and marks the Destination Broken only when the Transient budget runs out (delivery.transient_budget, 10 attempts within 30 minutes) or after a Fatal error.

Route it around Muster

Send this alert through an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster: the Destination it is about may be the one that would carry it.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• The Root messages of the Destination are not created or edited: people in that chat do not see new Alert Groups, and the messages they see may show an old status. Thread replies wait too.
  • Other Destinations, ingestion, Commands from the UI and the API, and timers keep working. The Alert Group pages show the current state, and the Alert Group list filter Delivery problem finds the affected Alert Groups.
  • Nothing is lost while deliveries wait: once the Destination answers again, Muster delivers the current state of each Root message, not every change it missed.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Open System status (/admin/system-status): Delivery queues shows how many deliveries wait per Destination, and Broken Destinations whether the Destination is already Broken.
  2. Open the Destination page (/destinations/<id>). Health says Healthy or Broken; a Broken Destination shows "Broken since HH:MM: {reason}. Muster tries again every {interval}."
  3. Look at the outcomes of its attempts: sum by (outcome) (increase(muster_delivery_attempts_total{job="muster",destination="<id>"}[15m])). transient and unknown point at the network or the messenger; retry_after at rate limits; fatal and markup_rejected at the configuration or the message; template_error at a template, see MusterTemplateError.
  4. Read the log lines delivery_attempt for the Destination (destination is its id): outcome, code (the HTTP status of the answer or the error_code of a Telegram answer, 0 when the outcome carries no status), reason (the masked error the messenger answered or the call failed with), attempt, duration_ms and retry_after_ms. outbound_blocked means that the outbound address policy refused the address or the proxy (rule names why); delivery_work_failed that the worker itself could not attempt, for example because the database connection was lost.
  5. Compare with all outbound calls of the delivery client class: sum by (outcome) (rate(muster_client_requests_total{job="muster",client="delivery"}[5m])). Failures across every Destination point at the network, a proxy or DNS rather than one messenger.
  6. Press Check on the Destination page, or run muster doctor, which prints one line per Mattermost, Slack, Telegram and Bridge Destination (destination <name>) with the result of its check.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Network, DNS or proxy: fix the path from the replicas to the messenger, the proxy of the Connection, or the Organization's Outbound addresses (/admin/organization/outbound) when outbound_blocked names the address.
  • Credentials or permissions: replace the bot token on the Connection, or give the bot back the rights the Destination check asks for, then press Check.
  • Telegram is blocked in your network: see Telegram in restricted networks.
  • When the Destination has become Broken, follow MusterDestinationBroken.
  • The alert resolves once a delivery to the Destination succeeds, or its queue is empty.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
A Destination has more than 100 deliveries waiting, and the number keeps growing. The chart rule is:

max by (destination) (muster_delivery_queue{job="muster"}) > 100 and max by (destination) (deriv(muster_delivery_queue{job="muster"}[15m])) > 0

It fires after 15 minutes, with severity warning and the label destination, the Destination's id; muster_destination_info gives its name. It is a chart rule only. muster_delivery_queue is counted by the Leader every 15 seconds: the pending deliveries and Thread replies that are due.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• The messages of that Destination fall further and further behind: new Alert Groups and their changes appear late. Deliveries are still made; nothing is lost.
  • Other Destinations, the UI and the API keep working.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Open System status (/admin/system-status): Delivery queues shows the waiting deliveries per Destination, Storms the Routes in a Storm and Broken Destinations whether the Destination stopped.
  2. Look at the outcomes of its attempts: sum by (outcome) (increase(muster_delivery_attempts_total{job="muster",destination="<id>"}[15m])). Many retry_after mean that the messenger limits the rate; transient or unknown that calls fail; few attempts of any kind that Muster's own limiter holds them back.
  3. Check whether a Storm feeds the queue: muster_storm_active by route and the log line storm_started. route.storm_threshold is 20 new Alert Groups per minute.
  4. For Telegram, compare the load with the limiters: destination.telegram.limiter allows 10 requests per minute per Destination, sends and edits together, in the channel and its discussion group. For Slack, destination.slack.limiter allows 30 requests per minute per Destination, sends and edits together, and connection.slack.limiter 50 requests per minute per Connection.
  5. When no delivery succeeds at all, follow MusterDeliveryFailing instead.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Reduce what feeds the Destination: tune the grouping of its Routes, create an Alertmanager silence for a noisy source, or move some Routes to another Destination.
  • When calls fail, fix the cause as in MusterDeliveryFailing.
  • A queue that only grows during a Storm shrinks after it: Muster coalesces the changes of a Root message, so it delivers the current state rather than every change.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
Deliveries are slow: the 95th percentile of the time from receiving a Snapshot to the API call that delivers the resulting change is above 5 seconds, the objective Muster keeps while its rate limiters have room. The chart rule is:

histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(muster_delivery_latency_seconds_bucket{job="muster"}[15m]))) > 5

It fires after 15 minutes, with severity warning. It is a chart rule only and has no labels of its own: it covers every Destination together. Changes made by Commands or timers are not measured, only those caused by Snapshots.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• New Alert Groups and their changes appear in the messengers later than usual. Nothing is lost.
  • The UI and the API show the current state without delay; Commands keep working.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Find the slow Destinations: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, destination) (rate(muster_delivery_latency_seconds_bucket{job="muster"}[15m]))). muster_destination_info gives their names.
  2. Look for rate limits: increase(muster_delivery_attempts_total{job="muster",outcome="retry_after"}[15m]) by destination. A messenger that answers "retry after" makes Muster wait as long as it asks.
  3. Look for a Storm: muster_storm_active by route, the log line storm_started and Storms on the System status page (/admin/system-status). More than route.storm_threshold (20) new Alert Groups per minute on a Route fill the limiters.
  4. Check Muster's own limiters. Telegram: destination.telegram.limiter (10 requests per minute per Destination, sends and edits together, in the channel and its discussion group) and connection.telegram.limiter (15 messages per second per Connection). Slack: destination.slack.limiter (30 requests per minute per Destination, sends and edits together) and connection.slack.limiter (50 requests per minute per Connection). A busy Destination waits for its limiter, which is expected and not a fault.
  5. Check the latency of the calls themselves: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, outcome) (rate(muster_client_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="muster",client="delivery"}[15m]))). Slow calls point at the network, a proxy or the messenger.
  6. Check Delivery queues on the System status page; when a queue keeps growing, see MusterDeliveryQueueGrowing.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• A Storm or a noisy Route: tune the Route's grouping so that one problem makes one Alert Group, or create an Alertmanager silence for the source. The Storm summary already replaces separate messages while the Storm lasts.
  • Rate limits of one chat: spread the Routes of that Destination over more Destinations (chats or channels).
  • Slow calls: fix the network path or the proxy of the Connection; for Telegram in a restricted network, see Telegram in restricted networks.
  • The alert clears once the 95th percentile over 15 minutes is back under 5 seconds.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
A Destination is Broken: Muster stopped sending to it after a Fatal error — the messenger refused the bot or the request for good — or after its Transient budget ran out (delivery.transient_budget, 10 attempts within 30 minutes). Muster then probes it every delivery.broken_probe_interval (5 minutes) with the oldest waiting delivery, or with the Destination check when nothing waits, and ends the Broken state on the first success.

This alert has two sources with the same name, severity critical and this page:

  • The Internal alert, raised by Muster itself as an Alert of the built-in "Muster" Integration when the Destination becomes Broken, with the labels destination (the Destination's id) and destination_name. It is resolved when a probe, the Destination check or a test message succeeds, and when the Destination is deleted.

  • The chart rule, the backup for when Muster cannot deliver the Internal alert:

    max by (destination) (muster_destination_broken{job="muster"}) == 1

    It fires after 5 minutes with the label destination. muster_destination_broken is set by the Leader.

Route it around Muster

Send the chart rule through an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster. Route the Internal alert to a Destination of another kind than the Broken one — a Broken Telegram Destination usually means that Telegram is unreachable for every Telegram Destination, so send MusterDestinationBroken of Telegram Destinations to Mattermost or an outgoing webhook.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• Nothing is sent to the Destination: no new Root messages, no edits, no Thread replies. Its deliveries wait, and the Alert Groups that wait for it show a delivery problem; the Alert Group list filter Delivery problem finds them.
  • Other Destinations, ingestion, Commands and timers keep working.
  • When the Broken state ends, Muster brings every waiting Root message to its current state; it does not replay the changes it missed one by one.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Open System status (/admin/system-status): Broken Destinations lists every Broken Destination and since when. The Destination list (/destinations) has the filter Broken Destinations too.
  2. Open the Destination page (/destinations/<id>). The banner says "Broken since HH:MM: {reason}. Muster tries again every {interval}." The reason is the error the messenger answered, with secrets masked.
  3. Find the log line destination_broken (destination, cause, reason): cause is fatal after a Fatal error and unavailable after the Transient budget ran out. outbound_blocked lines for the same address mean that the outbound address policy refused it.
  4. Press Check on the Destination page to run the Destination check now, or run muster doctor, which prints a line destination <name> with the failing step. For a Connection problem, press Check connection on the Connection page (/connections/<id>).

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• cause fatal: fix what the reason names. Typical cases are a revoked bot token (replace it on the Connection), a bot that lost its admin rights in a Telegram channel or its discussion group, a bot removed from a Slack channel (invite it again with /invite) or a Slack channel that was archived, a deleted channel or chat, or an outgoing webhook that answers with a permanent error. Then press Check: a check that passes ends the Broken state at once.
  • cause unavailable: the messenger or the path to it was down long enough to use up the Transient budget. Fix the network, the proxy of the Connection or the Outbound addresses (/admin/organization/outbound); the next probe ends the Broken state by itself, or press Check to end it now.
  • Slack answers 429: it limits each method per app and workspace. Muster holds the whole Connection for the seconds of Retry-After and does not count that as a failed attempt, so a 429 with Retry-After does not make a Destination Broken. A 429 without it counts as a transient failure, and enough of them use up the Transient budget (cause unavailable): lower the limiters or spread the load. See Rate limits.
  • Telegram is unreachable from your network: see Telegram in restricted networks.
  • Send test message on the Destination page also ends the Broken state when every step succeeds.
  • The Internal alert resolves and destination_recovered (destination, broken_for_s) is logged when the Broken state ends; the chart rule resolves at the Leader's next update of muster_destination_broken.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
Prometheus cannot scrape a Muster replica: the target of the job muster is down. The chart rule is:

up{job="muster"} == 0

It fires after 2 minutes, with severity critical and one alert per scrape target (instance). It is a chart rule only; Muster cannot raise it about itself.

Route it around Muster

Send this alert through an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster, for example straight to a pager or a chat that Muster does not manage. While Muster is down it cannot deliver anything, this alert included.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• With every replica down, nothing is ingested, no message is sent or edited, and the UI, the API and the buttons in the messengers do not answer. Alertmanager retries its failed notifications, and each later notification carries the whole Alertmanager group again, so Muster catches up once it is back.
  • With one replica of several down, the others keep working: ingestion, delivery and timers run on every replica, and another replica takes over the Leader tasks if the stopped one was the Leader.
  • After the downtime, the new Leader records it (downtime_recorded) and Muster recovers: see Recovery after downtime on the System status page.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Find out whether the process runs at all: the pod or the container, its restarts and its exit code.
  2. Ask the internal listener (MUSTER_LISTEN_INTERNAL, :8082 by default) directly. GET /health/live answers 200 while the process serves; GET /health/ready answers 503 while the database does not answer or the shutdown has begun.
  3. Read the last log lines of the replica:
    • startup_failed: start-up stopped; its error says what to fix — the database cannot be reached, a migration failed or a listener cannot listen.
    • listener_failed: a listener stopped with an error and the process exits so that it is restarted.
    • shutdown_requested: the replica received SIGTERM, for example during a rollout.
  4. When the process runs but the scrape fails, check the scrape configuration against MUSTER_LISTEN_INTERNAL: the port, the path /metrics and the network policy between Prometheus and the replica.
  5. Run muster doctor with the replica's settings. The lines database, session_connection and key_canary name a database that cannot be reached, a session connection whose advisory locks or LISTEN do not work, and master keys that do not decrypt the stored data.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Fix what startup_failed or muster doctor names: the database URL or its credentials, the master keys, a port that another process holds.
  • When the database is down, bring it back first; Muster becomes ready as soon as it answers.
  • When only the scrape fails, correct the scrape target or the network policy.
  • Once Muster is back, open Recovery after downtime on the System status page (/admin/system-status) and the Alert Group list: Alertmanager's next notifications bring the state up to date.
  • Set up an outgoing heartbeat (Organization → Outgoing heartbeat, /admin/organization/outgoing-heartbeat) to an external dead man's switch, so that a stopped Muster is noticed even when Prometheus cannot report it.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
An Integration is Heartbeat lost: its Heartbeat is on, and no signal arrived within its Heartbeat timeout (integration.heartbeat_timeout, 5 minutes by default). Something on the path from Prometheus through Alertmanager and the network to Muster has stopped; see Heartbeat.

This alert has two sources with the same name, severity critical and this page:

  • The Internal alert, raised by the Leader's Heartbeat check, which runs every 10 seconds, as an Alert of the built-in "Muster" Integration. Its labels are integration (the Integration's id), integration_name and the Integration's Static labels, so a Route can send it to the team of that cluster. It is resolved by the next signal, by turning the Heartbeat off, and by deleting the Integration.

  • The chart rule, the backup for when Muster itself cannot deliver the Internal alert:

    max by (integration) (muster_heartbeat_lost{job="muster"}) == 1

    It fires after 1 minute with the label integration. muster_heartbeat_lost is set by the Leader's Heartbeat check.

Route it around Muster

Send the chart rule through an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster, so that it reaches people even when the path through Muster is the one that broke.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• Alerts from that Alertmanager may not reach Muster: new problems in that cluster may go unnoticed.
  • Stale resolution pauses for the Integration: the time without a live Heartbeat does not count towards an alert's time to go Stale, so nothing is resolved as Stale until the signal returns.
  • Other Integrations, delivery and Commands keep working.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Open the Integration page (/integrations/<id>): the banner says "No contact with Alertmanager since HH:MM…", the time of the last signal. System status (/admin/system-status) lists the Integration under Integrations needing attention as "Heartbeat lost since …".
  2. Find the log line heartbeat_lost (integration, last_signal_at). The signal returning logs heartbeat_live with first false.
  3. Check Alertmanager: is it running, and does it still have the Heartbeat route and receiver? Its own metrics show failed notifications to the Heartbeat receiver.
  4. Check Prometheus: the always-firing alert (MusterHeartbeat, or Watchdog in kube-prometheus-stack) must be firing, so the rule evaluation and the connection from Prometheus to Alertmanager work.
  5. Check the path to Muster's ingest listener (MUSTER_INGEST_URL): DNS, ingress, certificates and network policies. Requests that arrive with a wrong or revoked token are refused with 401 and logged as ingest_rejected; see MusterIngestRejected.
  6. When many Integrations are Heartbeat lost at once, the problem is likely on Muster's side: its ingest listener or the network in front of it.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Restart or repair Alertmanager or Prometheus, or restore the Heartbeat route and receiver from the snippet (The snippet).
  • Fix the network path or the ingress to MUSTER_INGEST_URL.
  • Replace a revoked token in the Heartbeat receiver with a token of the Integration.
  • When the cluster was retired on purpose, turn the Heartbeat off or delete the Integration; both resolve the alert.
  • The next signal makes the Heartbeat live again and resolves the Internal alert; see When the Heartbeat is lost.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
Processing falls behind ingestion: more than 1,000 Stored Snapshots wait to be processed, or the 95th percentile of the time from receiving a Snapshot to the end of its processing is above 60 seconds. The chart rule is:

max(muster_ingest_backlog{job="muster"}) > 1000 or histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(muster_ingest_processing_delay_seconds_bucket{job="muster"}[5m]))) > 60

It fires after 5 minutes, with severity warning. It is a chart rule only. muster_ingest_backlog is counted by the Leader over every Organization. Ingestion itself keeps answering Alertmanager: Muster stores each Snapshot first and processes it afterwards, in arrival order per Alertmanager group.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• New Alerts reach their Alert Groups late, and so do resolves: Alert Groups appear, change and resolve in the UI and in the messengers later than Alertmanager sent them.
  • Nothing is lost: the Stored Snapshots wait and are processed in order.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Find the slow Integrations: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, integration) (rate(muster_ingest_processing_delay_seconds_bucket{job="muster"}[5m]))).
  2. List what waits for one Integration: GET /api/v1/stored-snapshots?integration=<id>&state=pending, or the Stored Snapshots of the Integration page (/integrations/<id>).
  3. Read the log lines snapshot_processing_interrupted (integration, error): the processing worker stopped because the database failed or the connection was lost, and tries again after a growing pause.
  4. Check the database pool of each replica: muster_db_pool_connections by state against muster_db_pool_max_connections, and the rate of muster_db_pool_acquire_wait_seconds_total. A pool that is always fully acquired, with the wait time growing, means that the replicas need more connections.
  5. Check whether failures add to the load: muster_ingest_failed_snapshots_total by integration and the log line snapshot_failed (integration, stored_snapshot, error). A failed Snapshot is not retried by itself; the Snapshots behind it are processed.
  6. Check the database itself: CPU, I/O, locks and slow queries.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Restore the database or the connection to it; the worker resumes on its own.
  • Give the replicas more connections (pool_max_conns of MUSTER_DATABASE_URL, by default the larger of 10 and the number of CPUs), or run more replicas. Each Integration processes processing.parallel_groups (2) Alertmanager groups at the same time.
  • Reduce the input: an Alertmanager that sends very often or very large groups makes more work. Check its group_interval and repeat_interval.
  • After fixing the cause of snapshot_failed, process the failed Snapshots again with muster ingest replay --since <duration> [--integration <name>] --actor <name>, for example muster ingest replay --since 2h --integration prod-eu --actor "Jane Doe". Processing is idempotent, so Snapshots that were processed change nothing.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
Muster refused ingestion requests within 15 minutes: an oversized one, or more than 10 without a valid Integration token, counted per value of the label integration. The chart rule is:

sum by (integration, outcome) (increase(muster_ingest_requests_total{job="muster",outcome="too_large"}[15m])) > 0 or sum by (integration, outcome) (increase(muster_ingest_requests_total{job="muster",outcome="unauthorized"}[15m])) > 10

It fires at once (for: 0m), with severity warning and the labels integration — the id of the token's Integration, or unknown when the token matched none — and outcome. It is a chart rule only.

  • too_large: the body was larger than ingest.body_limit (16 MB) and was refused with 413.
  • unauthorized: the token was missing, wrong or revoked, belonged to a deleted Integration, or was an API token instead of an Integration token; refused with 401.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• The refused requests are not stored or processed. When they come from an Alertmanager, its Alerts do not reach Muster, and with a Heartbeat on, the Integration soon becomes Heartbeat lost.
  • Requests with a valid Integration token and a body within ingest.body_limit keep working.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. See which Integration and outcome: sum by (integration, outcome) (increase(muster_ingest_requests_total{job="muster"}[15m])).
  2. Read the log lines ingest_rejected (integration, outcome, route_pattern, client_address): the route pattern tells ingestion from the Heartbeat, and the client address which host sent it. Muster never logs a token.
  3. For unauthorized, open the Integration page (/integrations/<id>) and compare its tokens and their last use with the Alertmanager receivers that send to it. integration="unknown" means the token matched no Integration at all: a mistyped token, one of a deleted Integration, an API token, or a scanner probing the ingest listener.
  4. For too_large, find the Alertmanager group that produces such a Snapshot: a group with very many Alerts or very long annotations.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• A revoked or old token still in use: put a current token into the Alertmanager receiver and reload Alertmanager; see Token rotation.
  • An API token in a receiver: replace it with a token of the Integration; ingestion accepts only Integration tokens.
  • Traffic from unknown addresses: restrict who may reach the ingest listener (MUSTER_INGEST_URL) with a network policy or the ingress.
  • too_large: split the Alertmanager group with a finer group_by, or shorten the annotations that make it large.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
A burst of failed sign-ins: more than 20 for one method within 10 minutes. The chart rule is:

sum by (method) (increase(muster_login_failures_total{job="muster"}[10m])) > 20

It fires at once (for: 0m), with severity warning and the label method: local for a wrong login or password, totp for a wrong TOTP or recovery code, oidc for a refused OIDC sign-in. It is a chart rule only. Attempts that the sign-in throttle refuses before evaluating them are not counted.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• Someone may be guessing passwords or codes. The sign-in throttle (auth.signin_throttle) slows them down: after 3 consecutive failures per account or source address, each attempt waits twice as long as the previous one, up to 60 seconds.
  • Legitimate users of the same account or address wait longer between attempts.
  • With oidc, people may be unable to sign in at all because the identity provider or its settings fail.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. See the method: sum by (method) (increase(muster_login_failures_total{job="muster"}[10m])).
  2. For local and totp, open the Audit log (Organization → Audit log, /admin/audit-log) and look for the actions session.sign_in_failed and session.second_factor_failed: each names the account, when it is known, and the source address.
  3. For oidc, read the log lines oidc_sign_in_failed (reason, error): the identity provider reported an error, could not be reached, or answered with an ID token that did not verify. A clock that is off also makes ID tokens fail; see MusterClockSkew.
  4. Tell an attack from a mistake: many accounts from few addresses look like guessing; one account from its usual address looks like a forgotten password or a script with an old one.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Guessing from outside: block the source addresses at the ingress or the firewall, and restrict who may reach the UI.
  • A forgotten password or a lost authenticator: on the user's page (/admin/users/<id>), create a New password setup link or Reset TOTP. Without an Admin who can sign in, use the emergency commands muster admin reset-password --actor <name> <login> and muster admin reset-totp --actor <name> <login>.
  • A script or a tool with old credentials: give it a Personal access token or an API token of a Service account instead of a password.
  • oidc failures: fix the identity provider, or the OIDC settings (/admin/oidc) and their Check connection; see Sign-in with Keycloak. Local sign-in stays available meanwhile.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
Every replica of Muster reports that it is not the Leader. The chart rule is:

max(muster_leader{job="muster"}) == 0

It fires after 2 minutes, with severity critical. It is a chart rule only. One replica, the Leader, holds a lock in the database and runs the Leader tasks; when it cannot confirm its lock within leader.fencing_timeout (15 s) it stops them, and any replica may take the lock. This alert means that none has for 2 minutes.

Route it around Muster

Send this alert through an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster. Muster still delivers without a Leader, but the problem behind the missing Leader — usually the database — may stop delivery next.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
What stops while no replica leads:

  • Telegram polling: Connections in the long polling update mode receive no button presses and no messages from the discussion group.
  • Bridge polling: Bridge Connections in the poll event delivery mode receive no events — no button presses, Text commands, Account link requests or reports of deleted messages — until a replica leads again. A press or a Text command that is older than bridge.event_max_age (1 hour) by then is dropped unanswered.
  • Slack's Socket Mode: Slack Connections in the socket event mode hold no Socket Mode connection, so a button press made meanwhile is lost — the person sees Slack's error — until a replica leads again and connects. Muster does not count on Slack to send such presses again.
  • The Heartbeat check and the Stale check: no Integration becomes Heartbeat lost, and no alert is resolved as Stale.
  • Partition maintenance, retention and the pruning of short-lived state, the outgoing heartbeat, the expiry check of the OIDC client secret and the Leader-only metrics (muster_alert_groups, muster_delivery_queue, muster_destination_broken, muster_heartbeat_lost, muster_ingest_backlog, muster_storm_active), which go stale or disappear.

What keeps working: ingestion, delivery to every Destination, timers (the end of a Snooze, Ack timeouts and Reminders), the UI, the API, the webhook update mode of Telegram, the push event delivery mode of Bridge Connections and the http event mode of Slack Connections, whose presses any replica receives. After leader.absence_notice (2 minutes) without a Leader, the UI shows the banner "No replica is leading: Telegram and Bridge polling, Slack's Socket Mode, Heartbeat and Stale checks are paused."

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Open System status (/admin/system-status). Replicas lists every replica that refreshed its record, when it last did ("Refreshed …"), and which one is the Leader; with no Leader, no replica carries the flag.
  2. Check muster_leader per replica: max by (instance) (muster_leader{job="muster"}). A replica that does not appear at all is not scraped; see MusterDown.
  3. Read the logs of the replicas:
    • leadership_lost (replica, error): the Leader could not confirm its lock within leader.fencing_timeout, or its lock session failed.
    • leadership_acquired (replica): a replica took the lock. Alternating lost and acquired lines mean that the lock keeps breaking.
    • leader_task_failed (task, error): a Leader task failed, usually because the database was unavailable.
  4. Run muster doctor with the replicas' settings. session_connection must say "advisory locks and LISTEN work": the Leader lock is an advisory lock on the session connection. Behind a pooler in transaction mode, such as PgBouncer, advisory locks do not hold, and MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_URL must point at the database directly or at a pool in session mode.
  5. Check the database itself: its availability, failovers, connection limits and the latency between the replicas and the database.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Restore the database or the network path to it. Once the session connection works again, a replica takes the lock within seconds and the banner disappears.
  • Set MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_URL when the main connection goes through a pooler in transaction mode, and restart the replicas.
  • Raise the database's connection limit if the session connections are refused: each replica holds about three of them besides its main pool.
  • Once a Leader returns, the paused tasks run again at their next interval: the new Leader polls Telegram and the bridges and connects Slack's Socket Mode, and the Heartbeat and Stale checks resume from the signals and Snapshots that ingestion recorded meanwhile.
  • A Slack Connection that must not lose a press while no replica leads uses the http event mode, which every replica serves.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
The OIDC client secret expires soon: the date entered as Client secret expires on in the OIDC settings is within oidc.secret_expiry_lead (14 days).

It is an Internal alert only, severity warning, with no labels besides alertname and severity. The Leader checks the date every 5 minutes and raises it as an Alert of the built-in "Muster" Integration; it is resolved when the date is changed to a later one or cleared.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• Nothing yet. Once the secret expires, the identity provider refuses Muster's back-channel requests, and OIDC sign-in fails for everyone.
  • Local sign-in keeps working, so an Admin with a local password can still fix the settings.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Open the OIDC settings (/admin/oidc): the banner says "The client secret expires on {date}. Issue a new one in the identity provider and enter it here."
  2. The log line oidc_secret_expiring (expires_on) is written once per raise.
  3. In the identity provider, look up the client's secret and its real expiry date; the date in Muster is only what someone entered.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
1. Issue a new client secret in the identity provider, for Keycloak under the client's Credentials; see Sign-in with Keycloak.
  2. Enter the new secret in the OIDC settings, set Client secret expires on to its new expiry date, or clear it if the new secret does not expire, and save. With the API, PUT /api/v1/oidc-settings takes the fields client_secret and client_secret_expires_on.
  3. Press Check connection, then sign in once through OIDC to confirm.

The alert resolves within 5 minutes, at the Leader's next check.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
Alertmanager truncates the Snapshots of an Integration: it left Alerts out of a Snapshot because of the max_alerts limit of its webhook receiver, or, for Grafana, the Max alerts limit of its webhook contact point. Muster treats each Snapshot as the whole Alertmanager group, so a Truncated Snapshot hides Alerts from it.

It is an Internal alert only, severity warning, raised by Muster as an Alert of the built-in "Muster" Integration when the first Alertmanager group (groupKey) of the Integration arrives truncated. Its labels are integration (the Integration's id) and integration_name. It is resolved when no group of the Integration is truncated any more: each group's next untruncated Snapshot ends its truncation, and so does a group that has sent nothing for as long as it takes an Alert to go Stale.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• The Alerts that Alertmanager left out do not reach their Alert Groups: Muster may show fewer Alerts than fire, miss an Alert Group entirely, or keep an Alert open that Alertmanager no longer lists.
  • For Grafana, when a whole group resolves, its last Snapshot lists only the first alerts, up to Max alerts, and Grafana sends nothing more for the group until one of its alerts fires again. The Alerts it left out stay firing in Muster until they go Stale, which needs a live Heartbeat; the Heartbeat through Grafana has not been verified (see Connect Grafana).
  • Everything else of the Integration keeps working.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Open the Integration page (/integrations/<id>): the banner says "Alertmanager truncates Snapshots for N groups. Set max_alerts: 0 on the Alertmanager receiver." Its Alertmanager routes list shows the Truncated groups.
  2. System status (/admin/system-status) lists the Integration under Integrations needing attention with "Snapshots truncated".
  3. muster_ingest_truncated_snapshots_total by integration counts the truncated Snapshots; the log line internal_alert_raised (alertname, fingerprint, entity) marks when the alert was raised.
  4. Open a recent Stored Snapshot of the Integration (/integrations/<id>/snapshots/<id>): a Truncated Snapshot has truncatedAlerts above 0.
  5. In the Alertmanager configuration, find the webhook_configs entry of the receiver that sends to Muster and its max_alerts. For Grafana, open the webhook contact point that sends to Muster and check its Max alerts (maxAlerts in a provisioning file).

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Set max_alerts: 0 on the Alertmanager receiver that sends to Muster, so that every Alert of the group is sent, and reload Alertmanager; see Connect Alertmanager.
  • For Grafana, set Max alerts to 0, the default, on the webhook contact point that sends to Muster; see Connect Grafana. Max alerts 0 does not end the Alerts that a wholly resolved group of Grafana's left firing: they go Stale while the Heartbeat is live, or end once the group fires again and sends untruncated Snapshots. Resolving their Alert Group by hand does not end them either: Alerts still firing when its Grace period ends start a new Alert Group.
  • The alert resolves once each truncated group has sent an untruncated Snapshot, at its next notification. A group of Grafana's that resolved wholly sends none until one of its alerts fires again, so its truncation ends as Meaning says.

items.title: Meaning
items.text:
A template failed to render. This alert has two sources with the same name, severity warning and this page:

  • The Internal alert, raised by Muster as an Alert of the built-in "Muster" Integration when a template of a Route or of a Destination starts failing, and resolved when that template renders again or, for a Route, when a new template of that kind is saved; for a Destination, also when the Destination is deleted. Its labels are route and route_name for a template of a Route — the Root message, the Alert line or the Ack timeout notice (template is root_message, line or ack_timeout_notice) — or destination and destination_name for a request template of an outgoing webhook (template is webhook_request).

  • The chart rule, on every failure counted in the last 15 minutes:

    sum by (route, destination, template) (increase(muster_template_errors_total{job="muster"}[15m])) > 0

    It fires at once (for: 0m) with the labels route, destination (one of them empty) and template. The counter also counts the URL templates of Link rules (template="link_rule"), which raise no Internal alert, so the chart rule can fire where the Internal alert does not.

items.title: Impact
items.text:
• A Route template that fails: the message is rendered with the Fallback template instead — every label under Muster's heading, with the footer and the buttons. People still see and act on the Alert Group, in a plainer format.
  • A request template of an outgoing webhook that fails: that request is not sent; the delivery or the Thread reply ends as Not delivered, with no fallback body.
  • A Link rule that fails: its link is left out of the Alert Group's links.
  • Everything else keeps working.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.text:
1. Open System status (/admin/system-status): Template errors lists every Route and Destination whose template fails, with the kind — Root message, Alert line, Ack timeout notice, Link rule or Request template.
  2. Open the Route page (/routes/<id>): the banner says "Template error since HH:MM: {error}." with the line and column that failed. The Route list marks the Route with "Template error".
  3. Read the log lines:
    • fallback_template_used (route, group, template, error): a Route template failed and the message used the Fallback template.
    • webhook_template_failed (destination, group, request, error): a request template of an outgoing webhook failed.
    • link_rule_failed (link_rule, route, group, error): the URL template of a Link rule failed.
  4. Check which labels the template reads: a template that works for most Alert Groups often fails on one whose Alerts lack a label or carry an unexpected value.

items.title: Fix
items.text:
• Correct the template so that it handles the missing or unexpected value, and check it with the preview before you save it. For outgoing webhooks, see Template errors.
  • For a Link rule, correct its URL template under Organization → Link rules (/admin/organization/link-rules).
  • The Internal alert resolves when the next message of the Route renders with the template (logged as template_recovered) or when a new template of that kind is saved on the Route, and when the next request of the Destination renders or the Destination is deleted. Deleting a Route does not resolve it. The chart rule resolves 15 minutes after the last failure.

items.title: Outgoing webhook: events mode
items.text:
An outgoing webhook Destination in the events mode sends one HTTP POST for every lifecycle event of every Alert Group on its Routes: an ordered, signed stream of versioned JSON events that an automation can record, react to or forward. Muster renders nothing for a chat here; for a chat with a REST API, use the template mode instead.

In the examples, MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL is https://muster.example.org and the receiving endpoint is https://automation.example.org/muster.

items.title: Create the Destination
items.text:
In the web UI:

  1. Open Destinations, select Create destination and choose Outgoing webhook. Keep the Mode Events.

  2. Under Events request, enter the URL and, with Add header, each header's name and value; a value reads a Secret as {{ .Secrets.<name> }}. Set the Proxy if the endpoint needs one, and give the Destination a Name. Select Save.

  3. Muster shows the Signing secret once: copy it to the receiving endpoint, which verifies the signatures with it (see Verify the signature), and close the dialog.

  4. The saved Destination shows its type and health, its Routes and its settings, with the tab Request log beside Settings. Add it to a Route to send it events. In the screenshots, the receiving endpoint is https://hooks.example.org.

Through the API, create a Destination of type webhook with the mode events:

{
  "type": "webhook",
  "name": "automation",
  "mode": "events",
  "events": {
    "url": "https://automation.example.org/muster",
    "headers": [{ "name": "Authorization", "value": "Bearer {{ .Secrets.token }}" }]
  },
  "proxy": { "enabled": false },
  "mentions": { "...": "Mention settings, as for any Destination" },
  "limiter": { "limit": 5, "per_seconds": 1 }
}
  • The URL and the header values are Go templates. They can read the Destination's Secrets as {{ .Secrets.<name> }} (or {{ $.Secrets.<name> }}, or {{ index .Secrets "<name>" }}) and nothing else; any other use of .Secrets, such as {{ with .Secrets }} or {{ $s := .Secrets }}, is refused, because Muster could not check that the Secret exists. They are parsed and run on a dry run when you save; an error names the field, its line and its column.
  • Muster sets Content-Type, webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature itself; a header template may not name them. Every request also carries User-Agent: Muster/<version> unless a header template sets its own.
  • The proxy is the Destination's own; the requests never read HTTP_PROXY or HTTPS_PROXY.
  • The limiter defaults to 5 requests per second in the form (destination.webhook.limiter).
  • An outgoing webhook has no Connection and no Destination check: checking it answers 422 check_not_supported.

The answer to the creation carries the Signing secret once, in signing_secret. Store it where the endpoint verifies the signatures; Muster never shows it again.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
Credentials the endpoint needs go into the Destination's Secrets, never into the URL or a header as text.

  1. On the page of the Destination, under Secrets, select Add secret. Enter the Name, such as token, and the Value, and select Save.

  2. The list shows the Secret's name, that it is set and when it changed, and its reference, {{ .Secrets.token }}, which the URL and the headers read. Replace sets a new value and Remove deletes it; the value is never shown again.

Through the API:

curl -X PUT https://muster.example.org/api/v1/destinations/DSK7M3QX9P2RTA/secrets/token \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"value":"the-token-of-the-endpoint"}'
  • A Secret name is a letter or an underscore followed by letters, digits and underscores.
  • Values are write-only: GET …/secrets lists names, whether they are set and when they last changed, with an ETag that If-Match on PUT and DELETE compares with.
  • Everyone who can read Destinations sees the URL and header templates as written, with the references only.
  • Secret values and the Signing secrets are masked as [redacted] in delivery errors, the Timeline and the logs.
  • A template that reads a Secret the Destination does not have fails: that event is not sent and ends as Not delivered.

A header named Authorization, or a URL whose user information or query holds a literal value instead of a {{ .Secrets.<name> }} reference, gives the Destination the warning literal_credential with the JSON Pointer of the field, for example /events/headers/0/value: the value is shown to everyone who can read Destinations.

items.title: What is sent
items.text:
One POST per lifecycle event, with the version 1 body as application/json:

{
  "version": 1,
  "event": "created",
  "notify": true,
  "mentions": [{ "type": "user", "id": "SR2K9D1VW3MPTE", "name": "Alice Smith", "login": "alice" }],
  "sequence": 1,
  "occurred_at": "2026-10-03T09:41:07Z",
  "actor": { "kind": "system", "transport": "system" },
  "alert_group": {
    "number": 412,
    "id": "AGK7M3QX9P2RTA",
    "title": "HighErrorRate payments-api",
    "summary": "Error rate above 5% for 10 minutes",
    "status": "firing",
    "route": { "id": "RT8Q2M4X7K1P3B", "name": "payments" },
    "urgent": false,
    "severity_level": "critical",
    "started_at": "2026-10-03T09:41:07Z",
    "resolved_at": null,
    "snooze_until": null,
    "reopen_count": 0,
    "url": "https://muster.example.org/alert-groups/AGK7M3QX9P2RTA"
  },
  "alerts": [
    {
      "fingerprint": "6f1c2b0e9d4a7c31",
      "status": "firing",
      "labels": { "alertname": "HighErrorRate", "service": "payments-api" },
      "annotations": { "summary": "Error rate above 5%" },
      "starts_at": "2026-10-03T09:31:07Z",
      "resolved_at": null,
      "resolve_reason": null,
      "generator_url": "https://prometheus.example.org/graph?g0.expr=…"
    }
  ]
}
version 1. event The lifecycle event, one of the names below. notify true exactly when the event is Loud. mentions Who the event mentions under the Destination's Mention settings, as data: {"type": "everyone"}, {"type": "group", "name": …} or {"type": "user", "id": …, "name": …, "login": …}. Always [] for a Quiet event. sequence The Alert Group's lifecycle event number. It grows with every lifecycle event of the Alert Group, may have gaps, and does not start at 1 for a Destination added to the Route later: rely only on "greater means newer". occurred_at When the event was recorded. actor Who made the change: a user or service_account with id, name (and the user's login, or the token_name used) and the transport (ui, api, mattermost, telegram, bridge, slack, cli), or system with the reason, for example timer. alert_group The Alert Group as it was when the event was recorded: number, id, title, summary, status, the owner (id, name, login) while acknowledged, Route, Urgent, Severity level, times, Reopen count and its page in Muster. alerts One element per Alert, by fingerprint, with its status, labels, annotations, times and the resolve reason.

The body is rendered when the event is recorded, so a retry hours later still carries the state the event described.

items.title: Event names
items.text:
Every row of the lifecycle event tables is one event, Quiet ones and those with nothing to show in a messenger included. What delivery itself does — a Publication, a Storm summary, a final edit — is not a lifecycle event and is never sent.
