items.title: Sign-in
items.text:
Everything in the web UI and the API works only after sign-in. No page and no read of the API is open to someone who has not signed in. What is open is a short list of endpoints that cannot ask for a session:

  • the sign-in itself: the list of sign-in methods, the password sign-in, the OpenID Connect redirect and its callback, and the page where a person sets a password from a setup link;
  • ingestion and the Heartbeat, which take an Integration token;
  • the callbacks that Mattermost, Slack, Telegram and a Bridge send to Muster, which each carry a secret or a signature of their own;
  • the served API specification;
  • the health checks and /metrics, on the internal listener, which is not meant to be reachable from outside the cluster.

Everything else answers 401 without a session or a token.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Each User and Service account has one of three Roles, each a fixed set of Permissions:

Role May Admin everything: also configures Integrations, Routes, Connections and Destinations, manages Users, the OIDC settings, Service accounts, the Organization's settings, and reads the Audit log and the System status Responder what a Viewer reads, and acts on Alert Groups: acknowledges and takes over, resolves, snoozes, adds Notes and answers Reminders Viewer reads Alert Groups, Alerts, Integrations, Routes, Connections, Destinations, Link rules and Lookup tables, with secret values masked

Every signed-in person also manages their own profile: password, TOTP, Account links and Personal access tokens. Every operation in the API reference names the Permission it needs.

items.title: Ways to sign in
items.text:
• Local users. An Admin creates a user with a login, and Muster returns a single-use link, valid for 24 hours (auth.password_setup_link_ttl), where the person sets a password of at least 12 characters (auth.password_min_length). Muster sends no email; the Admin hands the link over. The first Admin comes from MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL and its password at the first start, as the Quick start shows.
  • OpenID Connect. People sign in at your identity provider, and a mapping from the groups in their token to Roles decides what they may do. Sign-in with Keycloak and Sign-in with GitLab are complete walkthroughs.
  • TOTP. A second step with a one-time code from an authenticator app, for local and OIDC users alike; the Organization can require it. See TOTP.
  • Personal access tokens. A person creates them in the profile for scripts. A token acts as its User, with at most that User's Permissions, and can be narrowed to fewer. It can expire (token.expiry; a token has no expiry unless you set one, and the page warns about that), and the Audit log names the token with the person. The API limits each token (api.rate_limit). See API tokens and automation.
  • Service accounts. An identity that is not a person, for automation such as a pipeline. It has a Role and any number of tokens, cannot sign in to the web UI, and cannot become the Owner of an Alert Group.

Operations that change one's own account, such as the password, TOTP, tokens and Account links, need the web session; a token is refused there.

A web session ends after 12 hours without a request (auth.session_idle_timeout), or 7 days after sign-in (auth.session_lifetime). Both are built in. A session of an OIDC user whose identity provider granted no offline token — or, as GitLab, offers none — ends 12 hours after sign-in (auth.oidc_fallback_session_lifetime), and a background re-check asks the identity provider about every OIDC user who has an offline token and a live session or a usable Personal access token, every 15 minutes (auth.oidc_recheck_interval).

When the identity provider is in a network that Muster cannot reach, see Closed networks.

items.title: Add a User
items.text:
An Admin adds a local user; a person who signs in through OpenID Connect gets their User at their first sign-in.

  1. Open Access → Users and select Create user. Enter the Name, the Login and, if you like, the Email (optional), and choose the Role. Select Create.

  2. Muster shows the Password setup link once. Copy it with Copy and hand it to the person yourself: Muster sends no email. The link works once, until the time the dialog names. In the screenshot it starts with http://localhost:8080, the address of a development installation; yours starts with your MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL.

  3. The Users list shows the new User with the Role, the source, the sign-in method, the last sign-in, TOTP and the status. If the link is lost or expires, open the User and select New password setup link.

  4. The person opens the link, sets a password, and signs in on Sign in to Muster with the login and the password. With OpenID Connect on, the page also offers Sign in with {name}.

items.title: Your profile
items.text:
Every signed-in person opens their own profile from the user menu, their name at the top right: Profile.

  1. Under Details, change your Name and select Save. Under Language and time zone, choose the Language and the Time zone of the web UI; they apply at once. The time zone also sets when the Snooze presets you press in messengers end.

  2. Under Password, enter the Current password and the new one twice, and select Change password; your other sessions are signed out. Sessions lists where you are signed in, and Sign out everywhere ends them all, this one too.

The profile also holds TOTP, the messenger accounts and the Personal access tokens.

items.title: Sign-in needs HTTPS or localhost
items.text:
The session cookie is Secure, so browsers keep it only on a page served over HTTPS or from the browser's own machine: localhost, a name under .localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]. On plain http:// to any other address, such as http://192.0.2.10:8080, the browser drops the cookie and every sign-in returns to the sign-in page. Muster says so in two places:

  • the sign-in page shows "Sign-in needs HTTPS or localhost" above the form when the browser does not treat the page as secure;
  • the server logs public_url_insecure at WARN when it starts with MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL set to an http:// address on any other host.

There are two ways out:

  • HTTPS. Put a reverse proxy or an Ingress with a certificate in front of the app port 8080, set MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL to its https:// address and restart Muster.
  • An SSH tunnel to localhost, to try Muster on another machine without a certificate. On your own machine, run ssh -L 8080:localhost:8080 <host>, keep it open and browse to http://localhost:8080, with MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL set to http://localhost:8080. Safari may drop the cookie on localhost too: if sign-in still returns to the sign-in page there, use HTTPS or another browser.

items.title: Link your messenger accounts
items.text: A button in Mattermost, Slack or Telegram acts as a Muster User only if the person who presses it has linked their messenger account to their User. People do it themselves, from their profile, as Link your messenger accounts describes. Admins cannot do it for them: they see the links of every User and can remove them, but they cannot create one for someone else. A press from an unlinked account changes nothing, and the person is answered privately with a link to their profile.

items.title: Closed networks
items.text:
OpenID Connect needs a back channel: Muster itself calls the identity provider, to read its configuration and keys, to exchange the code for tokens, and to check the sessions again later. Where Muster is outside the network of the identity provider and cannot reach it, OpenID Connect cannot work, even though the people's browsers can. Typical cases are an identity provider inside a company network and Muster in a cloud or a different site.

If a proxy can bring Muster to the provider, set it in the OIDC settings first: see Proxies. When it cannot, use local users with TOTP. The Keycloak page describes the symptoms of an unreachable provider and does not repeat them here.

items.title: Set it up
items.text:
1. Sign in as the bootstrap Admin, whose email and password come from MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL and its password variable at the first start.
  2. Under Access → Users, create a user for each person, with a login and a Role.
  3. Hand each person the one-time setup link that Muster shows. It is valid for 24 hours and works once. Muster sends no email, so you pass it on yourself. The person sets a password of at least 12 characters.
  4. Under Organization → Security, set TOTP required to local users, or to everyone. With the policy, the person enrols TOTP right after the first sign-in and saves the 10 recovery codes. Without it, the policy would only be a wish: enrolment would be each person's choice.
  5. Add Personal access tokens for scripts and Service accounts for automation. They do not depend on the identity provider.

Take care of the way back: keep at least two Admins, and keep the recovery codes of each. If the last Admin loses the second factor, muster admin reset-totp --actor <name> <login> resets it from the command line, and muster admin reset-password --actor <name> <login> sets a new password.

Local sign-in and OpenID Connect can run side by side. If the provider becomes reachable later, configure OIDC and let people link it from their profile; their TOTP stays.

items.title: Sign-in with GitLab
items.text:
This page sets up sign-in through GitLab with OpenID Connect (OIDC), on https://gitlab.com or on GitLab self-managed. GitLab is an OIDC provider for its own users: a person signs in to Muster with their GitLab account, and the groups they belong to in GitLab decide their Role.

GitLab differs from Keycloak in two ways that matter here:

  • it puts group paths such as platform/sre into the groups claims, and it has two of them, groups and groups_direct;
  • it does not offer the scope offline_access, so Muster cannot re-check its users in the background.

Muster talks to GitLab over the back channel: it fetches the provider metadata (discovery) and the signing keys, and exchanges the authorization code for tokens itself. Muster must therefore reach GitLab over the network, directly or through the proxy of the OIDC settings. If it cannot, use local users with TOTP instead.

In the examples, GitLab self-managed runs at https://gitlab.example.org, and MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL is https://muster.example.org. On https://gitlab.com, replace the first with https://gitlab.com.

items.title: 1. Create the application
items.text:
Muster is an OAuth application in GitLab. Create it where it suits you; in recent GitLab versions the pages are:

  • instance-wide, on GitLab self-managed: Admin → Applications → New application;
  • for a group: the group's Settings → Applications → Add new application;
  • for a user: Edit profile → Access → Applications → Add new application.

Whoever owns the application, every user of that GitLab can authorize it; the Role mapping of step 3 decides who gets in.

Every GitLab account can reach the sign-in

On https://gitlab.com, any gitlab.com account can authorize Muster's application. Keep Role for users without a matching group at None and map only groups of your own, so that a stranger's sign-in is refused. On GitLab self-managed the same applies to every user of the instance.

Fill in the form:

Setting Value Name Muster — GitLab shows it when it asks a person to authorize the application Redirect URI https://muster.example.org/api/v1/sessions/oidc/callback and https://muster.example.org/api/v1/me/oidc-identity/callback, one per line Confidential checked: Muster keeps the secret on the server Trusted optional, in the Admin area only: checked skips the screen where a person authorizes Muster at their first sign-in Scopes openid, profile and email

Both redirect URIs are MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL followed by a path: /api/v1/sessions/oidc/callback ends a sign-in, and /api/v1/me/oidc-identity/callback ends linking an existing account to GitLab from its profile. Register both, with exactly the scheme, host and port of MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL.

Select Save application, then copy the Application ID and the Secret. GitLab shows the secret in full only now; Renew secret makes a new one later.

items.title: 2. Configure Muster
items.text:
Sign in to Muster as an Admin and open Access → OIDC, or use PUT /api/v1/oidc-settings:

Setting Value Issuer URL https://gitlab.example.org: the base URL of GitLab, including its relative URL path if it has one (for example https://example.org/gitlab), or https://gitlab.com Client ID the Application ID of step 1 Client secret the Secret of step 1; it is write-only: Muster shows only whether it is set and when it changed Display name the name on the button "Sign in with {name}", for example GitLab; by default the host of the issuer URL Scopes profile email; openid is always added, and offline_access is not, because GitLab does not offer it Groups claim groups or groups_direct, see step 3 Group mapping group paths to Roles, see step 3

Every scope in the list must be one of the application's scopes: GitLab refuses a sign-in that asks for any other scope with invalid_scope, so never add offline_access to the list for GitLab. The Role for users without a matching group stays None, as the warning in step 1 says. The other settings — Role sync, skipping TOTP and the proxy — work as on the Keycloak page.

items.title: 3. Map groups to Roles
items.text:
GitLab names each group by its full path, such as platform or platform/sre, and offers two claims:

groups The paths of every group the person is a member of, directly or through an ancestor group: a member of platform is listed with platform and with each of its subgroups, such as platform/sre. GitLab puts it in the userinfo answer, not in the ID token, and Muster reads it from there. groups_direct The paths of the groups the person is a direct member of, without the subgroups they reach through an ancestor. GitLab puts it in the ID token.

Choose groups when membership of a parent group should count for its subgroups, as it does in GitLab itself; choose groups_direct when a Role should follow only the groups a person was added to by name. For example, with the groups claim groups:

IdP group Role platform/muster-admins Admin platform/sre Responder platform Viewer

Every member of platform is a Viewer at least, and also a member of platform/sre through it, so a Responder. To keep platform members Viewers, use groups_direct: then only the people added to platform/sre itself are Responders. When a person's groups map to several Roles, the highest wins.

A group path is matched exactly, letter case included, so copy it from the group's URL.

items.title: 4. Check the connection
items.text: Press Check connection. The check fetches discovery through the saved settings and proxy and shows how the request travelled, how long it took, the endpoints GitLab announced, the Requested scopes of a sign-in (openid profile email with the scopes above) and that Offline access is not offered. That is expected for GitLab and is not a problem: it only means the rules of No offline access apply.

items.title: 5. Sign in
items.text: Open Muster and press Sign in with {display name}. GitLab asks the person to authorize Muster once, unless the application is trusted, and the first sign-in creates their Muster user with the Role of their groups. The login is GitLab's username (preferred_username). As with any provider, Muster never merges accounts by login or email, and a person whose groups map to no Role is refused; the Keycloak page lists the errors of the sign-in page.

items.title: No offline access
items.text:
GitLab's discovery does not list offline_access in scopes_supported, so Muster does not request it. GitLab still returns a refresh token, but without offline_access Muster does not keep it. Sign-in works, and for every person who signs in through GitLab:

  • there are no background re-checks;
  • each OIDC session ends auth.oidc_fallback_session_lifetime (12 hours) after sign-in, even while in use, so that a person blocked or removed in GitLab is signed out within that time;
  • their Personal access tokens work only while their last OIDC sign-in is within auth.oidc_token_grace (7 days); after that, the tokens are refused until they sign in through GitLab again.

The Keycloak page describes the same rules; see also Ways to sign in.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: idp_error with invalid_scope in the log event oidc_sign_in_failed GitLab refused a scope Muster asked for: a scope in Muster's Scopes that the application does not have, or offline_access typed into that list. Remove it from the list, or add it to the application in GitLab. The Role is not the one you expect Check the groups claim: with groups_direct, membership through a parent group does not count. The Audit log entry session.oidc_refused of a refused sign-in lists the groups GitLab sent.

items.title: Sign-in with Keycloak
items.text:
This page sets up sign-in through Keycloak with OpenID Connect (OIDC). Other identity providers work the same way: Muster needs a confidential client with the authorization code flow, a claim that lists the person's groups, and, for the background re-checks, the scope offline_access where the provider offers it. Sign-in with GitLab covers a provider that does not.

Muster talks to Keycloak over the back channel: it fetches the provider metadata (discovery) and the signing keys, and exchanges the authorization code for tokens itself. Muster must therefore reach Keycloak over the network, directly or through the proxy of the OIDC settings. If it cannot — Keycloak sits in a closed network and Muster outside it — use local users with TOTP instead.

In the examples, Keycloak runs at https://keycloak.example.org with the realm ops, and MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL is https://muster.example.org.

items.title: 1. Create the client
items.text:
In the Keycloak admin console, open the realm, then Clients → Create client:

Setting Value Client type OpenID Connect Client ID muster Client authentication On (a confidential client with a client secret) Authentication flow Standard flow only; switch off Direct access grants, Implicit flow and Service accounts Valid redirect URIs https://muster.example.org/api/v1/sessions/oidc/callback and https://muster.example.org/api/v1/me/oidc-identity/callback Web origins leave empty: the browser never calls Keycloak from Muster's pages

Both redirect URIs are MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL followed by a path: /api/v1/sessions/oidc/callback ends a sign-in, and /api/v1/me/oidc-identity/callback ends linking an existing account to Keycloak from its profile. Register both, with exactly the scheme, host and port of MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL.

Under Advanced → Advanced settings, set Proof Key for Code Exchange Code Challenge Method to S256. Muster always sends a PKCE challenge, so this only makes Keycloak insist on it.

Then open Credentials and copy the Client secret. Note when it expires, if your realm rotates client secrets: Muster warns two weeks before the date you enter (oidc.secret_expiry_lead).

items.title: 2. Add the groups claim
items.text:
Muster gives each person a Role from their groups. Keycloak puts groups into tokens only through a mapper:

  1. Open the client → Client scopes → muster-dedicated → Add mapper → By configuration → Group Membership.
  2. Set Name to groups and Token Claim Name to groups.
  3. Switch Full group path off, so that the claim carries oncall rather than /oncall.
  4. Switch on Add to ID token and Add to userinfo.

Muster reads the groups from the ID token, and from the userinfo endpoint when the ID token lacks the claim; the userinfo answer must be plain JSON, not a signed JWT. The name of the claim is the Groups claim of the OIDC settings; it is groups unless you change both.

items.title: 3. Allow offline_access
items.text:
Muster asks for the scope offline_access at every sign-in, besides the scopes of the settings, from every identity provider whose discovery lists it in scopes_supported or lists no scopes at all; Keycloak lists it. With it, Keycloak returns an offline token, which Muster keeps encrypted and uses to re-check every OIDC user in the background every 15 minutes (auth.oidc_recheck_interval): a person disabled or removed in Keycloak loses their Muster sessions at the next re-check, without waiting for them to end.

Another identity provider may support offline_access without listing it in its discovery. Add offline_access to the Scopes of the settings for it, and Muster requests it too. Never do so for GitLab, which offers no offline_access and refuses such a sign-in with invalid_scope (Sign-in with GitLab).

To allow it in Keycloak:

  1. Make sure the realm role offline_access is a default role of the realm (Realm settings → User registration → Default roles), which it is in a new realm, or give it to the groups that use Muster.
  2. Open the client → Client scopes and check that the client scope offline_access is assigned as Optional.

items.title: Without offline_access
items.text:
Sign-in still works when Keycloak does not grant offline_access, but Muster cannot re-check the person in the background:

  • there are no background re-checks for them;
  • each of their OIDC sessions ends auth.oidc_fallback_session_lifetime (12 hours) after sign-in, even while in use, so that a person disabled in Keycloak is signed out within that time;
  • their Personal access tokens work only while their last OIDC sign-in is within auth.oidc_token_grace (7 days); after that, the tokens are refused until they sign in through OIDC again.

items.title: 4. Configure Muster
items.text:
Sign in to Muster as an Admin and open OIDC settings, or use PUT /api/v1/oidc-settings:

Setting Value Issuer URL https://keycloak.example.org/realms/ops — the issuer of https://keycloak.example.org/realms/ops/.well-known/openid-configuration. Use https: over http the client secret and the tokens cross the network in clear text Client ID muster Client secret the secret of step 1; it is write-only: Muster shows only whether it is set and when it changed Client secret expires on the expiry date of the secret, if it has one Display name the name on the button "Sign in with {name}"; by default the host of the issuer URL Scopes profile email; openid is always added, and offline_access because Keycloak offers it Groups claim groups Group mapping for example muster-admins → Admin, oncall → Responder; when a person's groups map to several Roles, the highest wins Role for users without a matching group none (the default) refuses their sign-in; Viewer or Responder lets them in Sync Role at sign-in on (the default): Keycloak decides the Role at every sign-in and re-check; off: the mapping applies only when the user is created Skip TOTP when the IdP asserted MFA off by default; on skips Muster's own TOTP step when the ID token's amr claim says that Keycloak used multi-factor authentication. Keycloak sends amr only when the client has an Authentication Method Reference (AMR) mapper Proxy the HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS5 proxy through which Muster reaches Keycloak, if it needs one

The settings behind the three rows above Proxy are oidc.unmatched_role (none: sign-in is refused), oidc.sync_role (on) and oidc.skip_totp_with_idp_mfa (off).

In the web UI:

  1. Open Access → OIDC. Under Identity provider, turn on Allow sign-in through OIDC and fill in the Issuer URL, the Provider name (the display name), the Client ID, the Client secret — Set a value, or Replace once one is set —, Client secret expires on and the Scopes.

  2. Under Roles, enter the Groups claim and map each group with Add IdP group: the group's name and its Role. Choose the Role for users without a matching group, and whether to Sync the Role at every sign-in and to Skip TOTP when the identity provider confirmed multi-factor authentication. Set the proxy below if Muster needs one, and select Save.

The screenshots show the form filled in, before Save.

Then press Check connection. The check fetches discovery through the saved settings and proxy and shows how the request travelled (direct or proxy), how long it took, the endpoints Keycloak announced, the Requested scopes of a sign-in (openid offline_access profile email) and that Offline access is offered. When the outbound address policy blocks Keycloak or the proxy, the error names the rule.

Keycloak lists only standard claims in claims_supported, so until the first sign-in the check shows the warning No sign-in has carried the groups claim ‘groups’ yet, so group mappings have not matched anyone yet (groups_claim_missing) although the mapper of step 2 exists. The warning goes away at the first sign-in whose ID token or userinfo carries the groups claim, and later checks no longer raise it; changing the groups claim, the issuer, the client ID or the scopes starts over. A sign-in without the claim changes nothing: Keycloak leaves it out for a user in no group. If the warning stays after a sign-in of a user in a group, the mapper is missing or not added to the ID token. A mapper removed after it worked raises no warning: you notice it through refused sign-ins, whose Audit log entry session.oidc_refused lists no groups.

The settings also warn when the mapping is empty and users without a matching group get no Role (nobody_can_sign_in), and two weeks before the client secret expires.

items.title: 5. Sign in
items.text:
Open Muster and press Sign in with {display name}. The first sign-in of a person creates their Muster user with the Role of their groups. The login is Keycloak's preferred_username, else the email, else the subject. Muster never merges accounts by login or email: when a local user already has the login, the sign-in is refused with "An account with this login already exists. Sign in with it and link OIDC in your profile."

A person whose groups map to no Role is refused with "You have no access to Muster. Contact your administrator.", and the Audit log entry session.oidc_refused lists the groups their token carried. A user with TOTP gives the code after Keycloak, unless Keycloak asserted multi-factor authentication and the setting above skips it.

Other errors on the sign-in page: account_disabled (the Muster user is disabled or deleted), oidc_disabled (OIDC was switched off), invalid_request (the sign-in took longer than 10 minutes, oidc.auth_request_ttl, or was started in another browser) and idp_error (Keycloak reported an error, could not be reached, or answered with a token that did not verify; the log event oidc_sign_in_failed says which).

items.title: When Muster cannot reach the identity provider
items.text:
OIDC needs the back channel from Muster to Keycloak. When Keycloak is inside a closed network that Muster cannot reach, even through a proxy, use local users instead:

  • an Admin creates each user and hands over the one-time password setup link (Users → Create);
  • set Organization → Security → TOTP required to everyone, so that every user enrols TOTP at their first sign-in.

Local sign-in is always available, also next to OIDC, and the bootstrap Admin or muster admin reset-password --actor <name> lets an operator in when the OIDC settings are broken.

items.title: TOTP
items.text: TOTP is a second step in the sign-in: a six-digit code from an authenticator app, which changes every 30 seconds (RFC 6238). Every User, local or from OpenID Connect, can enrol it. It adds protection to a password that leaks, and it is the second factor of installations that cannot use an identity provider: see Closed networks.

items.title: Enrol
items.text:
People enrol from their profile: they scan a QR code with the authenticator app and confirm with the first code. Enrolment gives the person 10 recovery codes (auth.totp_recovery_codes), each of ten characters and usable once. They are shown once: save them somewhere safe. In the profile a person can generate new recovery codes, which replace the unused ones, and remove TOTP. Removing it needs the current password (a local user) or a current code or recovery code.

  1. Open your Profile and, under Two-factor authentication (TOTP), select Set up TOTP.

  2. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app, or enter the Secret by hand. Enter the code the app shows in Code from the app and select Confirm.

  3. Muster shows the recovery codes once: Copy codes, keep them somewhere safe, and select Continue.

  4. The profile says since when TOTP is on and how many recovery codes are left, with Regenerate recovery codes and Remove TOTP.

A User has one enrolment. From then on, every sign-in asks for a code after the password, or after the redirect from the identity provider: Two-factor authentication asks for the Code, and Use a recovery code instead takes a recovery code.

A recovery code is accepted in place of a code, and is then used up. Until the code is given, the session can only read itself, sign out and give the code.

A wrong password or code counts as a failure, and failures slow the next attempts down per account and per source address: after 3 in a row, each attempt waits twice as long as the one before, from 1 second up to 60 seconds.

items.title: The policy
items.text:
The Organization's policy TOTP required (organization.totp_required), under Organization → Security, has three values:

Value Who must have TOTP nobody (the default) no one; everyone may enrol if they want local users every account that has a password everyone every account, local or from OpenID Connect
  1. Open Organization → Security.

  2. Under Two-factor authentication, choose TOTP required: Nobody, Local users or Everyone. Select Save.

A person who falls under the policy and has no TOTP yet must enrol right after sign-in, before they can do anything else. An account that signs in through OpenID Connect, whether created by it or linked to it, does not count as a local user for this policy.

items.title: OpenID Connect and the identity provider's multi-factor authentication
items.text: An identity provider may already ask for a second factor. When the OIDC setting oidc.skip_totp_with_idp_mfa (skip TOTP when the identity provider asserted multi-factor authentication; off by default) is on, Muster skips its own code for a sign-in where the provider's token says so in its amr claim. With the setting off, Muster asks for its own code whenever the User has TOTP. See Sign-in with Keycloak.

items.title: A lost authenticator
items.text:
A person who lost both the device and the recovery codes needs a reset.

  • An Admin resets it under Access → Users: Reset TOTP.
  • From the command line, when no Admin can sign in:
muster admin reset-totp --actor ops-alice alice

--actor names the person who runs the command, and is required; the last argument is the login of the account. The command works on the database, with the same settings as the server.

A reset removes the TOTP and its recovery codes and ends the account's sessions. Under a policy that covers the account, the person enrols again at the next sign-in. Without the policy, they can enrol again from the profile.

items.title: What the Audit log records
items.text: The Audit log, under Organization → Audit log, records TOTP enrolled, removed and reset, with the User, who did it, and the Transport (cli for the command). It never records a code. Failed sign-ins, with a wrong code too, are counted in the metric muster_login_failures_total with the method totp; the chart rule MusterLoginFailures watches it.
